courses.title: Conversational Arabic
courses.tagline: Read, write, and speak Arabic: master the script, essential grammar, and everyday dialogues with clear transliteration.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational Arabic is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday Arabic from your very first lesson. You learn the way real conversations work: how the Arabic script and sounds work, the core grammar behind daily sentences, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. Every phrase appears in Arabic script with transliteration and an English translation, so you can speak from lesson one while your reading catches up. The course teaches Modern Standard Arabic — the form used in news, books, and formal settings and understood across the Arab world. The first half builds your foundation — the script and pronunciation, greetings, essential sentence patterns, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, restaurant and travel conversations, and longer everyday exchanges. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep improving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:

You learn the way real conversations work: how the Arabic script and sounds work, the core grammar behind daily sentences, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. The course teaches Modern Standard Arabic — the form used in news, books, and formal settings and understood across the Arab world. The first half builds your foundation — the script and pronunciation, greetings, essential sentence patterns, numbers, and asking questions. syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will be able to: read and write the Arabic alphabet, recognize letter forms, and pronounce the sounds that do not exist in English; greet people, introduce yourself, and use survival phrases when you do not understand; build sentences with correct word order, the definite article, gender, and present-tense verbs; count fluently, tell the time, and use days, months, and dates; ask and answer questions about directions, prices, and everyday topics; talk about things you did using the past tense; make plans and invitations and hold a full restaurant or travel conversation; and run a simple daily practice routine that keeps your speaking improving.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read one lesson at a time, and read every Arabic line out loud — saying the words with your mouth, not just your eyes, is what builds speaking skill. Each lesson opens with what it teaches, explains the concept with concrete examples in Arabic script plus transliteration and English, includes full example dialogues with translations, warns you about common beginner mistakes, and ends with a clearly labeled Practice exercise. Do the practice before moving on; the lessons build on each other, and Lesson 3's grammar depends on Lesson 1's script. Aim for one lesson per day, and re-read the previous lesson's dialogues the next morning as a warm-up. There are no grades and no timers — steady repetition beats cramming. Keep a notebook for writing out the practice exercises by hand, especially the Arabic letters.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites. This course starts from zero and assumes you have never studied Arabic before. Everything — even how to write your first Arabic letter and how to make each new sound — is explained from scratch. If you already know a little Arabic, Lesson 1's pronunciation rules are still worth reading, because correcting a bad pronunciation habit early saves months later. You do not need any textbook or prior grammar knowledge; a notebook for writing out the practice exercises is the only thing that will help.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes — it is a text/workbook course, and everything you need is on the page: explanations, example sentences in Arabic script with transliteration and English translations, translated dialogues, and practice exercises. The materials section includes a phrase cheat sheet, an alphabet quick-reference chart, and a verb conjugation worksheet you can print and reuse. The course teaches Modern Standard Arabic; everyday spoken dialects differ by region, and this is noted where it matters. It makes no promise of fluency timelines or test scores; your results depend on the speaking practice you put in. Created with Planet Leads.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The Arabic Script — Alphabet, Letter Forms, and Pronunciation
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to read and write the Arabic alphabet — 28 letters written right to left, with shapes that change depending on position. Arabic script looks intimidating for exactly one week; then its logic clicks and it becomes one of the most phonetic writing systems you will ever learn. Your goal today: recognize every letter, write the basic forms, and pronounce the sounds that don't exist in English.

Arabic is written right to left. There are no capital letters. Most letters connect to their neighbors, and each letter has up to four forms: isolated, initial (start of a word), medial (middle), and final (end). Six letters never connect to the following letter: ا (alif), د (dal), ذ (dhal), ر (ra), ز (zay), و (waw). Learn the alphabet in this order, with transliteration: ا (a), ب (b), ت (t), ث (th as in "think"), ج (j), ح (ḥ — a deep breathy h from the throat), خ (kh as in Scottish "loch"), د (d), ذ (dh as in "this"), ر (r — rolled), ز (z), س (s), ش (sh), ص (ṣ — deep, emphatic s), ض (ḍ — deep, emphatic d), ط (ṭ — deep, emphatic t), ظ (ẓ — deep, emphatic "th" as in "this"), ع (ʿ — a voiced sound from deep in the throat, the hardest for beginners), غ (gh — like a gargled French r), ف (f), ق (q — a deep k from the back of the throat), ك (k), ل (l), م (m), ن (n), هـ (h), و (w/long ū), ي (y/long ī).

The sounds that don't exist in English need deliberate practice. ح (ḥ): breathe out strongly with your throat open, like fogging a mirror from deep in the throat — compare هـ (h, normal h) in هواء (hawāʾ, air) vs حار (ḥārr, hot). ع (ʿ): tighten your throat muscles and voice from deep down — practice with عين (ʿayn, eye). The emphatic letters ص ض ط ظ are pronounced with the tongue pulled back and the mouth hollowed, giving a "dark" quality: سين (sīn, the letter s) vs صين? — better pair: سار (sāra, walked) vs صار (ṣāra, became). ق (q): make a k but much further back, almost a soft pop in the throat — قلب (qalb, heart/dog? no: قلب qalb = heart). خ (kh): gargle lightly — خبز (khubz, bread).

Short vowels are marks written above or below consonants: َ (fatḥa = a), ُ (ḍamma = u), ِ (kasra = i). Long vowels use letters: ا (ā), و (ū), ي (ī). Most printed Arabic omits the short-vowel marks, which is why this course always gives you transliteration — you learn the word's sound first, and the unvowelled spelling becomes readable with practice. The ة (tāʾ marbūṭah) marks feminine words and sounds like "ah": مدرسة (madrasah, school). The ال (al-) prefix means "the": الكتاب (al-kitāb, the book).

One famous rule: sun and moon letters. The 14 sun letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن) assimilate the l of ال in pronunciation: الشمس (ash-shams, the sun — pronounced "ash-shams," not "al-shams"). The 14 moon letters keep it: القمر (al-qamar, the moon). You don't need to produce this perfectly yet — just recognize why الشمس is pronounced "ash-shams."

Common beginner mistakes to fix now. First, writing left to right — train your hand from day one: start at the right margin. Second, pronouncing ح as a normal h and ع as a glottal stop — they are distinct letters with distinct sounds, and mixing them changes words. Third, ignoring the emphatic letters — ص and س are different letters; صبر (ṣabr, patience) is not سبر.

Practice: Write the full alphabet in order, right to left, three times, saying each letter's name aloud. Then write these words and read them: باب (bāb, door), بيت (bayt, house), كتاب (kitāb, book), قلم (qalam, pen), مدرسة (madrasah, school), شمس (shams, sun), قمر (qamar, moon). Finally, read this sentence aloud slowly: أنا طالب (anā ṭālib — I am a student). It uses only sounds from this lesson, and it is your first real Arabic sentence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully.

The universal greeting is السلام عليكم (as-salāmu ʿalaykum) — peace be upon you. It works with everyone, everywhere. The reply is وعليكم السلام (wa ʿalaykum as-salām) — and upon you be peace. مرحبا (marḥaban) is a friendly hello; أهلا وسهلا (ahlan wa sahlan) is a warm welcome — literally "you have come to family and ease." Time-based greetings: صباح الخير (ṣabāḥ al-khayr, good morning), answered with صباح النور (ṣabāḥ an-nūr); مساء الخير (masāʾ al-khayr, good evening), answered with مساء النور (masāʾ an-nūr). For introductions: ما اسمك؟ (mā ismuk? — what is your name? — to a man; mā ismuki? to a woman). أنا اسمي... (anā ismī... — my name is...). من أين أنت؟ (min ayna anta? — where are you from? — to a man; anti to a woman). تشرفنا (tasharrafnā) — pleased to meet you. Goodbyes: مع السلامة (maʿa as-salāmah, goodbye — literally "with safety"), إلى اللقاء (ilā al-liqāʾ, see you later).

Politeness words carry enormous weight. شكرا (shukran) is thank you — add جزيلا (jazīlan) for "thank you very much." عفوا (ʿafwan) is you're welcome. من فضلك (min faḍlik — to a man; min faḍliki — to a woman) means please. آسف (āsif — said by a man; آسفة āsifah — said by a woman) is I'm sorry. A frequent beginner mistake is using the wrong gender form — Arabic addresses men and women differently, so learn both forms of من فضلك and آسف/آسفة from the start.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. لا أفهم (lā afham) — I don't understand. تكلم ببطء من فضلك (takallam bi-buṭʾ min faḍlik) — speak slowly, please. هل تتكلم الإنجليزية؟ (hal tatakallam al-inglīziyyah? — do you speak English?). أين الحمام؟ (ayna al-ḥammām? — where is the bathroom?). ساعدني من فضلك (sāʿidnī min faḍlik) — please help me. These five phrases will rescue you anywhere Arabic is spoken, and people respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Two cultural notes that prevent real mistakes. First, greetings are longer and warmer than in English — rushing past السلام عليكم to your question feels abrupt; exchange the greeting fully first. Second, the right hand is used for giving, receiving, and eating — offer things with your right hand as a sign of respect.

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with transliteration and translations:

Layla: السلام عليكم! ما اسمك؟ (As-salāmu ʿalaykum! Mā ismuk?) — Peace be upon you! What is your name?
Omar: وعليكم السلام! أنا اسمي عمر. وأنت؟ (Wa ʿalaykum as-salām! Anā ismī ʿUmar. Wa ant?) — And upon you be peace! My name is Omar. And you?
Layla: أنا اسمي ليلى. من أين أنت؟ (Anā ismī Laylā. Min ayna ant?) — My name is Layla. Where are you from?
Omar: أنا من مصر. وأنت؟ (Anā min Miṣr. Wa ant?) — I am from Egypt. And you?
Layla: أنا من أمريكا. تشرفنا! (Anā min Amrīkā. Tasharrafnā!) — I am from America. Pleased to meet you!
Omar: تشرفنا! هل تتكلمين الإنجليزية؟ (Tasharrafnā! Hal tatakallamīn al-inglīziyyah?) — Pleased to meet you! Do you (feminine) speak English?
Layla: نعم، قليلا. تكلمي ببطء من فضلك. (Naʿam, qalīlan. Takallamī bi-buṭʾ min faḍlik.) — Yes, a little. Speak slowly, please.
Omar: لا مشكلة. مع السلامة! (Lā mushkilah. Maʿa as-salāmah!) — No problem. Goodbye!

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, one thing about yourself, pleased to meet you) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then drill the survival phrases: cover the Arabic, read the English, and say the Arabic from memory until you can do all five without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with the throat sounds from Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Core Grammar — Word Order, ال, Gender, and Present Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the sentence patterns behind most Arabic conversation: word order, the definite article ال, masculine and feminine gender, and present-tense verbs. Arabic has a famous feature beginners love: there is no "to be" in the present tense — "I am a student" is simply أنا طالب (anā ṭālib), "I student." Master this lesson and you can build thousands of correct sentences.

Arabic word order is flexible, but beginners should use subject-verb-object like English: أنا أدرس العربية (anā adrusu al-ʿarabiyyah) — I study Arabic. أخي يشرب القهوة (akhī yashrabu al-qahwah) — my brother drinks coffee. Verb-first order (يدرس الطالب — yadrusu aṭ-ṭālibu, studies the student) is also correct and very common, but SVO keeps you safe while learning.

The definite article ال (al-) means "the" and attaches to the front of the word: كتاب (kitāb, a book) → الكتاب (al-kitāb, the book). مدرسة (madrasah, a school) → المدرسة (al-madrasah, the school). Remember the sun letters from Lesson 1: with sun letters the l assimilates — الشمس is pronounced ash-shams (the sun), while moon letters keep al-: القمر al-qamar (the moon). There is no indefinite article — كتاب alone means "a book."

Gender shapes everything. Every noun is masculine or feminine; feminine nouns usually end in ة (tāʾ marbūṭah): مدرسة (school), سيارة (sayyārah, car), طالبة (ṭālibah, female student). Adjectives match the noun's gender: طالب مجتهد (ṭālib mujtahid — a hardworking male student) vs طالبة مجتهدة (ṭālibah mujtahidah — a hardworking female student). Pronouns: أنا (anā, I), أنتَ (anta, you masculine), أنتِ (anti, you feminine), هو (huwa, he), هي (hiya, she), نحن (naḥnu, we). Demonstratives: هذا (hādhā, this masculine), هذه (hādhihi, this feminine), ذلك (dhālika, that masculine), تلك (tilka, that feminine). هذا كتاب (hādhā kitāb — this is a book), هذه مدرسة (hādhihi madrasah — this is a school).

Present-tense verbs use prefixes: أ (a) for I, ت (ta) for you/he-she, ي (ya) for he, ن (na) for we. With the verb درس (darasa, to study): أنا أدرس (anā adrusu — I study), أنتَ تدرس (anta tadrusu — you study), هو يدرس (huwa yadrusu — he studies), هي تدرس (hiya tadrusu — she studies), نحن ندرس (naḥnu nadrusu — we study). Learn one more verb fully — كتب (kataba, to write): أكتب (aktubu), تكتب (taktubu), يكتب (yaktubu), نكتب (naktubu). Two verbs fully conjugated gives you the pattern for hundreds.

Negation: لا (lā) before a present verb — لا أدرس (lā adrusu) — I don't study. For "to be" sentences, use ليس (laysa): لست طالبا (lastu ṭāliban) — I am not a student; ليس كبيرا (laysa kabīran) — it is not big. Questions: add هل (hal) at the start for yes/no — هل تدرس؟ (hal tadrusu? — do you study?) — or use question words in place (Lesson 5).

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, inserting a "to be" verb in the present — أنا أكون طالب is wrong; أنا طالب is correct. Save كان (kāna) for the past (Lesson 6). Second, mismatching adjective gender — طالبة مجتهد is wrong; the ة on the noun demands ة on the adjective: طالبة مجتهدة.

Dialogue — coworkers at lunch:

Samir: أين تعمل؟ (Ayna taʿmal?) — Where do you work?
Nadia: أعمل في بنك. أنا موظفة. وأنت؟ (Aʿmalu fī bank. Anā muwaẓẓafah. Wa ant?) — I work in a bank. I am an employee (feminine). And you?
Samir: أنا مدرس. أعمل في مدرسة. (Anā mudarris. Aʿmalu fī madrasah.) — I am a teacher (masculine). I work in a school.
Nadia: هل أنت متعب اليوم؟ (Hal anta mutʿab al-yawm?) — Are you tired today?
Samir: لا، أنا بخير. هل تريدين أن تأكلي معي؟ (Lā, anā bi-khayr. Hal turīdīn an taʾkulī maʿī?) — No, I'm fine. Do you want to eat with me?
Nadia: نعم، أريد. هل نذهب إلى المطعم؟ (Naʿam, urīd. Hal nadhhabu ilā al-maṭʿam?) — Yes, I want to. Shall we go to the restaurant?
Samir: هيا بنا. أنا جائع. (Hayyā binā. Anā jāʾiʿ.) — Let's go. I'm hungry.

Practice: Write ten أنا sentences about yourself (identity, profession, origin) — no verb needed. Write eight present-tense verb sentences using أدرس and أكتب with different pronouns. Then write six noun-adjective pairs with correct gender matching (three masculine, three feminine). Say every sentence aloud. Finally, translate: "She is a doctor. She works in a hospital. She is tired today. She wants coffee." Check: هي طبيبة (hiya ṭabībah). تعمل في مستشفى (taʿmalu fī mustashfā). هي متعبة اليوم (hiya mutʿabah al-yawm). تريد قهوة (turīdu qahwah).

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Arabic numbers have one famous quirk — the numerals ٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩ look different from Western digits — plus gender agreement rules that surprise beginners. Learn the system exactly, and numbers become pure utility: prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules.

First, the numerals. Arabic uses Eastern Arabic numerals: ٠ (0), ١ (1), ٢ (2), ٣ (3), ٤ (4), ٥ (5), ٦ (6), ٧ (7), ٨ (8), ٩ (9). You will see these on clocks, prices, and license plates across the Middle East. Western digits (0–9) are also common, especially in the Levant and Gulf — learn to read both, and you will never be stuck.

Numbers 1–10 with transliteration: واحد (wāḥid, 1), اثنان (ithnān, 2), ثلاثة (thalāthah, 3), أربعة (arbaʿah, 4), خمسة (khamsah, 5), ستة (sittah, 6), سبعة (sabʿah, 7), ثمانية (thamāniyah, 8), تسعة (tisʿah, 9), عشرة (ʿasharah, 10). Eleven and twelve: أحد عشر (aḥada ʿashar, 11), اثنا عشر (ithnā ʿashar, 12). Tens: عشرون (ʿishrūn, 20), ثلاثون (thalāthūn, 30), أربعون (arbaʿūn, 40), خمسون (khamsūn, 50). One hundred: مائة (miʾah, 100). One thousand: ألف (alf, 1000). Compound numbers join with و (wa, and): خمسة وعشرون (khamsah wa ʿishrūn, 25).

The gender rule: numbers 3–10 take the OPPOSITE gender of the noun they count — ثلاثة كتب (thalāthatu kutub, three books — feminine number with masculine noun), خمس سيارات (khamsu sayyārāt, five cars — masculine-looking number with feminine noun). Numbers 1 and 2 match the noun's gender and usually follow it: كتاب واحد (kitāb wāḥid, one book), سيارة واحدة (sayyārah wāḥidah, one car). This feels backwards at first; drill it with real nouns until it is automatic.

Telling time: الساعة (as-sāʿah) means both "hour" and "o'clock." الساعة الواحدة (as-sāʿah al-wāḥidah, 1 o'clock), الساعة الثالثة (as-sāʿah ath-thālithah, 3 o'clock) — hours use ordinal numbers. Minutes: الساعة الثالثة وعشر دقائق (3:10), والنصف (wa an-niṣf, half past) — الساعة الثالثة والنصف (3:30), والربع (wa ar-rubʿ, quarter past) — الساعة الثالثة والربع (3:15), إلا الربع (illā ar-rubʿ, quarter to) — الساعة الرابعة إلا الربع (3:45). صباحا (ṣabāḥan) is AM, مساء (masāʾan) is PM. Ask the time with كم الساعة؟ (kam as-sāʿah? — what time is it?).

Days of the week: الأحد (al-aḥad, Sunday), الاثنين (al-ithnayn, Monday), الثلاثاء (ath-thulāthāʾ, Tuesday), الأربعاء (al-arbiʿāʾ, Wednesday), الخميس (al-khamīs, Thursday), الجمعة (al-jumuʿah, Friday), السبت (as-sabt, Saturday). اليوم (al-yawm) is today, غدا (ghadan) is tomorrow, أمس (amsi) is yesterday. Months: يناير (yanāyir, January), فبراير (fibrāyir, February), مارس (māris, March), أبريل (ibrīl, April), مايو (māyū, May), يونيو (yūnyū, June), يوليو (yūlyū, July), أغسطس (aghusṭus, August), سبتمبر (sibtambir, September), أكتوبر (uktūbir, October), نوفمبر (nūfambir, November), ديسمبر (dīsambir, December). Dates: الخامس من مايو (al-khāmis min māyū, May 5th).

Money and shopping vocabulary, since numbers live there: بكم؟ (bi-kam? — how much?), بكم هذا؟ (bi-kam hādhā? — how much is this?). غال جدا (ghālin jiddan) — very expensive. رخيص (rakhīṣ) — cheap. أريد هذا (urīdu hādhā) — I want this one.

Dialogue — at a market:

Customer: السلام عليكم! بكم هذا؟ (As-salāmu ʿalaykum! Bi-kam hādhā?) — Peace be upon you! How much is this?
Vendor: وعليكم السلام! بعشرة. تريد كم؟ (Wa ʿalaykum as-salām! Bi-ʿasharah. Turīdu kam?) — And upon you be peace! Ten. How many do you want?
Customer: أريد ثلاثة. وكم سعر هذه؟ (Urīdu thalāthah. Wa kam siʿru hādhihi?) — I want three. And what is the price of this one?
Vendor: خمسة للواحدة. (Khamsah lil-wāḥidah.) — Five for one.
Customer: غال جدا! أرخص قليلا من فضلك. (Ghālin jiddan! Arkhaṣ qalīlan min faḍlik.) — Very expensive! Cheaper, a little, please.
Vendor: حسنا، أربعة. (Ḥasanan, arbaʿah.) — Okay, four.
Customer: اتفقنا. أريد اثنتين. (Ittafaqnā. Urīdu ithnatayn.) — Agreed. I want two.

Practice: Count aloud from 1 to 20 without stopping, then backwards from 20 to 1. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in Arabic. Drill the gender rule with five masculine nouns and five feminine nouns (ثلاثة كتب، خمس سيارات pattern). Finally, memorize the market dialogue's price lines and role-play buying three different items, asking بكم هذا؟ each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to use every question word, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in an Arabic-speaking place. The good news: Arabic questions keep statement word order — you just swap in a question word where the answer goes, or start with هل for yes/no questions.

The core question words: ماذا (mādhā, what), أين (ayna, where), متى (matā, when), كيف (kayfa, how), كم (kam, how much/many), من (man, who), لماذا (limādhā, why). They sit where the answer would be: ما هذا؟ (mā hādhā? — what is this?), أين تذهب؟ (ayna tadhhab? — where are you going?), من هو؟ (man huwa? — who is he?), متى تأتي؟ (matā taʾtī? — when are you coming?). For yes/no questions, start with هل (hal): هل تذهب؟ (hal tadhhab? — are you going?). A classic beginner mistake is translating English word order — "Where are you going?" never scrambles the Arabic; keep أين تذهب؟.

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. أين...؟ (ayna...? — where is...?): أين المحطة؟ (ayna al-maḥaṭṭah? — where is the station?). كيف أذهب إلى...؟ (kayfa adhhabu ilā...? — how do I get to...?). يمين (yamīn, right), يسار (yasār, left), إلى الأمام (ilā al-amām, straight ahead), قريب (qarīb, near), بعيد (baʿīd, far), عند الزاوية (ʿinda az-zāwiyah, at the corner), إشارة المرور (ishārat al-murūr, traffic light). If you are lost: أنا ضائع (anā ḍāʾiʿ — said by a man; ḍāʾiʿah for a woman) — I'm lost. The lifesaver follow-up: هل يمكنك أن تريني على الخريطة؟ (hal yumkinuka an turīyanī ʿalā al-kharīṭah? — can you show me on the map?). When someone answers, listen for انعطف يمينا (inʿaṭif yamīnan, turn right) and استمر مباشرة (istamirr mubāsharatan, continue straight).

Shopping questions beyond prices: هل عندك...؟ (hal ʿindak...? — do you have...?): هل عندك مقاس كبير؟ (hal ʿindaka miqās kabīr? — do you have a large size?). هل يمكنني أن أجرب؟ (hal yumkinunī an ujarrib? — can I try it on?). هل تقبلون البطاقة؟ (hal taqbalūn al-biṭāqah? — do you take card?). متى تفتحون؟ (matā taftaḥūn? — when do you open?). Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: من أين أنت؟ (min ayna ant? — where are you from?), ما هي مهنتك؟ (mā hiya mihnatuk? — what is your profession?), منذ متى وأنت هنا؟ (mundhu matā wa anta hunā? — how long have you been here?), هل تحب هذه المدينة؟ (hal tuḥibbu hādhihi al-madīnah? — do you like this city?), ماذا تنصحني؟ (mādhā tanṣaḥunī? — what do you recommend?).

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Tourist: عفوا، أين المتحف؟ (ʿAfwan, ayna al-matḥaf?) — Excuse me, where is the museum?
Local: قريب. اذهب مباشرة ثم انعطف يسارا عند إشارة المرور. (Qarīb. Idhhab mubāsharatan thumma inʿaṭif yasāran ʿinda ishārat al-murūr.) — Near. Go straight, then turn left at the traffic light.
Tourist: هل هو بعيد مشيا؟ (Hal huwa baʿīd mashyan?) — Is it far on foot?
Local: لا، خمس دقائق. هو بين البنك والصيدلية. (Lā, khamsu daqāʾiq. Huwa bayna al-bank wa aṣ-ṣaydaliyyah.) — No, five minutes. It's between the bank and the pharmacy.
Tourist: شكرا جزيلا! ما اسم هذا الشارع؟ (Shukran jazīlan! Mā ismu hādhā ash-shāriʿ?) — Thank you very much! What is this street called?
Local: هذا شارع النيل. (Hādhā shāriʿ an-Nīl.) — This is Nile Street.

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Sara: من أين أنت؟ (Min ayna ant?) — Where are you from?
Karim: أنا من لبنان. وأنت؟ (Anā min Lubnān. Wa ant?) — I am from Lebanon. And you?
Sara: أنا من هنا، من القاهرة. منذ متى وأنت هنا؟ (Anā min hunā, min al-Qāhirah. Mundhu matā wa anta hunā?) — I am from here, from Cairo. How long have you been here?
Karim: منذ أسبوعين. أحب هذه المدينة كثيرا. (Mundhu usbūʿayn. Uḥibbu hādhihi al-madīnah kathīran.) — Two weeks. I love this city a lot.
Sara: ماذا تنصحني أن أزور؟ (Mādhā tanṣaḥunī an azūr?) — What do you recommend I visit?
Karim: أريد أن أذهب إلى الحديقة غدا. لماذا لا تأتي؟ (Urīdu an adhhabu ilā al-ḥadīqah ghadan. Limādhā lā taʾtī?) — I want to go to the park tomorrow. Why don't you come?
Sara: فكرة جيدة! في أي ساعة؟ (Fikrah jayyidah! Fī ayyi sāʿah?) — Good idea! At what time?
Karim: في العاشرة. نلتقي هنا. (Fī al-ʿāshirah. Naltaqī hunā.) — At ten. We meet here.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud. Memorize the direction sequence (إلى الأمام, يمين, يسار, عند الزاوية) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in Arabic, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with changed details (your city, your time, your plan) until the question patterns feel automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The Past Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: ماذا فعلت أمس؟ (mādhā faʿalta amsi? — what did you do yesterday?). Arabic past tense uses suffixes on the verb stem — learn the pattern once and it works for every verb.

The past tense adds endings to the three-letter stem. With كتب (kataba, to write): كتبتُ (katabtu — I wrote), كتبتَ (katabta — you masculine wrote), كتبتِ (katabti — you feminine wrote), كتب (kataba — he wrote), كتبتْ (katabat — she wrote), كتبنا (katabnā — we wrote). The full pattern to memorize: ـتُ (tu, I), ـتَ (ta, you m.), ـتِ (ti, you f.), ـَ (a, he — no ending), ـتْ (at, she), ـنا (nā, we). Apply it to درس (darasa, to study): درستُ (darastu — I studied), درستَ (darasta), درستِ (darasti), درس (darasa), درستْ (darasat), درسنا (darasnā). Two verbs fully conjugated gives you the engine for every regular verb.

The negative past uses لم (lam) + the present-tense verb without its final vowel: لم أدرس (lam adrus — I didn't study), لم يذهب (lam yadhhab — he didn't go). This is a hard rule — لم always pairs with the shortened present form, never with the past suffixes. Saying لم درستُ is wrong; لم أدرس is correct.

For "was" in the past, use كان (kāna): كان الطقس جميلا (kāna aṭ-ṭaqsu jamīlan — the weather was beautiful), كنت متعبا (kuntu mutʿaban — I was tired, masculine; mutʿabatan feminine). كان conjugates like any past verb: كنتَ (kunta, you m. were), كانت (kānat, she was), كنا (kunnā, we were).

Time words anchor the past: أمس (amsi, yesterday), أول أمس (awwala amsi, the day before yesterday), الأسبوع الماضي (al-usbūʿ al-māḍī, last week), الشهر الماضي (ash-shahr al-māḍī, last month), السنة الماضية (as-sanah al-māḍiyah, last year), قبل قليل (qabla qalīl, a little while ago). Combine them with the past tense: شاهدت فيلما أمس (shāhadtu filman amsi — I watched a movie yesterday), ذهبت إلى دمشق الأسبوع الماضي (dhahabtu ilā Dimashq al-usbūʿ al-māḍī — I went to Damascus last week). To list several past actions, chain them with و (wa, and): شاهدت فيلما وتسوقت (shāhadtu filman wa tasawwaqtu — I watched a movie and went shopping).

Two beginner warnings. First, don't mix لم with past suffixes — لم is always followed by the present stem: لم أكتب (lam aktub — I didn't write). Second, remember gender agreement in the past: هي ذهبتْ (hiya dhahabat — she went) needs the تْ ending; هو ذهب (huwa dhahaba — he went) takes none. Dropping the feminine تْ is the most common past-tense error.

Dialogue — talking about the weekend:

Nour: ماذا فعلت في عطلة نهاية الأسبوع؟ (Mādhā faʿalta fī ʿuṭlat nihāyat al-usbūʿ?) — What did you do on the weekend?
Tariq: ذهبت إلى الشاطئ مع عائلتي يوم السبت. (Dhahabtu ilā ash-shāṭiʾ maʿa ʿāʾilatī yawm as-sabt.) — I went to the beach with my family on Saturday.
Nour: كيف كان؟ هل كان الطقس جميلا؟ (Kayfa kān? Hal kāna aṭ-ṭaqsu jamīlan?) — How was it? Was the weather beautiful?
Tariq: نعم، كان مشمسا جدا! سبحنا وأكلنا السمك. (Naʿam, kāna mushmisan jiddan! Sabaḥnā wa akalnā as-samak.) — Yes, very sunny! We swam and ate fish.
Nour: جميل! بقيت في البيت. شاهدت فيلما وقرأت كتابا. (Jamīl! Baqītu fī al-bayt. Shāhadtu filman wa qaraʾtu kitāban.) — Lovely! I stayed home. I watched a movie and read a book.
Tariq: هل أعجبك الفيلم؟ (Hal aʿjabak al-film?) — Did you like the movie?
Nour: نعم، أحببته كثيرا. وماذا فعلت يوم الأحد؟ (Naʿam, aḥbabtuhu kathīran. Wa mādhā faʿalta yawm al-aḥad?) — Yes, I loved it. And what did you do Sunday?
Tariq: نمت حتى وقت متأخر وزرت والدي. (Nimtu ḥattā waqtin mutaʾakhkhir wa zurtu wāliday.) — I slept in late and visited my parents.

Practice: Write a paragraph of 8–10 sentences about what you did yesterday, using at least five different past-tense verbs with correct pronoun endings. Read it aloud twice. Then conjugate in writing: درس، كتب، ذهب — full past tense, all persons. Finally, answer aloud in complete Arabic sentences: ماذا أكلت أمس؟ في أي ساعة استيقظت؟ ماذا فعلت في عطلة نهاية الأسبوع الماضية؟

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Making Plans — Future Expressions + Restaurant and Travel Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to talk about the future — making plans, expressing wants, inviting people — and handles two of the most useful real-world conversations: ordering in a restaurant and navigating travel. Future talk turns you from a visitor into someone who can actually live in Arabic: booking, inviting, promising, and planning.

Arabic marks the future with سوف (sawfa) or the prefix سـ (sa-) before the present verb: سوف أذهب (sawfa adhhabu) or سأذهب (sa-adhhabu) — I will go. سوف نأكل (sawfa naʾkulu) or سنأكل (sa-naʾkulu) — we will eat. سـ is shorter and more common in speech; سوف is slightly more formal. Future time words: غدا (ghadan, tomorrow), بعد غد (baʿda ghad, the day after tomorrow), الأسبوع القادم (al-usbūʿ al-qādim, next week), الشهر القادم (ash-shahr al-qādim, next month), السنة القادمة (as-sanah al-qādimah, next year), الليلة (al-laylah, tonight). Combine freely: سأذهب إلى القاهرة الأسبوع القادم (sa-adhhabu ilā al-Qāhirah al-usbūʿ al-qādim — I will go to Cairo next week).

To say you want something, use أريد (urīdu — I want): أريد أن أذهب (urīdu an adhhab — I want to go), أريد قهوة (urīdu qahwah — I want coffee). The negative: لا أريد (lā urīd — I don't want). Invitations: هل تريد أن...؟ (hal turīdu an...? — do you want to...?): هل تريد أن تأكل معنا؟ (hal turīdu an taʾkula maʿanā? — do you want to eat with us?). Accept with نعم، بكل سرور (naʿam, bi-kulli surūr — yes, with pleasure). Decline softly with مرة أخرى إن شاء الله (marrah ukhrā in shāʾ Allāh — another time, God willing) — a graceful, culturally natural no.

Restaurant phrases. The staff greets you with أهلا وسهلا (ahlan wa sahlan) — welcome. Ask for the menu: قائمة الطعام من فضلك (qāʾimat aṭ-ṭaʿām min faḍlik — the menu, please). Ask for a recommendation: ماذا تنصحني؟ (mādhā tanṣaḥunī? — what do you recommend?). Order with أريد... من فضلك: أريد هذا من فضلك (urīdu hādhā min faḍlik — I want this, please). React to food: لذيذ جدا! (ladhīdh jiddan! — very delicious!). Dietary needs: بدون لحم (bidūn laḥm — without meat), بدون سكر (bidūn sukkar — without sugar). Ask for the bill: الحساب من فضلك (al-ḥisāb min faḍlik — the check, please). Common mistake: calling the waiter with a loud whistle or snap — a raised hand with عفوا (ʿafwan) is polite and effective.

Travel phrases. المطار (al-maṭār, airport), الطائرة (aṭ-ṭāʾirah, airplane), الفندق (al-funduq, hotel), القطار (al-qiṭār, train), تذكرة (tadhkirah, ticket), حجز (ḥajz, reservation). At the hotel: عندي حجز (ʿindī ḥajz — I have a reservation), أريد أن أسجل الدخول (urīdu an usajjila ad-dukhūl — I'd like to check in), في أي ساعة يبدأ الفطور؟ (fī ayyi sāʿah yabdaʾ al-fuṭūr? — at what time does breakfast start?). Problems: فقدت جواز سفري (faqadtu jawāza safarī — I lost my passport), ساعدني من فضلك (sāʿidnī min faḍlik — please help me).

Dialogue 1 — at a restaurant:

Waiter: أهلا وسهلا! كم شخص؟ (Ahlan wa sahlan! Kam shakhṣ?) — Welcome! How many people?
Hassan: شخصان. هل يوجد طاولة بجانب النافذة؟ (Shakhṣān. Hal yūjadu ṭāwilah bi-jānib an-nāfidhah?) — Two people. Is there a table by the window?
Waiter: نعم، تفضل. هذه قائمة الطعام. (Naʿam, tafaḍḍal. Hādhihi qāʾimat aṭ-ṭaʿām.) — Yes, please come. Here is the menu.
Hassan: ماذا تنصحني؟ (Mādhā tanṣaḥunī?) — What do you recommend?
Waiter: المشويات لذيذة جدا. (Al-mashwiyyāt ladhīdhah jiddan.) — The grilled meats are very delicious.
Hassan: حسنا، أريد المشويات وكوبين من العصير من فضلك. (Ḥasanan, urīdu al-mashwiyyāt wa kūbayn min al-ʿaṣīr min faḍlik.) — Good, I want the grilled meats and two glasses of juice, please.
(later) Hassan: لذيذ جدا! الحساب من فضلك. (Ladhīdh jiddan! Al-ḥisāb min faḍlik.) — Very delicious! The check, please.
Waiter: خمسة وثمانون. (Khamsah wa thamānūn.) — Eighty-five.

Dialogue 2 — making weekend plans:

Rania: ماذا ستفعلين يوم السبت؟ (Mādhā sa-tafʿalīn yawm as-sabt?) — What will you do Saturday?
Salem: أريد أن أذهب إلى السوق. وأنت؟ (Urīdu an adhhabu ilā as-sūq. Wa ant?) — I want to go to the market. And you?
Rania: سأذهب إلى الحديقة. هل تريد أن تأتي معي؟ (Sa-adhhabu ilā al-ḥadīqah. Hal turīdu an taʾtiya maʿī?) — I will go to the park. Do you want to come with me?
Salem: نعم، بكل سرور! في أي ساعة نلتقي؟ (Naʿam, bi-kulli surūr! Fī ayyi sāʿah naltaqī?) — Yes, with pleasure! At what time shall we meet?
Rania: في العاشرة صباحا، أمام المسجد. (Fī al-ʿāshirah ṣabāḥan, amāma al-masjid.) — At ten in the morning, in front of the mosque.
Salem: اتفقنا! أراك غدا. (Ittafaqnā! Arāk ghadan.) — Agreed! See you tomorrow.

Practice: Write three plans for next week using سوف or سـ, and three wants using أريد. Write a full restaurant dialogue (8+ lines) where you enter, order two dishes and drinks, react to the food, and ask for the bill. Say it all aloud. Finally, invite a friend somewhere in Arabic using هل تريد أن...؟, and answer your own invitation.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Conversation Practice Drills + Your 30-Day Practice Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson does two things: it gives you structured conversation drills that combine everything from Lessons 1–7, and it hands you a concrete 30-day plan so your Arabic keeps growing after the course ends. A course can teach you the material, but only a routine turns material into skill — so treat this lesson as the most important one to actually do.

Drill 1 — The Two-Minute Monologue. Set a timer for two minutes and talk about your day — present for routines (أستيقظ في الساعة السابعة كل يوم — astayqiẓu fī as-sāʿah as-sābiʿah kull yawm, I wake up at seven every day), past for what already happened (أكلت الفطور — akaltu al-fuṭūr, I ate breakfast), future for what is next (سأذهب إلى السوق الآن — sa-adhhabu ilā as-sūq al-ān, I will go to the market now). Do not stop to look up words; describe around them. Keeping going matters more than being perfect. Do this drill daily — it is the single highest-value exercise in this course.

Drill 2 — Question Tennis. Write 20 question words and topics on slips of paper (ماذا, أين, من, متى, كيف). Draw one and answer in two full sentences, then ask a follow-up question. Example: draw أين → أين تذهب؟ أذهب إلى المدرسة. وأنت؟ Draw ماذا → ماذا أكلت؟ أكلت خبزا. If you practice with a partner, rally: they answer your question, then ask you one back. Ten minutes of question tennis covers more ground than an hour of passive review.

Drill 3 — Situation Cards. Write real situations on cards: "Your hotel has no hot water — explain politely," "Ask a stranger for directions to the station," "Order dinner for two at a restaurant," "Small talk with a taxi driver for five minutes." Draw a card and perform it aloud, both roles. These force you to combine vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation under mild pressure — exactly what real conversations feel like. Rotate through all your cards weekly.

Two mistakes that stall learners at this stage. First, the perfection trap: refusing to speak until every ending is certain. Arabic speakers are generous with beginners who try; they cannot help beginners who stay silent. Speak with 70% accuracy today rather than 100% accuracy never. Second, passive consumption: re-reading lessons and calling it study. Reading feels productive but builds recognition, not production. Every minute of speaking aloud counts triple compared to silent review — your mouth needs the reps, especially for ع, ح, and the emphatic letters.

Your 30-day practice plan. Week 1 — Foundations lock-in: 20 minutes daily. Days 1–2: re-read Lessons 1–2 dialogues aloud, reading the Arabic script. Days 3–4: write the full alphabet from memory, then check the chart. Days 5–7: number and time drills from Lesson 4 until 1–20 and the gender rule are automatic. Week 2 — Conversation ignition: 25 minutes daily. Daily two-minute monologue plus question tennis; re-do the Lesson 5 dialogues with changed details. Week 3 — Real situations: 30 minutes daily. One situation card per day performed aloud; write a daily journal of five Arabic sentences about your day (present + past + future mix). Week 4 — Live fire: 30+ minutes daily. Have at least three real conversations — with a tutor, a language-exchange partner, an Arabic-speaking neighbor, or ordering food in Arabic at a restaurant. Note your three most frequent errors and drill them the following week.

Track it simply: a notebook page per day with the date, minutes practiced, and one line about what felt easier than last week. If you miss a day, never miss twice — the streak matters more than any single session. After 30 days, repeat the cycle with harder situation cards and longer monologues; you now own a system, not just a course.

Practice: Do Drill 1 right now — two full minutes about your day in Arabic, out loud, no stopping. Then write out your personal Week 1 schedule with exact times (for example, "7:30 AM, 20 minutes, alphabet writing"). Finally, write five situation cards of your own based on your life — travel you plan, restaurants you visit, people you meet — and perform the first one today. بالتوفيق (bi at-tawfīq) — good luck! You are an Arabic speaker now. Keep speaking.

courses.title: Bible Study Foundations: Texts, Theology & Methods
courses.tagline: Understand the Bible deeply: its storyline, key themes, and proven study methods.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Bible Study Foundations is an introductory course designed for readers who want to move beyond isolated verses and understand the Bible as a whole. Across eight lessons, you will learn practical study approaches, walk through the storyline of the Old and New Testaments, explore central theological themes such as covenant, grace, and the kingdom, and practice reading different literary genres on their own terms. The course treats the Bible as Christians have read it for centuries: a collection of texts that Christians hold to be authoritative and that present a unified story centered on God and, in the Christian reading, Jesus Christ. The tone is educational and respectful throughout; no denominational position is assumed or argued, and you are encouraged to reflect honestly on your own questions as you study.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
