syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: You will learn what data analytics is and the four types of data (numbers, categories, text, and dates) plus how each one behaves. You will learn to use a spreadsheet to sort, filter, and run formulas on a dataset of hundreds of rows. You will learn a repeatable process for cleaning messy data: handling missing values, fixing inconsistent formats, removing duplicates, and checking your work. You will learn descriptive statistics in plain English — mean, median, mode, range, and standard deviation — and when each one is the right summary. You will learn visualization principles: which chart type fits which question, how to avoid misleading charts, and how to label honestly. You will learn SQL basics: selecting columns, filtering rows, sorting, grouping, and calculating averages and counts across a database table. You will learn to design a simple dashboard with key metrics, trend charts, and comparison views. Finally, you will walk through a complete case study from question to recommendation and get a roadmap for what to learn next.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: Work through the lessons in order, because each one builds on the previous. After reading a lesson, redo its worked examples yourself — in a spreadsheet for Lessons 2 through 5 and 7, and in any free SQL practice environment or even on paper for Lesson 6. Typing the formulas and queries yourself is what makes the skills stick; reading alone is not enough. When you reach the Practice exercise at the end of a lesson, do it before moving on — each one takes thirty to sixty minutes and uses small datasets included in the lesson text. Keep a working spreadsheet file for the course where you save your practice datasets and answers; by Lesson 8 you will have a small portfolio of analyses. Expect to make errors — a wrong formula or a chart that looks strange is feedback, not failure. Check the 'common mistakes' notes in each lesson when something looks off, and re-read the concept it points to. Plan roughly one to two hours per lesson including the exercises.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: You need a computer with any spreadsheet program installed — the free options built into most systems or available at no cost online all work, since the course uses standard features (sorting, filtering, common formulas, charts) that every spreadsheet program has. You need basic comfort with files and folders, such as creating a folder and saving a file. No programming experience is required, and the math never goes beyond arithmetic plus a few new averages explained from zero. Everything else — vocabulary, techniques, and habits — is taught inside the lessons. If you can follow written instructions and are willing to experiment with a spreadsheet, you are ready.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This is a written course package: eight text lessons, this syllabus, and three practical reference materials (a data-cleaning checklist, a formula and SQL cheat sheet, and a dashboard planning worksheet) that you can print or keep open while you work. There is no video content, no audio, and no live sessions — everything is designed to be read, worked through, and kept as a reference you return to. The datasets in the lessons are small illustrative examples for practice, not claims about any real business or population. The course makes no promise of jobs, income, or certification; it teaches data analysis skills, and your results will depend on the practice you put in. Read at your own pace, repeat lessons as needed, and keep your practice files — they are the start of your analytics portfolio.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What Data Analytics Is and the Types of Data
lessons.text:
This lesson defines data analytics in plain terms and teaches you the four types of data you will work with throughout the course. By the end you will be able to explain what an analyst actually does day to day, tell the four data types apart on sight, and match each type to the questions it can and cannot answer. Everything in this course — cleaning, statistics, charts, SQL — sits on top of these foundations, so take the time to get comfortable here.

Data analytics is the practice of turning raw records into answers that help someone make a decision. Raw records are facts captured in the course of activity: each sale rung up, each order shipped, each customer sign-up. An analyst takes those records and does four things. First, they clarify the question: "Which product should we restock?" is answerable, while "Are we doing well?" is too vague. Second, they gather the relevant data and check that it is trustworthy. Third, they analyze it — count, group, compare, summarize — to find patterns. Fourth, they present the finding clearly, often with a chart, plus a recommendation. Notice what is not on the list: guessing, cherry-picking one favorable number, or dressing up a weak finding with a fancy chart. The analyst's credibility comes from honest handling of the data, and Lessons 3 through 5 teach the techniques that keep you honest.

Data comes in four types, and the type decides what you are allowed to do with it. Numerical data (also called quantitative) is numbers where arithmetic makes sense: sales amounts, temperatures, ages, quantities. You can add and average these. Categorical data (qualitative) is labels that group things: product names, colors, payment methods, customer segments. You can count how many fall in each category, but averaging "red" and "blue" is meaningless. Text data is free-form writing: reviews, comments, descriptions. You can search it and count words, but it needs processing before it behaves like the other types. Date and time data marks when things happened: order dates, timestamps. You can sort by it, group by month or week, and measure gaps between events. A single dataset usually mixes all four — an order record has a date, a product name (category), a quantity and price (numbers), and a customer note (text).

Here is a small sample dataset you will see referenced through the course — a neighborhood bakery's daily records. Each row is one day:

Date | Loaves sold | Revenue | Busiest hour | Weather | Staff note
2026-10-26 | 84 | 210.00 | 8 AM | sunny | "Ran out of rye by 10"
2026-10-27 | 61 | 152.50 | 9 AM | rainy | "Slow morning"
2026-10-28 | 77 | 192.50 | 8 AM | cloudy | ""
2026-10-29 | 95 | 237.50 | 8 AM | sunny | "Extra batch at noon"
2026-10-30 | 58 | 145.00 | 10 AM | rainy | "Two staff out sick"

Loaves sold and Revenue are numerical. Busiest hour and Weather are categorical. The date is date data. The staff note is text. Already you can see real questions this answers: which weather brings more sales, what a typical day looks like, whether staffing notes explain the slow days. An analyst would start by asking the bakery owner which decision the answer feeds — for example, how many loaves to bake tomorrow — and only then compute.

Two beginner mistakes start in this lesson. First, treating categories like numbers: assigning 1 = sunny, 2 = rainy and then "averaging" the weather to 1.4 is nonsense, even though a spreadsheet will happily compute it. Always ask: does arithmetic mean anything here? If not, count instead of averaging. Second, jumping to analysis before defining the question. It is tempting to open a dataset and start calculating everything, but analysis without a question produces trivia. Write the question in one sentence first — "Do rainy days sell fewer loaves?" — and let it choose which numbers you compute. The habit of question-first analysis is the single most valuable thing this lesson teaches.

Practice: Invent a small dataset of your own with ten rows about something you can observe this week — your daily cups of water, minutes spent on chores, or items in your shopping cart. Include at least one numerical column, one categorical column, and a date column. Then write three one-sentence questions your dataset could answer and three it could not (for example, water data cannot tell you about sleep). Finally, label each column in the bakery dataset above with its data type, and explain in one sentence why "busiest hour" is categorical rather than numerical even though it contains a number.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Spreadsheets for Analysis — Sorting, Filtering, and Formulas
lessons.text:
This lesson makes you fluent in the analyst's daily tool: the spreadsheet. By the end you will sort and filter a dataset of hundreds of rows, write formulas that calculate new columns, and use the core functions — SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MIN, MAX, IF, and VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP — correctly. Spreadsheets handle a surprising share of professional analysis, and everything you learn here transfers to the dashboard and statistics lessons later.

Start with a clean layout. Put your data in a proper table: one header row with short, clear names (date, loaves, revenue), one row per record below it, no blank rows in the middle, and no merged cells. Keep raw data on one sheet and do your analysis on another, so the originals are never at risk. This discipline feels fussy until the day a careless sort scrambles your data — and sorting is the first skill. Select your data and sort by a column: sorting the bakery data by loaves sold from largest to smallest instantly shows the best and worst days. The golden rule of sorting is to select ALL columns before sorting, or use your program's "sort range with headers" feature, so each row stays intact. Sorting one column alone while the others stay put silently destroys your data — this is the most damaging beginner error in spreadsheets, and the habit of selecting the whole table first prevents it.

Filtering lets you look at a slice without deleting anything. Turn on filters for your header row, then use the dropdown on the weather column to show only rainy days: the spreadsheet hides the other rows and, crucially, functions like SUBTOTAL adjust to show only the visible rows. Filtering answers questions like "what is our average revenue on sunny days?" in seconds: filter to sunny, then average the revenue column. A filter never changes the underlying data — it only changes the view — so it is always safe to experiment. Combine filters across columns to narrow further: rainy days AND loaves below 65. When you are done, clear the filter to bring everything back.

Formulas turn raw columns into answers. Every formula starts with = and can reference cells: =B2*2.5 computes double the value in B2. The functions you will use constantly are SUM (total), AVERAGE (mean), COUNT (how many numbers), COUNTA (how many non-empty cells), MIN and MAX. So =AVERAGE(C2:C31) gives average daily revenue for a month, and =MAX(B2:B31) finds the best sales day. IF makes decisions: =IF(B2>80,"Strong day","Normal day") labels each day, and you can nest conditions for more bands. VLOOKUP (or XLOOKUP in newer programs) pulls matching data from another table — for example, looking up each product's category from a price list by its product code. When you copy a formula down a column, references shift relatively (B2 becomes B3), which is usually what you want; put a $ before the letter or number to lock a reference, like $B$2, when it must not move — for example, a tax rate stored in one cell that every row's formula uses.

Two more mistakes to engrave in memory. First, numbers stored as text: values that look like numbers but were typed or pasted as text will not sort or average correctly, and your totals will silently undercount. The symptom is SUM returning 0 or AVERAGE ignoring cells; the fix is to convert the column to numbers (most programs offer "convert to number" or multiplying by 1 in a helper column). Second, dividing by zero or referencing empty cells in AVERAGE: empty cells are ignored by AVERAGE, which is usually fine, but a truly missing value is different from a zero — a day the bakery was closed should be blank, not 0, or your average will sink unfairly. Lesson 3 goes deeper on exactly this distinction.

Practice: Rebuild the five-day bakery dataset from Lesson 1 in a spreadsheet. Add a sixth and seventh day of your own invention. Then: (1) sort by revenue, largest first, and confirm whole rows moved together; (2) filter to rainy days and compute their average loaves with AVERAGE; (3) add a column with =IF(B2>75,"Big day","Regular day") and copy it down; (4) at the bottom, compute total revenue with SUM, average loaves with AVERAGE, and the best day with MAX. Save this file — you will extend it in Lessons 3, 4, and 5.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Cleaning Messy Data
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the least glamorous and most important analyst skill: cleaning messy data. By the end you will run a repeatable cleaning routine — checking for missing values, fixing inconsistent formats, removing duplicates, and validating your work — on any dataset. Real-world data is never as tidy as textbook examples: entries are misspelled, dates arrive in three formats, half the rows are missing something. Analysts commonly spend most of a project's time cleaning, because every analysis built on dirty data is wrong in ways that look convincing.

Start with a cleaning mindset: never edit the raw data. Make a copy or work on a duplicate sheet, and keep a short log of what you changed — "removed 3 duplicate rows", "filled 2 missing revenues with the daily average". This log is your proof that the final numbers are honest, and it lets you or anyone else redo the work. Then inspect before you fix: sort each column, scan for odd values, and use filters to spot blanks. A quick scan of a customer list might reveal "New York", "new york", "NY", and "Nwe York" all meaning the same city, plus two identical rows and a phone column mixing (555) 123-4567 with 555.123.4567. Each of these is a different defect with a different fix.

Missing values are the most common defect, and the fix depends on why the value is missing. A blank revenue on a day the shop was closed is not a zero — it is "not applicable," and the honest treatment is to leave it blank so averages skip it, as Lesson 2 noted. A blank in a survey response where someone skipped the question is genuinely unknown. Your options are: leave it blank (best when few are missing and the analysis tolerates it), fill it with a sensible substitute like the column's average or median (acceptable when you disclose it in your log), or drop the row (only when the row is unusable otherwise). What you must never do is silently treat blanks as zeros without thinking — zeros drag averages down and can flip a conclusion. As a rule, if more than a small fraction of a column is missing, the problem is in how the data was collected, and you should say so in your findings rather than patch over it.

Inconsistent formats are the next defect. Standardize text with find-and-replace and consistent capitalization: pick "New York" and convert every variant to it. Standardize dates to one format (2026-10-26 style, year-month-day, sorts correctly as text too). Standardize numbers: strip currency symbols and commas into plain numbers in one column, keeping the original if you like. Remove exact duplicates — most spreadsheet programs have a "remove duplicates" command — but check first that the rows are truly identical and not two legitimate identical-looking records (two separate $20 sales on the same day are real; a pasted-twice import is not). Finally, validate: recompute your row counts before and after (you removed exactly the duplicates, nothing else), spot-check ten random rows against the raw copy, and re-run your key formulas. If the totals changed in a way you cannot explain from your log, something went wrong — go back.

Two mistakes define this lesson. First, cleaning without a log: a month later you will not remember whether you deleted those rows because they were duplicates or because they were inconvenient, and neither will anyone checking your work. Second, "fixing" data by deleting rows that contradict the story you want. Removing a terrible sales day because it spoils the trend is not cleaning — it is fabrication. The rule is simple: you may only remove or change values for documented data-quality reasons (duplicate, impossible value like a negative age, obvious typo), never because you dislike the result. When in doubt, keep the row and note the oddity.

Practice: Take your bakery spreadsheet from Lesson 2 and deliberately mess up a copy: misspell one weather entry, enter one date in a different format, duplicate one row, delete one revenue value, and add a stray space to a product name if you have one. Then clean the copy using this lesson's routine — inspect, log each fix, standardize, dedupe, validate — and write a five-line cleaning log. Confirm your totals match the original file afterward. Keep the log format; the checklist in your materials packet is built from exactly this routine.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Descriptive Statistics in Plain English
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches descriptive statistics — the handful of numbers that summarize a dataset — in plain English with no mathematical jargon unexplained. By the end you will compute and interpret the mean, median, and mode (three kinds of "average"), measure spread with range and standard deviation, and know which summary fits which situation. These summaries are the vocabulary of analysis: nearly every report, dashboard, and business conversation about data uses them.

Start with the three averages, because each answers a slightly different question. The mean is what most people mean by "average": add everything up and divide by the count. The bakery's loaves over five days — 84, 61, 77, 95, 58 — sum to 375, divided by 5 gives a mean of 75. The median is the middle value when the numbers are lined up in order: 58, 61, 77, 84, 95, so the median is 77. The mode is the most frequent value — with these five distinct numbers there is no mode, but in a month of weather data the mode might be "sunny". The crucial difference: the mean is pulled by extremes, the median is not. Add one catering order of 400 loaves and the mean jumps to about 129 while the median barely moves. That is why analysts report the median for things with occasional huge values — incomes, house prices, order sizes — and the mean when values are well-behaved. When someone quotes an "average" without saying which one, ask; the choice can completely change the story.

Spread tells you how much the numbers vary, and a summary without spread is half a story. "Average 75 loaves a day" could mean every day sells 73 to 77, or it could mean alternating 40 and 110 — same average, wildly different bakery. The range is the simplest measure: max minus min, here 95 − 58 = 37. The standard deviation is the more useful one: roughly, the typical distance of a day's sales from the mean. A small standard deviation means consistent days; a large one means volatile days. You do not need to compute it by hand — every spreadsheet has a STDEV function — but you need the intuition: two shops can share an average while one is predictable and the other is a roller coaster, and the standard deviation is the number that reveals which is which. Percentiles add one more useful lens: the 90th percentile is the value that 90% of days fall below, handy for questions like "how big a day should we be ready for?"

Choosing the right summary is a small decision tree. Describing a typical value? Use the median if outliers exist, the mean otherwise, the mode for categories. Describing consistency? Use range for a quick sense, standard deviation for the real picture. Comparing two groups — sunny versus rainy days, this month versus last? Compute the same summary for each group side by side and look at the gap. And always sanity-check summaries against the raw data: if the median says 77 but a glance at the column shows mostly 50s and 60s, something is off — perhaps a filter is still on, or text-numbers are being ignored. Summaries compress reality; the raw column is the ground truth you check against.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, quoting the mean for skewed data without mentioning it: saying "average order value is $85" when one giant order did most of the work misleads whoever plans inventory from that number. Report the median alongside, or at least note the outlier. Second, confusing correlation with cause, which starts here because summaries invite it: rainy days averaging fewer loaves does not prove rain causes low sales — perhaps rainy days in your data were also the days staff were out sick (remember October 30). A difference between groups is a clue that deserves investigation, not a conclusion. Write "rainy days averaged 15 fewer loaves in this data" — a true statement — rather than "rain causes slow days" — a claim the data alone cannot support.

Practice: Extend your bakery spreadsheet to fourteen days (invent seven more rows, keeping the same columns). Compute the mean, median, and mode of loaves sold, plus the range and standard deviation (STDEV). Then split the days into sunny versus not-sunny and compute the mean loaves for each group. Write three honest sentences summarizing what you found — using "in this data" language, not causal claims. Finally, add one extreme day (a 300-loaf catering order) and watch what happens to the mean versus the median; write one sentence explaining which summary you would report to the bakery owner and why.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Data Visualization Principles and Chart Types
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to turn numbers into pictures that tell the truth quickly. By the end you will choose the right chart for each question, build clean honest charts in a spreadsheet, and spot the tricks that make charts misleading — including in other people's work. A good chart lets a busy person grasp in five seconds what a table of numbers takes five minutes to reveal; a bad chart does the opposite, and sometimes lies.

Every chart answers one of a few question types, and the question picks the chart. Comparing categories? Use a bar chart: loaves sold per weekday, revenue per product. Showing change over time? Use a line chart: daily revenue across the month, where the eye naturally follows the trend. Showing parts of a whole? Use a pie chart only for a few slices (two to five) — payment method shares, for example — or a stacked bar when there are more. Showing the relationship between two numbers? Use a scatter plot: each day is a dot with temperature on one axis and loaves on the other, revealing whether hotter days sell more. Showing a distribution? Use a histogram: how many days fell into each sales band. When in doubt, a bar chart is the safest default — it is the hardest chart to misread. Match the chart to the question before touching any formatting; a beautiful wrong chart is still wrong.

Honest charts follow a short set of principles. Start bar charts at zero: a bar's length encodes its value, so cutting the axis at 70 makes a 75-to-80 difference look enormous when it is actually small. Label everything: chart title stating the finding, axis labels with units ("Revenue, dollars"), and data labels on key points. Keep it simple: one message per chart, no 3D effects, no decorative images, no rainbow of fifteen colors when two will do. Use color to highlight, not decorate — gray for the background data, one strong color for the point you want noticed. And keep the data visible: a chart should never hide the numbers behind so much styling that the reader cannot check your work. These rules are not about taste; each one prevents a specific misunderstanding.

Learn to spot misleading charts, because you will meet them in reports, news, and sales pitches. The truncated axis is the classic: bars or lines that start at a non-zero value to exaggerate a tiny change — always check where the axis begins. The cherry-picked timeframe: a line chart starting right after a dip to show "amazing growth" — ask what the longer history looks like. The area trick: using pictures (coins, people icons) sized by height when the eye reads area, doubling the visual exaggeration — if the value doubles, the icon's area quadruples. The missing context: "sales up 50%" with no mention that last month was the worst on record. And the dual-axis trap: two lines on different scales engineered to look correlated. Your defense is one habit: before reacting to any chart, read the axes, the labels, and the source note. Ten seconds of skepticism defeats most chart tricks.

The workflow for building a chart is: question first, then the right data slice, then the right chart type, then honest formatting, then a one-sentence takeaway written beneath it. For example: question — "are weekends stronger than weekdays?" Slice — average revenue grouped by day of week. Chart — bar chart of the seven averages, axis from zero, titled "Average daily revenue by weekday, October". Takeaway — "In this data, Saturday averaged the highest revenue and Monday the lowest." Notice the takeaway describes the data without claiming why. Build every chart this way and your visuals will be trustworthy by construction.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, charting raw unsorted tables: a line chart of dates in random order produces spaghetti that hides the trend — sort by date first, always. Second, pie charts with too many slices: a twelve-slice pie is unreadable; if you have many categories, use a bar chart sorted largest to smallest, or group the small ones into "Other". If your reader has to work to decode the chart, the chart has failed.

Practice: In your bakery spreadsheet, build three charts from your fourteen-day dataset: (1) a line chart of daily revenue over time, sorted by date, with labeled axes; (2) a bar chart comparing average loaves on sunny versus rainy versus cloudy days, axis starting at zero; (3) a pie chart of days by weather type (keep it to the weather categories you have). Under each chart write a one-sentence honest takeaway. Then deliberately make a misleading version of chart 2 by starting the axis just below your smallest value, and compare the two side by side — notice how different the story feels, and write one sentence about why the honest version is the one you would show the bakery owner.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: SQL Basics for Querying Data
lessons.text:
This lesson introduces SQL, the standard language for asking questions of databases. By the end you will write queries that select columns, filter rows, sort results, group data, and compute counts and averages — the core of real database analysis. Spreadsheets are wonderful up to tens of thousands of rows; databases hold millions, and SQL is how analysts reach into them. The good news: basic SQL reads almost like English, and everything in this lesson works in any standard database.

Picture a database table as a spreadsheet that lives on a server: named columns, one row per record. Our running example is an orders table with columns order_id, order_date, product, quantity, price, and region. The simplest query asks for columns:

SELECT product, quantity, price FROM orders;

This returns every row but only those three columns. SELECT * returns all columns — fine for exploring, but name your columns in real work so results are predictable. Add a filter with WHERE, which keeps only rows matching a condition:

SELECT product, quantity FROM orders WHERE region = 'North';

Text values go in single quotes; numbers do not: WHERE quantity > 10. Combine conditions with AND, OR, and NOT: WHERE region = 'North' AND quantity > 10. Sort with ORDER BY: ORDER BY order_date gives oldest first, ORDER BY price DESC gives most expensive first (DESC means descending; ASC is the default). Limit huge results with LIMIT 20 while exploring, so a mistaken query returns twenty rows instead of twenty million. Read a query top to bottom as a sentence: "select these columns from this table where these rows, ordered this way." That reading habit makes SQL far less intimidating.

Aggregation is where SQL earns its keep: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups and computes one summary row per group. Total revenue per product:

SELECT product, SUM(quantity * price) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

SUM, COUNT, and AVG do the adding, counting, and averaging; AS names the result column so it reads clearly. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(price) counts non-empty prices. Filter groups with HAVING, which is WHERE's counterpart after grouping: HAVING SUM(quantity * price) > 1000 keeps only products above that revenue. A common beginner confusion is WHERE versus HAVING: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping ("only northern orders"), HAVING filters the grouped results after ("only products totaling over 1000"). You will often use both in one query. Date filtering uses the same comparisons: WHERE order_date >= '2026-10-01' AND order_date < '2026-11-01' grabs October cleanly — note the pattern of "from the first of the month up to but not including the first of next month," which avoids missing the last day's late orders.

Two more essentials round out the basics. DISTINCT removes duplicates: SELECT DISTINCT region FROM orders lists each region once — the quickest way to see what values a column actually contains, which doubles as a data-quality check (expecting three regions and finding five spellings is a Lesson 3 problem surfacing in SQL). And NULL marks missing values: a blank in a database is NULL, and it needs special tests — WHERE price IS NULL finds the missing ones, because = NULL never matches anything (a classic gotcha: the query runs fine and returns nothing, silently). Treat NULL with the same care Lesson 3 taught for blanks: understand why it is missing before deciding what to do with it.

Two mistakes dominate early SQL. First, forgetting that SQL is case-insensitive for keywords but your data may not be: 'North' and 'north' can be different values in the region column, so a filter that returns nothing might be a capitalization mismatch — check with SELECT DISTINCT first. Second, grouping errors: every column in your SELECT must either be in the GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregation like SUM. SELECT product, region, SUM(quantity) ... GROUP BY product is an error (or worse, silently wrong in lenient databases) because region is neither grouped nor aggregated. The rule is mechanical: if it is not aggregated, it must be in the GROUP BY.

Practice: On paper or in any free SQL practice tool, imagine the orders table with ten rows you invent (mix products, regions, quantities, and include one NULL price and one duplicate-looking row). Write and "run" in your head: (1) all orders from the North region sorted by price, highest first; (2) total revenue per product, highest first; (3) the count of orders per region; (4) products with total revenue above 500. For each query, write one sentence saying what business question it answers. Then write the query that finds rows with missing prices, and explain why = NULL would fail where IS NULL succeeds.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Building a Simple Dashboard
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to build a dashboard: one page that shows the key numbers for a business at a glance and updates as new data arrives. By the end you will choose the right metrics, lay out a clean one-page dashboard in a spreadsheet, wire it to update automatically, and avoid the clutter that ruins most dashboards. A dashboard is the analyst's main product — the thing a busy owner actually looks at every morning — so building one well is a career-level skill.

A dashboard answers three questions in under a minute: how are we doing, is it getting better or worse, and where should I look closer? Everything on the page must serve one of those. Start by picking four to six key metrics with the decision-maker, not alone: for the bakery, daily revenue, loaves sold, average order value, and waste (unsold loaves) cover health, volume, value, and efficiency. Each metric needs three properties: a clear definition (is "daily revenue" before or after refunds?), a target or comparison (versus last week, versus a goal), and an owner who acts when it moves. A metric nobody acts on is decoration — cut it. Resist the temptation to show everything; a dashboard with thirty numbers is a report nobody reads. The discipline is: if removing a number would change no decision, remove it.

Lay out the page in three zones. The top strip holds the key metrics as big numbers with their comparison: "Revenue today: $212 (up $18 vs last 7-day average)". Big, current, instantly readable. The middle holds two or three trend charts: revenue over the last 30 days as a line, loaves by weekday as bars — the "getting better or worse" zone from Lesson 5's principles, axes honest and labeled. The bottom holds one breakdown that invites closer looks: sales by product or by hour, so a dip in the top number can be investigated one glance down. One page, no scrolling if you can manage it, consistent formatting, and a small "data as of" timestamp so nobody acts on stale numbers. White space is not wasted space — it is what lets the eye find the important thing.

The "updates itself" part is simpler than it sounds. Keep one sheet as the raw data log where new rows are appended daily (date, loaves, revenue, and so on), and build the dashboard on a second sheet whose cells reference the log with formulas. Today's revenue is a lookup of the latest date's row; the 7-day average is AVERAGE of the last seven rows; the 30-day trend chart's data range covers the log's recent rows. When you append today's numbers to the log, every metric and chart refreshes — no rebuilding, no copy-paste. Use structured references or a defined table so formulas extend automatically as rows are added, and put data validation on the log's key columns (dates as dates, weather from a dropdown list) so tomorrow's entry cannot silently break the dashboard with a typo. This append-only log plus formula-driven display is the entire architecture of most small-business dashboards.

Two mistakes ruin dashboards. First, the vanity metric: totals that only go up and never inform a decision, like "total loaves sold since opening" — impressive, useless. Every metric must pass the "so what?" test: if it dropped 20% tomorrow, would someone do something specific? If not, replace it. Second, the stale dashboard: a beautiful page whose data is three weeks old because updating it was manual and annoying. Automate the update path (the log-plus-formulas design), put the "data as of" date where it cannot be missed, and if you cannot keep it fresh, take it down — a stale dashboard actively misleads, which is worse than none.

Practice: Build a one-page bakery dashboard in a new spreadsheet file. Sheet 1 is the log: your fourteen days of data in clean table form. Sheet 2 is the dashboard: a top strip with four big-number metrics (latest revenue, 7-day average revenue, total loaves this week, average loaves per day) each with a comparison to the prior period; a middle zone with a 14-day revenue line chart and a weekday bar chart; a bottom zone with a small table of average loaves by weather. Add a "data as of" date. Then append a fifteenth day to the log and confirm every metric and chart updates without you touching Sheet 2. Show it to someone and time how long it takes them to answer "how is the bakery doing" — under a minute means you built it right.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: End-to-End Case Study and Where to Go Next
lessons.text:
This final lesson walks a complete analysis from question to recommendation, using every skill in the course, and then maps where your learning goes next. By the end you will see how the pieces connect in a realistic project, know how to structure your own analyses, and have a clear next-steps roadmap. This is the lesson that turns eight separate skills into one professional workflow.

The case: the bakery owner asks, "Should I start baking on Sundays? I'm currently closed." That is a good question — specific, tied to a decision, answerable with data. Step one is planning: what data would answer it? Current Saturday sales (the closest proxy for Sunday demand), foot-traffic observations, and the costs of opening (staff wages, ingredients, utilities). The owner has six months of daily sales records — a spreadsheet with date, loaves, revenue, and weather. Step two is cleaning: you scan the data and find the problems Lesson 3 trained you for — three dates typed in a different format, one week where revenue was entered as text with dollar signs, two duplicate rows from a double-import, and four days with blank revenue that turn out to be holidays when the shop was closed (blanks, not zeros — you log every fix). Step three is analysis. Saturdays average 118 loaves versus a 75-loaf weekday average, and the median tells the same story, so the demand signal is real and not driven by outliers. Weather splits show the pattern holds on rainy Saturdays too. A scatter plot of temperature versus loaves shows no strong relationship, so you set that aside rather than forcing a finding.

Step four is the part beginners skip: checking the finding before presenting it. You ask the hard questions. Is six months enough? It covers summer and fall but not the holiday season or deep winter — you note that limit openly. Could something else explain strong Saturdays? They follow payday Fridays for many customers and have full staffing — you cannot prove cause, so you report the pattern without claiming why, exactly as Lesson 4 taught. What would it cost? Staff wages for a Sunday shift plus ingredients run about $180, and at the Saturday average revenue of roughly $295 with typical ingredient costs, the margin looks positive — but you present this as an estimate with stated assumptions, not a promise. Step five is the presentation: a one-page summary with three visuals — Saturday versus weekday bar chart, a six-month Saturday trend line, and the cost-versus-revenue comparison — each with a one-sentence takeaway, plus your recommendation: trial Sundays for eight weeks, track the same metrics on the dashboard from Lesson 7, and decide with real Sunday data. Notice the recommendation includes how to verify it — good analysis always says what would prove it wrong.

That workflow — question, plan, clean, analyze, check, present, verify — is the template for every analysis you will ever do. Write it on a card and keep it visible. The checking step is what separates analysts from spreadsheet operators: anyone can compute an average, but the professional asks "what could make this wrong?" and answers honestly in the report. Your materials packet's checklist is built around this workflow.

Where to go next depends on what pulled you. If databases excited you, go deeper into SQL: joins across multiple tables, subqueries, and window functions are the next tier, and any free SQL tutorial plus practice datasets will carry you. If statistics grabbed you, the next concepts are correlation, basic probability, and hypothesis testing — introductory statistics textbooks written for non-mathematicians are the right level. If dashboards and presentation were the thrill, learn a dedicated dashboard tool and study information design: how layout, color, and typography guide attention. If you want it all to scale, learning a programming language for data work lets you automate cleaning and analysis on datasets far beyond spreadsheet size. Whichever path you take, the method stays the same: small real datasets, question first, clean carefully, check honestly, present clearly.

Practice: Run your own end-to-end mini case. Pick a question about your own life that data could answer — for example, "do I spend more on weekdays or weekends?" or "which days am I most productive?" Collect two weeks of simple data in a log (date plus two or three columns), clean it with your checklist, compute one comparison with statistics, build one honest chart, and write a half-page summary with a recommendation — including one paragraph on what could make your finding wrong and what data would check it. Save the spreadsheet and the summary together; this is the first full case study in your portfolio, and it demonstrates the complete workflow to anyone who sees it.

courses.title: Data Science Foundations
courses.tagline: Turn raw data into clear answers, one careful step at a time.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Data Science Foundations is a written, self-paced course that teaches you how to turn raw data into clear answers. It is written for complete beginners: no prior experience with data work is assumed, and no math beyond everyday arithmetic is used. Every idea is introduced in plain language and worked through with small sample datasets you can follow by hand or in a spreadsheet program. The first lessons explain what data science is and how to work with data tables. The middle lessons teach the core craft: cleaning messy data, describing data with summaries, and drawing charts that tell the truth. The later lessons introduce prediction in plain terms, show you how to present findings so other people can act on them, and close with a small end-to-end project that runs from a question to a recommendation. Each of the eight lessons opens by stating exactly what you will learn, explains concepts with worked examples, warns you about the mistakes beginners make most often, and ends with a practice exercise. By the final lesson you will have completed a full small project and will know exactly where to go next.

syllabus.body:

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: You will learn what data science is and how a data project moves from a question to an answer. You will learn to read and work with data tables: rows, columns, and the four types of data. You will learn a repeatable process for cleaning messy data: handling missing values, fixing inconsistent formats, removing duplicates, and checking your work. You will learn to describe data with summaries: averages, medians, ranges, and counts, and when each one is the right choice. You will learn to build honest charts and to spot charts that mislead. You will learn the idea behind prediction: using patterns in past data to make a careful forecast, and how to test whether a prediction is any good. You will learn to present findings clearly, with a short written summary and a few good charts. Finally, you will carry out a complete small project from start to finish.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: Work through the lessons in order, because each one builds on the previous one. After reading a lesson, redo its worked examples yourself, by hand on paper or in a spreadsheet program. Typing the numbers and formulas yourself is what makes the skills stick; reading alone is not enough. When you reach the Practice exercise at the end of a lesson, do it before moving on. Each one takes thirty to sixty minutes and uses small datasets included in the lesson text. Keep a working spreadsheet file for the course where you save your practice datasets and answers; by Lesson 8 you will have a small portfolio of analyses. Expect to make errors: a wrong formula or a chart that looks strange is feedback, not failure. Check the common mistakes notes in each lesson when something looks off, and re-read the concept it points to. Plan roughly one to two hours per lesson including the exercises.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: You need a computer with any spreadsheet program installed: the free options built into most systems or available at no cost online all work, since the course uses standard features such as sorting, filtering, common formulas, and charts that every spreadsheet program has. You need basic comfort with files and folders, such as creating a folder and saving a file. No programming experience is required, and the math never goes beyond arithmetic plus a few new averages explained from zero. The course is tool-agnostic: it describes concepts and plain steps that work in any spreadsheet program or on paper, and it does not require any one specific paid product. Everything else, vocabulary, techniques, and habits, is taught inside the lessons. If you can follow written instructions and are willing to experiment with a spreadsheet, you are ready.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This is a written course package: eight text lessons, this syllabus, and three practical reference materials (a data science glossary and cheat sheet, a cleaning and checking checklist, and a practice plan) that you can print or keep open while you work. This package contains written lessons and worksheets only, no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes. Everything is designed to be read, worked through, and kept as a reference you return to. The datasets in the lessons are small illustrative examples for practice, not claims about any real business or population. The course makes no promise of jobs, income, or certification; it teaches data science skills, and your results will depend on the practice you put in. Read at your own pace, repeat lessons as needed, and keep your practice files: they are the start of your data portfolio.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What Data Science Is
lessons.text:
This lesson defines data science in plain terms and shows you how a data project moves from a vague worry to a clear answer. By the end you will be able to explain what data science is, describe the five steps of a data project, tell the four types of data apart on sight, and write a good question that data can actually answer. Everything in this course, cleaning, summarizing, charting, predicting, presenting, sits on top of these foundations, so take the time to get comfortable here.

Data science is the practice of turning raw records into answers that help someone make a decision. Raw records are facts captured in the course of activity: each harvest weighed, each book borrowed, each order placed. A data scientist takes those records and does five things. First, they clarify the question: "How much should we plant next month?" is answerable, while "Are we doing well?" is too vague to work with. Second, they gather the relevant data and check that it is trustworthy. Third, they clean it, because real data is messy. Fourth, they analyze it: count, group, compare, and summarize to find patterns. Fifth, they present the finding clearly, often with a chart, plus a recommendation. Notice what is not on the list: guessing, cherry-picking one favorable number, or dressing up a weak finding with a fancy chart. Credibility in data work comes from honest handling of the data, and Lessons 3 through 5 teach the techniques that keep you honest.

Here is a small sample dataset you will see referenced through the course: a community garden's weekly harvest log. Each row is one week:

Week ending | Kilograms harvested | Beds in use | Volunteers | Weather | Notes
2026-10-03 | 42 | 8 | 6 | sunny | "Extra tomatoes"
2026-10-10 | 31 | 8 | 4 | rainy | "Two beds flooded"
2026-10-17 | 38 | 9 | 5 | cloudy | ""
2026-10-24 | 47 | 9 | 7 | sunny | "New bed planted"
2026-10-31 | 28 | 9 | 3 | rainy | "Several volunteers away"

Kilograms harvested and volunteers are numbers. Beds in use is also a number, a count. Weather is a category. The week-ending date is date data. The notes column is free text. Already you can see real questions this answers: which weather brings bigger harvests, what a typical week looks like, whether volunteer numbers explain the slow weeks. A data scientist would start by asking the garden coordinator which decision the answer feeds, for example how many beds to plant next season, and only then compute. That question-first habit is the single most valuable thing this lesson teaches.

Data comes in four types, and the type decides what you are allowed to do with it. Numerical data is numbers where arithmetic makes sense: kilograms, temperatures, ages, counts. You can add and average these. Categorical data is labels that group things: weather, crop names, bed numbers used as labels, volunteer roles. You can count how many fall in each category, but averaging "sunny" and "rainy" is meaningless. Text data is free-form writing: notes, comments, descriptions. You can search it and count words, but it needs processing before it behaves like the other types. Date and time data marks when things happened: harvest dates, loan dates. You can sort by it, group by month or week, and measure gaps between events. A single dataset usually mixes all four: a garden record has a date, a weather label, a harvest weight, and a note.

Two beginner mistakes start in this lesson. First, treating categories like numbers: assigning 1 to sunny and 2 to rainy and then averaging the weather to 1.4 is nonsense, even though a spreadsheet will happily compute it. Always ask: does arithmetic mean anything here? If not, count instead of averaging. Second, jumping to analysis before defining the question. It is tempting to open a dataset and start calculating everything, but analysis without a question produces trivia. Write the question in one sentence first, "Do rainy weeks harvest less?" and let it choose which numbers you compute. A good question names the thing you want to compare and the decision it will inform. "Do rainy weeks harvest less, so we know whether to add covered beds?" is a question with a decision attached, and that is the standard to aim for.

Practice: Invent a small dataset of your own with ten rows about something you can observe this week: your daily cups of water, minutes spent on chores, pages read, or items in your shopping cart. Include at least one numerical column, one categorical column, and a date column. Then write three one-sentence questions your dataset could answer and three it could not: water data cannot tell you about sleep, for example. Finally, label each column in the garden dataset above with its data type, and explain in one sentence why "beds in use" is numerical while "weather" is categorical, even though both can be written as short values in a table.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Working with Data Tables
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to work confidently with data tables: the rows and columns that hold almost all data you will meet. By the end you will read a table correctly, sort and filter it, add calculated columns, and use the core spreadsheet functions for totals, averages, and counts. Tables are the basic unit of data work, and fluency here makes every later lesson faster.

Start with the shape of a table. A table has one header row with short, clear column names, such as week ending, kilograms, beds, volunteers, and weather, and one row per record below it. Each row is one observation: one week, one order, one person. Each column is one measurement or label, the same kind of thing all the way down. A cell is where one row meets one column: a single value. Keep your table tidy: no blank rows in the middle, no merged cells, no titles or notes sitting inside the data area, and one kind of value per column. If a column mixes numbers and text, such as "42" in some cells and "about forty" in others, formulas will fail or silently skip cells. Put titles and notes above the table or on a separate sheet, and keep the data area clean. This discipline feels fussy until the day a careless sort scrambles your data, and sorting is the first skill.

Sorting rearranges rows so a column runs in order. Sort the garden data by kilograms harvested, largest to smallest, and the best and worst weeks jump out at once. The golden rule of sorting is to select all columns before sorting, or to use your program's sort-with-headers feature, so each row stays intact. Sorting one column alone while the others stay put silently destroys your data: the harvest numbers move but the dates do not, and every row becomes a lie. This is the most damaging beginner error in spreadsheet work, and the habit of selecting the whole table first prevents it. Sorting is also a quick way to inspect data: sort a column from smallest to largest and scan the extremes for odd values, such as a negative harvest or a date in the wrong year.

Filtering lets you look at a slice without deleting anything. Turn on filters for your header row, then use the dropdown on the weather column to show only rainy weeks: the spreadsheet hides the other rows and functions such as SUBTOTAL adjust to show only the visible rows. Filtering answers questions like "what is our average harvest on sunny weeks?" in seconds: filter to sunny, then average the kilograms column. A filter never changes the underlying data, it only changes the view, so it is always safe to experiment. Combine filters across columns to narrow further: rainy weeks with fewer than five volunteers. When you are done, clear the filter to bring everything back. Filtering is also how you spot problems: filter a column for blanks and you see at once how many values are missing, a question Lesson 3 takes up in full.

Calculated columns turn raw columns into answers. A formula in a spreadsheet starts with an equals sign and can reference cells: =B2*2 computes double the value in B2, and =B2/C2 divides one column by another. Add a column called kilograms per bed, with the formula =B2/C2 copied down, and you can compare weeks fairly even when the number of beds changed. The functions you will use constantly are SUM for a total, AVERAGE for a mean, COUNT for how many numbers there are, COUNTA for how many non-empty cells there are, and MIN and MAX for the smallest and largest values. So =AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives the average weekly harvest, and =MAX(B2:B6) finds the best week. IF makes decisions: =IF(B2>40,"Big week","Regular week") labels each week, and you can build on that with a second IF for more bands. When you copy a formula down a column, references shift relatively, B2 becomes B3, which is usually what you want. Put a dollar sign before the letter or number to lock a reference, like $B$2, when it must not move, for example a target value stored in one cell that every row's formula uses.

Two more mistakes to engrave in memory. First, numbers stored as text: values that look like numbers but were pasted as text will not sort or average correctly, and your totals will silently undercount. The symptom is SUM returning zero or AVERAGE ignoring cells; the fix is to convert the column to numbers, which most programs offer as a convert-to-number command or by multiplying by one in a helper column. Second, dividing by zero or by an empty cell: a week with zero beds in use cannot give kilograms per bed, and the formula will show an error. That error is honest feedback, not a bug to hide: it tells you the row needs attention, and Lesson 3 teaches you how to handle it.

Practice: Rebuild the five-week garden dataset from Lesson 1 in a spreadsheet program. Add a sixth and seventh week of your own invention. Then do these four steps: sort by kilograms harvested, largest first, and confirm whole rows moved together; filter to rainy weeks and compute their average kilograms with AVERAGE; add a column with =IF(B2>40,"Big week","Regular week") and copy it down; add a column for kilograms per bed with =B2/C2 and copy it down. At the bottom, compute total kilograms with SUM, average kilograms with AVERAGE, and the best week with MAX. Save this file: you will extend it in Lessons 3, 4, and 5.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Cleaning Messy Data
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the least glamorous and most important data skill: cleaning messy data. By the end you will run a repeatable cleaning routine, checking for missing values, fixing inconsistent formats, removing duplicates, and validating your work, on any dataset. Real-world data is never as tidy as textbook examples: entries are misspelled, dates arrive in three formats, half the rows are missing something. People who work with data commonly spend most of a project's time cleaning, because every analysis built on dirty data is wrong in ways that look convincing.

Start with a cleaning mindset: never edit the raw data. Make a copy or work on a duplicate sheet, and keep a short log of what you changed: "removed 2 duplicate rows", "filled 1 missing harvest with the weekly average". This log is your proof that the final numbers are honest, and it lets you or anyone else redo the work. Then inspect before you fix: sort each column, scan for odd values, and use filters to spot blanks. A quick scan of a garden log might reveal "sunny", "Sunny", "SUNNY", and "suny" all meaning the same weather, plus two identical weeks and a volunteer column mixing "6" with "six". Each of these is a different defect with a different fix, and the inspection step is what tells you which defects you actually have, instead of guessing.

Missing values are the most common defect, and the fix depends on why the value is missing. A blank harvest on a week the garden was closed for a holiday is not a zero: it is not applicable, and the honest treatment is to leave it blank so averages skip it, as Lesson 2 noted. A blank in a survey response where someone skipped the question is genuinely unknown. Your options are: leave it blank, which is best when few are missing and the analysis tolerates it; fill it with a sensible substitute like the column's average or median, which is acceptable when you disclose it in your log; or drop the row, which is only right when the row is unusable otherwise. What you must never do is silently treat blanks as zeros without thinking: zeros drag averages down and can flip a conclusion. As a rule, if more than a small share of a column is missing, the problem is in how the data was collected, and you should say so in your findings rather than patch over it.

Inconsistent formats are the next defect. Standardize text with find-and-replace and consistent capitalization: pick "sunny" and convert every variant to it. Standardize dates to one format, year-month-day, which also sorts correctly as text. Standardize numbers: strip units and commas into plain numbers in one column, keeping the original if you like. Remove exact duplicates, most spreadsheet programs have a remove-duplicates command, but check first that the rows are truly identical and not two legitimate identical-looking records: two separate weeks with the same harvest are real, while a pasted-twice import is not. Finally, validate: recompute your row counts before and after, so you removed exactly the duplicates and nothing else; spot-check ten random rows against the raw copy; and re-run your key formulas. If the totals changed in a way you cannot explain from your log, something went wrong, so go back and find it before analyzing further.

Impossible values deserve their own check. A harvest of negative kilograms, a week with 400 volunteers when the garden has never had more than ten, or a date in the wrong year are all signals that something was typed wrong. Do not just delete them: check the raw source first, such as the paper log the numbers came from, and fix the value if the source shows the truth. If the source cannot be checked, remove the row and log it, saying why. The same care applies to outliers, values that are unusual but possible. A 90-kilogram week after a new bed opened might be real, while a 900-kilogram week is almost certainly a typing error, an extra zero. Investigate outliers instead of deleting them on sight, because a real outlier often carries the most interesting story in the data.

Two mistakes define this lesson. First, cleaning without a log: a month later you will not remember whether you deleted those rows because they were duplicates or because they were inconvenient, and neither will anyone checking your work. Second, fixing data by deleting rows that contradict the story you want. Removing a terrible harvest week because it spoils the trend is not cleaning, it is fabrication. The rule is simple: you may only remove or change values for documented data-quality reasons, a duplicate, an impossible value, an obvious typo, never because you dislike the result. When in doubt, keep the row and note the oddity in your findings.

Practice: Take your garden spreadsheet from Lesson 2 and deliberately mess up a copy: misspell one weather entry, enter one date in a different format, duplicate one row, delete one harvest value, and add a stray space to a weather entry. Then clean the copy using this lesson's routine: inspect, log each fix, standardize, dedupe, and validate, and write a five-line cleaning log. Confirm your totals match the original file afterward. Keep the log format; the checklist in your materials packet is built from exactly this routine, and you will use it again in the final project.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Describing Data with Summaries
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches descriptive summaries: the handful of numbers that describe a dataset in plain terms. By the end you will compute and interpret the mean, median, and mode, three kinds of average, measure spread with range and standard deviation, and know which summary fits which situation. These summaries are the vocabulary of data work: nearly every report, dashboard, and conversation about data uses them, and choosing the wrong one is one of the easiest ways to mislead, even by accident.

Start with the three averages, because each answers a slightly different question. The mean is what most people mean by average: add everything up and divide by the count. The garden's harvests over five weeks, 42, 31, 38, 47, and 28 kilograms, sum to 186, divided by 5 gives a mean of 37.2. The median is the middle value when the numbers are lined up in order: 28, 31, 38, 42, 47, so the median is 38. The mode is the most frequent value: with these five distinct numbers there is no mode, but in a season of weather data the mode might be sunny. The crucial difference is that the mean is pulled by extremes while the median is not. Add one bumper week of 120 kilograms and the mean jumps to about 51 while the median barely moves. That is why people who work with data report the median for things with occasional huge values, such as incomes, house prices, and order sizes, and the mean when values are well-behaved. When someone quotes an average without saying which one, ask; the choice can completely change the story.

Spread tells you how much the numbers vary, and a summary without spread is half a story. "Average 37 kilograms a week" could mean every week harvests 35 to 39, or it could mean alternating 20 and 55: same average, wildly different garden. The range is the simplest measure: the largest value minus the smallest, here 47 minus 28, which is 19. The standard deviation is the more useful one: roughly, the typical distance of a week's harvest from the mean. A small standard deviation means consistent weeks; a large one means volatile weeks. You do not need to compute it by hand: every spreadsheet program has a STDEV function, but you need the intuition. Two gardens can share an average while one is predictable and the other is a roller coaster, and the standard deviation is the number that reveals which is which. Percentiles add one more useful lens: the 90th percentile is the value that 90 percent of weeks fall below, handy for questions like "how big a week should we be ready for?"

Choosing the right summary is a small decision tree. Describing a typical value? Use the median if outliers exist, the mean otherwise, and the mode for categories. Describing consistency? Use range for a quick sense and standard deviation for the real picture. Comparing two groups, sunny versus rainy weeks, this month versus last? Compute the same summary for each group side by side and look at the gap. And always sanity-check summaries against the raw data: if the median says 38 but a glance at the column shows mostly 20s, something is off, perhaps a filter is still on, or text-numbers are being ignored. Summaries compress reality; the raw column is the ground truth you check against. Counts deserve the same care: a count of weeks is simple, but a count of distinct values, such as how many different crops were harvested, answers a different question from a count of rows, so name exactly what you counted.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, quoting the mean for skewed data without mentioning it: saying "average harvest is 51 kilograms" when one bumper week did most of the work misleads whoever plans planting from that number. Report the median alongside it, or at least note the outlier. Second, confusing a difference with a cause, which starts here because summaries invite it: rainy weeks averaging fewer kilograms does not prove rain causes low harvests. Perhaps rainy weeks in your data were also the weeks few volunteers showed up, remember the week of October 31, with only three volunteers. A difference between groups is a clue that deserves investigation, not a conclusion. Write "rainy weeks averaged fewer kilograms in this data", a true statement, rather than "rain causes low harvests", a claim the data alone cannot support. That careful wording is the mark of honest data work.

Practice: Extend your garden spreadsheet to fourteen weeks, inventing seven more rows and keeping the same columns. Compute the mean, median, and mode of kilograms harvested, plus the range and standard deviation using STDEV. Then split the weeks into sunny versus not sunny and compute the mean harvest for each group. Write three honest sentences summarizing what you found, using "in this data" language, not causal claims. Finally, add one extreme week, a 120-kilogram bumper harvest, and watch what happens to the mean versus the median. Write one sentence explaining which summary you would report to the garden coordinator and why.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Charts That Tell the Truth
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to turn numbers into pictures that tell the truth quickly. By the end you will choose the right chart for each question, build clean honest charts in a spreadsheet program, and spot the tricks that make charts misleading, including in other people's work. A good chart lets a busy person grasp in five seconds what a table of numbers takes five minutes to reveal. A bad chart does the opposite, and sometimes it misleads without the reader noticing.

Every chart answers one of a few question types, and the question picks the chart. Comparing categories? Use a bar chart: kilograms harvested per crop, volunteers per week. Showing change over time? Use a line chart: weekly harvest across the season, where the eye naturally follows the trend. Showing parts of a whole? Use a pie chart only for a few slices, two to five, such as the share of harvest by crop, or use a stacked bar when there are more. Showing the relationship between two numbers? Use a scatter plot: each week is a dot with volunteers on one axis and kilograms on the other, revealing whether more volunteers go with bigger harvests. Showing a distribution? Use a histogram: how many weeks fell into each harvest band. When in doubt, a bar chart is the safest default: it is the hardest chart to misread. Match the chart to the question before touching any formatting, because a beautiful wrong chart is still wrong.

Honest charts follow a short set of principles. Start bar charts at zero: a bar's length encodes its value, so cutting the axis at 30 makes a 35-to-40 difference look enormous when it is actually small. Label everything: a chart title stating the finding, axis labels with units, such as "Kilograms harvested", and data labels on key points. Keep it simple: one message per chart, no 3D effects, no decorative images, no rainbow of fifteen colors when two will do. Use color to highlight, not decorate: gray for the background data and one strong color for the point you want noticed. Keep the data visible: a chart should never hide the numbers behind so much styling that the reader cannot check your work. These rules are not about taste; each one prevents a specific misunderstanding, and together they make your charts trustworthy by construction.

Learn to spot misleading charts, because you will meet them in reports, news, and sales pitches. The truncated axis is the classic: bars or lines that start at a non-zero value to exaggerate a tiny change. Always check where the axis begins. The cherry-picked timeframe: a line chart starting right after a dip to show amazing growth. Ask what the longer history looks like. The area trick: using pictures, such as baskets or people icons, sized by height when the eye reads area, doubling the visual exaggeration. If the value doubles, the icon's area quadruples. The missing context: "harvest up by half" with no mention that last month was the worst on record. The dual-axis trap: two lines on different scales engineered to look correlated. Your defense is one habit: before reacting to any chart, read the axes, the labels, and the source note. Ten seconds of skepticism defeats most chart tricks, and it is a habit worth building now.

The workflow for building a chart is: question first, then the right data slice, then the right chart type, then honest formatting, then a one-sentence takeaway written beneath it. For example, take the question "are weekends stronger than weekdays?" and translate it to the garden: "do sunny weeks harvest more than rainy weeks?" Slice the data into average harvest grouped by weather. Chart it as a bar chart of the averages, axis starting at zero, titled "Average weekly harvest by weather". Takeaway: "In this data, sunny weeks averaged the highest harvest and rainy weeks the lowest." Notice the takeaway describes the data without claiming why. Build every chart this way and your visuals will be trustworthy by construction. Also keep the underlying table near the chart, or available on request, so a reader who doubts the picture can check the numbers it came from.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, charting raw unsorted tables: a line chart of dates in random order produces spaghetti that hides the trend, so sort by date first, always. Second, pie charts with too many slices: a twelve-slice pie is unreadable. If you have many categories, use a bar chart sorted largest to smallest, or group the small ones into "Other". If your reader has to work to decode the chart, the chart has failed. A third, quieter mistake is charting a summary without saying what it is: a bar labeled "average" with no note of whether it is a mean or a median leaves the reader guessing, so label the summary type in the title or in a note beneath the chart.

Practice: In your garden spreadsheet, build three charts from your fourteen-week dataset: a line chart of weekly harvest over time, sorted by date, with labeled axes; a bar chart comparing average kilograms on sunny versus rainy versus cloudy weeks, axis starting at zero; and a pie chart of weeks by weather type, keeping it to the weather categories you have. Under each chart write a one-sentence honest takeaway. Then deliberately make a misleading version of the bar chart by starting the axis just below your smallest value, and compare the two side by side. Notice how different the story feels, and write one sentence about why the honest version is the one you would show the garden coordinator.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: An Introduction to Prediction
lessons.text:
This lesson introduces prediction in plain terms: using patterns in past data to make a careful forecast about what might happen next. By the end you will understand what a prediction is and is not, build a simple forecast from a trend, test it by holding back recent data, and know the limits that keep predictions honest. Prediction is the part of data science that sounds most magical, so this lesson is deliberately careful: a forecast is a reasoned guess with stated assumptions, not a promise.

A prediction answers a question like "how much will we harvest next week?" or "how many books will be borrowed next month?" It works by finding a pattern in past data and extending it forward. The simplest pattern is a trend: harvests rising by a few kilograms each week suggest next week will be a little higher again. A second pattern is a group average: sunny weeks in your data averaged 44 kilograms, so a sunny week ahead might harvest around that amount. A third pattern is a relationship between two columns: weeks with more volunteers tended to harvest more, so knowing next week's volunteer count gives a clue about its harvest. None of these patterns is a law of nature. They are summaries of what happened before, and they only help if the future resembles the past. That condition is the heart of honest prediction.

Build a simple trend forecast by hand so you can see every step. Take the garden's last six weekly harvests in order: 28, 31, 38, 35, 42, 47 kilograms. The numbers rise overall, with a small dip in the middle. A plain way to forecast is to average the last three weeks, 35, 42, and 47, which gives about 41 kilograms, and to use that as the forecast for next week. A second way is to look at the change from week to week: the jumps are 3, 7, minus 3, 7, and 5, averaging about 4 kilograms a week, so adding 4 to the latest week gives about 51. Those two reasonable methods give different answers, 41 and 51, and that disagreement is informative: it tells you the forecast is uncertain and that the method matters. Report a forecast as a range, "around 41 to 51 kilograms", rather than a single false-precision number. A range admits what you do not know, and a reader who plans planting from it can plan for both ends.

Testing a prediction is what separates guessing from data science. The method is simple and powerful: hold back the most recent data, build your forecast from the earlier data only, and then compare the forecast with the weeks you held back. Suppose you forecast week 14 from weeks 1 through 13 and predicted 40 kilograms, but the actual harvest was 33. The error is 7 kilograms, and the direction matters: you overestimated. Repeat this for several weeks, one at a time, and average the errors to get a sense of how far off your method usually is. If the average error is small compared with the harvests themselves, the method is useful. If the errors are large, or if the method keeps overestimating in rainy weeks and underestimating in sunny weeks, the pattern is telling you something is missing, perhaps weather, and you should add it to the forecast. Never test a prediction on the same data you used to build it: that is like setting an exam from questions you already memorized, and it will flatter the method.

Prediction also has limits you must respect. First, the future may not resemble the past: a new pest, a broken water pipe, or a change in opening hours can break every pattern at once, and no method built on old data can see that coming. Say so in your findings. Second, predictions about people carry extra care: a forecast that a certain group will behave a certain way can become a self-fulfilling label, so report patterns about groups with caution and never present a group average as a fact about one person. Third, a prediction is not a cause: finding that volunteer numbers and harvests rise together does not prove that adding volunteers causes bigger harvests. Perhaps good weather brings both more volunteers and better growth. Use the language of association, "weeks with more volunteers tended to harvest more", and let a proper test, such as trying extra volunteers for a few weeks and comparing, decide the cause.

Two mistakes dominate this lesson. First, false precision: reporting "47.382 kilograms" when your method is only accurate to within several kilograms. Round the forecast to the precision your data supports, and give a range. Second, forecasting far ahead: a one-week forecast built on recent weeks is reasonable, while a forecast for a year ahead built on the same data is mostly imagination. The further ahead you forecast, the wider the range should be, and the more clearly you should state the assumptions it rests on.

Practice: Using your fourteen-week garden data, build two forecasts for week 15: the average of the last three weeks, and the latest week plus the average weekly change over the last five weeks. Write both forecasts as a range and note which method you trust more and why. Then test your method properly: use weeks 1 through 10 to forecast week 11, compare with the actual week 11 value, and write down the error. Repeat for weeks 12, 13, and 14, each time using only the data before the week you forecast. Compute the average error across the four tests and write one paragraph: is your method good enough to plan planting from, and what would make it better?

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Presenting Your Findings
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to present findings so other people can understand them and act on them. By the end you will structure a short findings report, write a clear one-page summary, choose a few good charts, and explain limits honestly. Analysis that nobody understands is wasted work: the presentation is where data science earns its keep, and a clear, honest report beats a clever analysis that nobody can follow.

A findings report has a simple structure that works for almost any project. Start with the question, in one sentence, and the decision it will inform. Then describe the data: where it came from, how many rows it has, what time period it covers, and what cleaning you did, in a few lines. Then give the findings, each as a short statement with its evidence: a number, a comparison, or a chart. Then give the recommendation: what should happen next, and what would prove the recommendation wrong. End with limits: what the data cannot tell you, and what extra data would help. That structure, question, data, findings, recommendation, limits, fits on two pages for a small project and scales to longer reports. A reader who only reads the first page should still walk away with the question, the main finding, and the recommendation.

The one-page summary is the most important page you will write. It opens with the question and the answer in plain language: "Sunny weeks harvest more than rainy weeks in this data, by about 12 kilograms a week on average." It follows with two or three supporting numbers, each with its context: the sunny average, the rainy average, and the number of weeks behind each. It includes one chart, the best one, with a title that states the finding. It closes with the recommendation and the limit: "Consider covered beds for rainy weeks, and track the next eight weeks to check whether the pattern holds." Notice what the summary does not do: it does not list every calculation, it does not use jargon without explaining it, and it does not hide uncertainty. If a term must appear, define it in the sentence where it appears: "the median, the middle value when weeks are lined up in order, was 38 kilograms."

Choosing charts for a presentation follows the same rules as Lesson 5, with one addition: fewer is better. A report with one excellent chart is more persuasive than a report with eight mediocre ones. Pick the chart that answers the main question, and add a second only if it answers a different question the reader needs. Every chart gets a title that states the finding, not just the topic: "Sunny weeks averaged the highest harvest" is a title, while "Harvest by weather" is only a label. Put the takeaway in words beneath the chart, so a reader who skims still gets the point. Keep the underlying table available, on a second page or in an appendix, so a skeptical reader can check the numbers.
