A resume coach belongs where job seekers gather; a meal-planning service belongs where busy parents scroll. One platform done well beats three done badly; you can expand after 90 days. Set up a simple profile: a clear photo or logo, one line saying who you help and how ('Weekly dinner plans for busy parents'), and one link to your offer or trial.

Run four content pillars in rotation so you never stare at a blank screen. 1) Teach: one useful tip from your expertise ('The 3-ingredient rule for 20-minute dinners'). 2) Prove: show your work and results — before/after, a customer story (with permission), your process on camera or in screenshots. 3) Relate: your story and opinions — why you started, a mistake you made, what you believe about your niche. 4) Invite: the offer — trials, customer stories (shared with permission), limited spots, direct calls to message you. The ratio: roughly 4 teach/prove/relate posts for every 1 invite post. Nobody follows an account that only sells; everybody respects one that teaches generously and sells occasionally.

The weekly routine (about 4 hours total). Monday: write 5 posts in one 60-minute batch (one per pillar plus one extra teach). Tuesday–Saturday: publish one daily and spend 20 minutes engaging — answer every comment, comment thoughtfully on 5 accounts in your niche, reply to every direct message. Sunday: 30-minute review — which post got the most saves, shares, or replies? Do more of that next week; drop what flopped twice. Batching beats daily inspiration, and engagement beats posting into the void — platforms reward conversations, so be conversational.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, perfectionism: spending two hours on one post's design while posting twice a month. Frequency with honest, useful content beats rare polished content — your 50th post will be better than your 5th because you made the first 49. Second, vanity metrics: chasing follower counts while ignoring the only metrics that matter at this stage — profile visits, direct messages, and trial signups. A hundred followers with five customers beats ten thousand followers with zero; track business outcomes weekly.

Make engagement do the heavy lifting with a simple daily outreach habit alongside posting. Each day, send five genuine direct messages to people who engaged with your niche: answer a question they asked publicly, share a tip relevant to their post, or invite them to your free trial when it truly fits. This is not spam — it is being helpful in public and continuing the conversation in private, and it is how small accounts grow without ad spend. Also repurpose everything: one teaching post becomes a short video script, three tips become one carousel, and your five best posts become a pinned 'start here' collection. Repurposing multiplies each hour of writing into a week of presence. And protect the routine: schedule your content batch like an appointment, because 'post when inspired' quietly becomes 'never post.' Thirty focused minutes a day for ninety days will teach you more about your market than any course about social media ever could.

                Practice: Choose your one platform and rewrite your profile using the formula. Write next week's five posts now (one per pillar + one teach), each under 150 words with one clear takeaway. Publish the first today, then do 20 minutes of genuine engagement. Set up a simple tracker: date, post topic, pillar, saves/shares/replies, profile visits, DMs, trial signups — review it every Sunday for four weeks and write one line on what to change.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Money Basics — Costs, Break-Even, and Tracking
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you the money basics every founder needs: knowing your costs, calculating your break-even point, and tracking your numbers on one page. You do not need accounting software or a finance background — you need a clear-eyed list of what goes out, what comes in, and the exact number of sales that makes the business sustain itself. Founders who track money monthly make calm decisions; founders who avoid the numbers make anxious ones.

Start by listing all costs in two buckets. Fixed costs happen every month whether you sell or not: tool subscriptions, website hosting, insurance, a phone plan used for business. Variable costs happen per sale: materials, packaging, shipping, payment processing fees (roughly 3% per transaction), and any per-customer labor. Worked example: Priya sells handmade soap gift sets online. Fixed: $29/month website + $15/month email tool = $44. Variable per set: $6 materials + $3 packaging + $5 shipping + 3% fees on a $32 price (~$1) = $15. Her contribution per sale (price minus variable cost) is $32 − $15 = $17. That $17 is the number that matters — it is what each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and then toward earnings.

Now the break-even point: fixed costs ÷ contribution per sale. Priya: $44 ÷ $17 = 2.6, so 3 sets per month covers all costs; sale #4 onward contributes to earnings. This single calculation answers the most important question in early business: 'How many do I need to sell to not lose money?' Compute yours now with real numbers — not hopeful ones. Then set two targets above it: your 'sustain' target (covers costs + pays you a modest amount for your time) and your 'grow' target (sustain + reinvestment). Write all three numbers on one line and pin it where you work.

Track with a one-page monthly sheet — no fancy tools needed. Columns: date, description, money in, money out, running balance. Once a month (pick a fixed date, like the 1st), fill in five summary numbers: total revenue, total costs, net (revenue − costs), units sold, and cash in the business account. Compare against your three targets. The discipline is the product: 20 minutes a month of honest numbers beats any dashboard you never open. Keep business money in a separate account or at least a separate ledger from personal spending — mixing them is the #1 source of 'where did the money go?' panic.

Two money mistakes beginners make. First, forgetting their own time: pricing as if your labor is free makes the business look profitable while you earn nothing per hour. Always include a time cost in your math, even roughly. Second, confusing revenue with profit: 'I made $1,000 this month!' while costs were $900 is a $100 month, not a $1,000 month. Celebrate revenue, but decide based on net. And a standing rule from this course: never spend money you cannot afford to lose on unproven ideas — validate with conversations and manual MVPs first, spend on tools and ads only after paying customers exist.

Build a small buffer before you need it. Once revenue covers costs, set aside a fixed slice of each month's net — even ten percent — into a separate business savings spot for slow months, refunds, or surprise expenses. Beginners often spend every dollar of a good month and then panic in a quiet one; a buffer turns volatility from a crisis into an inconvenience. Also decide your pay rule in advance: for example, you pay yourself a fixed modest amount monthly once the business sustains it, rather than draining whatever is left. A business that cannot pay you and still grow is sending you a message about its pricing or costs — listen to it via the numbers, not via stress. Revisit this lesson quarterly: update your fixed costs, recompute break-even, and confirm your three targets still match reality. Fifteen minutes with honest numbers beats hours of worrying without them.

                Practice: Build your one-page monthly tracker (on paper or a spreadsheet) with the five columns. Fill in last month's real numbers, even if they are zeros. Calculate your fixed costs, variable cost per unit, contribution per sale, and break-even units. Write your three targets (break-even / sustain / grow) and schedule a recurring monthly 20-minute 'money date' with yourself. Bring this sheet to every future pricing and spending decision.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Launch Checklist + Your 90-Day Action Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson gets you launched: a concrete pre-launch checklist that catches the things beginners forget, and a 90-day action plan that turns this course into a working business. Launch does not mean a big announcement — it means real customers can find you, pay you, and receive value, starting this week. Everything before this lesson was preparation; this lesson is the starting gun.

The launch checklist — verify each item honestly before you announce. Offer: one clear offer with a price, written in one sentence a stranger understands. Payment: a working way to accept money, tested with a small transaction. Delivery: the MVP from Lesson 3 is built and you have delivered it at least once (even free). Proof: three interview notes or early customer reactions that confirm the pain is real. Presence: your one social platform set up per Lesson 6, with five posts scheduled. Pipeline: your list of 100 prospects started and first 10 outreach messages ready. Numbers: your break-even and targets from Lesson 7 written down. Legal basics: check your local rules for business registration, taxes, and any permits your offer needs — this course cannot give legal advice, so verify locally. If any item is missing, that missing item is your task for this week, not a reason to delay everything else.

Your 90-day action plan. Days 1–30 (Prove): finish validation interviews, build the MVP, set the price, win customers 1–10 by hand. Weekly scoreboard: interviews done, outreach sent, customers won, revenue. Days 31–60 (Stabilize): deliver excellently to the first ten, collect their feedback and referrals, start the social media routine, raise the price once using the ladder method if demand is strong. Weekly scoreboard adds: referrals received, posts published, repeat buyers. Days 61–90 (Systematize): document your delivery process so it takes less of your time, productize the most repeatable part (template, guide, or package), set the next 90-day targets. End-of-quarter review: revenue vs. targets, what worked, what to stop, one big bet for next quarter. The full template is in the materials section — print it and fill it in today.

Two launch mistakes to avoid. First, the endless polish loop: 'I'll launch when the website is perfect / the logo is done / I feel ready.' Launch is a date on the calendar, not a feeling — pick a date within 14 days and announce it to someone who will hold you to it. Second, launching to everyone instead of to your list: a launch post to strangers converts poorly; personal messages to your 100 prospects convert well. Launch quietly to warm contacts first, gather proof, then go wider.

A final honest note, because this course teaches process, not promises: doing everything here does not guarantee success — markets are uncertain and some good ideas still fail. What it does guarantee is that you will fail fast and cheap if the idea is wrong (Lessons 1–3), price sanely (Lesson 4), learn directly from customers (Lesson 5), build an audience asset (Lesson 6), know your numbers (Lesson 7), and execute in focused 90-day cycles (this lesson). That is the entire game: run the cycle, keep what works, cut what does not, repeat. Most people never finish one cycle. Finish yours.

Practice: Run the launch checklist now and mark each item done or missing with a date to fix it. Pick your launch date (within 14 days) and tell one person. Fill in the 90-day action plan template from the materials with your actual numbers and dates. Send your first 10 outreach messages this week. Your business starts the day a stranger pays you — make that day soon.

courses.title: Conversational French
courses.tagline: Speak French from day one: pronunciation, core grammar, and real everyday dialogues.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational French is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday French from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. The first half builds your foundation — pronunciation, greetings, etre and avoir, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep moving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational French is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday French from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. The first half builds your foundation — pronunciation, greetings, etre and avoir, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep moving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will be able to: pronounce French words clearly using the main vowel sounds, nasal vowels, and consonant rules; greet people, introduce yourself, and handle survival phrases when you do not understand; use etre and avoir correctly and build sentences in the present tense with regular and common irregular verbs; count to one hundred and beyond, tell the time, and use days, months, and dates; ask and answer questions about directions, prices, and everyday topics; talk about things you did using the passe compose; make plans for the future and hold a full restaurant or travel conversation; and run a simple daily practice routine that keeps your speaking improving.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read one lesson at a time, out loud wherever you see French — saying the words with your mouth, not just your eyes, is what builds speaking skill. Each lesson opens with what it teaches, explains the concept with concrete examples, includes full example dialogues with English translations, warns you about common beginner mistakes, and ends with a clearly labeled Practice exercise. Do the practice before moving on, even if it feels easy; the lessons build on each other, and Lesson 3's verbs depend on Lesson 1's sounds. Aim for one lesson per day, and re-read the previous lesson's dialogues the next morning as a warm-up. There are no grades and no timers — steady repetition beats cramming.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites. This course starts from zero and assumes you have never studied French before. Everything — even how to make each vowel sound — is explained from scratch. If you already know a little French, Lesson 1's pronunciation rules are still worth reading, because correcting a bad accent habit early saves months later. You do not need any textbook, app, or prior grammar knowledge; a notebook for writing out the practice exercises is the only thing that will help.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes — it is a text/workbook course, and everything you need is on the page: explanations, example sentences, translated dialogues, and practice exercises. The materials section includes a vocabulary cheat sheet and a 30-day practice plan template you can print and reuse. Work through the lessons in order, do the exercises in writing and out loud, and you will finish with usable, spoken French for real everyday situations.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronunciation — French Vowels, Nasal Sounds, and Silent Letters
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to pronounce French clearly from the start. French spelling looks intimidating, but the sounds follow patterns you can learn in one sitting. Your goal in this lesson is not a perfect accent — it is clarity. If your vowels are clean and you respect the nasal sounds and silent letters, French speakers will understand you even while you are still learning words.

Start with the pure vowels, which are steadier than English vowels. A sounds like 'ah' in father: papa (pah-PAH, dad). E has several sounds: the closed E sounds like 'ay' in day — café (kah-FAY, coffee); the open E sounds like 'eh' in bed — lait (leh, milk); and the unstressed E in the middle of words is often a soft 'uh' or dropped entirely — fromage (froh-MAHZH, cheese). I sounds like 'ee' in see: merci (mehr-SEE, thank you). O sounds like 'oh' in go: bonjour (bohn-ZHOOR, hello). U is the famous hard one: round your lips as if to say 'oo' but say 'ee' instead — tu (tew, you), rue (rew, street). The letter combination OU is the regular 'oo' sound: vous (voo, you formal), bonjour's 'jour'. Practice the pair tu (tew) versus tout (too) until your mouth feels the difference.

Now the nasal vowels — the sounds that make French sound like French. A nasal vowel is produced by letting air flow through your nose while the vowel is voiced. Do not pronounce the N or M fully; they just signal the nose. AN/EN: en (ahn) — enfant (ahn-FAHN, child), vent (vahn, wind). IN/AIN/EIN: vin (vahn — yes, it sounds like vent's cousin, thinner) — vin (wine), pain (pahn, bread). ON: on (ohn) — bon (bohn, good), maison (meh-ZOHN, house). UN: un (uhn) — brun (bruhn, brown). Train each one: hold the vowel, then let your nose join in, and stop before your tongue touches the roof of your mouth for the N. Beginners often pronounce the N like an English N — bon becomes 'bonn' — and it instantly sounds wrong, so drill this daily.

Silent letters are everywhere in French, and they are your friends once you know the rules. Final consonants are usually silent: petit is pronounced puh-TEE (the T is silent), and parlez drops its Z sound to become pahr-LAY. But C, R, F, and L are often pronounced at the end — remember 'CaReFuL': sac (sahk, bag), mer (mehr, sea), vif (veef, lively), cheval (shuh-VAHL, horse). The H is always silent in French: hôtel (oh-TEHL, hotel), homme (ohm, man). The E at the end of words is silent too: table (tahbl, table), porte (pohrt, door). Liaison is the elegant connecting rule: when a word ends in a normally silent consonant and the next word starts with a vowel, you link them — les amis is pronounced lay-ZAH-mee (the friends), nous avons becomes noo-ZAH-vohn (we have). You will hear this constantly.

French word stress is simple: it almost always falls on the LAST syllable of a phrase group, lightly and evenly. Bonjour is bohn-ZHOOR, merci is mehr-SEE, restaurant is reh-stoh-RAHN. Do not stress French words the English way — never say 'RES-tau-rant' in French. The rhythm is flatter and more even than English; think of each syllable getting roughly equal time with a gentle lift at the end.

Here is a short dialogue using only sounds from this lesson. Read it aloud slowly:

Marie: Bonjour ! Comment vous appelez-vous ? (bohn-ZHOOR koh-mahn voo zah-play VOO) — Hello! What is your name?
Pierre: Je m'appelle Pierre. Et vous ? (zhuh mah-pehl pee-YEHR ay voo) — My name is Pierre. And you?
Marie: Je m'appelle Marie. Enchantée. (zhuh mah-pehl mah-REE ahn-shahn-TAY) — My name is Marie. Delighted to meet you.
Pierre: Enchanté. Vous parlez français ? (ahn-shahn-TAY voo pahr-LAY frahn-SEH) — Delighted. Do you speak French?
Marie: Oui, un peu. (wee uhn puh) — Yes, a little.

Say the whole dialogue five times today; it is your first French conversation.

Practice: Write out these ten words, mark the nasal vowels, and say each aloud three times: enfant, bon, maison, vin, pain, comment, chanson, temps, pont. Next, pair up tu/tout, rue/roue, dessus/dessous and say each pair until the U versus OU difference is obvious. Finally, read the dialogue above aloud five times, then cover the pronunciation hints and read it again — you should be able to produce the sounds from the spelling alone.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully.

Start with greetings. Bonjour (bohn-ZHOOR) means hello or good day and works from morning until evening. Bonsoir (bohn-SWAHR) is good evening, used after about 6 PM. Salut (sah-LEW) is hi/bye among friends — never use it with a shopkeeper or official on first meeting. Au revoir (oh ruh-VWAHR) is goodbye, à bientôt (ah bee-ahn-TOH) is see you soon, and bonne journée (bohn zhoor-NAY) means have a good day — shopkeepers say it to you as you leave. For introductions: Je m'appelle... (zhuh mah-PEHL) means 'my name is'. Comment vous appelez-vous? (koh-mahn voo zah-play VOO) asks someone's name formally; Comment tu t'appelles? (koh-mahn tew tah-PEHL) is the informal version for friends and peers. Enchanté (m) or enchantée (f) means delighted to meet you.

Now the small-talk core. Comment allez-vous ? (koh-mahn tah-lay VOO) is 'how are you' formally; Comment ça va ? (koh-mahn sah vah) is the casual version everyone uses. Common answers: Très bien, merci (treh bee-ahn mehr-SEE — very well, thanks), Ça va (it is going okay), Comme ci, comme ça (so-so), Je suis fatigué (m) / fatiguée (f) (I am tired). Et vous ? (ay voo) means 'and you?' — short and essential. S'il vous plaît (seel voo pleh) is please (formal), s'il te plaît the informal; merci is thank you, merci beaucoup is thank you very much, de rien (duh ree-AHN) or je vous en prie is you're welcome. A frequent beginner mistake is answering Comment ça va? with a long life story; a short answer plus Et vous? keeps the conversation balanced and gives you twice the practice.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. Je ne comprends pas (zhuh nuh kohn-PRAHN pah) — I don't understand. Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ? (poo-vay VOO ray-pay-TAY) — Can you repeat, please? Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît (pahr-LAY plew lahn-tuh-MAHN) — Speak more slowly, please. Parlez-vous anglais ? (pahr-lay VOO ahn-GLEH) — Do you speak English? Pardon (pahr-DOHN) — excuse me / sorry. Excusez-moi (ehk-sew-zay MWAH) — excuse me (to get attention). Je suis désolé (m) / désolée (f) — I'm sorry. Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ? (kehs kuh sah vuh deer) — What does that mean? These phrases will rescue you in any French-speaking place, and people respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Watch for this social mistake: France runs on the tu/vous distinction. Use vous with strangers, shopkeepers, elders, and in any formal setting; switch to tu only when the other person does or with clear peers and friends. Using tu with a stranger is not a grammar failure — it is a social one, and it can come across as rude. When in doubt, start with vous. A second classic trap: saying 'je suis chaud' to mean 'I am hot' (temperature). With être, chaud means aroused — say j'ai chaud (zhay shoh — I have heat) instead, which you will meet properly in Lesson 3.

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with the translations:

Claire: Bonjour ! Comment vous appelez-vous ? — Hello! What is your name?
Thomas: Bonjour. Je m'appelle Thomas. Et vous ? — Hello. My name is Thomas. And you?
Claire: Je m'appelle Claire. Enchantée. — My name is Claire. Delighted to meet you.
Thomas: Enchanté, Claire. Vous êtes d'où ? — Delighted, Claire. Where are you from?
Claire: Je suis de Londres. Et vous ? — I am from London. And you?
Thomas: Je suis de Lyon. Vous parlez français ? — I am from Lyon. Do you speak French?
Claire: Un peu. Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît. — A little. Speak more slowly, please.
Thomas: Bien sûr. Comment allez-vous aujourd'hui ? — Of course. How are you today?
Claire: Très bien, merci. Et vous ? — Very well, thanks. And you?
Thomas: Très bien. Au revoir ! — Very well. Goodbye!

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, one feeling word, goodbye) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then practice the survival phrases: cover the French column, read the English, and say the French from memory until you can do all eight without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with the nasal vowels from Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Être, Avoir, and the Present Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson tackles the two most important verbs in French — être (to be) and avoir (to have) — plus the present tense, which lets you describe what you do every day. Être and avoir are the backbone of the language: they appear in nearly every sentence, and avoir doubles as the helper verb for the past tense you will meet in Lesson 6. Master their shapes now and everything later gets easier.

ÊTRE (to be) — memorize this table completely: je suis (zhuh swee — I am), tu es (tew ay — you are, informal), il/elle est (eel/ehl ay — he/she is), nous sommes (noo sohm — we are), vous êtes (voo zeht — you are, formal/plural), ils/elles sont (eel/ehl sohn — they are). Use it for identity, origin, description, profession, and location of people: Je suis américain (I am American), Elle est médecin (She is a doctor), Nous sommes à Paris (We are in Paris), Ils sont contents (They are happy). Note that French drops the article with professions — Elle est médecin, not 'elle est une médecin'.

AVOIR (to have) — equally essential: j'ai (zhay — I have), tu as (tew ah — you have), il/elle a (eel/ehl ah — he/she has), nous avons (noo zah-VOHN — we have), vous avez (voo zah-VAY — you have), ils/elles ont (eel/ehl zohn — they have). French uses avoir where English uses 'to be' for age, hunger, thirst, temperature, and need: J'ai vingt ans (I am twenty — literally 'I have twenty years'), J'ai faim (I am hungry), J'ai soif (I am thirsty), J'ai chaud (I am hot), J'ai froid (I am cold), J'ai besoin de... (I need...). This is the single most useful avoir pattern for daily life — learn j'ai faim, j'ai soif, j'ai chaud, j'ai froid as fixed phrases today.

Now the present tense of regular verbs. French verbs fall into three groups. First group (-ER, the biggest): drop -er and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Parler (to speak): je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent. Note that parle, parles, parlent all sound identical (pahr l) — spelling carries what the ear cannot, which is why context matters. Second group (-IR like finir, to finish): je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent. Third group is irregular and learned verb by verb. Practice with habiter (to live): J'habite à Paris (I live in Paris), and travailler (to work): Je travaille dans un bureau (I work in an office), Tu travailles le samedi ? (Do you work Saturdays?).

Essential irregular verbs to learn as vocabulary: ALLER (to go): je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. Je vais au marché (I go to the market). FAIRE (to do/make): je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font. Je fais du sport (I exercise). VOULOIR (to want): je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent. Je veux un café (I want a coffee). POUVOIR (to be able to): je peux, tu peux, il peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils peuvent. Je peux vous aider (I can help you). These four appear in nearly every conversation, so they repay memorization immediately.

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, translating English 'do' questions word-for-word: English 'Do you speak French?' is simply Parlez-vous français ? or Vous parlez français ? with rising intonation — French needs no helper verb. Second, forgetting that adjectives agree in gender and number: un homme content (a happy man) but une femme contente (a happy woman), des enfants contents (happy children). The -e for feminine and -s for plural are silent in speech but mandatory in writing.

Dialogue — two coworkers at lunch:

Julien: Où travailles-tu ? — Where do you work?
Sophie: Je travaille dans une banque. Je suis caissière. Et toi ? — I work at a bank. I am a cashier. And you?
Julien: Je suis professeur. Je travaille dans une école. — I am a teacher. I work at a school.
Sophie: Tu es fatigué aujourd'hui ? — Are you tired today?
Julien: Non, ça va. Tu veux déjeuner avec moi ? — No, I'm fine. Do you want to have lunch with me?
Sophie: Oui, je veux bien. On va au restaurant ? — Yes, I'd like to. Shall we go to the restaurant?
Julien: Allons-y. J'ai faim. — Let's go. I'm hungry.

Practice: Conjugate in writing: parler, finir, être, avoir, aller, faire. Then write six sentences about yourself: two with être (identity/origin/profession), two with avoir (age/needs/feelings), two with present-tense action verbs. Say each sentence aloud. Finally, translate to French: 'She is a doctor. She works in a hospital. She is tired today. She wants a coffee.' Check: Elle est médecin. Elle travaille dans un hôpital. Elle est fatiguée aujourd'hui. Elle veut un café.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Numbers are pure utility — prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules — and telling the time unlocks appointments, opening hours, and travel. French numbers have a few famous quirks (hello, quatre-vingts), so this lesson is built for repetition and out-loud drilling.

Numbers 0–20 (memorize these exactly): 0 zéro, 1 un/une, 2 deux, 3 trois, 4 quatre, 5 cinq, 6 six (sees), 7 sept (seht), 8 huit (weet), 9 neuf (nuhf), 10 dix (dees), 11 onze, 12 douze, 13 treize, 14 quatorze, 15 quinze, 16 seize, 17 dix-sept, 18 dix-huit, 19 dix-neuf, 20 vingt (vahn). Tens: 30 trente, 40 quarante, 50 cinquante, 60 soixante, 70 soixante-dix (sixty-ten!), 80 quatre-vingts (four-twenties!), 90 quatre-vingt-dix (four-twenty-ten!). Yes, 70–99 are built on 60 and 80: 71 = soixante-et-onze, 77 = soixante-dix-sept, 85 = quatre-vingt-cinq, 99 = quatre-vingt-dix-neuf. It feels strange for a week, then becomes automatic. 100 = cent, 200 = deux cents, 1,000 = mille. Un becomes une before feminine nouns: un café, une table.

Telling time: Quelle heure est-il ? (What time is it?). Il est une heure (1:00), Il est deux heures, Il est trois heures... Minutes: Il est quatre heures dix (4:10), Il est six heures et demie (6:30), Il est huit heures moins le quart (7:45 — 'eight minus a quarter', very common). Midi is noon, minuit is midnight. For appointments: le rendez-vous est à trois heures (the appointment is at three). French often uses the 24-hour clock in writing — 15h30 for 3:30 PM — so learn to read it: dix-huit heures = 6 PM. A classic mistake is forgetting heures is plural after one: Il est une heure but Il est deux heures.

Days of the week (masculine, never capitalized): lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche. Use le for 'on': le lundi = on Monday, le lundi as a habit = on Mondays. Months: janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre. Dates: le cinq mai, le vingt octobre. To say what day it is: Quel jour sommes-nous ? — Nous sommes mardi. What is the date? Quelle est la date ? — C'est le deux novembre. Note the order: day first, then month — le 2 novembre, never 'novembre 2'. Exception: the first of the month is le premier — le premier janvier.

Practical money and shopping vocabulary, since numbers live there: Combien ça coûte ? (How much does it cost?), Ça coûte dix euros (It costs ten euros), C'est très cher (It's very expensive), C'est bon marché (It's cheap), Vous avez la monnaie ? (Do you have change?), L'addition, s'il vous plaît (The check, please). In shops you will hear prices as bare numbers — 'quarante-cinq' for 45 — so number fluency pays off immediately. Phone numbers are read in pairs: 06 12 34 56 78 = zéro-six, douze, trente-quatre...

Dialogue — at a market:

Vendeur: Bonjour ! Vous désirez ? — Hello! What would you like?
Client: Je voudrais deux kilos de pommes, s'il vous plaît. — I'd like two kilos of apples, please.
Vendeur: Ça fait douze euros. Autre chose ? — That's twelve euros. Anything else?
Client: Combien coûtent les oranges ? — How much are the oranges?
Vendeur: Cinq euros le kilo. — Five euros a kilo.
Client: Donnez-m'en trois kilos. Vous fermez à quelle heure ? — Give me three kilos. What time do you close?
Vendeur: Nous fermons à huit heures. — We close at eight.
Client: Merci. Vous avez la monnaie de vingt ? — Thanks. Do you have change for twenty?
Vendeur: Oui, bien sûr. — Yes, of course.

Practice: Count aloud from 0 to 100 without stopping — including the tricky 70s, 80s, and 90s — then backwards from 50 to 0. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in French. Then drill time: say the current time in French every 15 minutes for two hours (Quelle heure est-il ? — Il est...). Finally, memorize the market dialogue's price lines and role-play a shopping trip where you buy three different items, asking Combien ça coûte ? each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to form every kind of question, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in a French-speaking place. The good news: you already know two of the three question patterns from the dialogues so far.

French has three ways to ask a question. 1) Rising intonation: keep normal word order and raise your voice at the end — Vous parlez français ? This is the most common in speech. 2) Est-ce que: put est-ce que (ehs-kuh) before a statement — Est-ce que vous parlez français ? Slightly more formal, very safe. 3) Inversion: flip subject and verb — Parlez-vous français ? Most formal, common in writing. All three mean the same thing; master intonation first, recognize the others. The core question words: que (what — Qu'est-ce que c'est ? = What is that?), qui (who), quel/quelle (which), où (where), quand (when), pourquoi (why), comment (how), combien (how much/many). Parce que (one phrase) means 'because' — do not confuse it with pourquoi.

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. Où est... ? (Where is...?), Comment aller à... ? (How do I get to...?), C'est près (It's near), C'est loin (It's far), à droite (to the right), à gauche (to the left), tout droit (straight ahead), au coin de la rue (on the street corner), entre... et... (between... and...). When someone answers, listen for: tournez (turn), traversez (cross), continuez (continue). Polite opener: Pardon, où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ? (Excuse me, where is the station, please?). And the lifesaver follow-up: Pouvez-vous me montrer sur le plan ? (Can you show me on the map?).

Shopping questions beyond prices: Vous avez... ? (Do you have...?), Il y a... ? (Is there...? / Are there...?), Je peux essayer ? (Can I try it on?), Vous avez une taille plus grande / plus petite ? (Do you have a bigger/smaller size?), Vous acceptez la carte ? (Do you take card?), Vous ouvrez à quelle heure ? (What time do you open?). Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: Vous êtes d'où ? (Where are you from?), Vous faites quoi dans la vie ? (What do you do?), Vous êtes ici depuis longtemps ? (Have you been here long?), Vous aimez la ville ? (Do you like the city?), Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez ? (What do you recommend?). Two mistakes to avoid: saying 'Quoi est votre nom ?' instead of Comment vous appelez-vous ? (nobody says the first), and answering a question you only half understood — use Je ne comprends pas bien, pouvez-vous répéter ? instead of guessing.

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Touriste: Pardon, où est le musée, s'il vous plaît ? — Excuse me, where is the museum, please?
Passant: C'est près. Continuez tout droit et tournez à gauche. — It's near. Keep going straight and turn left.
Touriste: C'est loin à pied ? — Is it far on foot?
Passant: Non, c'est à cinq minutes. C'est entre la banque et la pharmacie. — No, it's five minutes. It's between the bank and the pharmacy.
Touriste: Merci beaucoup. Comment s'appelle cette rue ? — Thank you very much. What is this street called?
Passant: C'est la rue Victor Hugo. — It's Victor Hugo Street.

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Léa: Vous êtes d'où ? — Where are you from?
Marc: Je suis de Belgique. Et vous ? — I'm from Belgium. And you?
Léa: Je suis d'ici, de Paris. Vous êtes ici depuis longtemps ? — I'm from here, from Paris. Have you been here long?
Marc: Depuis deux semaines. J'aime beaucoup la ville. — For two weeks. I like the city a lot.
Léa: Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez à visiter ? — What do you recommend visiting?
Marc: Je veux voir le parc demain. Pourquoi vous ne venez pas ? — I want to see the park tomorrow. Why don't you come?
Léa: Bonne idée ! À quelle heure ? — Good idea! At what time?
Marc: À dix heures. On se voit ici. — At ten. See you here.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with rising intonation. Then memorize the direction-giving sequence (tout droit, à droite, à gauche, au coin) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in French, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with a partner or alone, then change three details (city, time, place) and run it again — this is how small talk becomes automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The Passé Composé
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense — the passé composé — so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: Qu'est-ce que vous avez fait hier ? (What did you do yesterday?). The passé composé covers completed, finished actions with a clear end: yesterday, last week, this morning.

The passé composé has a beautifully simple formula: AVOIR (or ÊTRE) in the present + the past participle. For regular -ER verbs, the past participle is the stem + é: parler → parlé, manger → mangé, visiter → visité. So: j'ai parlé (I spoke), tu as mangé (you ate), il a visité (he visited), nous avons fini (we finished — finir → fini), vous avez pris (you took — prendre → pris, irregular), ils ont vu (they saw — voir → vu, irregular). Common irregular past participles to memorize now: fait (faire), dit (dire), pris (prendre), mis (mettre), vu (voir), su (savoir), pu (pouvoir), voulu (vouloir), dû (devoir), eu (avoir), été (être). Time words anchor the past: hier (yesterday), hier soir (last night), la semaine dernière (last week), l'année dernière (last year), ce matin (this morning).

A small set of verbs — mostly verbs of movement and change of state — use ÊTRE instead of avoir as the helper. Remember them with the 'house of être' picture: aller/venir (go/come), arriver/partir (arrive/leave), entrer/sortir (enter/go out), monter/descendre (go up/go down), naître/mourir (be born/die), rester (stay), tomber (fall), retourner (return), passer (pass by). With être, the participle AGREES with the subject: elle est allée (she went — extra -e), ils sont partis (they left — extra -s), nous sommes arrivés. With avoir there is no agreement in basic sentences: elle a mangé, ils ont fini. This agreement rule is the most tested point of French past-tense grammar — drill it.

Negation wraps around the helper verb: je n'ai pas parlé (I didn't speak), elle n'est pas venue (she didn't come). Questions work three ways as in Lesson 5: Tu as mangé ? / Est-ce que tu as mangé ? / As-tu mangé ? Two beginner warnings. First, French has a second past tense — the imparfait, for ongoing and habitual past actions — and this course teaches only the passé composé, which is enough for everyday conversation. Using the passé composé for everything at first is understandable and will not block communication. Second, the agreement trap: writing 'elle a allée' (wrong helper AND wrong agreement) instead of 'elle est allée'. Check two things every time: is the helper avoir or être, and if être, does the participle match the subject?

Dialogue — talking about the weekend:

Lucie: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ce week-end ? — What did you do this weekend?
Antoine: Je suis allé à la plage avec ma famille. — I went to the beach with my family.
Lucie: C'était comment ? Il a fait beau ? — How was it? Was the weather nice?
Antoine: Oui, il a fait très beau. Nous avons nagé et nous avons mangé du poisson. — Yes, it was very sunny. We swam and ate fish.
Lucie: Génial ! Moi, je suis restée à la maison. J'ai regardé un film et j'ai lu un livre. — Great! I stayed home. I watched a movie and read a book.
Antoine: Le film t'a plu ? — Did you like the movie?
Lucie: Oui, je l'ai adoré. Et dimanche, qu'est-ce que tu as fait ? — Yes, I loved it. And Sunday, what did you do?
Antoine: J'ai dormi tard et j'ai rendu visite à mes parents. — I slept in and visited my parents.

Practice: Write a paragraph of 8–10 sentences about what you did yesterday, using at least five different passé composé verbs (mix avoir and être helpers). Read it aloud twice. Then conjugate in writing: parler, finir, aller, venir, prendre — full passé composé, all persons, with correct agreements for the être verbs. Finally, answer these aloud in complete French sentences: Qu'est-ce que vous avez mangé hier ? À quelle heure vous êtes-vous levé ? Qu'est-ce que vous avez fait le week-end dernier ? Vous avez vu un film cette semaine ?

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Making Plans — Future Expressions + Restaurant and Travel Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to talk about the future — making plans, accepting invitations, and handling two of the most useful real-world conversations: ordering in a restaurant and navigating travel. Future talk is what turns you from a tourist into someone who can actually live in French: booking, inviting, promising, and planning.

French has two easy ways to express the future. The everyday one is ALLER + INFINITIVE — the 'near future': Je vais étudier (I'm going to study), Nous allons voyager (We are going to travel), Tu vas venir ? (Are you coming?). Just conjugate aller (je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont) and add any infinitive — this one structure covers most future needs. The second is the futur simple, formed on the infinitive + endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont: je parlerai, tu mangeras, il viendra (venir is irregular: viendr-), nous finirons, vous prendrez, ils seront (être → ser-), j'aurai (avoir → aur-). Use it for promises, predictions, and formal plans: Je t'appellerai demain (I will call you tomorrow), Il fera beau (It will be sunny). For this level, default to aller + infinitive in conversation and recognize the futur simple when you hear it.

Restaurant vocabulary and phrases. La carte / le menu (the menu), le plat du jour (dish of the day), l'entrée (starter), le plat principal (main course), le dessert (dessert), la boisson (drink). Ordering: Je voudrais... (I would like... — polite), Pour moi... (For me...), Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez ? (What do you recommend?). During the meal: C'est délicieux (It's delicious), Vous pouvez m'apporter... ? (Can you bring me...?), L'addition, s'il vous plaît (The check, please). Common mistake: saying 'je suis chaud' for 'I'm hot' (temperature) — say j'ai chaud. Another: barking 'je veux' at the waiter is grammatically fine but socially blunt — je voudrais or j'aimerais sounds much better. Tipping: service is included in French restaurants (service compris), so leaving a tip is optional and small.

Travel phrases. À l'aéroport (at the airport): Où est la porte... ? (Where is gate...?), Mon vol part à... (My flight leaves at...), J'ai une réservation (I have a reservation). À l'hôtel: Je voudrais une chambre double (I'd like a double room), Le petit-déjeuner est à quelle heure ? (What time is breakfast?), Vous avez le wifi ? (Do you have wifi?). Problems: J'ai perdu mon passeport (I lost my passport), J'ai besoin d'aide (I need help), Où y a-t-il une pharmacie ? (Where is there a pharmacy?). Note how much of this reuses Lessons 2–5 — the course is compounding.

Dialogue 1 — at a restaurant:

Serveur: Bonsoir. Vous avez une réservation ? — Good evening. Do you have a reservation?
Claire: Oui, au nom de Claire. — Yes, under Claire.
Serveur: Par ici, s'il vous plaît. Vous voulez voir la carte ? — This way, please. Would you like to see the menu?
Claire: Oui, merci. Quel est le plat du jour ? — Yes, thanks. What is the dish of the day?
Serveur: C'est du poulet avec du riz. C'est délicieux. — It's chicken with rice. It's delicious.
Claire: Je voudrais ça, et une salade. Et toi, Julien ? — I'd like that, and a salad. And you, Julien?
Julien: Pour moi, le poisson. Vous pouvez m'apporter de l'eau, s'il vous plaît ? — For me, the fish. Can you bring me water, please?
Serveur: Tout de suite. — Right away.
(plus tard) Claire: L'addition, s'il vous plaît. — The check, please.
Serveur: Ça fait trente-cinq euros. — It's thirty-five euros.

Dialogue 2 — making weekend plans:

Nicolas: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire samedi ? — What are you going to do Saturday?
Emma: Je vais rendre visite à ma sœur. Et toi ? — I'm going to visit my sister. And you?
Nicolas: Je vais aller au marché le matin. Tu veux venir ? — I'm going to go to the market in the morning. Do you want to come?
Emma: Oui, avec plaisir. On se voit à quelle heure ? — Yes, gladly. What time shall we meet?
Nicolas: À neuf heures. Après, on va déjeuner ensemble. — At nine. Afterwards we'll have lunch together.
Emma: Parfait. Je t'appellerai vendredi pour confirmer. — Perfect. I'll call you Friday to confirm.

Practice: Write three plans for next week using aller + infinitive, and three promises using the futur simple. Then write a full restaurant dialogue (8+ lines) where you order a starter, main, drink, and dessert, ask for the check, and react to the food. Say it all aloud. Finally, plan a real weekend in French: where you will go, who you will see, what you will eat — five sentences minimum, out loud.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Conversation Practice Drills + Your 30-Day Practice Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson does two things: it gives you structured conversation drills that combine everything from Lessons 1–7, and it hands you a concrete 30-day plan so your French keeps growing after the course ends. A course can teach you the material, but only a routine turns material into fluency — so treat this lesson as the most important one to actually do.

Drill 1 — The Two-Minute Monologue. Set a timer for two minutes and talk about your day — present for routines (Je me lève à sept heures...), passé composé for what already happened (J'ai pris un café...), future for what is next (Je vais travailler...). Do not stop to look up words; describe around them (la chose pour écrire = the thing for writing, if you forget 'pen'). Fluency is built by keeping going, not by being perfect. Do this drill daily — it is the single highest-value exercise in this course.

Drill 2 — Question Tennis. Write 20 question words and topics on slips of paper (Où...?, Quand...?, Pourquoi...?). Draw one and answer in two full sentences, then ask a follow-up question. Example: draw 'Où ?' → Où êtes-vous né ? Je suis né en Ohio. Draw 'Pourquoi ?' → Pourquoi apprenez-vous le français ? J'apprends le français parce que je veux voyager. If you practice with a partner, rally: they answer your question, then ask you one back. Ten minutes of question tennis covers more ground than an hour of passive review.

Drill 3 — Situation Cards. Write real situations on cards: 'Your hotel has no hot water — complain politely', 'Ask a stranger for directions to the pharmacy', 'Order dinner for two including a dietary restriction', 'Small talk with a taxi driver for five minutes'. Draw a card and perform it aloud, both roles. These force you to combine vocabulary, grammar, and politeness under mild pressure — exactly what real conversations feel like. Rotate through all your cards weekly.

Two mistakes that stall learners at this stage. First, the perfection trap: refusing to speak until every conjugation is certain. French speakers are generous with beginners who try; they cannot help beginners who stay silent. Speak with 70% accuracy today rather than 100% accuracy never. Second, passive consumption: re-reading lessons and calling it study. Reading feels productive but builds recognition, not production. Every minute of speaking aloud counts triple compared to silent review — your mouth needs the reps.

Your 30-day practice plan. Week 1 — Foundations lock-in: 20 minutes daily. Days 1–2: re-read Lessons 1–2 dialogues aloud. Days 3–4: conjugate être/avoir/present verbs from Lesson 3 out loud. Days 5–7: number and time drills from Lesson 4 until 0–100 is automatic. Week 2 — Conversation ignition: 25 minutes daily. Daily two-minute monologue plus question tennis; re-do the Lesson 5 and 6 dialogues with changed details. Week 3 — Real situations: 30 minutes daily. One situation card per day performed aloud; write a daily journal of five French sentences about your day (present + passé composé + future mix). Week 4 — Live fire: 30+ minutes daily. Have at least three real conversations — with a tutor, a language-exchange partner, a French-speaking neighbor, or even ordering food in French. Record one, listen back, and note your three most frequent errors to drill next month.

Track it simply: a notebook page per day with the date, minutes practiced, and one line about what felt easier than last week. If you miss a day, never miss twice — the streak matters more than any single session. After 30 days, repeat the cycle with harder situation cards and longer monologues; you now own a system, not just a course.

Practice: Do Drill 1 right now — two full minutes about your day in French, out loud, no stopping. Then write out your personal Week 1 schedule with exact times (e.g., '7:30 AM, 20 minutes, Lessons 1–2 dialogues'). Finally, write five situation cards of your own based on your life — travel you plan, restaurants you visit, people you meet — and perform the first one today. Bonne chance — you are a French speaker now. Keep speaking.

courses.title: Conversational German
courses.tagline: Speak German from day one: pronunciation, core grammar, and real everyday dialogues.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational German is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday German from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. The first half builds your foundation — pronunciation, greetings, sein and haben, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep moving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational German is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday German from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. The first half builds your foundation — pronunciation, greetings, sein and haben, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep moving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will be able to: pronounce German words clearly using the main vowel sounds, umlauts, and consonant rules; greet people, introduce yourself, and handle survival phrases when you do not understand; use sein and haben correctly and build sentences in the present tense with regular and common irregular verbs; count to one hundred and beyond, tell the time, and use days, months, and dates; ask and answer questions about directions, prices, and everyday topics; talk about things you did using the Perfekt tense; make plans for the future and hold a full restaurant or travel conversation; and run a simple daily practice routine that keeps your speaking improving.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read one lesson at a time, out loud wherever you see German — saying the words with your mouth, not just your eyes, is what builds speaking skill. Each lesson opens with what it teaches, explains the concept with concrete examples, includes full example dialogues with English translations, warns you about common beginner mistakes, and ends with a clearly labeled Practice exercise. Do the practice before moving on, even if it feels easy; the lessons build on each other, and Lesson 3's verbs depend on Lesson 1's sounds. Aim for one lesson per day, and re-read the previous lesson's dialogues the next morning as a warm-up. There are no grades and no timers — steady repetition beats cramming.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites. This course starts from zero and assumes you have never studied German before. Everything — even how to make each vowel sound — is explained from scratch. If you already know a little German, Lesson 1's pronunciation rules are still worth reading, because correcting a bad accent habit early saves months later. You do not need any textbook, app, or prior grammar knowledge; a notebook for writing out the practice exercises is the only thing that will help.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes — it is a text/workbook course, and everything you need is on the page: explanations, example sentences, translated dialogues, and practice exercises. The materials section includes a vocabulary cheat sheet and a 30-day practice plan template you can print and reuse. Work through the lessons in order, do the exercises in writing and out loud, and you will finish with usable, spoken German for real everyday situations.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronunciation — German Vowels, Umlauts, and Consonant Rules
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to pronounce German clearly from the start. German spelling is remarkably consistent: once you learn the sound rules, you can read almost any word correctly. Your goal in this lesson is not a perfect accent — it is clarity. If your vowels are clean and your consonant clusters are crisp, German speakers will understand you even while you are still learning words.

Start with the pure vowels, which are shorter and steadier than English vowels. A sounds like 'ah' in father: danke (DAHN-kuh, thank you). E sounds like 'eh' in bed: Bett (beht, bed). I sounds like 'ee' in see: Liebe (LEE-buh, love). O sounds like 'oh' in go, but shorter: Brot (broht, bread). U sounds like 'oo' in moon: gut (goot, good). Keep every vowel short and pure — do not let them glide into a second sound the way English habits push you to. A very common beginner mistake is reading German vowels with English values — for example, saying 'mein' (mine) like the English word 'main' instead of 'mine'. When in doubt, keep vowels short.

Now the umlauts — ä, ö, ü — the sounds that make German sound like German. Ä sounds like 'eh': Mädchen (MEHD-khen, girl). Ö: round your lips as if to say 'oh' but say 'eh' instead — schön (shurn, beautiful). Ü: round your lips as if to say 'oo' but say 'ee' instead — Tür (tewr, door), grün (grewn, green). These are the famous hard sounds; practice them daily by alternating pairs: schon (already) versus schön (beautiful), Mutter (mother) versus Mütter (mothers). The letter combination EI sounds like the English 'eye': mein (mine), klein (small). IE is the reverse — a long 'ee': Liebe, Bier (beer). EU and ÄU sound like 'oy': heute (HOY-tuh, today), Häuser (HOY-zer, houses).

German consonants are crisp and firm. The CH has two sounds: after a, o, u it is a throaty scrape from the back of the throat — Bach (bahkh), Buch (bookh); after e, i, and umlauts it is a soft hiss like a cat — ich (ikh, I), Milch (milk). The R is rolled or gargled in the throat — rot (roht, red); a light throat gargle is perfectly acceptable and standard. W sounds like English V: Wasser (VAH-ser, water). V sounds like English F: Vater (FAH-ter, father). Z sounds like 'ts': Zeit (tsite, time). S before a vowel sounds like English Z: Sonne (ZON-nuh, sun); but SS and ß (Eszett) are a sharp S: Straße (SHTRAH-suh, street), Wasser. SCH is 'sh': schön, Schule (SHOO-luh, school). SP and ST at the start of a word add the sh: sprechen (SHPREH-khen, to speak), Stadt (shtat, city). J sounds like English Y: ja (yah, yes). Finally, German devoices consonants at the end of words: Tag (day) ends with a K sound, not G; Hund (dog) ends with a T sound, not D.

Word stress in German usually falls on the FIRST syllable of native words: DANke, GUTen Tag, WASser, MORgen. This is the opposite of French and one of the first things that makes your German sound right. Longer compound words stress the first part: HAUSaufgaben (homework), BAHNhof (train station). Trust first-syllable stress for everyday words and your rhythm will sound natural.

Here is a short dialogue using only sounds from this lesson. Read it aloud slowly:

Anna: Guten Tag! Wie heißen Sie? (GOO-tun tahk vee HIGH-sun zee) — Good day! What is your name?
Lukas: Ich heiße Lukas. Und Sie? (ikh HIGH-suh LOO-kahs oont zee) — My name is Lukas. And you?
Anna: Ich heiße Anna. Freut mich. (ikh HIGH-suh AH-nah froyt mikh) — My name is Anna. Pleased to meet you.
Lukas: Freut mich. Sprechen Sie Deutsch? (froyt mikh SHPREH-khen zee doytsh) — Pleased to meet you. Do you speak German?
Anna: Ja, ein bisschen. (yah ine BIS-khen) — Yes, a little.

Say the whole dialogue five times today; it is your first German conversation.

Practice: Write out these ten words and say each aloud three times, exaggerating the umlauts and CH sounds: schön, Tür, Mädchen, ich, Buch, sprechen, Wasser, Zeit, Straße, heute. Next, practice the pairs schon/schön, Mutter/Mütter, mein/meine until the differences are obvious. Finally, read the dialogue above aloud five times, then cover the pronunciation hints and read it again — you should be able to produce the sounds from the spelling alone.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully.

Start with greetings. Guten Tag (GOO-tun tahk) means good day and works all day. Guten Morgen (GOO-tun MOR-gun) is good morning, Guten Abend (GOO-tun AH-bent) is good evening. Hallo (hah-LOH) is hi — friendly and universal. Tschüss (tchewss) is bye among friends; Auf Wiedersehen (owf VEE-der-zay-un) is the formal goodbye. In southern Germany and Austria you will hear Grüß Gott (grewss got) and Servus (ZEHR-voos) as greetings — recognize them. For introductions: Ich heiße... (ikh HIGH-suh) means 'my name is'. Wie heißen Sie? (vee HIGH-sun zee) asks someone's name formally; Wie heißt du? (vee highst doo) is the informal version. Freut mich (froyt mikh) means pleased to meet you.

Now the small-talk core. Wie geht es Ihnen? (vee gayt ehs EE-nun) is 'how are you' formally; Wie geht's? (vee gayts) is the casual version everyone uses. Common answers: Sehr gut, danke (zayr goot DAHN-kuh — very well, thanks), Es geht (ehs gayt — it's going okay), Nicht so gut (not so good), Ich bin müde (ikh bin MEW-duh — I am tired). Und Ihnen? / Und dir? (oont EE-nun / oont deer) means 'and you?' — short and essential. Bitte (BIT-tuh) is please and you're welcome, danke is thank you, danke schön is thank you very much. A frequent beginner mistake is answering Wie geht's? with a long life story; a short answer plus Und dir? keeps the conversation balanced and gives you twice the practice.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. Ich verstehe nicht (ikh fehr-SHTAY-uh nikht) — I don't understand. Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? (KURN-nun zee dahs BIT-tuh vee-der-HOH-lun) — Can you repeat that, please? Sprechen Sie bitte langsamer (SHPREH-khen zee BIT-tuh LAHNG-zah-mer) — Please speak more slowly. Sprechen Sie Englisch? (SHPREH-khen zee EHNG-lish) — Do you speak English? Entschuldigung (ehnt-SHOOL-dee-goong) — excuse me / sorry. Es tut mir leid (ehs toot meer lite) — I'm sorry. Was bedeutet...? (vahs buh-DOY-tet) — What does ... mean? These phrases will rescue you in any German-speaking place, and people respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Watch for this social mistake: German runs on the du/Sie distinction. Use Sie with strangers, shopkeepers, elders, and in any formal setting; switch to du only when the other person offers it or with clear peers and friends. Using du with a stranger is not a grammar failure — it is a social one, and it can come across as rude. When in doubt, start with Sie. A second note: Germans value directness and punctuality in a way that surprises some visitors — a straightforward question is polite, and arriving on time matters.

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with the translations:

Julia: Guten Tag! Wie heißen Sie? — Good day! What is your name?
Felix: Guten Tag. Ich heiße Felix. Und Sie? — Good day. My name is Felix. And you?
Julia: Ich heiße Julia. Freut mich. — My name is Julia. Pleased to meet you.
Felix: Freut mich, Julia. Woher kommen Sie? — Pleased to meet you, Julia. Where are you from?
Julia: Ich komme aus England. Und Sie? — I come from England. And you?
Felix: Ich komme aus Berlin. Sprechen Sie Deutsch? — I come from Berlin. Do you speak German?
Julia: Ein bisschen. Sprechen Sie bitte langsamer. — A little. Please speak more slowly.
Felix: Natürlich. Wie geht es Ihnen heute? — Of course. How are you today?
Julia: Sehr gut, danke. Und Ihnen? — Very well, thanks. And you?
Felix: Sehr gut. Auf Wiedersehen! — Very well. Goodbye!

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, one feeling word, goodbye) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then practice the survival phrases: cover the German column, read the English, and say the German from memory until you can do all seven without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with the umlauts and CH sounds from Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Sein, Haben, and the Present Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson tackles the two most important verbs in German — sein (to be) and haben (to have) — plus the present tense, which lets you describe what you do every day. Sein and haben are the backbone of the language: they appear in nearly every sentence, and both double as helper verbs for the past tense you will meet in Lesson 6. Master their shapes now and everything later gets easier.

SEIN (to be) — memorize this table completely: ich bin (ikh bin — I am), du bist (doo bist — you are, informal), er/sie/es ist (ehr/zee/ehs ihst — he/she/it is), wir sind (veer zint — we are), ihr seid (eer zite — you are, plural informal), sie/Sie sind (zee zint — they are / you are, formal). Use it for identity, origin, description, profession, and location: Ich bin Amerikaner (I am American), Sie ist Ärztin (She is a doctor), Wir sind in München (We are in Munich), Sie sind freundlich (They are friendly). Note the Sie/sie overlap: capitalized Sie is formal 'you', lowercase sie is 'she' or 'they' — context and the verb make it clear.

HABEN (to have) — equally essential: ich habe (ikh HAH-buh — I have), du hast (doo hahst — you have), er/sie/es hat (ehr/zee/ehs haht — he/she/it has), wir haben (veer HAH-bun — we have), ihr habt (eer hahpt — you have), sie/Sie haben (zee HAH-bun — they have / you have). German uses haben for age, hunger, and need, like French: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt (I am twenty years old — literally 'I am twenty years old'), Ich habe Hunger (I am hungry), Ich habe Durst (I am thirsty), Ich habe keine Zeit (I have no time / I'm busy). Learn Ich habe Hunger, Ich habe Durst, and Ich habe keine Zeit as fixed phrases today.

Now the present tense of regular verbs. Drop the -en and add: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. Machen (to do/make): ich mache, du machst, er macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie machen. Wohnen (to live): Ich wohne in Hamburg (I live in Hamburg). Arbeiten (to work): Ich arbeite im Büro (I work in an office) — note that verbs whose stem ends in -t or -d insert an extra e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. Lernen (to learn): Ich lerne Deutsch (I am learning German). The pattern is beautifully regular, which is why German present tense is one of the easier parts of the grammar.

Essential irregular verbs to learn as vocabulary: GEHEN (to go): ich gehe, du gehst, er geht, wir gehen, ihr geht, sie gehen — Ich gehe zum Markt (I go to the market). ESSEN (to eat): ich esse, du isst, er isst, wir essen, ihr esst, sie essen — note the stem vowel change e→i in du/er forms. TRINKEN (to drink): ich trinke, du trinkst... (regular). MÖCHTEN (would like — the polite 'want'): ich möchte, du möchtest... Ich möchte einen Kaffee (I would like a coffee) — this is the politeness key for restaurants and shops. KÖNNEN (can/to be able): ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie können. WOLLEN (to want): ich will, du willst... These modal verbs appear in nearly every conversation.

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, word order: in a main clause the conjugated verb is ALWAYS in second position — Ich lerne heute Deutsch (I learn today German), Heute lerne ich Deutsch (Today learn I German). Time phrases can start the sentence, but the verb stays second. Second, translating English 'do' questions word-for-word: English 'Do you speak German?' is simply Sprechen Sie Deutsch? — verb first, no helper needed.

Dialogue — two coworkers at lunch:

Jonas: Wo arbeitest du? — Where do you work?
Lena: Ich arbeite in einer Bank. Ich bin Kassiererin. Und du? — I work at a bank. I am a cashier. And you?
Jonas: Ich bin Lehrer. Ich arbeite in einer Schule. — I am a teacher. I work at a school.
Lena: Bist du heute müde? — Are you tired today?
Jonas: Nein, es geht mir gut. Möchtest du mit mir essen? — No, I'm fine. Would you like to eat with me?
Lena: Ja, gern. Gehen wir ins Restaurant? — Yes, gladly. Shall we go to the restaurant?
Jonas: Gehen wir. Ich habe Hunger. — Let's go. I'm hungry.

Practice: Conjugate in writing: machen, wohnen, sein, haben, gehen, essen. Then write six sentences about yourself: two with sein (identity/origin/profession), two with haben (needs/feelings), two with present-tense action verbs — and put a time phrase first in two of them to practice verb-second order. Say each sentence aloud. Finally, translate to German: 'She is a doctor. She works in a hospital. She is tired today. She would like a coffee.' Check: Sie ist Ärztin. Sie arbeitet in einem Krankenhaus. Sie ist heute müde. Sie möchte einen Kaffee.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Numbers are pure utility — prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules — and telling the time unlocks appointments, opening hours, and travel. German numbers have one famous quirk — the reversed tens and units (vierundzwanzig = four-and-twenty) — so this lesson is built for repetition and out-loud drilling.

Numbers 0–20 (memorize these exactly): 0 null, 1 eins, 2 zwei, 3 drei, 4 vier, 5 fünf, 6 sechs (zehks), 7 sieben (ZEE-bun), 8 acht (ahkht), 9 neun (noyn), 10 zehn (tsayn), 11 elf, 12 zwölf (tsvurlf), 13 dreizehn, 14 vierzehn, 15 fünfzehn, 16 sechzehn, 17 siebzehn, 18 achtzehn, 19 neunzehn, 20 zwanzig (TSVAHN-tsikh). Tens: 30 dreißig, 40 vierzig, 50 fünfzig, 60 sechzig, 70 siebzig, 80 achtzig, 90 neunzig, 100 hundert. From 21 up, German says the unit FIRST, then 'und', then the ten: 21 = einundzwanzig (one-and-twenty), 47 = siebenundvierzig, 83 = dreiundachtzig. It feels backwards for a week, then becomes automatic — and it explains why phone numbers are read digit by digit. 1,000 = tausend. Note eins drops its -s before nouns: ein Kaffee, eine Tasse.

Telling time: Wie viel Uhr ist es? or Wie spät ist es? (What time is it?). Es ist ein Uhr (1:00), Es ist zwei Uhr, Es ist drei Uhr... Minutes: Es ist vier Uhr zehn (4:10), Es ist halb sieben (6:30 — careful! 'half seven' means half PAST six in German, the half counts toward the coming hour), Es ist viertel vor acht (7:45), Es ist viertel nach acht (8:15). Mittag is noon, Mitternacht is midnight. For appointments: Der Termin ist um drei Uhr (the appointment is at three). German uses the 24-hour clock constantly in writing and often in speech — 15:30 is fünfzehn Uhr dreißig, and 18:00 is achtzehn Uhr. A classic mistake is translating 'half seven' as halb sieben meaning 7:30 — it means 6:30. Learn this on day one.

Days of the week (masculine, capitalized — all German nouns are): Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag (or Sonnabend), Sonntag. Use am for 'on': am Montag = on Monday. Months: Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni, Juli, August, September, Oktober, November, Dezember. Dates: der fünfte Mai, der zwanzigste Oktober. To say what day it is: Welcher Tag ist heute? — Heute ist Dienstag. What is the date? Welches Datum haben wir? — Heute ist der zweite November. Note the order: day first, then month — der 2. November.

Practical money and shopping vocabulary, since numbers live there: Wie viel kostet das? (How much does that cost?), Das kostet zehn Euro (That costs ten euros), Das ist sehr teuer (That's very expensive), Das ist billig (That's cheap), Haben Sie Kleingeld? (Do you have change?), Die Rechnung, bitte (The check, please). In shops you will hear prices as bare numbers — 'fünfundvierzig' for 45 — so number fluency pays off immediately. Phone numbers are read digit by digit or in pairs: null-eins-sieben... or siebzehn...

Dialogue — at a market:

Verkäufer: Guten Tag! Was darf's sein? — Good day! What can I get you?
Kunde: Ich möchte zwei Kilo Äpfel, bitte. — I'd like two kilos of apples, please.
Verkäufer: Das macht zwölf Euro. Sonst noch etwas? — That's twelve euros. Anything else?
Kunde: Wie viel kosten die Orangen? — How much are the oranges?
Verkäufer: Fünf Euro das Kilo. — Five euros a kilo.
Kunde: Dann drei Kilo, bitte. Wann schließen Sie? — Then three kilos, please. When do you close?
Verkäufer: Wir schließen um acht Uhr. — We close at eight.
Kunde: Danke. Haben Sie Kleingeld für zwanzig? — Thanks. Do you have change for twenty?
Verkäufer: Ja, natürlich. — Yes, of course.

Practice: Count aloud from 0 to 100 without stopping — including the reversed 21–99 — then backwards from 50 to 0. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in German. Then drill time: say the current time in German every 15 minutes for two hours (Wie viel Uhr ist es? — Es ist...). Finally, memorize the market dialogue's price lines and role-play a shopping trip where you buy three different items, asking Wie viel kostet das? each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to form every kind of question, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in a German-speaking place. The good news: German questions follow one clean rule — the verb moves to first position.

To form a yes/no question, put the conjugated verb FIRST: Sprechen Sie Deutsch? (Do you speak German?), Kommen Sie aus Berlin? (Do you come from Berlin?). For information questions, put the question word first, then the verb: Wo wohnen Sie? (Where do you live?), Wann beginnt der Film? (When does the film start?). The core question words: was (what), wer (who), welcher/welche (which), wo (where), wohin (where to), woher (where from), wann (when), warum (why), wie (how), wie viel (how much), wie viele (how many). Weil (because) answers warum — do not confuse the two. Remember verb-second order still applies after the question word: Warum lernen Sie Deutsch? (Why learn you German?).

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. Wo ist...? (Where is...?), Wie komme ich zu...? (How do I get to...?), Es ist nah (It's near), Es ist weit (It's far), rechts (right), links (left), geradeaus (straight ahead), an der Ecke (on the corner), zwischen... und... (between... and...). When someone answers, listen for: biegen Sie ab (turn), gehen Sie über (go across), folgen Sie (follow). Polite opener: Entschuldigung, wo ist der Bahnhof? (Excuse me, where is the train station?). And the lifesaver follow-up: Können Sie es mir auf dem Stadtplan zeigen? (Can you show me on the city map?).

Shopping questions beyond prices: Haben Sie...? (Do you have...?), Gibt es...? (Is there...? / Are there...?), Kann ich das anprobieren? (Can I try it on?), Haben Sie eine Nummer größer / kleiner? (Do you have a size bigger / smaller?), Kann ich mit Karte zahlen? (Can I pay by card?), Wann öffnen Sie? (When do you open?). Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: Woher kommen Sie? (Where are you from?), Was machen Sie beruflich? (What do you do for work?), Wie lange sind Sie schon hier? (How long have you been here?), Gefällt Ihnen die Stadt? (Do you like the city?), Was empfehlen Sie? (What do you recommend?). Two mistakes to avoid: saying 'Was ist Ihr Name?' instead of Wie heißen Sie? (nobody says the first), and answering a question you only half understood — use Ich habe nicht ganz verstanden, können Sie das wiederholen? instead of guessing.

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Tourist: Entschuldigung, wo ist das Museum? — Excuse me, where is the museum?
Passant: Es ist nah. Gehen Sie geradeaus und biegen Sie links ab. — It's near. Go straight ahead and turn left.
Tourist: Ist es weit zu Fuß? — Is it far on foot?
Passant: Nein, fünf Minuten. Es ist zwischen der Bank und der Apotheke. — No, five minutes. It's between the bank and the pharmacy.
Tourist: Vielen Dank. Wie heißt diese Straße? — Thank you very much. What is this street called?
Passant: Das ist die Goethestraße. — That's Goethestraße.

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Mia: Woher kommen Sie? — Where are you from?
Paul: Ich komme aus Österreich. Und Sie? — I come from Austria. And you?
Mia: Ich komme von hier, aus Hamburg. Wie lange sind Sie schon hier? — I'm from here, from Hamburg. How long have you been here?
Paul: Seit zwei Wochen. Die Stadt gefällt mir sehr. — For two weeks. I like the city a lot.
Mia: Was empfehlen Sie zu besichtigen? — What do you recommend seeing?
Paul: Ich möchte morgen den Park sehen. Warum kommen Sie nicht mit? — I want to see the park tomorrow. Why don't you come along?
Mia: Gute Idee! Um wie viel Uhr? — Good idea! At what time?
Paul: Um zehn Uhr. Wir sehen uns hier. — At ten. See you here.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with the verb correctly in first or second position. Then memorize the direction-giving sequence (geradeaus, rechts, links, an der Ecke) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in German, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with a partner or alone, then change three details (city, time, place) and run it again — this is how small talk becomes automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The Perfekt Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense — the Perfekt — so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: Was haben Sie gestern gemacht? (What did you do yesterday?). The Perfekt covers completed, finished actions and is the tense of spoken German — in conversation, Germans use Perfekt, not the literary Präteritum.

The Perfekt formula: HABEN or SEIN in the present + the past participle (Partizip II) at the END of the sentence. Regular verbs form the participle with ge- + stem + -t: machen → gemacht, lernen → gelernt, spielen → gespielt. So: Ich habe gelernt (I learned), Du hast gespielt (You played), Er hat gemacht (He did/made). Note the participle's fixed home at the end: Ich habe gestern viel gelernt (I learned a lot yesterday). Irregular participles use ge- + stem (often with a vowel change) + -en: essen → gegessen, trinken → getrunken, sehen → gesehen, sprechen → gesprochen, nehmen → genommen, lesen → gelesen, schreiben → geschrieben, vergessen → vergessen, finden → gefunden. Memorize these as vocabulary — they are the verbs you use most.

A set of verbs — mostly movement and change of state — use SEIN instead of haben: gehen → ich bin gegangen (I went), kommen → ich bin gekommen (I came), fahren → ich bin gefahren (I drove/went), fliegen → ich bin geflogen (I flew), bleiben → ich bin geblieben (I stayed), sein → ich bin gewesen (I was/have been), werden → ich bin geworden (I became). Rule of thumb: if the verb describes moving from A to B or a change of state, it probably takes sein. Everything else takes haben. Time words anchor the past: gestern (yesterday), gestern Abend (last night), letzte Woche (last week), letztes Jahr (last year), heute Morgen (this morning).

Two structural details make or break your Perfekt. First, separable-prefix verbs: the ge- goes BETWEEN the prefix and the stem — anrufen (to call) → angerufen, aufstehen (to get up) → aufgestanden, einkaufen (to shop) → eingekauft.
