The literary environment matters too: the ancient Near East produced creation accounts, flood stories, law codes, and covenant treaties, and scholars study the Hebrew versions alongside these, not to reduce the text to its neighbors, but to see precisely where it follows convention and where it departs. A law collection's structure, a treaty's pattern of preamble, stipulations, and blessings, a genealogy's way of marking eras: recognizing these forms helps you read the Hebrew versions with understanding rather than confusion. The scholarly principle is comparative and careful: similarities illuminate the shared cultural vocabulary, while differences reveal what is distinctive.

A responsible approach to context also knows its limits. Historical background informs reading; it does not dictate it. Scholars debate dates, authorship, and composition history vigorously, and this course presents the questions as open where they are open rather than settling them by fiat. When you encounter a claim like this law reflects ancient Near Eastern practice, ask for the evidence and consider alternative explanations; when a commentary asserts a historical fact, distinguish it from the text itself. The goal is a richer reading, not a replacement of the text with background information. Keep the text central: context is the lighting, not the painting.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, presentism, judging ancient practices by modern standards without first understanding them on their own terms. The honest sequence is: understand what the text meant in its world, then reflect on what it means in yours. Skipping the first step produces criticism of a caricature. Second, the parallel fallacy, assuming that because a neighboring culture had a similar story, the Hebrew version means the same thing. Shared forms carry different messages; the differences are usually the point. Compare to distinguish, not to flatten.

Practice: (1) In your journal, write a one-page description of the ancient Near Eastern world, geography, politics, daily life, literacy, in your own words, as if explaining it to a friend. (2) Choose one law, for example a Sabbath regulation or a dietary rule, and write two paragraphs: first, what it would have meant practically to an ancient household; second, what questions a modern reader might ask about it, keeping the two perspectives explicitly separate. (3) Find one example of a shared ancient literary form, a law collection, a treaty pattern, or a genealogy, in the text's structure and describe in a paragraph what recognizing the form clarifies. (4) Write down three historical questions about the text that scholars debate, phrased neutrally without assuming an answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Methods for Close Reading — Peshat, Word Study, and Structure
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches methods for close reading of the Hebrew Bible: attention to plain meaning, word study, repetition, and structure. By the end you will be able to read a passage at several levels, trace a Hebrew word through the text, and explain how a passage's structure shapes its meaning. Method matters as much as content: two readers can look at the same verse and see different things depending on how they were taught to read, and disciplined method turns casual reading into study.

Begin with peshat, the plain or contextual meaning: what the words say in their grammar, vocabulary, and immediate context. This is the foundation, and every other level of reading builds on it. Practicing peshat means slowing down: identify the subject and verb of each sentence, notice repeated words, and ask what the passage meant to its first audience before asking what it means to a later reader. Consider the opening of Bereshit: the Hebrew syntax of the first verses has been analyzed for centuries, with readers debating how the clauses connect. That debate is peshat-level work, careful grammar in service of meaning. A useful discipline: paraphrase each verse in your own words before consulting any commentary. If you cannot paraphrase it, you have not yet understood its plain sense, and interpretation built on confusion will stay confused.

Word study is the second method, and your root knowledge from Lesson 3 makes it possible. Choose a word that repeats in a passage, find its root, and list other words from the same root. Then ask: what does the root's core idea contribute here? The word shalom and its root sh-l-m, for example, carry wholeness and completion, so a passage using shalom is saying more than a translation's single word for peace conveys. Check a word's range by looking at how it is used in different passages: chesed appears in contexts of loyalty, kindness, and obligation, and its meaning in any one verse is shaped by the whole range. Use a concordance or a word-study reference if you have access to one, and record your findings in your journal. Word study done carefully is one of the most rewarding forms of close reading, because it lets you hear the Hebrew behind the translation.

Repetition and structure are the third method. Ancient Hebrew narrative and poetry use repetition deliberately: repeated words mark themes, repeated scenes invite comparison, and repeated phrases frame a passage. When a word appears three times in a short passage, ask why. When two stories share a pattern but differ in one detail, ask what the difference signifies. Structure also carries meaning: a passage may be arranged as a chiasm, a symmetrical pattern where the first and last elements mirror each other and the center carries the emphasis, or as a sequence that builds toward a climax. Sketch the structure of a passage before interpreting it: list its scenes or stanzas in order, note repetitions and contrasts, and identify the turning point. That sketch often reveals the passage's argument more clearly than any commentary.

Comparison is the fourth method. Compare translations: place two or three renderings of the same passage side by side and note where they differ. Differences reveal ambiguities in the Hebrew or different translator philosophies, and each difference is a question worth investigating. Compare passages within the text: the text revisits events and laws more than once, and asking why the accounts differ is one of the oldest and most productive questions in the field. Compare with context: Lesson 6's historical background lets you ask what a passage's first audience would have heard. And compare commentaries: when two scholars read one verse differently, reconstruct each one's reasoning. The disagreement teaches more than either conclusion alone.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, jumping to interpretation before establishing the plain meaning: creative readings of a verse you have not parsed grammatically are built on sand. Peshat first, always, even advanced scholars circle back to it. Second, treating one translation as the text: every translation is already an interpretation, making hundreds of small decisions you cannot see. The student who reads only one translation mistakes the translator's choices for the text itself. Compare at least two, and remember that the Hebrew, which you can now approach through letters, roots, and vocabulary, is the anchor.

Practice: (1) Choose a short passage of ten to fifteen verses, for example the opening of the Joseph story or a psalm, and paraphrase each verse in your own words in your journal, peshat work with no commentaries yet. (2) Choose one repeated word in the passage, trace its root, list three other words from that root, and write a paragraph on what the root contributes to the passage. (3) Sketch the passage's structure in a simple outline, marking repetitions, contrasts, and the turning point. (4) Compare two translations of the same passage, list every difference you find, and write one question about each significant difference.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Your Study Plan — Building a Hebrew Reading Practice
lessons.text:
This final lesson helps you build a sustainable personal study plan and maps where to continue learning. By the end you will design a study routine fitted to your life, know how to structure individual sessions, have a one-year reading plan, and understand your options for deeper study. Courses end; study continues. This lesson is the bridge from guided lessons to independent learning, and the plan you write here is the document that carries your learning forward.

Design a routine you can actually keep, because the best method is the one you sustain. Be honest about your time: twenty focused minutes three times a week outperforms an ambitious two-hour session that collapses by month two. Anchor sessions to existing habits, after morning coffee, during a lunch break, before bed, since attached habits survive and floating intentions do not. Choose a regular place with your materials at hand: your translation, this course's lessons, your journal, and your glossary. Set a review rhythm: ten minutes each month rereading your journal entries, noting which questions got answered and which deepened. The journal review is where you will literally watch yourself becoming a better reader. It is also the most commonly skipped step, so schedule it now.

Structure each session in four movements. First, review, five minutes: reread your last session's notes and questions, since study compounds when sessions connect. Second, read, fifteen to twenty minutes: work through a short passage slowly, a few verses, not a chapter, paraphrasing as Lesson 7 taught, noting repetitions, surprises, and questions. Third, investigate, ten to fifteen minutes: pursue one question, compare a translation, check a term in the glossary, trace a root, or consider the context from Lesson 6. One question deeply beats five superficially. Fourth, record, five minutes: write what you found, what remains open, and where you will start next time. End every session with an unanswered question deliberately left open. It pulls you back next time far better than a feeling of completion. The study-session worksheet in your materials packet turns this structure into a reusable template.

Follow a reading plan that gives the text its proper shape. The traditional weekly-portion cycle, the parashot from Lesson 4, remains the finest year-long structure for the Torah: fifty-four portions, one per week, completing the Torah annually, and because the cycle is shared, study companions and published guides align with it. If a year feels long, begin with a focused alternative: read Bereshit straight through over about twelve weeks at this course's pace, or follow one theme from Lesson 5 across all three parts of the Tanakh, or reread the passages from your course exercises now that you have full methods. A second year could take you through the historical books of the Neviim, and a third through the Psalms and wisdom books, reading one psalm or one chapter of Proverbs per session. Whatever plan you choose, keep the journal going, dated entries, questions first, findings second, and revisit Lessons 2 through 7 as your reading raises new questions. The course is a reference work now, not just a sequence.

For deeper study, several paths open. Language study: learning Hebrew grammar beyond the alphabet and vocabulary of this course transforms your reading. Even recognizing roots, prefixes, and common verb patterns changes everything, and introductory Biblical Hebrew courses are widely available. Commentary study: work through one book with a classical commentary alongside a modern study edition, one portion per week. Academic study: university-level introductions to the Hebrew Bible, courses on the ancient Near East, and scholarly journals offer the critical dimension, and your local library is the free gateway. Community study: study groups, classes, and discussion partners multiply insight. Explaining your reading to another person is the fastest way to find its holes. Choose the path that matches your curiosity; they combine freely, and none requires any particular belief.

A final word on posture. The academic stance this course has maintained, descriptive, neutral, curious, is itself a discipline worth keeping. It lets you study a text sacred to millions with both respect and intellectual honesty: respect that takes the text seriously on its own terms, honesty that follows evidence where it leads and labels interpretation as interpretation. You will encounter readers who approach the Hebrew Bible devotionally, polemically, or dismissively; the studied reader can converse with all of them, because understanding a text deeply is independent of what anyone concludes about it. Your journal, your questions, and your growing precision with the language are the real credentials this course offers.

Practice: (1) Write your study charter: sessions per week, duration, anchored time, place, materials list, and monthly review date, sign and date it. (2) Do one full session using the four-movement structure and the worksheet, on a passage you have not studied in this course; file the completed worksheet as your template example. (3) Choose your reading plan, the annual portion cycle or a focused alternative, and write its first month of assignments with dates. (4) Reread your entire course journal start to finish; write a two-page reflection on how your questions, vocabulary, and reading precision changed from Lesson 1 to now, quoting your own early and late entries. That reflection is your graduation document, the proof, in your own words, of what eight lessons of disciplined study built.

courses.title: Conversational Hindi
courses.tagline: Speak practical everyday Hindi from day one: Devanagari sounds, core grammar, and real conversations.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational Hindi is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday Hindi from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. The first half builds your foundation — Devanagari sounds and script basics, greetings, hona and the present tense, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep moving after the last lesson. All Hindi words are written in transliteration (Roman letters) with English translations, so you can follow the whole course without knowing the Devanagari script.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational Hindi is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday Hindi from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. The first half builds your foundation — Devanagari sounds and script basics, greetings, hona and the present tense, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep moving after the last lesson. All Hindi words are written in transliteration (Roman letters) with English translations, so you can follow the whole course without knowing the Devanagari script.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will be able to: pronounce Hindi words clearly using the main vowel sounds, consonant groups, and the retroflex sounds that English does not have; recognize the Devanagari letters and read simple words; greet people, introduce yourself, and handle survival phrases when you do not understand; use hona correctly and build sentences in the present tense with correct masculine and feminine agreement; count to one hundred and beyond, tell the time, and use days, months, and dates; ask and answer questions about directions, prices, and everyday topics; talk about things you did using the past tense; make plans for the future and hold a full restaurant or travel conversation; and run a simple daily practice routine that keeps your speaking improving.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read one lesson at a time, out loud wherever you see Hindi — saying the words with your mouth, not just your eyes, is what builds speaking skill. Each lesson opens with what it teaches, explains the concept with concrete examples, includes full example dialogues with English translations, warns you about common beginner mistakes, and ends with a clearly labeled Practice exercise. Do the practice before moving on, even if it feels easy; the lessons build on each other, and Lesson 3's verbs depend on Lesson 1's sounds. Aim for one lesson per day, and re-read the previous lesson's dialogues the next morning as a warm-up. There are no grades and no timers — steady repetition beats cramming.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites. This course starts from zero and assumes you have never studied Hindi before. Everything — even how to make each sound and how the Devanagari script works — is explained from scratch, and every Hindi word is written in Roman letters so you can speak from the first page without learning a new alphabet first. If you already know a little Hindi, Lesson 1's pronunciation rules are still worth reading, because correcting a bad accent habit early saves months later. You do not need any textbook, app, or prior grammar knowledge; a notebook for writing out the practice exercises is the only thing that will help.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes — it is a text/workbook course, and everything you need is on the page: explanations, example sentences, translated dialogues, and practice exercises. The materials section includes a vocabulary cheat sheet and a 30-day practice plan template you can print and reuse. Work through the lessons in order, do the exercises in writing and out loud, and you will finish with usable, spoken Hindi for real everyday situations.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Devanagari Sounds and Script Basics
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to pronounce Hindi clearly from the start, and introduces the Devanagari script so you can recognize the letters you will see on signs, menus, and screens. Your goal in this lesson is not a perfect accent — it is clarity. If your vowels are clean and you can make the retroflex sounds, Hindi speakers will understand you even while you are still learning words. Every Hindi word in this course is written in transliteration — Roman letters — with an English translation, so you can speak from the first page. The Devanagari letters are shown alongside so you can start recognizing them, but you never need them to say a word.

Start with the vowels, which are pure and steady, unlike English vowels that glide. A sounds like the u in but: namaste (nah-mah-STAY, hello), kam (kahm, work). AA is the same sound held longer, like the a in father: naam (naahm, name), baat (baaht, talk). I sounds like the i in bit: din (din, day), dil (dil, heart). II is longer, like ee in see: neend (neend, sleep), jeena (JEE-nah, to live). U sounds like the oo in put: tum (toom, you), sun (soon, listen). UU is longer, like oo in food: door (door, far), bhool (bhool, mistake). E sounds like the ay in day: mera (MAY-rah, my), dekh (daykh, look). AI is a glide, like the i in bike: kaisa (KAY-sah, how), paisa (PAY-sah, money). O sounds like the o in go: mera dost (my friend), bol (bohl, speak). AU is a glide, like ow in cow: aur (owr, and/more), kaun (kown, who). The difference between short and long vowels matters: kam (work) versus kaam (work, with a long aa, also means work but spelled differently) — and din (day) versus deen (religion) are different words entirely. Practice each pair until your ear hears the length difference.

Now the consonants, which Devanagari organizes by where they are made in the mouth — a brilliantly logical system. The throat group (ka, kha, ga, gha): kaam (work), khaana (food), ghar (house), ghaas (grass). The palate group (cha, chha, ja, jha): chai (tea), chha (shade), jaana (to go), jhaad (broom). The retroflex group is the famous one: the tongue tip curls back to touch the roof of the mouth — ta, tha, da, dha, na with a dot underneath in transliteration. Practice: daal (lentils), thanda (cold), ladka (boy), bada (big). English speakers often say these as dental sounds; curling the tongue back even slightly makes a real difference. The dental group (ta, tha, da, dha, na) is made with the tongue on the teeth: tum (you), din (day), naam (name). The lip group (pa, pha, ba, bha, ma): paani (water), phal (fruit), baat (talk), bhaai (brother), mera (my). Then ya, ra, la, va, and the sibilants sha, sa, ha: shaam (evening), saal (year), haan (yes).

Three sound rules will save you constant confusion. First, the aspirated consonants: kha, gha, chha, tha, pha, bha are the same as ka, ga, cha, ta, pa, ba but with a strong puff of air. Hold your hand in front of your mouth: khaana (food) should blow air on your hand, kaam (work) should not. The difference matters: kaal means time or death depending on context, but khaal means skin. Second, the schwa: the short a at the end of a written word is usually dropped in speech. Namaste is written with a final a but said nah-mah-STAY, and Ram is written Raama but said Raam. Third, the nasal sounds: a dot above a vowel or the letters n and m make the vowel nasal — main (I) is said with the vowel through the nose, and gaan (to go) ends with a nasal glide.

The Devanagari script itself is simpler than it looks. It is written left to right, and each letter is a syllable: a consonant carries an inherent a sound unless a vowel sign changes it. The vowels have their own standalone letters and small marks (matras) that attach to consonants: ka becomes ki with the i mark, ku with the u mark, ke with the e mark. Consonants can join into combined letters (conjuncts) when two consonants meet with no vowel between them, as in namaste, where the s and t join. You do not need to write Devanagari to speak Hindi, but recognizing the letters helps you read signs, menus, and messages. Learn to recognize the ten most common letters first: ka, na, ma, ra, ta, ha, sa, pa, ba, ya — they appear in almost every word.

Here is a short dialogue using only sounds from this lesson. Read it aloud slowly:

Anita: Namaste! Aap ka naam kya hai? (nah-mah-STAY, aap kah naahm kyAH hay) — Hello! What is your name?
Rahul: Namaste. Mera naam Rahul hai. Aap ka? (MAY-rah naahm RAH-hool hay, aap kah) — Hello. My name is Rahul. And yours?
Anita: Mera naam Anita hai. Aap se milkar khushi hui. (MAY-rah naahm ah-NEE-tah hay, aap say mil-KAR KHOO-shee hoo-EE) — My name is Anita. Pleased to meet you.
Rahul: Mujhe bhi. Aap Hindi bolte hain? (moo-JAY bhee, aap HIN-dee BOHL-tay hayn) — Me too. Do you speak Hindi?
Anita: Haan, thoda. (haahn, THOH-dah) — Yes, a little.

Say the whole dialogue five times today; it is your first Hindi conversation.

Practice: Write out these ten words, mark the long vowels and retroflex consonants, and say each aloud three times: namaste, khaana, ghar, daal, paani, chai, ladka, thanda, mera, shaam. Next, pair up kam/kaam, din/deen, and sun/soon and say each pair until the short-versus-long difference is obvious. Finally, read the dialogue above aloud five times, then cover the pronunciation hints and read it again — you should be able to produce the sounds from the transliteration alone.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully. Hindi speakers are warm and encouraging with learners, and even a few Hindi sentences will change how people respond to you.

Start with greetings. Namaste (nah-mah-STAY) is the standard hello and goodbye, used any time of day and in any setting. Namaskar (nah-mah-SKAAR) is a slightly more formal version. Suprabhat (soo-prah-BHAAT) means good morning, shubh ratri (shoobh RAAT-ree) means good night, and phir milenge (phir mi-LEN-gay) means we will meet again — a warm goodbye. Alvida (ahl-vi-DAH) is a more formal farewell. For introductions: Mera naam... hai (My name is...). Aap ka naam kya hai? asks someone's name formally; Tumhara naam kya hai? is the informal version for friends and peers. Aap se milkar khushi hui (Pleased to meet you) and Mujhe bhi (Me too) complete the introduction. Kahan se hain aap? (Where are you from?) follows naturally.

Now the small-talk core. Aap kaise hain? (How are you? — formal) is the standard question; Tum kaise ho? is the informal version. Common answers: Main theek hoon (I am fine), Bahut achha (Very good), Sab theek hai (Everything is fine), Main thaka hua hoon (I am tired — masculine) or Main thaki hui hoon (I am tired — feminine). Aur aap? (And you?) keeps the conversation balanced. Kripya is please, dhanyavaad is thank you, bahut dhanyavaad is thank you very much, and koi baat nahi (no problem / it does not matter) is you are welcome. A frequent beginner mistake is answering Aap kaise hain? with a long life story; a short answer plus Aur aap? gives you twice the practice and sounds natural. Note the respectful word ji, added after a name or yes/no: Haan ji (Yes, respectfully), Rahul ji (Mr. Rahul) — it softens everything and shows good manners.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. Mujhe samajh nahi aaya (I did not understand). Kya aap dobara keh sakte hain? (Can you say it again?). Dheere boliye, kripya (Speak slowly, please). Kya aap angrezi bolte hain? (Do you speak English?). Maaf kijiye (Excuse me / Sorry). Mujhe madad chahiye (I need help). Iska matlab kya hai? (What does this mean?). Main thoda Hindi bolta hoon (I speak a little Hindi — masculine) or Main thoda Hindi bolti hoon (feminine). These phrases will rescue you in any Hindi-speaking place, and people respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Watch for this social mistake: Hindi runs on three levels of you — aap (formal, respectful), tum (informal, friends and peers), and tu (very informal, close friends, children, or someone younger). Use aap with strangers, shopkeepers, elders, and in any formal setting; switch to tum only when the other person does or with clear peers and friends. Using tu with a stranger is not a grammar failure — it is a social one, and it can come across as rude or condescending. When in doubt, start with aap. A second classic trap: saying Main bhooka hoon is fine for I am hungry, but feelings of heat and cold use a different pattern — Mujhe garmi lag rahi hai (I am feeling hot, literally heat is touching me) and Mujhe thand lag rahi hai (I am feeling cold) — which you will meet properly in Lesson 3.

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with the translations:

Priya: Namaste! Aap ka naam kya hai? — Hello! What is your name?
Arjun: Namaste. Mera naam Arjun hai. Aur aap ka? — Hello. My name is Arjun. And yours?
Priya: Mera naam Priya hai. Aap se milkar khushi hui. — My name is Priya. Pleased to meet you.
Arjun: Mujhe bhi, Priya ji. Aap kahan se hain? — Me too, Priya. Where are you from?
Priya: Main London se hoon. Aur aap? — I am from London. And you?
Arjun: Main Delhi se hoon. Kya aap Hindi bolti hain? — I am from Delhi. Do you speak Hindi?
Priya: Thoda. Dheere boliye, kripya. — A little. Speak slowly, please.
Arjun: Zaroor. Aap kaise hain aaj? — Of course. How are you today?
Priya: Main theek hoon, dhanyavaad. Aur aap? — I am fine, thank you. And you?
Arjun: Main bhi theek hoon. Phir milenge! — I am fine too. See you again!

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, one feeling word, goodbye) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then practice the survival phrases: cover the Hindi column, read the English, and say the Hindi from memory until you can do all eight without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with the retroflex sounds and long vowels from Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Hona, Gender, and the Present Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson tackles the most important verb in Hindi — hona (to be) — plus the present tense and the gender system, which lets you describe what you do every day. Hona appears in nearly every sentence, and the present tense is built from a verb stem plus a hona form, so mastering this one pattern unlocks hundreds of sentences. Hindi has two genders — masculine and feminine — and every noun, adjective, and verb ending must agree with the gender of its subject. It feels strange at first, but the patterns are regular and you will learn them by example.

HONA (to be) — memorize this table completely: main hoon (I am), tum ho (you are, informal), aap hain (you are, formal), vah hai (he/she/it is), ham hain (we are), ve hain (they are). Use it for identity, origin, description, profession, and location: Main American hoon (I am American), Vah doctor hai (She is a doctor), Ham Delhi mein hain (We are in Delhi), Ve khush hain (They are happy). Note that Hindi word order is subject-object-verb, so the verb comes last: Main Delhi mein hoon, not Main hoon Delhi mein. Also note that vah is used for both he and she — gender shows up in the verb and adjective endings instead. Aap hain is used with aap even for one person, because respect is grammatically plural in Hindi.

GENDER is the heart of Hindi grammar. Most masculine nouns end in -a: ladka (boy), ghar (house — an exception ending in a consonant but still masculine), kitaab is feminine despite ending in b. Most feminine nouns end in -i: ladki (girl), kursi (chair), nadi (river). Adjectives agree: achha ladka (good boy), achhi ladki (good girl), achhe ladke (good boys), bada ghar (big house), badi kursi (big chair). The masculine plural ending is -e, the feminine plural is usually -iyan or stays the same: ladkiyan (girls). When in doubt about a noun's gender, learn it with the word — say ek ladka, ek ladki — and the gender will stick with the vocabulary. Two high-value patterns use hona with feelings: Mujhe bhookh lagi hai (I am hungry — literally hunger has come to me) and Mujhe pyaas lagi hai (I am thirsty). Learn these as fixed phrases today, along with Mujhe garmi lag rahi hai (I feel hot) and Mujhe thand lag rahi hai (I feel cold).

Now the present tense. Take the verb stem, add -ta for masculine singular, -ti for feminine singular, -te for masculine plural or formal, and then the matching form of hona. Karna (to do): main karta hoon (m, I do), main karti hoon (f, I do), tum karte ho, aap karte hain, vah karta hai (m) / karti hai (f), ham karte hain, ve karte hain. Bolna (to speak): Main Hindi bolta hoon (m, I speak Hindi), Main Hindi bolti hoon (f). Jaana (to go): Main bazaar jaata hoon (m, I go to the market). Rahna (to live/stay): Main Delhi mein rehta hoon (m, I live in Delhi). Kaam karna (to work): Main ek bank mein kaam karta hoon (m, I work in a bank). The pattern never changes — stem plus ta/ti/te plus hona — which makes Hindi verbs wonderfully regular once you know the gender of the subject.

Essential verbs to learn as vocabulary: jaana (to go): main jaata hoon. Aana (to come): main aata hoon. Khaana (to eat): main khaata hoon. Peena (to drink): main peeta hoon. Dekhna (to see/watch): main dekhta hoon. Padhna (to read/study): main padhta hoon. Likhna (to write): main likhta hoon. Sona (to sleep): main sota hoon. Chahna (to want): main chahta hoon. Sakna (to be able to): main kar sakta hoon (m, I can do it), main kar sakti hoon (f). These appear in nearly every conversation, so they repay memorization immediately. Note that sakna follows another verb: Main Hindi bol sakta hoon (m, I can speak Hindi).

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, forgetting gender agreement: saying main karta hoon when you are a woman — it must be main karti hoon. The ending must match the speaker, not the listener. Second, putting the verb in the English position: Hindi is subject-object-verb, so Main khaana khaata hoon (I food eat) is correct, while Main khaata hoon khaana is wrong. Time words come early in the sentence: Main aaj bazaar jaata hoon (Today I go to the market), Main kal Delhi jaata hoon (Tomorrow I go to Delhi).

Dialogue — two coworkers at lunch:

Vikram: Aap kahan kaam karte hain? — Where do you work?
Meera: Main ek bank mein kaam karti hoon. Main cashier hoon. Aur aap? — I work at a bank. I am a cashier. And you?
Vikram: Main teacher hoon. Main ek school mein kaam karta hoon. — I am a teacher. I work at a school.
Meera: Kya aap aaj thake hue hain? — Are you tired today?
Vikram: Nahi, main theek hoon. Kya aap mere saath khaana khaana chahti hain? — No, I am fine. Do you want to eat lunch with me?
Meera: Haan, zaroor. Ham restaurant jaate hain? — Yes, of course. Shall we go to the restaurant?
Vikram: Chaliye. Mujhe bhookh lagi hai. — Let us go. I am hungry.

Practice: Conjugate in writing: karna, bolna, jaana, khaana, hona — masculine and feminine singular, all persons. Then write six sentences about yourself: two with hona (identity/origin/profession), two with feeling phrases (bhookh, pyaas, garmi, thand), two with present-tense action verbs. Say each sentence aloud, checking the gender endings. Finally, translate to Hindi: She is a doctor. She works in a hospital. She is tired today. She wants tea. Check: Vah doctor hai. Vah hospital mein kaam karti hai. Vah aaj thaki hui hai. Vah chai chahti hai.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Numbers are pure utility — prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules — and telling the time unlocks appointments, opening hours, and travel. Hindi numbers from one to twenty are irregular and must be memorized, but after twenty the pattern becomes regular, and after one hundred it is simple. This lesson is built for repetition and out-loud drilling, because numbers only become useful when they are automatic.

Numbers 0–20 (memorize these exactly): 0 shunya, 1 ek, 2 do, 3 teen, 4 chaar, 5 paanch, 6 chhah, 7 saat, 8 aath, 9 nau, 10 das, 11 gyaarah, 12 baarah, 13 terah, 14 chaudah, 15 pandrah, 16 solah, 17 satrah, 18 athaarah, 19 unnees, 20 bees. Tens: 30 tees, 40 chaalees, 50 pachaas, 60 saath, 70 sattar, 80 assi, 90 nabbe. 100 = sau, 200 = do sau, 1,000 = hazaar, 100,000 = lakh, 10,000,000 = crore. Numbers between tens follow a pattern: 21 = ikkees, 22 = baaees, 25 = pachchees, 33 = taintees, 45 = paintaalees, 99 = ninyanve. The in-between numbers are the hardest part of Hindi counting, so drill them in groups: all the twenties together, then the thirties, then the forties. Phone numbers are read digit by digit: nau aath saat shunya for 9870. Note that Hindi speakers in India often switch to English numbers for large figures in business, but market prices, times, and ages are always in Hindi.

Telling time: Samay kya hai? or Kitne baje hain? (What time is it?). Ek bajaa hai (It is one o'clock), Do baje hain (It is two o'clock), Teen baje hain (It is three). Minutes use special words: Sava do (2:15 — a quarter past two), Dhai baje (2:30 — two and a half), Paune teen (2:45 — a quarter to three). So the pattern is: sava + hour for quarter past, dhaai/saadhe + hour for half past, paune + next hour for quarter to. Saadhe teen is 3:30, paune chaar is 3:45. For appointments: Meri meeting teen baje hai (My meeting is at three o'clock). Dopahar is midday/afternoon, shaam is evening, raat is night, subah is morning. Hindi speakers often use the 12-hour clock in speech and add subah, dopahar, shaam, or raat to make the time clear: Teen baje shaam ko (Three in the evening).

Days of the week: Somvaar (Monday), Mangalvaar (Tuesday), Budhvaar (Wednesday), Guruvaar or Brihaspativaar (Thursday), Shukravaar (Friday), Shanivaar (Saturday), Ravivaar (Sunday). All end in -vaar, which means day — a handy memory hook. Months: the English month names are widely used in India — January, February, March — and you can use them freely. Traditional Hindi month names exist (Chaitra, Vaishakh) but are used mainly for festivals and the religious calendar. Dates: Paanch May, Bees October. To say what day it is: Aaj kaun sa din hai? — Aaj Mangalvaar hai. What is the date? Aaj ki tareekh kya hai? — Aaj do November hai. Today is aaj, tomorrow is kal, yesterday is also kal — context tells you which — this week is is hafte, next week is agle hafte, last week is pichhle hafte.

Practical money and shopping vocabulary, since numbers live there: Yeh kitne ka hai? (How much is this?), Yeh das rupay ka hai (This is ten rupees), Bahut mehenga hai (It is very expensive), Yeh sasta hai (It is cheap), Kya aap ke paas chutta hai? (Do you have change?), Bill dijiye, kripya (The bill, please). In markets you will hear prices as bare numbers — paintaalees for 45 — so number fluency pays off immediately. Bargaining is normal in markets: Kam kijiye (Reduce the price, please) and Thoda kam karo (Make it a little less) are useful, said with a smile. The rupee is the currency, and prices are often written with Devanagari numerals as well as Western numerals, so recognizing the Devanagari digits from Lesson 1 helps.

Dialogue — at a market:

Dukaandar: Namaste! Aap ko kya chahiye? — Hello! What do you want?
Graahak: Mujhe do kilo seb chahiye, kripya. — I would like two kilos of apples, please.
Dukaandar: Baarah rupay hue. Aur kuch? — That is twelve rupees. Anything else?
Graahak: Santre kitne ke hain? — How much are the oranges?
Dukaandar: Paanch rupay kilo. — Five rupees a kilo.
Graahak: Mujhe teen kilo dijiye. Aap kitne baje band karte hain? — Give me three kilos. What time do you close?
Dukaandar: Ham aath baje band karte hain. — We close at eight.
Graahak: Dhanyavaad. Kya aap ke paas bees rupay ke chutta hai? — Thanks. Do you have change for twenty rupees?
Dukaandar: Haan, zaroor. — Yes, of course.

Practice: Count aloud from 0 to 100 without stopping — including the irregular teens and the twenties and thirties — then backwards from 50 to 0. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in Hindi. Then drill time: say the current time in Hindi every 15 minutes for two hours (Kitne baje hain? — ... baje hain), paying special attention to sava, saadhe, and paune forms. Finally, memorize the market dialogue's price lines and role-play a shopping trip where you buy three different items, asking Yeh kitne ka hai? each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to form every kind of question, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in a Hindi-speaking place. The good news: Hindi questions are simple. You already know the main pattern from the dialogues so far, and this lesson makes it automatic.

Hindi has two main ways to ask a question. 1) Rising intonation: keep normal word order and raise your voice at the end — Aap Hindi bolte hain? (Do you speak Hindi?). This is the most common in speech. 2) Question word in place: put the question word where the answer would go — Aap kahan rehte hain? (Where do you live?), Yeh kitne ka hai? (How much is this?), Aap kab jaa rahe hain? (When are you going?). The verb stays at the end in both patterns, which is the golden rule of Hindi word order. The core question words: kya (what — Yeh kya hai? = What is this?), kaun (who), kaun sa (which), kahan (where), kab (when), kyun (why), kaise (how), kitna/kitne (how much/many). Note that kya at the start of a sentence turns it into a yes/no question — Kya aap Hindi bolte hain? — while kya in the middle asks what: Aap kya karte hain? (What do you do?). Kyunki (because) answers kyun — Kyun? Kyunki main thaka hua hoon (Why? Because I am tired).

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. Kahan hai...? (Where is...?), Main ... kaise jaaoon? (How do I get to...?), Kya yeh paas hai? (Is it near?), Kya yeh door hai? (Is it far?), daayein (to the right), baayein (to the left), seedha (straight ahead), kone par (on the corner), ... ke beech mein (between... and...). When someone answers, listen for: seedha jaaiye (go straight), daayein mudiye (turn right), baayein mudiye (turn left), paar kijiye (cross). Polite opener: Maaf kijiye, station kahan hai? (Excuse me, where is the station?). And the lifesaver follow-up: Kya aap mujhe map par dikha sakte hain? (Can you show me on the map?). Hindi uses postpositions where English uses prepositions — mein (in), par (on), se (from/with), ko (to), tak (until) come after the noun: bazaar mein (in the market), ghar se (from home), Delhi tak (until Delhi).

Shopping questions beyond prices: Kya aap ke paas... hai? (Do you have...?), Kya ... hai? (Is there...? / Are there...?), Kya main pehen kar dekh sakta hoon? (Can I try it on? — masculine) or Kya main pehen kar dekh sakti hoon? (feminine), Kya aap ke paas bada size / chhota size hai? (Do you have a bigger/smaller size?), Kya main card se bhugtan kar sakta hoon? (Can I pay by card?), Aap kitne baje kholte hain? (What time do you open?). Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: Aap kahan se hain? (Where are you from?), Aap kya karte hain? (What do you do?), Aap yahan kab se hain? (How long have you been here?), Kya aap ko sheher pasand hai? (Do you like the city?), Aap kya salaah denge? (What do you recommend?). Two mistakes to avoid: saying Aap ka naam kya hai? with tum endings by accident (keep aap with hain, tum with ho), and answering a question you only half understood — use Mujhe theek se samajh nahi aaya, kya aap dobara keh sakte hain? instead of guessing.

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Yatri: Maaf kijiye, museum kahan hai? — Excuse me, where is the museum?
Raahgir: Yeh paas hai. Seedha jaaiye aur baayein mudiye. — It is near. Go straight and turn left.
Yatri: Kya yeh paidal door hai? — Is it far on foot?
Raahgir: Nahi, paanch minute hai. Yeh bank aur pharmacy ke beech mein hai. — No, it is five minutes. It is between the bank and the pharmacy.
Yatri: Bahut dhanyavaad. Is sadak ka naam kya hai? — Thank you very much. What is this street called?
Raahgir: Yeh MG Road hai. — This is MG Road.

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Lata: Aap kahan se hain? — Where are you from?
Mark: Main Belgium se hoon. Aur aap? — I am from Belgium. And you?
Lata: Main yahin se hoon, Delhi se. Aap yahan kab se hain? — I am from here, from Delhi. How long have you been here?
Mark: Do hafte se. Mujhe sheher bahut pasand hai. — For two weeks. I like the city a lot.
Lata: Aap kya dekhne ki salaah denge? — What do you recommend seeing?
Mark: Main kal park jaana chahta hoon. Aap kyun nahi aate? — I want to go to the park tomorrow. Why do you not come?
Lata: Achha vichaar hai! Kitne baje? — Good idea! At what time?
Mark: Das baje. Ham yahin milte hain. — At ten. We meet here.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with rising intonation. Then memorize the direction-giving sequence (seedha, daayein, baayein, kone par) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in Hindi, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with a partner or alone, then change three details (city, time, place) and run it again — this is how small talk becomes automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The Past Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: Aap ne kal kya kiya? (What did you do yesterday?). Hindi past tense has one special feature — the word ne — but once you learn its pattern, the tense is regular and easy to use.

The past tense has two patterns. For intransitive verbs (verbs with no direct object, like go, come, sleep, stay), the formula is: stem + -a (masculine) / -i (feminine) / -e (masculine plural) + tha/thi/the. Main gaya (m, I went), Main gayi (f, I went), Main soya (m, I slept), Main soyi (f, I slept), Vah aaya (m, he came), Vah aayi (f, she came), Ham gaye (we went). For transitive verbs (verbs with a direct object, like eat, drink, see, buy, do), Hindi uses the ergative marker ne after the subject, and the verb agrees with the OBJECT, not the subject: Main ne khaana khaaya (m, I ate food — khaana is masculine so khaaya), Main ne kitaab padhi (f, I read a book — kitaab is feminine so padhi), Usne chai pee (He drank tea — chai is feminine so pee), Main ne film dekhi (f, I watched a movie — film is feminine so dekhi), Ham ne khaana khaaya (We ate food). This ne pattern is the single most important grammar point in Hindi — drill it until it feels natural.

Common past forms to memorize now: kiya (did — karna), khaaya/khaayi (ate — khaana), peeya/peeyi (drank — peena), dekha/dekhi (saw — dekhna), gaya/gayi (went — jaana), aaya/aayi (came — aana), liya/li (took — lena), diya/di (gave — dena), bola/boli (said — bolna), mila/mili (met/found — milna), soya/soyi (slept — sona), khareeda/khareedi (bought — khareedna). Time words anchor the past: kal (yesterday/tomorrow), kal raat (last night), pichhle hafte (last week), pichhle saal (last year), aaj subah (this morning). Note that tha/thi/the is often dropped in casual speech when the time is clear: Main kal bazaar gaya is understood as I went to the market yesterday, though Main kal bazaar gaya tha is the full form.

Negation goes before the verb: Main ne khaana nahi khaaya (I did not eat food), Vah nahi aaya (He did not come). Questions work as in Lesson 5: Aap ne khaana khaaya? / Kya aap ne khaana khaaya? with rising intonation is the everyday form. Two beginner warnings. First, forgetting ne: saying Main khaana khaaya instead of Main ne khaana khaaya is the most common beginner error in Hindi — ne is required with transitive verbs in the past tense. Second, agreeing the verb with the subject instead of the object: Main ne kitaab padha is wrong because kitaab is feminine, so it must be Main ne kitaab padhi. Check two things every time: is there a ne after the subject, and does the verb ending match the object?

Dialogue — talking about the weekend:

Anita: Aap ne is hafte ke ant mein kya kiya? — What did you do this weekend?
Rohan: Main apne parivaar ke saath samudra tat par gaya. — I went to the beach with my family.
Anita: Kaisa tha? Mausam achha tha? — How was it? Was the weather nice?
Rohan: Haan, mausam bahut achha tha. Ham ne tairna kiya aur machhli khaayi. — Yes, the weather was very nice. We swam and ate fish.
Anita: Badhiya! Main ghar par rahi. Main ne film dekhi aur kitaab padhi. — Great! I stayed home. I watched a movie and read a book.
Rohan: Kya aap ko film pasand aayi? — Did you like the movie?
Anita: Haan, mujhe bahut pasand aayi. Aur Ravivaar ko, aap ne kya kiya? — Yes, I loved it. And Sunday, what did you do?
Rohan: Main der tak soya aur apne mata-pita se mila. — I slept in and met my parents.

Practice: Write a paragraph of 8–10 sentences about what you did yesterday, using at least five different past-tense verbs (mix ne verbs and intransitive verbs, masculine and feminine objects). Read it aloud twice. Then conjugate in writing: jaana, khaana, dekhna, karna, peena — full past tense, masculine and feminine, with correct ne and correct object agreement. Finally, answer these aloud in complete Hindi sentences: Aap ne kal kya khaaya? Aap kitne baje uthe? Aap ne pichhle hafte ke ant mein kya kiya? Kya aap ne is hafte film dekhi?

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Making Plans — Future Expressions + Restaurant and Travel Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to talk about the future — making plans, accepting invitations, and handling two of the most useful real-world conversations: ordering in a restaurant and navigating travel. Future talk is what turns you from a tourist into someone who can actually live in Hindi: booking, inviting, promising, and planning.

Hindi has two easy ways to express the future. The everyday one is the future tense itself: stem + -unga (masculine singular, I), -ungi (feminine singular, I), -ega (masculine singular, he), -egi (feminine singular, she), -enge (plural/formal). Main jaaunga (m, I will go), Main jaaungi (f, I will go), Main khaaunga (m, I will eat), Main khaaungi (f, I will eat), Vah aayega (m, he will come), Vah aayegi (f, she will come), Ham jaayenge (we will go), Aap aayenge (you will come — formal). The second way is the present tense with a future time word, which is very common in casual speech: Kal main Delhi jaata hoon (Tomorrow I go to Delhi) is understood as a future plan. For this level, default to the future endings in conversation and recognize the present-tense-with-future-time pattern when you hear it. Promises use the future tense: Main aap ko kal phone karoonga (m, I will call you tomorrow), Main aap ko kal phone karoongi (f).

Restaurant vocabulary and phrases. Menu (the menu), shuruaat (starter), mukhya khaana (main course), meetha (dessert/sweets), peene ki cheez (drink). Ordering: Mujhe... chahiye (I would like...), Mere liye... (For me...), Aap kya salaah denge? (What do you recommend?). During the meal: Yeh bahut swaadisht hai (It is delicious), Kya aap mujhe... laa sakte hain? (Can you bring me...?), Bill dijiye, kripya (The bill, please). Common mistake: ordering with a bare Mujhe chahiye is fine, but adding kripya (please) and using aap forms with the waiter sounds much better. Tipping: a small tip is appreciated in restaurants, though service charges are sometimes included — check the bill. Indian food to know: roti (flatbread), naan (oven bread), chawal (rice), daal (lentils), sabzi (vegetables), samosa (fried pastry), thali (platter meal), chai (tea), lassi (yogurt drink), mithai (sweets). Vegetarian food is everywhere — Main shakahari hoon (I am vegetarian) is a useful sentence.

Travel phrases. Hawai adda par (at the airport): Gate kahan hai? (Where is the gate?), Meri flight ... baje hai (My flight is at...), Meri booking hai (I have a reservation). Hotel mein: Mujhe ek double kamra chahiye (I would like a double room), Nashta kitne baje hai? (What time is breakfast?), Kya aap ke paas wifi hai? (Do you have wifi?). Problems: Mera passport kho gaya hai (I lost my passport), Mujhe madad chahiye (I need help), Pharmacy kahan hai? (Where is a pharmacy?). At the station: Train kis platform se jaayegi? (From which platform does the train leave?), Delhi ke liye ek ticket dijiye, kripya (A ticket to Delhi, please). Note how much of this reuses Lessons 2–5 — the course is compounding.

Dialogue 1 — at a restaurant:

Waiter: Namaste. Kya aap ki booking hai? — Hello. Do you have a reservation?
Claire: Haan, Claire ke naam par. — Yes, under the name Claire.
Waiter: Is taraf, kripya. Kya aap menu dekhna chahti hain? — This way, please. Would you like to see the menu?
Claire: Haan, dhanyavaad. Aaj ka khaas khaana kya hai? — Yes, thanks. What is the special dish today?
Waiter: Yeh murghi aur chawal hai. Yeh bahut swaadisht hai. — It is chicken and rice. It is delicious.
Claire: Mujhe yeh chahiye, aur ek salad. Aur aap, Jeroen? — I would like that, and a salad. And you, Jeroen?
Jeroen: Mere liye machhli. Kya aap mujhe paani laa sakte hain, kripya? — For me, the fish. Can you bring me water, please?
Waiter: Abhi laata hoon. — Right away.
(baad mein) Claire: Bill dijiye, kripya. — The bill, please.
Waiter: Paintees rupay hue. — That is thirty-five rupees.

Dialogue 2 — making weekend plans:

Nikhil: Aap Shanivaar ko kya karenge? — What will you do on Saturday?
Emma: Main apni behen se milne jaaungi. Aur aap? — I am going to visit my sister. And you?
Nikhil: Main Shanivaar subah bazaar jaaunga. Kya aap aana chahti hain? — I am going to go to the market on Saturday morning. Do you want to come?
Emma: Haan, zaroor. Ham kitne baje milenge? — Yes, gladly. What time shall we meet?
Nikhil: Nau baje. Uske baad ham saath khaana khaayenge. — At nine. Afterwards we will eat lunch together.
Emma: Badhiya. Main aap ko Shukravaar ko phone karoongi. — Perfect. I will call you Friday to confirm.

Practice: Write three plans for next week using the future tense, and three promises using the future tense with a time word. Then write a full restaurant dialogue (8+ lines) where you order a starter, main, drink, and dessert, ask for the bill, and react to the food. Say it all aloud. Finally, plan a real weekend in Hindi: where you will go, who you will see, what you will eat — five sentences minimum, out loud.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Conversation Practice Drills + Your 30-Day Practice Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson does two things: it gives you structured conversation drills that combine everything from Lessons 1–7, and it hands you a concrete 30-day plan so your Hindi keeps growing after the course ends. A course can teach you the material, but only a routine turns material into fluency — so treat this lesson as the most important one to actually do. Hindi rewards speakers who try: even a short Hindi sentence earns goodwill, and every conversation you attempt makes the next one easier.

Drill 1 — The Two-Minute Monologue. Set a timer for two minutes and talk about your day — present for routines (Main saat baje uthta hoon...), past for what already happened (Main ne chai pee...), future for what is next (Main kaam par jaaunga...). Do not stop to look up words; describe around them (likhne wali cheez = the thing for writing, if you forget pen). Fluency is built by keeping going, not by being perfect. Do this drill daily — it is the single highest-value exercise in this course.

Drill 2 — Question Tennis. Write 20 question words and topics on slips of paper (Kahan...?, Kab...?, Kyun...?). Draw one and answer in two full sentences, then ask a follow-up question. Example: draw Kahan? → Aap kahan paida hue? Main Ohio mein paida hua. Draw Kyun? → Aap Hindi kyun seekh rahe hain? Main Hindi seekh raha hoon kyunki main yatra karna chahta hoon. If you practice with a partner, rally: they answer your question, then ask you one back. Ten minutes of question tennis covers more ground than an hour of passive review.

Drill 3 — Situation Cards. Write real situations on cards: Your hotel has no hot water — complain politely, Ask a stranger for directions to the pharmacy, Order dinner for two including a dietary restriction, Small talk with a taxi driver for five minutes. Draw a card and perform it aloud, both roles. These force you to combine vocabulary, grammar, and politeness under mild pressure — exactly what real conversations feel like. Rotate through all your cards weekly.

Two mistakes that stall learners at this stage. First, the perfection trap: refusing to speak until every conjugation is certain. Hindi speakers are generous with beginners who try; they cannot help beginners who stay silent. Speak with 70% accuracy today rather than 100% accuracy never. Second, passive consumption: re-reading lessons and calling it study. Reading feels productive but builds recognition, not production. Every minute of speaking aloud counts triple compared to silent review — your mouth needs the reps. A third Hindi-specific trap: mixing up aap, tum, and tu endings. When you switch levels mid-conversation, it confuses the listener — pick aap with strangers and stay with aap until the other person invites you to tum.

Your 30-day practice plan. Week 1 — Foundations lock-in: 20 minutes daily. Days 1–2: re-read Lessons 1–2 dialogues aloud. Days 3–4: conjugate hona and present-tense verbs from Lesson 3 out loud, masculine and feminine. Days 5–7: number and time drills from Lesson 4 until 0–100 is automatic, including the sava, saadhe, and paune time forms. Week 2 — Conversation ignition: 25 minutes daily. Daily two-minute monologue plus question tennis; re-do the Lesson 5 and 6 dialogues with changed details. Week 3 — Real situations: 30 minutes daily. One situation card per day performed aloud; write a daily journal of five Hindi sentences about your day (present + past + future mix). Week 4 — Live fire: 30+ minutes daily. Have at least three real conversations — with a tutor, a language-exchange partner, a Hindi-speaking neighbor, or even ordering food in Hindi. Record one, listen back, and note your three most frequent errors to drill next month.

Track it simply: a notebook page per day with the date, minutes practiced, and one line about what felt easier than last week. If you miss a day, never miss twice — the streak matters more than any single session. After 30 days, repeat the cycle with harder situation cards and longer monologues; you now own a system, not just a course.

Practice: Do Drill 1 right now — two full minutes about your day in Hindi, out loud, no stopping. Then write out your personal Week 1 schedule with exact times (e.g., 7:30 AM, 20 minutes, Lessons 1–2 dialogues). Finally, write five situation cards of your own based on your life — travel you plan, restaurants you visit, people you meet — and perform the first one today. Shubhkaamnaayein — you are a Hindi speaker now. Keep speaking.

courses.title: Islamic Studies Foundations: Theology, Law & Quranic Study
courses.tagline: A structured introduction to Islamic theology, jurisprudence, and Quranic study methods.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Islamic Studies Foundations is a written, self-paced introduction to the core areas of Islamic learning: theology (aqidah), the Quran, the life of the Prophet Muhammad (the Seerah), the essentials of Islamic law (fiqh) through the five pillars, practical daily worship, and Islamic ethics. It is written for beginners — new Muslims, students exploring the faith, and anyone who wants a structured path into a vast tradition rather than scattered fragments. The course explains what Muslims believe and practice in clear language, frames beliefs respectfully as the tradition understands them, and teaches you how to study: which sources to trust, how to read the Quran with understanding, and how to build a sustainable learning routine. Each of the eight lessons ends with a practice or reflection exercise, and the final lesson helps you design your own ongoing study path.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Islamic Studies Foundations is a written, self-paced introduction to the core areas of Islamic learning: theology (aqidah), the Quran, the life of the Prophet Muhammad (the Seerah), the essentials of Islamic law (fiqh) through the five pillars, practical daily worship, and Islamic ethics. It is written for beginners — new Muslims, students exploring the faith, and anyone who wants a structured path into a vast tradition rather than scattered fragments. The course explains what Muslims believe and practice in clear language, frames beliefs respectfully as the tradition understands them, and teaches you how to study: which sources to trust, how to read the Quran with understanding, and how to build a sustainable learning routine. Each of the eight lessons ends with a practice or reflection exercise, and the final lesson helps you design your own ongoing study path.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: You will learn how Muslims approach the study of their religion: the Quran and the Sunnah as primary sources, and the student's etiquette of sincerity, humility, and seeking qualified teachers. You will learn the six articles of faith that form Islamic theology. You will learn the structure of the Quran, its major themes, and methods for reading it with comprehension. You will learn the key periods of the Prophet's life and the lessons Muslims draw from them. You will learn the five pillars of Islam and how they function in daily practice, with practical guides to prayer and fasting. You will learn the Islamic framework of ethics — character, family, and community responsibilities. Finally, you will build a personal, lifelong study routine suited to your schedule and level.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read the lessons in order, one at a time, and complete the Practice or Reflection exercise at the end of each lesson — the exercises turn information into understanding and take about fifteen to thirty minutes each. Keep a study notebook for your answers and questions; you will return to it in the final lesson. If you are a new Muslim, pair this course with learning the basic acts of worship in Lesson 6 as early as possible, and consider finding a local teacher or study circle to learn alongside. There are no exams; your measure of progress is whether you can explain each core concept in your own words and whether your daily practice is growing steadier.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no formal prerequisites and no assumed background in Arabic or Islamic studies. All Arabic terms are introduced with plain explanations, and all concepts are built from first principles. You will need a notebook or document for the exercises, a copy of the Quran in a translation you can read comfortably (any reputable translation is fine for this course's purposes), and optionally the study-tracker material included in this package.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This is a written course package: eight text lessons, this syllabus, and three practical study materials you can reuse. There is no video content, no audio, and no live instruction — everything is designed to be read, reflected on, and kept as a reference. The course presents mainstream Islamic teachings in an educational, non-sectarian way; where scholars hold differing views on details, this is noted honestly rather than resolved. For personal religious rulings or deep questions, the course consistently directs you to qualified scholars and trusted teachers rather than treating these lessons as a final authority.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How to study Islam — the Quran and Sunnah as sources, a student's approach
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you how Muslims approach the study of Islam: what counts as a source, how the sources relate to each other, and the attitude and habits of a good student. Islam is a tradition with fourteen centuries of scholarship behind it, and beginners often feel lost between two extremes: random videos and articles of uneven quality on one side, and dense classical texts on the other. This lesson gives you a map before you start the journey, so the lessons that follow land in the right framework.

Muslims hold that Islam's primary sources are two: the Quran and the Sunnah. The Quran is the book Muslims believe was revealed by God to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Gabriel, and it is the central text of the faith — recited in worship, memorized by millions, and treated as the ultimate authority. The Sunnah is the Prophet's example: what he said, did, and approved of, preserved in reports called hadith. Islamic tradition holds that the Quran gives the principles and the Sunnah shows their lived application — the Quran commands prayer, for example, and the Sunnah shows how the Prophet prayed. Understanding this pair is the key to everything: whenever you encounter a teaching, a useful habit is to ask, 'Where does this come from — the Quran, the Sunnah, or a scholar's interpretation of them?' That single question protects you from treating someone's opinion as divine law and from dismissing genuine scholarship as mere opinion.

Beyond the two primary sources sits the scholarly tradition: centuries of jurists, theologians, and commentators who interpreted the sources, debated them, and organized them into the schools of thought and sciences you will meet in later lessons. A beginner does not need to master this literature — but you do need to respect it. When you find scholars disagreeing on a detail, that disagreement is usually a sign of a living, careful tradition, not a flaw in it. Your job as a student is not to declare winners between scholars; it is to learn the mainstream positions, understand why they differ, and follow qualified guidance for your own practice.

The student's approach matters as much as the sources. Islamic tradition emphasizes intention: learn to draw closer to God and to live better, not to win arguments or collect credentials. It emphasizes humility: the more you learn, the more you realize how much you do not know, and that realization is a sign of progress, not failure. It emphasizes teachers: while books and courses like this one are valuable, Muslims traditionally learn from qualified, trustworthy teachers who can correct misunderstandings before they harden. And it emphasizes gradualism: the Prophet's own teaching unfolded step by step over many years, and your learning should too. Do not try to master theology, law, and Arabic in a month; build steadily.

A common mistake is learning from unqualified or anonymous sources. The internet rewards confidence, not knowledge, and some of the loudest voices about Islam online have the thinnest credentials. Prefer teachers and writers with recognized training, a traceable scholarly lineage, and a reputation among other scholars — and be wary of anyone whose main credential is a large following. When something you read surprises or alarms you, check it against a second reputable source before accepting or spreading it.

A second common mistake is studying rulings before foundations. Beginners often dive into detailed legal debates — the fine points of this or that ruling — before they understand the theology and purposes behind the law. This produces rigid, anxious practice. The classical curriculum did the opposite: beliefs first, then worship, then the details of law. This course follows that order deliberately.

Practice: In your notebook, write a one-paragraph statement of your intention for studying — why you are learning and what you hope changes in your life. Then list three sources you currently learn from (people, books, sites, channels) and, for each, note what you actually know about the author's qualifications. Finally, write down one question about Islam you most want answered by the end of this course; keep it visible and revisit it in Lesson 8.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Aqidah — the six articles of faith explained
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the six articles of faith (aqidah) that form the foundation of Islamic theology: belief in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree. Muslims consider these the non-negotiable core of the religion — the creed that defines what it means to be a believer — and everything else in Islamic practice flows from them. Understanding them clearly is the prerequisite for every later lesson, because Islamic law, worship, and ethics all make sense as responses to these beliefs.

The first article is belief in God (Allah): that there is one God, without partner, who created and sustains everything. Muslims believe God is eternal, all-knowing, all-powerful, and utterly unlike His creation — the Quran's short chapter Al-Ikhlas describes Him as One, eternal, neither begetting nor begotten, with nothing comparable to Him. This strict monotheism (tawhid) is the axis of the entire faith: worship is directed to God alone, and associating partners with Him is considered the gravest wrong. Notice the practical consequence: if God alone is worthy of worship and God alone controls outcomes, then prayer, trust, and gratitude all have exactly one address.

The second article is belief in the angels: beings of light created by God who obey Him perfectly and carry out His commands. Muslims believe angels record human deeds, deliver revelation (Gabriel brought the Quran to Muhammad), and perform functions in the cosmos and in the afterlife. Belief in angels reinforces a Muslim's sense of being observed and accompanied — actions have witnesses, and no good deed goes unrecorded.

The third and fourth articles concern revelation: belief in God's books and His messengers. Muslims believe God sent guidance to humanity through scriptures — including the Torah given to Moses, the Psalms given to David, the Gospel given to Jesus — and that the Quran is the final, preserved revelation confirming what came before. Likewise, Muslims believe God sent messengers to every nation: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and finally Muhammad, whom Muslims regard as the last prophet. This framework explains Islam's relationship with Judaism and Christianity: Muslims honor their prophets and scriptures as genuinely from God, while holding that the Quran is the final and fully preserved message.

The fifth article is belief in the Last Day: that human life does not end at death, that all people will be resurrected and judged, and that the righteous will enter Paradise and the wicked will face punishment. Islamic tradition holds that this belief gives moral weight to every choice — justice may be delayed in this world, but it is certain in the next. It is also a source of hope: suffering borne patiently is not wasted, and no oppressor escapes accountability forever.

The sixth article is belief in divine decree (qadar): that God knows and has decreed all things, while humans still possess real choice and moral responsibility. This is the subtlest article, and scholars have written volumes on how divine knowledge and human freedom coexist. For the beginner, the practical teaching is balance: trust God's decree without fatalism — plan, work, and take the means — and accept outcomes without despair, knowing that what missed you was never meant for you.

A common mistake is treating theology as trivia to memorize rather than beliefs to internalize. The articles of faith are meant to reshape how you see reality: one God worthy of worship, a watched and meaningful life, accountability beyond death. If your study of aqidah does not change your prayer and your character, it has stayed on the surface.

A second common mistake is arguing about theological fine points before the foundations are firm. The classical scholars debated subtle questions for centuries; a beginner who dives into those debates usually ends up confused or partisan. Learn the six articles solidly first — the debates can wait.

Reflection: Write each of the six articles in your own words, in one sentence each, as if explaining them to a curious friend. Then pick the article you find hardest to grasp fully and write a paragraph on why — what questions does it raise for you? Finally, choose one article and write down one concrete way it should change your daily behavior this week (for example: belief in the Last Day might change how you handle a small injustice at work). Keep these notes; you will revisit them when you study ethics in Lesson 7.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The Quran — structure, major themes, reading with understanding
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you the structure of the Quran, its major themes, and practical methods for reading it with understanding rather than just moving your eyes across the page. Muslims regard the Quran as the literal word of God, the religion's central miracle, and the primary source of guidance — so learning how it is organized and how to approach it is one of the most important skills in this course.

Structurally, the Quran has 114 chapters called surahs, arranged roughly from longest to shortest (after the short opening chapter, Al-Fatihah). Each surah is divided into verses called ayahs. The surahs fall into two broad periods: the Meccan surahs, revealed before the migration to Medina, which focus on theology — God's oneness, the afterlife, the stories of earlier prophets — and the Medinan surahs, revealed after the Muslim community was established, which add law, social organization, and community guidance. Knowing which period a surah belongs to often unlocks its emphasis: a Meccan passage is usually building faith, while a Medinan one is usually organizing life. The Quran is not arranged chronologically, so a good translation with brief introductions to each surah is worth its weight for a beginner.

The major themes run through the whole book. First, tawhid — God's oneness and uniqueness — appears on nearly every page, in arguments, parables, and direct address. Second, prophethood: the stories of earlier prophets (Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and others) are retold not as history lessons but as moral mirrors — each story ends, implicitly or explicitly, with 'and what will you do?' Third, the afterlife: vivid descriptions of resurrection, judgment, Paradise, and Hellfire that make accountability feel immediate. Fourth, guidance for the community: worship, charity, family law, commerce, and relations with others. Fifth, reflection on the natural world: the Quran constantly points to the sky, the earth, and the human body as signs inviting thought. When you read, try naming which theme a passage serves — it turns reading from a chore into a conversation.

How should you read it? Start with method, not volume. First, read with a reputable translation and, when possible, a short commentary (tafsir) for context — verses were revealed in situations, and knowing the situation often clarifies the meaning. Second, read slowly and in small portions: a few verses with reflection beats a whole chapter skimmed. The Prophet's companions are reported to have learned the Quran in small sections, acting on what they learned before moving on — a model worth imitating. Third, ask three questions of every passage: What is God telling me about Himself? What is He telling me about how to live? What is one thing I will do differently because of this? Fourth, memorize gradually: begin with the short chapters at the end of the Quran, which are also the ones used most in daily prayer.

A common mistake is reading the Quran like a novel, cover to cover, and quitting in confusion around the long legal passages of the second chapter. There is nothing wrong with cover-to-cover reading, but beginners often do better starting with the shorter Meccan surahs at the end of the book, where the core message of faith is stated most directly, then working backward into the longer chapters with a commentary at hand.

A second common mistake is quoting verses without context to win arguments — with others or with yourself. A verse about a specific historical conflict is not a general license, and a verse about God's mercy is not a reason to ignore His commands. The classical scholars insisted that interpretation requires knowledge of context, language, and the broader text; humility before the text is part of reverence for it.

Practice: Choose one short surah from the end of the Quran (for example, Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, or An-Nas). Read it in translation three times, slowly. Then write: (1) what the surah says about God, in your own words; (2) which of the five major themes it belongs to; (3) one concrete action or attitude change it suggests for your week. If you can, listen to a recitation of the same surah afterward and note any verse that strikes you differently when heard.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The Seerah — key periods of the Prophet's life and their lessons
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the key periods of the Prophet Muhammad's life (the Seerah) and the lessons Muslims draw from each. Muslims regard Muhammad as the final prophet and the living embodiment of the Quran's teachings — his life is studied not as distant history but as a practical model. Understanding the arc of his life gives context to the Quran's revelation and to the origins of the Muslim community.

The story begins in Mecca. Muhammad was born into the tribe of Quraysh, orphaned young, and raised by his grandfather and then his uncle. Islamic tradition remembers him as known for honesty and trustworthiness long before prophethood — his community called him the trustworthy one. At the age of forty, while retreating in the cave of Hira, Muslims believe he received the first revelation through the angel Gabriel: 'Read.' He began calling people quietly, then publicly, to the worship of one God and to moral reform. For over a decade, the early Muslims faced ridicule, boycott, and persecution; some sought refuge in Abyssinia, and the Prophet himself lost his wife Khadijah and his protective uncle in the same difficult year. The lesson Muslims draw from the Meccan period is perseverance in principle under pressure: the message did not bend to make life easier, and faith was built before power was.

The turning point is the Hijrah, the migration to Medina. Invited by the people of Medina, the Prophet and his followers relocated, and this event marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina, the Muslim community took shape: a mosque was built as the community's center, bonds of brotherhood were established between the migrants and their hosts, a covenant organized relations with neighboring tribes, and revelations addressed law, worship, and social life. The Medinan period shows Islam as a complete way of organizing a community — not only personal devotion but justice, consultation, and care for the vulnerable. It also included defensive conflicts with Meccan forces; Islamic tradition frames these as fought under strict ethical limits — no targeting of noncombatants, no destruction of property or nature — limits that later scholars developed into a detailed ethics of warfare.

The final period brings the return to Mecca. After years of tension, the Prophet entered Mecca peacefully in a conquest remembered for its general amnesty — former enemies were forgiven rather than punished, a moment Muslims cite as the supreme example of mercy in victory. In his final years he consolidated the community, delivered the Farewell Sermon emphasizing equality, justice, and the sanctity of life and property, and passed away in Medina, where he is buried. The lesson of this period, as Muslims understand it, is that strength is completed by mercy: the community that had been persecuted chose forgiveness at the moment it could have chosen revenge.

How should a student study the Seerah? Read it for principles, not just events. After each episode, ask: what character trait is being modeled — patience, courage, forgiveness, consultation?
