You learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the three writing systems (hiragana, katakana, and kanji), the core grammar behind daily sentences, and full dialogues with English translations and romaji so you always know exactly what is being said. The first half builds your foundation — pronunciation, greetings, the です/ます sentence pattern, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, restaurant and travel conversations, and longer everyday exchanges. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep improving after the last lesson. Every phrase appears in Japanese script with romaji and an English translation, so you can speak from lesson one while your reading catches up.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will be able to: pronounce Japanese clearly using the five vowels, the special sounds, and the long-vowel and small-っ rules; read and write hiragana and katakana and recognize common kanji; greet people, introduce yourself, and use survival phrases when you do not understand; build sentences with the です/ます pattern, particles, and present-tense verbs; count fluently, tell the time, and use days, months, and dates; ask and answer questions about directions, prices, and everyday topics; talk about things you did using the past tense; make plans and invitations and hold a full restaurant or travel conversation; and run a simple daily practice routine that keeps your speaking improving.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read one lesson at a time, and read every Japanese line out loud — saying the words with your mouth, not just your eyes, is what builds speaking skill. Each lesson opens with what it teaches, explains the concept with concrete examples in Japanese script plus romaji and English, includes full example dialogues with translations, warns you about common beginner mistakes, and ends with a clearly labeled Practice exercise. Do the practice before moving on; the lessons build on each other, and Lesson 3's particles depend on Lesson 1's sounds. Aim for one lesson per day, and re-read the previous lesson's dialogues the next morning as a warm-up. There are no grades and no timers — steady repetition beats cramming. Keep a notebook for writing out kana and the practice exercises by hand.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites. This course starts from zero and assumes you have never studied Japanese before. Everything — even how to make each vowel sound and how to read your first hiragana character — is explained from scratch. If you already know a little Japanese, Lesson 1's pronunciation rules are still worth reading, because correcting a bad accent habit early saves months later. You do not need any textbook or prior grammar knowledge; a notebook for writing out the practice exercises is the only thing that will help.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes — it is a text/workbook course, and everything you need is on the page: explanations, example sentences in Japanese script with romaji and English translations, translated dialogues, and practice exercises. The materials section includes a phrase cheat sheet, a kana quick-reference, and a conjugation worksheet you can print and reuse. The course teaches the polite です/ます style used with strangers and in daily public life. It makes no promise of fluency timelines or test scores; your results depend on the speaking practice you put in. Created with Planet Leads.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronunciation and the Three Writing Systems
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to pronounce Japanese clearly and introduces the three writing systems you will see in every lesson: hiragana, katakana, and kanji. Japanese pronunciation is beautifully consistent — each character is pronounced the same way every time — so once you learn the sounds, you can read almost any word correctly. Your goal is not a perfect accent today; it is clarity. If your vowels are pure and your syllables get equal time, Japanese speakers will understand you.

Japanese uses three scripts together. Hiragana (ひらがな, hiragana) writes native Japanese words and grammar endings: わたし (watashi, I/me), たべます (tabemasu, eat). Katakana (カタカナ, katakana) writes foreign loanwords and names: コーヒー (kōhī, coffee), アメリカ (amerika, America). Kanji (かんじ, kanji) are characters that carry meaning: 日 (sun/day), 本 (book/origin), 人 (person) — together 日本 (nihon) means Japan. Beginners learn hiragana first, then katakana, then kanji word by word. In this course every Japanese phrase appears in Japanese script with romaji (Roman letters) beside it, so you can start speaking immediately while your reading catches up.

The five vowels are the foundation — learn them perfectly and everything else follows. あ (a) as in "father." い (i) as in "machine." う (u) as in "flute" but with unrounded lips — say "oo" without pursing your lips. え (e) as in "bed." お (o) as in "go" but short, without the English glide. Each vowel is short and pure, always the same sound. Practice these five words slowly: あめ (ame, rain), いぬ (inu, dog), うみ (umi, sea), えき (eki, station), おかね (okane, money). Give every syllable equal time — Japanese is mora-timed, so たべます (ta-be-ma-su) has four equal beats, never "taBEmaSU" with English-style stress.

Most consonants match English, but learn these four special sounds now. し is "shi" (not "si"). ち is "chi" (not "ti"). つ is "tsu" — say "ts" plus "oo," as in つき (tsuki, moon). ふ is "fu" — blow air gently with your lips nearly closed, halfway between English "who" and "foo." The ら-row (ra ri ru re ro) is a light flap: tap your tongue once against the ridge behind your upper teeth, softer than an English r and lighter than an l. Try らくだ (rakuda, camel).

Three spelling rules change meaning, so master them today. First, long vowels: a vowel held for two beats instead of one. おばさん (obasan) means aunt; おばあさん (obaasan) means grandmother. ビル (biru) is a building; ビール (bīru) is beer. In hiragana, a long "o" is usually written おう (とうきょう, tōkyō) and a long "e" as えい; in katakana a long dash ー marks it (コーヒー, kōhī). Second, the small っ doubles the following consonant with a tiny pause: きて (kite) means "come," but きって (kitte) means a stamp or ticket; がっこう (gakkō) means school. Third, ん (n) is its own syllable: ほん (hon, book) is two beats, ho-n, not one.

Three particles are pronounced differently from how they are written, and this confuses every beginner exactly once. は is pronounced "wa" when it marks the topic: わたしは (watashi wa, as for me). へ is pronounced "e" when it marks direction: とうきょうへ (tōkyō e, to Tokyo). を is pronounced "o" when it marks the object: すしを (sushi o). You now know the three exceptions, so they will never trick you.

Here is the basic hiragana chart — the 46 core characters. Each row shares a consonant: あいうえお (a i u e o), かきくけこ (ka ki ku ke ko), さしすせそ (sa shi su se so), たちつてと (ta chi tsu te to), なにぬねの (na ni nu ne no), はひふへほ (ha hi fu he ho), まみむめも (ma mi mu me mo), やゆよ (ya yu yo), らりるれろ (ra ri ru re ro), わをん (wa wo n). Katakana mirrors this structure exactly: アイウエオ, カキクケコ, and so on — learn hiragana solidly and katakana takes days, not weeks. Kanji each have readings you learn word by word: 日 is ひ (hi) in ひ (sun) and にち (nichi) in 日本 (nihon, Japan). For now, just recognize 日, 本, and 人 as a set.

Practice: Write the あ-row (あいうえお) five times by hand, saying each sound aloud as you write. Read these ten words aloud, giving every syllable equal time: あめ, いぬ, うみ, えき, おかね, さくら (sakura, cherry blossom), ともだち (tomodachi, friend), がっこう, コーヒー, きって. Then drill the long-vowel pairs: say おばさん/おばあさん and ビル/ビール until the two-beat difference is obvious. Finally, read this sentence aloud slowly: わたしは がくせいです (watashi wa gakusei desu — I am a student). It uses only sounds from this lesson, and it is your first real Japanese sentence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully.

Start with greetings, which change with the time of day. おはようございます (ohayō gozaimasu) is good morning — polite and safe everywhere; friends shorten it to おはよう (ohayō). こんにちは (konnichiwa) is hello, used from late morning through the afternoon. こんばんは (konbanwa) is good evening. おやすみなさい (oyasumi nasai) is good night, said before sleep. For introductions: はじめまして (hajimemashite) means "nice to meet you" and is used only the first time you meet someone. わたしはアンナです (watashi wa Anna desu) means "I am Anna" — swap in your own name. [place] からきました ([place] kara kimashita) means "I came from [place]" — for example, アメリカからきました (amerika kara kimashita, I came from America). Close every introduction with よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegai shimasu), which roughly means "please treat me well" — there is no English equivalent, and skipping it makes introductions feel unfinished to Japanese ears.

Politeness words carry enormous weight in Japan. ありがとうございます (arigatō gozaimasu) is thank you; ありがとう (arigatō) is the casual version for friends. どういたしまして (dō itashimashite) is you're welcome. すみません (sumimasen) is the hardest-working word in the language — it means excuse me, sorry, and "may I have your attention," depending on the situation. Use it to get a shop clerk's attention, to apologize for bumping someone, and to preface any request. ごめんなさい (gomen nasai) is sorry for a real mistake. For goodbyes: さようなら (sayōnara) sounds formal and final, like you may not meet again — for everyday partings say じゃあね (jā ne, see you) with friends or しつれいします (shitsurei shimasu, excuse me) when leaving a room or ending a meeting politely.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. わかりません (wakarimasen) — I don't understand. もういちどおねがいします (mō ichido onegai shimasu) — one more time, please. ゆっくりはなしてください (yukkuri hanashite kudasai) — please speak slowly. えいごがはなせますか (eigo ga hanasemasu ka) — can you speak English? トイレはどこですか (toire wa doko desu ka) — where is the bathroom? たすけてください (tasukete kudasai) — please help me. These six phrases will rescue you anywhere in Japan, and people respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Two common mistakes to avoid. First, overusing さようなら for casual goodbyes — it can sound oddly dramatic, as if you are leaving forever. Default to じゃあね with people you will see again. Second, answering the phone or greeting with もしもし (moshi moshi) in person — もしもし is phone-only; saying it face-to-face confuses people. In person, start with すみません or こんにちは.

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with the romaji and translations:

Yuki: はじめまして。わたしはゆきです。アメリカからきました。(Hajimemashite. Watashi wa Yuki desu. Amerika kara kimashita.) — Nice to meet you. I am Yuki. I came from America.
Ken: はじめまして。わたしはけんです。よろしくおねがいします。(Hajimemashite. Watashi wa Ken desu. Yoroshiku onegai shimasu.) — Nice to meet you. I am Ken. Please treat me well.
Yuki: よろしくおねがいします。にほんごがわかりません。(Yoroshiku onegai shimasu. Nihongo ga wakarimasen.) — Likewise. I don't understand Japanese.
Ken: だいじょうぶです。ゆっくりはなします。(Daijōbu desu. Yukkuri hanashimasu.) — It's fine. I'll speak slowly.
Yuki: ありがとうございます。(Arigatō gozaimasu.) — Thank you very much.
Ken: どういたしまして。じゃあね。(Dō itashimashite. Jā ne.) — You're welcome. See you.

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, one thing about yourself, よろしくおねがいします) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then drill the survival phrases: cover the Japanese, read the English, and say the Japanese from memory until you can do all six without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with equal syllable timing from Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Core Grammar — です/ます Sentences, Particles, and Present Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the sentence pattern behind most polite Japanese: the です (desu) and ます (masu) forms, plus the small particles that mark each word's job. Japanese word order is subject-object-verb — the verb always comes last — and particles, not word order, tell you who did what to whom. Master this lesson and you can build thousands of correct sentences with vocabulary you pick up anywhere.

The core pattern is XはYです (X wa Y desu) — "as for X, it is Y." わたしはがくせいです (watashi wa gakusei desu) — I am a student. これはほんです (kore wa hon desu) — this is a book. きょうはあついです (kyō wa atsui desu) — today is hot. The は (pronounced "wa") marks the topic — what the sentence is about. Make it negative with じゃありません: わたしはせんせいじゃありません (watashi wa sensei ja arimasen) — I am not a teacher. Make it a question by adding か at the end with rising intonation: がくせいですか (gakusei desu ka) — are you a student? Answer はい、がくせいです (yes, I am) or いいえ、がくせいじゃありません (no, I am not).

Particles are the grammar's engine. が (ga) marks the subject of a specific action or the thing that is: ねこがすきです (neko ga suki desu) — I like cats. を (pronounced "o") marks the direct object: すしをたべます (sushi o tabemasu) — I eat sushi. に (ni) marks a destination, a target, or a time: とうきょうにいきます (tōkyō ni ikimasu) — I go to Tokyo; さんじにあいます (sanji ni aimasu) — I meet at 3 o'clock. へ (pronounced "e") also marks direction: にほんへいきます (nihon e ikimasu) — I go to Japan. で (de) marks the place where an action happens or the means used: レストランでたべます (resutoran de tabemasu) — I eat at a restaurant; はしでたべます (hashi de tabemasu) — I eat with chopsticks. と (to) means "and" between nouns or "with" a person: ともだちときました (tomodachi to kimashita) — I came with a friend. の (no) shows possession like 's: わたしのほん (watashi no hon) — my book. も (mo) means "also": わたしもいきます (watashi mo ikimasu) — I will go too.

Present-tense verbs in polite speech end in ます. Learn these eight deeply, because they appear everywhere: たべます (tabemasu, eat), のみます (nomimasu, drink), いきます (ikimasu, go), きます (kimasu, come), します (shimasu, do), みます (mimasu, see/watch), かいます (kaimasu, buy), よみます (yomimasu, read). The negative replaces ます with ません: たべません (tabemasen) — I don't eat. The past (Lesson 6) changes ます to ました. A full sentence: まいにちコーヒーをのみます (mainichi kōhī o nomimasu) — I drink coffee every day. Notice the verb is last, the object takes を, and the time word まいにち (every day) floats near the front.

Adjectives come in two families. い-adjectives end in い and describe directly: たかい (takai, expensive/high), やすい (yasui, cheap), おいしい (oishii, delicious), あたらしい (atarashii, new), おおきい (ōkii, big), ちいさい (chiisai, small). な-adjectives need な before a noun: きれい (kirei, pretty/clean), しずか (shizuka, quiet), ゆうめい (yūmei, famous), べんり (benri, convenient). In polite sentences both take です: このケーキはおいしいです (kono kēki wa oishii desu) — this cake is delicious. とうきょうはべんりです (tōkyō wa benri desu) — Tokyo is convenient. この/その/あの (this/that/that over there) go before nouns: このほん (this book), そのかばん (that bag).

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, dropping particles because English doesn't need them — すしたべます is understandable but wrong; すしをたべます is correct. Particles are not decoration; they are the grammar. Second, putting the verb anywhere but last. English habits produce わたしはたべますすし (watashi wa tabemasu sushi) — always rearrange to わたしはすしをたべます.

Dialogue — two coworkers introducing themselves:

Aya: はじめまして。わたしはあやです。かいしゃいんです。(Hajimemashite. Watashi wa Aya desu. Kaishain desu.) — Nice to meet you. I am Aya. I am an office worker.
Riku: はじめまして。わたしはりくです。がくせいです。(Hajimemashite. Watashi wa Riku desu. Gakusei desu.) — Nice to meet you. I am Riku. I am a student.
Aya: まいにちでんしゃでかいしゃへいきます。(Mainichi densha de kaisha e ikimasu.) — I go to the office by train every day.
Riku: わたしはあるいてがっこうへいきます。(Watashi wa aruite gakkō e ikimasu.) — I walk to school.
Aya: がっこうはとおいですか。(Gakkō wa tōi desu ka.) — Is the school far?
Riku: いいえ、ちかいです。とてもべんりです。(Īe, chikai desu. Totemo benri desu.) — No, it's close. It's very convenient.

Practice: Write ten sentences using XはYです with words about yourself (name, job, origin, hobby). Then write eight verb sentences using the eight verbs above, each with a particle (を, に, へ, or で). Say every sentence aloud. Finally, translate to Japanese: "I drink coffee every day. I go to Tokyo by train. This book is interesting (おもしろい)." Check: まいにちコーヒーをのみます。でんしゃでとうきょうへいきます。このほんはおもしろいです。

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Numbers are pure utility — prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules — and telling the time unlocks appointments, opening hours, and travel. Japanese has a few sound changes in its numbers that you must learn exactly, so this lesson is built for repetition and out-loud drilling.

Numbers 1–10: いち (ichi, 1), に (ni, 2), さん (san, 3), よん (yon, 4 — し shi is avoided because it also means death), ご (go, 5), ろく (roku, 6), なな (nana, 7 — しち shichi also exists), はち (hachi, 8), きゅう (kyū, 9 — く ku also exists), じゅう (jū, 10). From 11 up, combine: じゅういち (jūichi, 11), にじゅう (nijū, 20), さんじゅうご (sanjūgo, 35). Hundreds: ひゃく (hyaku, 100) — but watch the sound changes: さんびゃく (sanbyaku, 300), ろっぴゃく (roppyaku, 600), はっぴゃく (happyaku, 800). Thousands: せん (sen, 1000) — さんぜん (sanzen, 3000), はっせん (hassen, 8000). Ten thousand: いちまん (ichiman, 10000) — Japanese counts in ten-thousands, so 100000 is じゅうまん (jūman). Drill these changes until they are automatic; they appear in every price you will ever hear.

Counting things uses counters, and the counter changes with what you count. The general counter 〜つ (tsu) works for small numbers of objects: ひとつ (hitotsu, 1), ふたつ (futatsu, 2), みっつ (mittsu, 3), よっつ (yottsu, 4), いつつ (itsutsu, 5), むっつ (muttsu, 6), ななつ (nanatsu, 7), やっつ (yattsu, 8), ここのつ (kokonotsu, 9), とお (tō, 10). People: ひとり (hitori, 1 person), ふたり (futari, 2 people), then さんにん (sannin, 3 people), よにん (yonin, 4). Age: 〜さい — にじゅうごさい (nijūgosai, 25 years old). Flat things like paper and shirts: 〜まい — さんまい (sanmai, 3). Long things like bottles and pencils: 〜ほん — いっぽん (ippon, 1), さんぼん (sanbon, 3). Books: 〜さつ — いっさつ (issatsu, 1). Times/frequency: 〜かい — いっかい (ikkai, once). The pattern ひとつ/ふたつ/みっつ is worth memorizing cold, because it is the fallback when you forget a specific counter.

Telling time: add じ (ji) to the number — いちじ (ichiji, 1 o'clock), にじ (niji, 2), さんじ (sanji, 3) — but memorize the three irregulars: よじ (yoji, 4 o'clock), しちじ (shichiji, 7 o'clock), くじ (kuji, 9 o'clock). Minutes use ふん/ぷん: いっぷん (ippun, 1 minute), にふん (nifun, 2), さんぷん (sanpun, 3), よんぷん (yonpun, 4), ろっぷん (roppun, 6), はっぷん (happun, 8), じゅっぷん (juppun, 10). はん (han) means half: さんじはん (sanjihan, 3:30). ごぜん (gozen) is AM, ごご (gogo) is PM: ごごさんじ (gogo sanji, 3 PM). Ask the time with いまなんじですか (ima nanji desu ka) — what time is it now? A classic mistake is saying いちふん for one minute — the ぷん sound change is mandatory: いっぷん.

Days of the week: にちようび (nichiyōbi, Sunday), げつようび (getsuyōbi, Monday), かようび (kayōbi, Tuesday), すいようび (suiyōbi, Wednesday), もくようび (mokuyōbi, Thursday), きんようび (kinyōbi, Friday), どようび (doyōbi, Saturday). きょう (kyō) is today, あした (ashita) is tomorrow, きのう (kinō) is yesterday. Months: いちがつ (ichigatsu, January) through じゅうにがつ (jūnigatsu, December), with three irregulars: しがつ (shigatsu, April), しちがつ (shichigatsu, July), くがつ (kugatsu, September). Dates of the month reuse the 〜つ counting for days 1–10: ついたち (tsuitachi, the 1st), ふつか (futsuka, 2nd), みっか (mikka, 3rd), よっか (yokka, 4th), いつか (itsuka, 5th), むいか (muika, 6th), なのか (nanoka, 7th), ようか (yōka, 8th), ここのか (kokonoka, 9th), とおか (tōka, 10th) — then じゅうよっか (jūyokka, 14th), はつか (hatsuka, 20th), にじゅうよっか (nijūyokka, 24th). So May 5th is ごがついつか (gogatsu itsuka).

Money and shopping vocabulary, since numbers live there: いくらですか (ikura desu ka) — how much is it? 〜えん (en) marks yen: せんえん (sen'en, 1000 yen). たかいですね (takai desu ne) — it's expensive, isn't it. やすいですね (yasui desu ne) — it's cheap, isn't it. これをください (kore o kudasai) — this one, please.

Dialogue — at a shop:

Customer: すみません。これはいくらですか。(Sumimasen. Kore wa ikura desu ka.) — Excuse me. How much is this?
Clerk: さんぜんえんです。(Sanzen'en desu.) — It's 3000 yen.
Customer: たかいですね。もうすこしやすいのはありますか。(Takai desu ne. Mō sukoshi yasui no wa arimasu ka.) — That's expensive. Do you have a slightly cheaper one?
Clerk: はい、これです。にせんえんです。(Hai, kore desu. Nisen'en desu.) — Yes, this one. It's 2000 yen.
Customer: じゃあ、これをふたつください。(Jā, kore o futatsu kudasai.) — Then I'll take two of these, please.
Clerk: ありがとうございます。よんせんえんです。(Arigatō gozaimasu. Yonsen'en desu.) — Thank you. That's 4000 yen.

Practice: Count aloud from 1 to 100 without stopping, then backwards from 50 to 1. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in Japanese. Drill the irregular times (よじ, しちじ, くじ) and minutes (いっぷん, さんぷん, ろっぷん, はっぷん, じゅっぷん) until they are automatic. Finally, memorize the shop dialogue's price lines and role-play buying three different items, asking いくらですか each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to use every question word, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in Japan. The good news: Japanese questions are simple — add か to a statement with rising intonation, and question words just slot into the sentence where the answer would go.

The core question words: だれ (dare, who), なに/なん (nani/nan, what), どこ (doko, where), いつ (itsu, when), なぜ/どうして (naze/dōshite, why), どうやって (dōyatte, how — by what means), いくら (ikura, how much), どれ (dore, which one), どの (dono, which — before a noun), いくつ (ikutsu, how many). One rule to memorize: use なん before words starting with d, t, or n sounds, and なに everywhere else. なんですか (nan desu ka) — what is it? なんじですか (nanji desu ka) — what time is it? なにをたべますか (nani o tabemasu ka) — what will you eat? Question words never take は — they take が: だれがきましたか (dare ga kimashita ka) — who came? A classic beginner mistake is だれはきましたか, which sounds wrong to every Japanese ear.

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. 〜はどこですか (〜 wa doko desu ka) — where is 〜? えきはどこですか (eki wa doko desu ka) — where is the station? みぎ (migi, right), ひだり (hidari, left), まっすぐ (massugu, straight), ちかく (chikaku, near), とおく (tōku, far), かど (kado, corner), しんごう (shingō, traffic light). Ask how to get somewhere: とうきょうえきへいくにはどうやって (tōkyō eki e iku ni wa dōyatte) — how do I get to Tokyo station? If you are lost: みちにまよいました (michi ni mayoimashita) — I'm lost. The lifesaver follow-up: ちずをみせてください (chizu o misete kudasai) — please show me on the map. When someone answers, listen for みぎにいってください (please go right) and ひだりをまがってください (please turn left).

Shopping questions beyond prices use これ/それ/あれ (this one near me / that one near you / that one over there): これはなんですか (kore wa nan desu ka) — what is this? それはいくらですか (sore wa ikura desu ka) — how much is that? あれをみせてください (are o misete kudasai) — please show me that one over there. Sizes: おおきいサイズはありますか (ōkii saizu wa arimasu ka) — do you have a large size? Payment: カードでおねがいします (kādo de onegai shimasu) — by card, please. Bargaining politely: もうすこしやすくしてください (mō sukoshi yasuku shite kudasai) — please make it a little cheaper. Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: しゅみはなんですか (shumi wa nan desu ka) — what is your hobby? どこからきましたか (doko kara kimashita ka) — where did you come from? にほんははじめてですか (nihon wa hajimete desu ka) — is this your first time in Japan? なにがすきですか (nani ga suki desu ka) — what do you like?

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Tourist: すみません。えきはどこですか。(Sumimasen. Eki wa doko desu ka.) — Excuse me. Where is the station?
Local: あそこです。まっすぐいって、かどをみぎにまがってください。(Asoko desu. Massugu itte, kado o migi ni magatte kudasai.) — Over there. Go straight and turn right at the corner.
Tourist: あるいてとおいですか。(Aruite tōi desu ka.) — Is it far on foot?
Local: いいえ、ちかいです。ごふんぐらいです。(Īe, chikai desu. Gofun gurai desu.) — No, it's close. About five minutes.
Tourist: ありがとうございます。(Arigatō gozaimasu.) — Thank you very much.

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Emi: しゅみはなんですか。(Shumi wa nan desu ka.) — What is your hobby?
Dan: えいががすきです。あなたは。(Eiga ga suki desu. Anata wa.) — I like movies. And you?
Emi: わたしはりょうりがすきです。にほんははじめてですか。(Watashi wa ryōri ga suki desu. Nihon wa hajimete desu ka.) — I like cooking. Is this your first time in Japan?
Dan: はい、はじめてです。らいしゅうきょうとへいきます。(Hai, hajimete desu. Raishū kyōto e ikimasu.) — Yes, my first time. Next week I'm going to Kyoto.
Emi: きょうとはとてもきれいですよ。(Kyōto wa totemo kirei desu yo.) — Kyoto is very beautiful.
Dan: たのしみです。(Tanoshimi desu.) — I'm looking forward to it.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with rising intonation on か. Memorize the direction sequence (まっすぐ, みぎ, ひだり, かど) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in Japanese, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with changed details (your hobby, your next trip) until the question patterns feel automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The ました Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: きのうなにをしましたか (kinō nani o shimashita ka) — what did you do yesterday? Japanese past tense is wonderfully regular: change the ます ending you already know.

For verbs, replace ます with ました: たべます (I eat) → たべました (tabemashita, I ate). のみました (I drank), いきました (I went), きました (I came), しました (I did), みました (I watched), かいました (I bought), よみました (I read). The negative past replaces ません with ませんでした: たべませんでした (tabemasendeshita) — I didn't eat. For です sentences, です becomes でした: がくせいでした (gakusei deshita) — I was a student. The negative: じゃありませんでした (ja arimasendeshita) — I was not. Read those aloud and feel the pattern — one ending change covers every verb you know, with no irregular verbs to memorize at this level.

い-adjectives form the past by changing the final い to かった: たかい (expensive) → たかかった (takakatta, was expensive). おいしい → おいしかった (oishikatta, was delicious). あたらしい → あたらしかった (was new). The negative past: たかくなかった (takakunakatta, was not expensive). な-adjectives and nouns use でした: きれいでした (kirei deshita, was pretty), しずかでした (shizuka deshita, was quiet), たのしかったです is actually an い-adjective — たのしい (tanoshii, fun) → たのしかった (tanoshikatta, was fun). Two stars of past-tense conversation: よかったです (yokatta desu, it was good) and たのしかったです (it was fun) — you will use these constantly when talking about your weekend.

Time words anchor the past: きのう (kinō, yesterday), おととい (ototoi, the day before yesterday), せんしゅう (senshū, last week), せんげつ (sengetsu, last month), きょねん (kyonen, last year), さっき (sakki, a little while ago). Combine them with the past tense: きのうえいがをみました (kinō eiga o mimashita) — I watched a movie yesterday. せんしゅうとうきょうへいきました (senshū tōkyō e ikimashita) — I went to Tokyo last week. You can also list several past actions with 〜たり〜たりします: えいがをみたり、かいものをしたりしました (eiga o mitari, kaimono o shitari shimashita) — I did things like watching a movie and shopping. This "doing things like X and Y" pattern is extremely natural in conversation.

Two beginner warnings. First, don't use the past tense for things still true now: if you still live in Osaka, say おおさかにすんでいます, not すみました. The past tense means finished and over. Second, watch the い-adjective past spelling: たかい → たかかった doubles the か — writing たかいでした is the classic beginner error. For な-adjectives it really is でした (きれいでした), so keep the two families straight.

Dialogue — talking about the weekend:

Sora: しゅうまつはなにをしましたか。(Shūmatsu wa nani o shimashita ka.) — What did you do on the weekend?
Hana: どようびにとうきょうへいきました。(Doyōbi ni tōkyō e ikimashita.) — I went to Tokyo on Saturday.
Sora: どうでしたか。たのしかったですか。(Dō deshita ka. Tanoshikatta desu ka.) — How was it? Was it fun?
Hana: はい、とてもたのしかったです。ともだちとすしをたべました。(Hai, totemo tanoshikatta desu. Tomodachi to sushi o tabemashita.) — Yes, it was really fun. I ate sushi with a friend.
Sora: いいですね。わたしはいえでえいがをみました。(Ī desu ne. Watashi wa ie de eiga o mimashita.) — Nice. I watched a movie at home.
Hana: おもしろかったですか。(Omoshirokatta desu ka.) — Was it interesting?
Sora: はい、とてもおもしろかったです。にちようびはかいものをしました。(Hai, totemo omoshirokatta desu. Nichiyōbi wa kaimono o shimashita.) — Yes, very interesting. On Sunday I went shopping.

Practice: Write a paragraph of 8–10 sentences about what you did yesterday, using at least five different past-tense verbs plus one い-adjective past and one でした sentence. Read it aloud twice. Then convert these to the past: のみます, かいます, よみます, たかいです, きれいです, がくせいです. Finally, answer aloud in complete Japanese sentences: きのうなにをたべましたか。せんしゅうどこへいきましたか。しゅうまつはたのしかったですか。Then write three more sentences using 〜たり〜たりしました to describe a busy day, and read your whole paragraph to a friend or record yourself and listen carefully for the ました endings on every verb.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Making Plans — Future, Invitations + Restaurant and Travel Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to talk about the future — making plans, expressing wants, inviting people — and handles two of the most useful real-world conversations: ordering in a restaurant and navigating travel. Future talk turns you from a visitor into someone who can actually live in Japanese: booking, inviting, promising, and planning.

Japanese has no separate future tense — the present ます form plus a future time word does the job: あしたとうきょうへいきます (ashita tōkyō e ikimasu) — I will go to Tokyo tomorrow. らいしゅうともだちにあいます (raishū tomodachi ni aimasu) — I will meet a friend next week. らいねんにほんへいきます (rainen nihon e ikimasu) — I will go to Japan next year. Future time words: あした (tomorrow), あさって (day after tomorrow), こんしゅう (this week), らいしゅう (next week), らいげつ (next month), らいねん (next year), こんばん (tonight).

To say you want to do something, change ます to たいです: たべたいです (tabetai desu) — I want to eat. にほんへいきたいです (nihon e ikitai desu) — I want to go to Japan. すしをたべたいです (sushi o tabetai desu) — I want to eat sushi. The negative is たくないです: いきたくないです (ikitakunai desu) — I don't want to go. Note that たいです only describes your own wants or asks about someone else's in a question — never state what a third person wants with たいです alone; use 〜たがっています for others, which this course mentions only so you recognize it.

Invitations have two friendly patterns. 〜ませんか invites: いっしょにたべませんか (issho ni tabemasen ka) — won't you eat with me? えいがをみませんか (eiga o mimasen ka) — shall we watch a movie? 〜ましょう proposes "let's": いきましょう (ikimashō) — let's go. たべましょう (tabemashō) — let's eat. Accept with いいですね、いきましょう (ii desu ne, ikimashō) — sounds good, let's go. Decline softly with ちょっと… (chotto…) — "a little…" — which every Japanese speaker understands as a polite no.

Restaurant phrases. The staff greets you with いらっしゃいませ (irasshaimase) — welcome. Ask for the menu: メニューをください (menyū o kudasai). Ask for a recommendation: おすすめはなんですか (osusume wa nan desu ka). Order with 〜をください or the softer 〜をおねがいします: すしをおねがいします (sushi o onegai shimasu). React to food: おいしいです (oishii desu) — delicious. Ask for the check: おかんじょうをおねがいします (okanjō o onegai shimasu). After eating, say ごちそうさまでした (gochisōsama deshita) — thank you for the meal. Common mistake: pointing and saying just これ (kore, this) — it works but sounds blunt; これをください is polite and natural.

Travel phrases. くうこう (kūkō, airport), ひこうき (hikōki, airplane), ホテル (hoteru, hotel), でんしゃ (densha, train), きっぷ (kippu, ticket), よやく (yoyaku, reservation). At the hotel: よやくがあります (yoyaku ga arimasu) — I have a reservation. チェックインをおねがいします (chekkuin o onegai shimasu) — check-in, please. あさごはんはなんじからですか (asagohan wa nanji kara desu ka) — from what time is breakfast? Problems: パスポートをなくしました (pasupōto o nakushimashita) — I lost my passport. たすけてください (tasukete kudasai) — please help me.

Dialogue 1 — at a restaurant:

Staff: いらっしゃいませ。なんめいさまですか。(Irasshaimase. Nanmeisama desu ka.) — Welcome. How many people?
Ren: ふたりです。(Futari desu.) — Two people.
Staff: こちらへどうぞ。メニューをどうぞ。(Kochira e dōzo. Menyū o dōzo.) — This way, please. Here is the menu.
Ren: おすすめはなんですか。(Osusume wa nan desu ka.) — What do you recommend?
Staff: さしみがおすすめです。(Sashimi ga osusume desu.) — The sashimi is recommended.
Ren: じゃあ、さしみとごはんをおねがいします。(Jā, sashimi to gohan o onegai shimasu.) — Then sashimi and rice, please.
(later) Ren: おいしかったです。おかんじょうをおねがいします。(Oishikatta desu. Okanjō o onegai shimasu.) — It was delicious. The check, please.
Staff: さんぜんごひゃくえんです。(Sanzen gohyaku'en desu.) — That's 3500 yen.

Dialogue 2 — making weekend plans:

Kaito: どようびなにをしますか。(Doyōbi nani o shimasu ka.) — What will you do Saturday?
Mei: ともだちとえいがをみたいです。あなたは。(Tomodachi to eiga o mitai desu. Anata wa.) — I want to watch a movie with a friend. And you?
Kaito: ぼくはかいものをしたいです。いっしょにいきませんか。(Boku wa kaimono o shitai desu. Issho ni ikimasen ka.) — I want to go shopping. Won't you come along?
Mei: いいですね。なんじにあいますか。(Ī desu ne. Nanji ni aimasu ka.) — Sounds good. What time shall we meet?
Kaito: じゅうじにえきのまえであいましょう。(Jūji ni eki no mae de aimashō.) — Let's meet in front of the station at ten.
Mei: わかりました。たのしみです。(Wakarimashita. Tanoshimi desu.) — Got it. I'm looking forward to it.

Practice: Write three plans for next week using the ます form with future time words, and three wants using たいです. Write a full restaurant dialogue (8+ lines) where you enter, order food and a drink, react to the meal, and ask for the check. Say it all aloud. Finally, invite a friend somewhere in Japanese using 〜ませんか, and answer your own invitation with 〜ましょう.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Conversation Practice Drills + Your 30-Day Practice Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson does two things: it gives you structured conversation drills that combine everything from Lessons 1–7, and it hands you a concrete 30-day plan so your Japanese keeps growing after the course ends. A course can teach you the material, but only a routine turns material into skill — so treat this lesson as the most important one to actually do.

Drill 1 — The Two-Minute Monologue. Set a timer for two minutes and talk about your day — present for routines (まいにちしちじにおきます — I wake up at seven every day), past for what already happened (あさごはんをたべました — I ate breakfast), future for what is next (これからかいものをします — I will go shopping now). Do not stop to look up words; describe around them (たべるもの for food if you forget a word). Keeping going matters more than being perfect. Do this drill daily — it is the single highest-value exercise in this course.

Drill 2 — Question Tennis. Write 20 question words and topics on slips of paper (だれ, どこ, いつ, なぜ, いくら). Draw one and answer in two full sentences, then ask a follow-up question. Example: draw どこ → どこにすんでいますか。おおさかにすんでいます。Draw なに → なにをたべましたか。すしをたべました。If you practice with a partner, rally: they answer your question, then ask you one back. Ten minutes of question tennis covers more ground than an hour of passive review.

Drill 3 — Situation Cards. Write real situations on cards: "Your hotel has no hot water — explain politely," "Ask a stranger for directions to the station," "Order dinner for two at a restaurant," "Small talk with a taxi driver for five minutes." Draw a card and perform it aloud, both roles. These force you to combine vocabulary, grammar, and politeness under mild pressure — exactly what real conversations feel like. Rotate through all your cards weekly.

Two mistakes that stall learners at this stage. First, the perfection trap: refusing to speak until every particle is certain. Japanese speakers are generous with beginners who try; they cannot help beginners who stay silent. Speak with 70% accuracy today rather than 100% accuracy never. Second, passive consumption: re-reading lessons and calling it study. Reading feels productive but builds recognition, not production. Every minute of speaking aloud counts triple compared to silent review — your mouth needs the reps, especially for the ら-row flap and long vowels.

Your 30-day practice plan. Week 1 — Foundations lock-in: 20 minutes daily. Days 1–2: re-read Lessons 1–2 dialogues aloud, shadowing the romaji. Days 3–4: write all 46 hiragana from memory, then check the chart. Days 5–7: number and time drills from Lesson 4 until 1–100 and the irregular times are automatic. Week 2 — Conversation ignition: 25 minutes daily. Daily two-minute monologue plus question tennis; re-do the Lesson 5 dialogues with changed details. Week 3 — Real situations: 30 minutes daily. One situation card per day performed aloud; write a daily journal of five Japanese sentences about your day (present + past + future mix). Week 4 — Live fire: 30+ minutes daily. Have at least three real conversations — with a tutor, a language-exchange partner, a Japanese-speaking neighbor, or ordering food in Japanese at a restaurant. Note your three most frequent errors and drill them the following week.

Track it simply: a notebook page per day with the date, minutes practiced, and one line about what felt easier than last week. If you miss a day, never miss twice — the streak matters more than any single session. After 30 days, repeat the cycle with harder situation cards and longer monologues; you now own a system, not just a course.

Practice: Do Drill 1 right now — two full minutes about your day in Japanese, out loud, no stopping. Then write out your personal Week 1 schedule with exact times (for example, "7:30 AM, 20 minutes, hiragana writing"). Finally, write five situation cards of your own based on your life — travel you plan, restaurants you visit, people you meet — and perform the first one today. がんばってください (ganbatte kudasai) — do your best. You are a Japanese speaker now. Keep speaking.

courses.tagline: Learn Java from zero to real programs, one clear step at a time.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Java Programming is a written, self-paced course that takes you from installing Java to writing real programs you can run on your own computer. It is written for complete beginners: no prior coding experience is assumed, and every new idea is introduced with a plain explanation followed by a short code example you can type and run yourself. The first lessons build your core skills: setting up Java, variables and types, decisions with conditionals, repetition with loops, and organizing code into methods. The later lessons teach arrays for working with collections of values, and classes and objects for modeling real things in code. The course closes with a small final project that brings every skill together: a simple catalog program built from classes, arrays, loops, and methods. Each of the eight lessons opens by stating exactly what you will learn, explains concepts in everyday language, shows worked code examples, warns you about the mistakes beginners make most often, and ends with a practice exercise. By the final lesson you will have written several working programs and will know exactly where to go next.

You will learn variables and the main types: whole numbers, decimal numbers, text, single characters, and true-or-false values. You will learn to make decisions with if, else if, and else, and to choose between options with switch. You will learn to repeat work with for loops and while loops. You will learn to organize code into methods with parameters and return values so you can reuse logic instead of copying it. You will learn arrays for storing and processing many values of the same type. You will learn classes and objects: how to define a class with fields and methods, create objects from it, and use constructors. Finally, you will apply all of it in a guided final project: a small catalog program with adding, listing, and searching.

syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course with hands-on exercises: you learn by typing and running code, not by reading alone. Work through the lessons in order, because each one builds on the previous one. After reading a lesson, type its code examples into your own computer and run them; do not just copy and paste. Typing forces you to notice details like semicolons, braces, and capital letters that your eyes skip when reading. When you reach the Practice exercise at the end of a lesson, do it before moving on, even if you think you understood the material. Expect to get stuck: that is normal and part of learning. When an error appears, read the error message carefully, check the lesson's common mistakes notes, and try one fix at a time. Plan roughly one to two hours per lesson including the exercises, and revisit earlier lessons whenever a project asks for a skill you have not used in a while.

syllabus.body: You need a computer you are allowed to install software on, and basic comfort using files and folders, such as creating a folder and saving a file. You will need an internet connection once, to download Java, and a plain text editor for writing code; any plain text editor works, and no specific editor or tool is required for this course. Everything else, concepts, vocabulary, and habits, is taught from zero inside the lessons. If you can follow written instructions and are willing to experiment, you are ready.

syllabus.body: This is a written course package: eight text lessons, this syllabus, and three practical reference materials (a Java quick-reference cheat sheet, a common errors checklist, and a practice plan) that you can print or keep open while you work. This package contains written lessons and worksheets only, no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes. Everything is designed to be read, typed out, and kept as a reference you return to. The lessons teach real, runnable Java using only the standard Java library, so every example works with a normal Java installation and nothing extra to buy or install. The course makes no promise of jobs, income, or certification; it teaches programming skills, and your results will depend on the practice you put in. Read at your own pace, repeat lessons as needed, and keep your project files: they are the start of your programming portfolio.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Setup and Your First Script
lessons.text:
This lesson gets you running JavaScript with zero installation, using the browser you already have. By the end you will know how to open the developer console and run code instantly, how to put a script inside a web page with script tags, and how to store values in variables with let and const. You will also write your first real code: console.log() for showing output. Everything in this lesson is about getting comfortable with the tools, so run every example yourself as you read. JavaScript was born in the browser, which means your setup is already done. Open your browser, press F12 (or right-click any page and choose Inspect), and click the Console tab. You will see a prompt where you can type JavaScript and press Enter to run it immediately. Try typing console.log("Hello, world!") and pressing Enter — the message appears in the console. Try 2 + 3 and you will see 5. The console is your scratchpad for the whole course: whenever you wonder what a piece of code does, test it here in seconds instead of guessing. Nothing you type in the console changes the website permanently — reloading the page wipes it clean, so experiment freely. The console is great for experiments, but real JavaScript lives inside web pages. Create a file called hello.html in a plain text editor, type the following, save it, and open it in your browser by double-clicking the file:

My first script

The script tags mark where JavaScript lives inside the HTML. When the browser loads the page, it runs the code between them top to bottom. Open the console (F12) with this page open and you will see both messages — the page itself shows the heading, while the console shows your script's output. That split is normal: console.log() is a developer tool for seeing what your code is doing, and you will use it in every lesson to check your work. Variables store values under names so you can reuse them. JavaScript has two main ways to declare them: let name = "Maya"; let age = 30; const birthYear = 1995; Use let for values that will change (age = 31 later is fine) and const for values that should never be reassigned — trying birthYear = 2000 after declaring it const is an error. The const habit protects you: most values in a program never need to change, and const makes accidental changes impossible. Names follow the same rules as in most languages: letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs, but no starting with a digit and no spaces. JavaScript convention writes multi-word names in camelCase — firstName, totalPrice — so adopt that style from day one. Like Python, JavaScript is case-sensitive: Age and age are different variables. One more console trick that will save you hours: when something goes wrong, the console shows the error in red with a line number. Clicking the line number jumps to the failing code. Get into the habit of keeping the console open whenever you test a page — silent pages hide their errors, but the console always tells the truth. Two beginner mistakes cause most Lesson 1 frustration. First, quoting: console.log("hi') fails because the opening double quote must close with a double quote. Pick one style per string and match it. Second, forgetting to save the file before reloading the browser, then wondering why nothing changed — the browser only knows about the saved version, so save, then reload, then check the console. If your script "does nothing," those two checks solve it most of the time. Practice: Create greeting.html with a script that declares a const called name holding your name, a let called hobby holding your favorite hobby, and uses console.log() to print two lines, for example "Hi, I'm ..." and "I enjoy ...". Open the page, open the console, and confirm both lines appear. Then, in the console itself (not the file), experiment: type let testScore = 95; then testScore + 5; then const city = "Austin"; then try city = "Denver"; and read the error message. Notice how the console tells you assignment to a constant is not allowed — reading errors calmly is a skill you will use in every lesson.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Types, Operators, and Conditionals
Lesson 3: Functions, Arrays, and Objects
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to organize code into reusable functions and to manage collections of data with arrays and objects. By the end you will define functions with parameters and return values, create and manipulate arrays, model real things with objects, and loop over collections. Functions plus collections are the engine room of JavaScript: nearly every interactive page you build from Lesson 4 onward runs on these three ideas.

A function is a named, reusable block of code. You have already used built-in ones like console.log() and Number(); defining your own looks like this:

function greet(name) {
  return "Hello, " + name + "!";
}

const message = greet("Ava");
console.log(message);       // Hello, Ava!
console.log(greet("Ben"));  // Hello, Ben!

The function line names it (greet) and lists its parameters — the inputs it expects. Calling greet("Ava") passes "Ava" in as the argument, so name becomes "Ava" for that call. The return statement sends a value back to the caller: message receives "Hello, Ava!". The rule of thumb: console.log() is for showing humans, return is for giving values back to your program so it can keep working with them. A function without return still runs, but calling it gives back undefined. Parameters can have defaults — function greet(name, greeting = "Hello") — making them optional, and a function can call other functions, which is how small pieces compose into bigger behavior.

An array is an ordered list written with square brackets: const scores = [85, 92, 78]. Items are numbered from 0, so scores[0] is 85. Useful tools: scores.length gives the count, scores.push(90) adds to the end, scores.pop() removes and returns the last item. Loop over arrays with a classic for loop or the friendlier for...of: for (const score of scores) { console.log(score); } visits each item in order. Arrays hold the lists of things your apps display — tasks, products, messages — so get fluent with them now.

An object groups related values under named keys, written with curly braces: const person = { name: "Ava", age: 30, city: "Austin" }. Read values with dot notation — person.name — or bracket notation — person["name"] — which is handy when the key is stored in a variable. Add or change with person.email = "ava@example.com", and nest freely: objects inside arrays, arrays inside objects. A task in our capstone app will be an object like { text: "Buy milk", done: false }, and the whole list will be an array of those objects — a pattern you will see in real applications everywhere. Loop over an object's keys with for (const key in person) when you need to inspect every property.

Scope determines where a variable can be seen. Variables declared with let or const inside a function exist only while it runs; variables declared at the top level of your script are visible everywhere below. A classic mistake is declaring a variable inside an if block with let and trying to use it after the block ends — it does not exist there. The fix is to declare it in the wider scope first, then assign inside the block. Keeping data flowing through parameters and return values, rather than shared globals, makes functions predictable and testable.

Two mistakes are classic here. First, the off-by-one error: the last item of a 4-item array is scores[3], not scores[4], and scores[4] gives undefined instead of crashing — JavaScript fails silently where other languages shout, so always double-check indexes. Second, treating undefined as a value: reading a misspelled property like person.nam gives undefined, and then person.nam.toUpperCase() crashes. When you see "cannot read properties of undefined", look one step earlier — the property name or the object itself is not what you think.

Practice: Create contacts.html with a script that stores contacts as an array of objects, starting with two you invent ({ name, phone, email } keys). Write three functions: addContact(list, name, phone, email) that pushes a new object and returns the list; findContact(list, name) that loops and returns the matching object or null; and showContacts(list) that logs each contact on one readable line. At the bottom, call them in sequence: show the starting list, add a third contact, show the list again, and search for a name that does not exist — confirm your function returns null without crashing. Test everything in the console and read each output line to verify it says what you expect.
