courses.title: Conversational Korean
courses.tagline: Read, write, and speak Korean: master hangul in lesson one, then build real conversation skills step by step.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational Korean is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday Korean from your very first lesson. You learn the way real conversations work: how the hangul alphabet builds every syllable, the core grammar behind daily sentences, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. Every phrase appears in hangul with romanization and an English translation, so you can speak from lesson one while your reading catches up. The first half builds your foundation — hangul and pronunciation, greetings, essential sentence patterns, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, restaurant and travel conversations, and longer everyday exchanges. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep improving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational Korean is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday Korean from your very first lesson. You learn the way real conversations work: how the hangul alphabet builds every syllable, the core grammar behind daily sentences, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. Every phrase appears in hangul with romanization and an English translation, so you can speak from lesson one while your reading catches up. The first half builds your foundation — hangul and pronunciation, greetings, essential sentence patterns, numbers, and asking questions. The second half takes you into the past tense, making plans, restaurant and travel conversations, and longer everyday exchanges. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day practice plan so you keep improving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will be able to: read and write the entire hangul alphabet and pronounce syllable blocks correctly; greet people, introduce yourself, and use survival phrases when you do not understand; build sentences with particles, the present polite verb form, and correct negation; count fluently with both number systems, tell the time, and use days, months, and dates; ask and answer questions about directions, prices, and everyday topics; talk about things you did using the past tense; make plans and invitations and hold a full restaurant or travel conversation; and run a simple daily practice routine that keeps your speaking improving.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read one lesson at a time, and read every Korean line out loud — saying the words with your mouth, not just your eyes, is what builds speaking skill. Each lesson opens with what it teaches, explains the concept with concrete examples in hangul plus romanization and English, includes full example dialogues with translations, warns you about common beginner mistakes, and ends with a clearly labeled Practice exercise. Do the practice before moving on; the lessons build on each other, and Lesson 3's verbs depend on Lesson 1's hangul. Aim for one lesson per day, and re-read the previous lesson's dialogues the next morning as a warm-up. There are no grades and no timers — steady repetition beats cramming. Keep a notebook for writing out the practice exercises by hand.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites. This course starts from zero and assumes you have never studied Korean before. Everything — even how to read your first hangul character — is explained from scratch. If you already know a little Korean, Lesson 1's pronunciation rules are still worth reading, because correcting a bad pronunciation habit early saves months later. You do not need any textbook or prior grammar knowledge; a notebook for writing out the practice exercises is the only thing that will help.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes — it is a text/workbook course, and everything you need is on the page: explanations, example sentences in hangul with romanization and English translations, translated dialogues, and practice exercises. The materials section includes a phrase cheat sheet, a hangul quick-reference chart, and a verb conjugation worksheet you can print and reuse. The course teaches the polite 요 form used in daily public life. It makes no promise of fluency timelines or test scores; your results depend on the speaking practice you put in. Created with Planet Leads.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Hangul — The Korean Alphabet and Pronunciation
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to read and write hangul, the Korean alphabet — one of the most logical writing systems in the world. Hangul was designed so that each letter's shape hints at how your mouth makes the sound, and the whole alphabet can be learned in a day of focused study. Once you can read hangul, every sign, menu, and message in Korea opens up to you. Your goal today: read every character below and pronounce syllable blocks correctly.

Hangul has 14 consonants and 10 basic vowels. The consonants: ㄱ (g/k), ㄴ (n), ㄷ (d/t), ㄹ (r/l), ㅁ (m), ㅂ (b/p), ㅅ (s), ㅇ (silent at the start of a syllable, "ng" at the end), ㅈ (j), ㅊ (ch), ㅋ (k), ㅌ (t), ㅍ (p), ㅎ (h). The vowels: ㅏ (a), ㅑ (ya), ㅓ (eo — like the "u" in "cut"), ㅕ (yeo), ㅗ (o), ㅛ (yo), ㅜ (u — "oo"), ㅠ (yu), ㅡ (eu — say "oo" with lips spread flat), ㅣ (i — "ee"). The ㅓ/ㅗ and ㅡ distinctions are the hardest for English speakers: ㅓ (eo) is open and relaxed, ㅗ (o) is rounded. Practice the pair: 거 (geo) vs 고 (go), and 서 (seo) vs 소 (so).

Letters stack into syllable blocks, read left-to-right, top-to-bottom. A block always starts with a consonant: 가 = ㄱ + ㅏ (ga), 나 = ㄴ + ㅏ (na), 다 = ㄷ + ㅏ (da). With a final consonant (called batchim) underneath: 한 = ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ (han), 국 = ㄱ + ㅜ + ㄱ (guk). The silent ㅇ fills the first slot when a syllable starts with a vowel: 아 (a), 어 (eo), 오 (o). Read these real words now: 한국 (han-guk, Korea), 한국어 (han-gu-geo, Korean language), 서울 (seo-ul, Seoul), 김치 (gim-chi, kimchi), 사랑 (sa-rang, love). Notice each block is one syllable — say them block by block.

Five pronunciation rules make your Korean sound natural. Rule 1: consonants soften between vowels — the ㄱ in 아기 (a-gi, baby) sounds like "g," but at the start of a word like 가방 (ga-bang, bag) it is a light "k." Rule 2: double consonants ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ, ㅉ are tense and unaspirated — say 아까 (a-kka, a while ago) with tight, held consonants, no puff of air. Rule 3: final consonants (batchim) neutralize — a syllable-final ㄱ, ㅋ, or ㄲ all sound like a soft unreleased "k," so 부엌 (bu-eok, kitchen) ends with a stopped "k," never a released one. Rule 4: ㅅ before ㅣ, ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ sounds like "sh" — 시 (shi, as in 시간, time). Rule 5: ㄹ is a light flap between vowels (like the quick "tt" in American "butter") and an "l" at the end of a syllable: 사랑 (sa-rang) flaps, 서울 (seo-ul) ends with "l."

Combined vowels (diphthongs) complete the set: ㅐ (ae, as in "cat"), ㅔ (e, as in "bed"), ㅒ (yae), ㅖ (ye), ㅘ (wa), ㅙ (wae), ㅚ (oe — round your lips for "o" but say "eh"), ㅝ (wo), ㅞ (we), ㅟ (wi), ㅢ (ui). The ㅐ/ㅔ pair sounds nearly identical in modern speech — don't stress the difference. Practice words: 왜 (wae, why), 뭐 (mwo, what — colloquial), 의사 (ui-sa, doctor), 교회 (gyo-hoe, church).

Common beginner mistakes to fix now. First, pronouncing every consonant with English force — Korean consonants are lighter and less aspirated than English ones; say 다 (da) softly, not with a burst. Second, reading blocks letter-by-letter instead of syllable-by-syllable — train yourself to see 한 as "han," one unit. Third, ignoring batchim: 한국 is "han-guk," two syllables — beginners who say "ha-n-gu-k" as four beats sound choppy.

Practice: Write all 14 consonants and 10 vowels from memory, then check. Read these words aloud block by block: 가방 (bag), 나비 (butterfly), 다리 (leg/bridge), 라면 (noodles), 머리 (head), 바다 (sea), 사과 (apple), 우유 (milk), 전화 (phone), 학교 (school). Then write your name in hangul as best you can using today's letters, and read this sentence: 저는 학생입니다 (jeo-neun hak-saeng-im-ni-da — I am a student). It is your first real Korean sentence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully.

The universal greeting is 안녕하세요 (an-nyeong-ha-se-yo) — hello. It works morning, noon, and night, with everyone. When parting: 안녕히 가세요 (an-nyeong-hi ga-se-yo) to someone who is leaving, 안녕히 계세요 (an-nyeong-hi gye-se-yo) to someone who is staying — mixing these up is the classic beginner error, so learn the pair together: 가세요 = go well (you leave), 계세요 = stay well (you stay). For introductions: 처음 뵙겠습니다 (cheo-eum boep-ge-sseum-ni-da) — nice to meet you (formal, first meeting). 저는 민준입니다 (jeo-neun Minjun-im-ni-da) — I am Minjun (use your own name). 저는 [place]에서 왔어요 (jeo-neun [place]-e-seo wa-sseo-yo) — I come from [place]. 저는 스물다섯 살이에요 (jeo-neun seu-mul-da-seot sa-ri-e-yo) — I am 25 years old. 만나서 반갑습니다 (man-na-seo ban-gap-seum-ni-da) — pleased to meet you.

Politeness words carry enormous weight. 감사합니다 (gam-sa-ham-ni-da) is thank you — formal and safe everywhere; 고맙습니다 (go-map-seum-ni-da) is equally polite and slightly warmer. 고마워요 (go-ma-wo-yo) is the casual version for friends. 천만에요 (cheon-ma-ne-yo) is you're welcome. 죄송합니다 (joe-song-ham-ni-da) is I'm sorry for a real mistake; 실례합니다 (sil-lye-ham-ni-da) is excuse me to get attention or to pass by. A frequent beginner mistake is using 반말 (casual speech) with strangers because it sounds easier — with anyone older or unfamiliar, stay in the polite 요/습니다 forms this course teaches.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. 잘 모르겠어요 (jal mo-reu-ge-sseo-yo) — I don't understand well. 천천히 말씀해 주세요 (cheon-cheo-ni mal-sseum-hae ju-se-yo) — please speak slowly. 영어 하세요? (yeong-eo ha-se-yo? — do you speak English?). 화장실이 어디예요? (hwa-jang-si-ri eo-di-ye-yo? — where is the bathroom?). 도와주세요 (do-wa-ju-se-yo) — please help me. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주세요 (da-shi han beon mal-sseum-hae ju-se-yo) — please say it once more. These six phrases will rescue you anywhere in Korea, and people respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Two cultural notes that prevent real mistakes. First, bowing accompanies greetings — a small nod with 안녕하세요 is natural; a deep bow is for formal apologies or elders. Second, Koreans often ask age early in conversation (몇 살이에요? — how old are you?) — it is not rude; age determines speech levels and social roles, so answer cheerfully.

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with romanization and translations:

Jiwon: 안녕하세요! 처음 뵙겠습니다. (An-nyeong-ha-se-yo! Cheo-eum boep-ge-sseum-ni-da.) — Hello! Nice to meet you.
Minjun: 안녕하세요! 저는 민준입니다. (An-nyeong-ha-se-yo! Jeo-neun Min-jun-im-ni-da.) — Hello! I am Minjun.
Jiwon: 저는 지원입니다. 미국에서 왔어요. (Jeo-neun Ji-won-im-ni-da. Mi-gu-ge-seo wa-sseo-yo.) — I am Jiwon. I come from America.
Minjun: 아, 그렇군요. 만나서 반갑습니다. (A, geu-reo-kun-yo. Man-na-seo ban-gap-seum-ni-da.) — Ah, I see. Pleased to meet you.
Jiwon: 한국어를 잘 못해요. 천천히 말씀해 주세요. (Han-gu-geo-reul jal mo-tae-yo. Cheon-cheo-ni mal-sseum-hae ju-se-yo.) — I'm not good at Korean. Please speak slowly.
Minjun: 네, 알겠습니다. (Ne, al-ge-sseum-ni-da.) — Yes, understood.
Jiwon: 감사합니다! 안녕히 가세요. (Gam-sa-ham-ni-da! An-nyeong-hi ga-se-yo.) — Thank you! Goodbye (you're leaving).

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, your age or job, nice to meet you) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then drill the survival phrases: cover the Korean, read the English, and say the Korean from memory until you can do all six without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with correct syllable blocks.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Core Grammar — Particles, Present Tense, and Word Order
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the sentence patterns behind most Korean conversation: particles that mark each word's role, the present polite verb form, and subject-object-verb word order. Korean puts the verb last — always — and particles, not word order, tell you who did what to whom. Master this lesson and you can build thousands of correct sentences.

The basic order is subject-object-verb: 저는 밥을 먹어요 (jeo-neun ba-beul meo-geo-yo) — I eat rice. 저는 물을 마셔요 (jeo-neun mu-reul ma-syeo-yo) — I drink water. 저는 학교에 가요 (jeo-neun hak-gyo-e ga-yo) — I go to school. Time words go before the verb: 저는 내일 가요 (jeo-neun nae-il ga-yo) — I go tomorrow.

Particles are the grammar's engine. 은/는 (eun/neun) marks the topic — what the sentence is about: 저는 학생이에요 (jeo-neun hak-saeng-i-e-yo) — as for me, I am a student. Use 는 after vowels (저는), 은 after consonants (이름은 — i-reu-meun, as for the name). 이/가 (i/ga) marks the subject of a specific action or description: 비가 와요 (bi-ga wa-yo) — rain comes (it's raining). 누가 왔어요? (nu-ga wa-sseo-yo? — who came?). 을/를 (eul/reul) marks the object: 밥을 먹어요 (ba-beul meo-geo-yo), 를 after vowels (사과를 — sa-gwa-reul). 에 (e) marks destination or time: 학교에 가요 (to school), 세 시에 만나요 (se shi-e man-na-yo — meet at 3 o'clock). 에서 (e-seo) marks where an action happens or where you come from: 집에서 먹어요 (ji-be-seo meo-geo-yo — I eat at home), 미국에서 왔어요 (I came from America). 와/과 (wa/gwa) means "and/with": 친구와 갔어요 (chin-gu-wa ga-sseo-yo — I went with a friend). 도 (do) means "also": 저도 가요 (jeo-do ga-yo — I go too). 의 (ui) shows possession: 제 이름 (je i-reum — my name).

Present-tense verbs in the polite 요 form follow one rule. Take the verb stem (가다 → 가): if the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아요; otherwise add 어요; 하다 verbs become 해요. 가다 (to go) → 가요. 먹다 (to eat) → 먹어요. 보다 (to see) → 봐요. 오다 (to come) → 와요. 하다 (to do) → 해요. 있다 (to be/exist) → 있어요. 없다 (not exist) → 없어요. Learn these eight deeply — they appear everywhere. 저는 영화를 봐요 (jeo-neun yeong-hwa-reul bwa-yo) — I watch movies. Negative with 안: 안 가요 (an ga-yo) — I don't go. Or with 지 않다: 가지 않아요 (ga-ji a-na-yo). "Cannot" uses 못: 못 가요 (mot ga-yo) — I can't go.

입니다/입니까 handles "is" sentences: 저는 학생입니다 (I am a student). 이것은 책입니다 (i-geo-seun chae-gim-ni-da — this is a book). Question: 학생입니까? (are you a student?). In the 요 form: 학생이에요 / 학생이에요? Adjectives work like verbs in Korean — they conjugate: 예쁘다 (to be pretty) → 예뻐요. 크다 (to be big) → 커요. 좋다 (to be good) → 좋아요. 저는 행복해요 (jeo-neun haeng-bo-kae-yo) — I am happy.

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, dropping particles because English doesn't need them — 밥 먹어요 is understandable but wrong; 밥을 먹어요 is correct. Second, putting the verb anywhere but last. English habits produce 저는 먹어요 밥을 — always rearrange to 저는 밥을 먹어요. The verb is the anchor at the end.

Dialogue — coworkers introducing themselves:

Sujin: 처음 뵙겠습니다. 저는 수진입니다. 회사원이에요. (Cheo-eum boep-ge-sseum-ni-da. Jeo-neun Su-jin-im-ni-da. Hoe-sa-wo-ni-e-yo.) — Nice to meet you. I am Sujin. I am an office worker.
Taehyun: 처음 뵙겠습니다. 저는 태현입니다. 학생이에요. (Cheo-eum boep-ge-sseum-ni-da. Jeo-neun Tae-hyeon-im-ni-da. Hak-saeng-i-e-yo.) — Nice to meet you. I am Taehyun. I am a student.
Sujin: 매일 지하철로 회사에 가요. (Mae-il ji-ha-cheol-lo hoe-sa-e ga-yo.) — I go to the office by subway every day.
Taehyun: 저는 걸어서 학교에 가요. (Jeo-neun geo-reo-seo hak-gyo-e ga-yo.) — I walk to school.
Sujin: 학교가 멀어요? (Hak-gyo-ga meo-reo-yo?) — Is the school far?
Taehyun: 아니요, 가까워요. 아주 편해요. (A-ni-yo, ga-kka-wo-yo. A-ju pyeo-nae-yo.) — No, it's close. Very convenient.

Practice: Write ten 입니다/이에요 sentences about yourself (name, job, origin). Write eight verb sentences using the eight verbs above, each with a particle (을/를, 에, or 에서). Say every sentence aloud. Finally, translate to Korean: "I drink coffee every day. I go to Seoul by subway. This book is interesting (재미있다)." Check: 저는 매일 커피를 마셔요. 지하철로 서울에 가요. 이 책은 재미있어요.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Korean has TWO number systems — native Korean and Sino-Korean — and using the wrong one is the classic beginner giveaway. Learn which system goes where, and numbers become pure utility: prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules.

Native Korean numbers (for counting things, age, hours): 하나 (ha-na, 1), 둘 (dul, 2), 셋 (set, 3), 넷 (net, 4), 다섯 (da-seot, 5), 여섯 (yeo-seot, 6), 일곱 (il-gop, 7), 여덟 (yeo-deol, 8), 아홉 (a-hop, 9), 열 (yeol, 10). Eleven is 열하나, twelve 열둘, twenty 스물 (seu-mul), thirty 서른 (seo-reun). Before a counter, 1–4 shorten: 한 (han), 두 (du), 세 (se), 네 (ne) — 한 개 (han gae, one thing), 두 명 (du myeong, two people), 세 살 (se sal, three years old).

Sino-Korean numbers (for money, minutes, dates, phone numbers): 일 (il, 1), 이 (i, 2), 삼 (sam, 3), 사 (sa, 4), 오 (o, 5), 육 (yuk, 6), 칠 (chil, 7), 팔 (pal, 8), 구 (gu, 9), 십 (ship, 10). Eleven is 십일, twenty is 이십, one hundred is 백 (baek), one thousand is 천 (cheon), ten thousand is 만 (man) — Korean counts in ten-thousands like Japanese: 십만 (ship-man) is 100,000.

Which system goes where — memorize this table. Native: age (스물다섯 살 — 25 years old), counting objects with counters (사과 세 개 — three apples), hours (세 시 — 3 o'clock). Sino: money (삼천 원 — 3000 won), minutes (삼십 분 — 30 minutes), months and dates (3월, 5일), phone numbers, floors. The hour/minute split is the famous one: 세 시 삼십 분 (se shi sam-ship bun) — 3:30 — native 세 for the hour, Sino 삼십 for the minutes. Mixing them (삼 시 세십 분) is wrong every time.

Counters pair with native numbers: 개 (gae, things), 명/분 (myeong/bun, people — 분 is respectful), 살 (sal, age), 잔 (jan, cups), 병 (byeong, bottles), 마리 (ma-ri, animals), 권 (gwon, books), 장 (jang, flat sheets), 대 (dae, machines/cars). Examples: 커피 두 잔 (keo-pi du jan — two cups of coffee), 책 세 권 (chaek se gwon — three books), 고양이 한 마리 (go-yang-i han ma-ri — one cat).

Telling time: native number + 시 (shi) for hours — 한 시 (1 o'clock), 두 시 (2), 열두 시 (12). Sino number + 분 (bun) for minutes — 십 분 (10 minutes), 사십오 분 (45 minutes). 반 (ban) means half: 세 시 반 (3:30). 오전 (o-jeon) is AM, 오후 (o-hu) is PM: 오후 세 시 (3 PM). Ask the time with 지금 몇 시예요? (ji-geum myeot shi-ye-yo? — what time is it now?). A classic mistake is saying 삼 시 for 3 o'clock — hours are native: 세 시.

Days of the week: 월요일 (wo-ryo-il, Monday), 화요일 (hwa-yo-il, Tuesday), 수요일 (su-yo-il, Wednesday), 목요일 (mo-gyo-il, Thursday), 금요일 (geu-myo-il, Friday), 토요일 (to-yo-il, Saturday), 일요일 (i-ryo-il, Sunday). 오늘 (o-neul) is today, 내일 (nae-il) is tomorrow, 어제 (eo-je) is yesterday. Months: Sino number + 월 (wol) — 1월 (i-rwol, January), 12월 (shi-bi-wol, December). Dates: Sino number + 일 (il) — 5일 (o-il, the 5th). So May 5th, Monday is 5월 5일 월요일 (o-wol o-il wo-ryo-il). The order is always biggest to smallest: year, month, day.

Money and shopping vocabulary: 얼마예요? (eol-ma-ye-yo? — how much is it?). 원 (won) is the currency: 삼천 원 (sam-cheon won, 3000 won). 비싸요 (bi-ssa-yo) — expensive. 싸요 (ssa-yo) — cheap. 이거 주세요 (i-geo ju-se-yo) — this one, please.

Dialogue — at a shop:

Customer: 이거 얼마예요? (I-geo eol-ma-ye-yo?) — How much is this?
Clerk: 삼천 원이에요. (Sam-cheon wo-ni-e-yo.) — It's 3000 won.
Customer: 비싸네요. 좀 싼 거 있어요? (Bi-ssa-ne-yo. Jom ssan geo i-sseo-yo?) — That's expensive. Do you have a cheaper one?
Clerk: 네, 이거는 이천 원이에요. (Ne, i-geo-neun i-cheon wo-ni-e-yo.) — Yes, this one is 2000 won.
Customer: 그럼 이거 두 개 주세요. (Geu-reom i-geo du gae ju-se-yo.) — Then give me two of these, please.
Clerk: 감사합니다. 사천 원입니다. (Gam-sa-ham-ni-da. Sa-cheon wo-nim-ni-da.) — Thank you. That's 4000 won.

Practice: Count aloud 1–20 in both systems without stopping. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in Korean. Drill the hour/minute split (세 시 삼십 분) until it is automatic. Finally, memorize the shop dialogue's price lines and role-play buying three different items, asking 얼마예요? each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to use every question word, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in Korea. The good news: Korean questions keep statement word order — you just swap in a question word where the answer goes, with rising intonation.

The core question words: 뭐/무엇 (mwo/mu-eot, what — 뭐 is casual speech, 무엇 is the full form), 어디 (eo-di, where), 누구 (nu-gu, who), 언제 (eon-je, when), 어떻게 (eo-tteo-ke, how), 얼마 (eol-ma, how much), 왜 (wae, why), 몇 (myeot, how many — before counters). They sit where the answer would be: 이게 뭐예요? (i-ge mwo-ye-yo? — what is this?), 어디에 가요? (eo-di-e ga-yo? — where are you going?), 누구예요? (nu-gu-ye-yo? — who is it?), 언제 와요? (eon-je wa-yo? — when are you coming?). Question words take 이/가, never 은/는: 누가 왔어요? (nu-ga wa-sseo-yo? — who came?) — saying 누가는 is the classic beginner error. 몇 pairs with counters: 몇 개? (myeot gae? — how many things?), 몇 살이에요? (myeot sa-ri-e-yo? — how old are you?).

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. ...이/가 어디예요? (...i/ga eo-di-ye-yo? — where is...?): 역이 어디예요? (yeo-gi eo-di-ye-yo? — where is the station?). 어떻게 가요? (eo-tteo-ke ga-yo? — how do I get there?). 오른쪽 (o-reun-jjok, right), 왼쪽 (oen-jjok, left), 직진 (jik-jin, straight ahead), 가까워요 (ga-kka-wo-yo, it's near), 멀어요 (meo-reo-yo, it's far), 사거리 (sa-geo-ri, intersection), 신호등 (sin-ho-deung, traffic light). If you are lost: 길을 잃었어요 (gi-reul i-reo-sseo-yo) — I'm lost. The lifesaver follow-up: 지도에서 보여 주세요 (ji-do-e-seo bo-yeo ju-se-yo) — please show me on the map. When someone answers, listen for 오른쪽으로 가세요 (go to the right) and 왼쪽으로 도세요 (turn left).

Shopping questions beyond prices: ...있어요? (...i-sseo-yo? — do you have...?): 큰 사이즈 있어요? (keun sa-i-jeu i-sseo-yo? — do you have a large size?). 입어 봐도 돼요? (i-beo bwa-do dwae-yo? — may I try it on?). 카드 돼요? (ka-deu dwae-yo? — can I pay by card?). 몇 시에 열어요? (myeot shi-e yeo-reo-yo? — what time do you open?). 깎아 주세요 (kka-kka ju-se-yo) — please give me a discount. Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: 어디에서 왔어요? (eo-di-e-seo wa-sseo-yo? — where did you come from?), 무슨 일을 하세요? (mu-seun i-reul ha-se-yo? — what work do you do?), 여기 온 지 얼마나 됐어요? (yeo-gi on ji eol-ma-na dwae-sseo-yo? — how long have you been here?), 이 도시가 마음에 들어요? (i do-shi-ga ma-eu-me deu-reo-yo? — do you like this city?), 뭐가 맛있어요? (mwo-ga ma-shi-sseo-yo? — what is delicious here?).

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Tourist: 실례합니다. 박물관이 어디예요? (Sil-lye-ham-ni-da. Bang-mul-gwa-ni eo-di-ye-yo?) — Excuse me. Where is the museum?
Local: 가까워요. 직진하시고 신호등에서 왼쪽으로 도세요. (Ga-kka-wo-yo. Jik-jin-ha-shi-go sin-ho-deung-e-seo oen-jjo-geu-ro do-se-yo.) — It's near. Go straight and turn left at the traffic light.
Tourist: 걸어서 멀어요? (Geo-reo-seo meo-reo-yo?) — Is it far on foot?
Local: 아니요, 오 분쯤 걸려요. 은행하고 약국 사이에 있어요. (A-ni-yo, o bun-jjeum geol-lyeo-yo. Eun-haeng-ha-go yak-guk sa-i-e i-sseo-yo.) — No, about five minutes on foot. It's between the bank and the pharmacy.
Tourist: 감사합니다! (Gam-sa-ham-ni-da!) — Thank you!

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Hana: 어디에서 왔어요? (Eo-di-e-seo wa-sseo-yo?) — Where did you come from?
Jun: 부산에서 왔어요. 하나 씨는요? (Bu-sa-ne-seo wa-sseo-yo. Ha-na sshi-neun-yo?) — I came from Busan. And you, Hana?
Hana: 저는 서울 사람이에요. 여기 온 지 얼마나 됐어요? (Jeo-neun Seo-ul sa-ra-mi-e-yo. Yeo-gi on ji eol-ma-na dwae-sseo-yo?) — I'm from Seoul. How long have you been here?
Jun: 두 주 됐어요. 서울이 정말 좋아요. (Du ju dwae-sseo-yo. Seo-u-ri jeong-mal jo-a-yo.) — Two weeks. I really like Seoul.
Hana: 뭐가 제일 좋아요? (Mwo-ga je-il jo-a-yo?) — What do you like most?
Jun: 음식이요! 내일 공원에 갈 거예요. 같이 가실래요? (Eum-shi-gi-yo! Nae-il gong-wo-ne gal geo-ye-yo. Ga-chi ga-shil-lae-yo?) — The food! I'm going to the park tomorrow. Want to come along?
Hana: 좋아요! 몇 시에 만날까요? (Jo-a-yo! Myeot shi-e man-nal-kka-yo?) — Sounds good! What time shall we meet?
Jun: 열 시에 여기서 만나요. (Yeol shi-e yeo-gi-seo man-na-yo.) — Let's meet here at ten.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with rising intonation. Memorize the direction sequence (직진, 오른쪽, 왼쪽, 사거리) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in Korean, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with changed details (your city, your time, your plan) until the question patterns feel automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The 았/었어요 Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: 어제 뭐 했어요? (eo-je mwo hae-sseo-yo? — what did you do yesterday?). Korean past tense follows the same vowel rule you learned for the present.

Form the past by adding 았어요/었어요 to the verb stem: if the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요; otherwise add 었어요; 하다 verbs become 했어요. 가다 → 갔어요 (ga-sseo-yo, went). 먹다 → 먹었어요 (meo-geo-sseo-yo, ate). 보다 → 봤어요 (bwa-sseo-yo, saw). 오다 → 왔어요 (wa-sseo-yo, came). 하다 → 했어요 (hae-sseo-yo, did). 사다 → 샀어요 (sa-sseo-yo, bought). 자다 → 잤어요 (ja-sseo-yo, slept). 읽다 → 읽었어요 (il-geo-sseo-yo, read). Feel the pattern — it mirrors the 아요/어요 rule exactly, so the present lesson does double duty. The formal past is 았습니다/었습니다: 갔습니다, 먹었습니다.

The negative past has two forms. Use 안 + past: 안 갔어요 (an ga-sseo-yo) — I didn't go. Or the past of 지 않다: 가지 않았어요 (ga-ji a-na-sseo-yo). Both are natural; 안 is shorter and more common in speech. For "couldn't," use 못 + past: 못 잤어요 (mot ja-sseo-yo) — I couldn't sleep.

Adjectives conjugate the same way: 예쁘다 → 예뻤어요 (ye-ppeo-sseo-yo, was pretty). 좋다 → 좋았어요 (jo-a-sseo-yo, was good). 크다 → 컸어요 (keo-sseo-yo, was big). Two stars of past-tense conversation: 좋았어요 (it was good) and 재미있었어요 (jae-mi-i-sseo-sseo-yo, it was fun/interesting) — you will use these constantly when talking about your weekend.

Time words anchor the past: 어제 (eo-je, yesterday), 그저께 (geu-jeo-kke, the day before yesterday), 지난주 (ji-nan-ju, last week), 지난달 (ji-nan-dal, last month), 작년 (jang-nyeon, last year), 아까 (a-kka, a little while ago). Combine them with the past tense: 어제 영화를 봤어요 (eo-je yeong-hwa-reul bwa-sseo-yo) — I watched a movie yesterday. 지난주에 서울에 갔어요 (ji-nan-ju-e Seo-u-re ga-sseo-yo) — I went to Seoul last week. To list several past actions, chain them with -고: 영화를 보고 쇼핑했어요 (yeong-hwa-reul bo-go syo-ping-hae-sseo-yo) — I watched a movie and went shopping.

Two beginner warnings. First, don't use the past tense for states still true now: if you still live in Busan, say 부산에 살아요, not 살았어요. The past means finished and over. Second, watch the vowel rule on irregular stems: 크다 (to be big) contracts to 컸어요, not 크었어요 — vowel-contracting verbs (크다, 트다) drop the stem vowel. When in doubt, memorize the common ones: 컸어요 (was big), 좋았어요 (was good), 봤어요 (saw).

Dialogue — talking about the weekend:

Dae: 주말에 뭐 했어요? (Ju-ma-re mwo hae-sseo-yo?) — What did you do on the weekend?
Rin: 토요일에 경복궁에 갔어요. (To-yo-i-re gyeong-bok-gung-e ga-sseo-yo.) — I went to Gyeongbokgung Palace on Saturday.
Dae: 어땠어요? 재미있었어요? (Eo-ttae-sseo-yo? Jae-mi-i-sseo-sseo-yo?) — How was it? Was it fun?
Rin: 네, 정말 재미있었어요! 사진도 많이 찍었어요. (Ne, jeong-mal jae-mi-i-sseo-sseo-yo! Sa-jin-do ma-ni jji-geo-sseo-yo.) — Yes, really fun! I took lots of photos too.
Dae: 좋았겠네요. 저는 집에서 영화를 봤어요. (Jo-a-kke-nne-yo. Jeo-neun ji-be-seo yeong-hwa-reul bwa-sseo-yo.) — Sounds great. I watched a movie at home.
Rin: 영화 재미있었어요? (Yeong-hwa jae-mi-i-sseo-sseo-yo?) — Was the movie fun?
Dae: 네, 정말 좋았어요. 일요일에는 장을 봤어요. (Ne, jeong-mal jo-a-sseo-yo. I-ryo-i-re-neun jang-eul bwa-sseo-yo.) — Yes, really good. On Sunday I did the grocery shopping.

Practice: Write a paragraph of 8–10 sentences about what you did yesterday, using at least five different past-tense verbs plus one adjective past. Read it aloud twice. Then convert these to the past: 마시다, 사다, 읽다, 예쁘다, 좋다. Finally, answer aloud in complete Korean sentences: 어제 뭐 먹었어요? 몇 시에 일어났어요? 지난 주말에 뭐 했어요? 한국에 가 본 적 있어요?

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Making Plans — Future Expressions + Restaurant and Travel Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to talk about the future — making plans, expressing wants, inviting people — and handles two of the most useful real-world conversations: ordering in a restaurant and navigating travel. Future talk turns you from a visitor into someone who can actually live in Korean: booking, inviting, promising, and planning.

Korean marks the future with (으)ㄹ 거예요 attached to the verb stem: add ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel stem, 을 거예요 after a consonant stem. 가다 → 갈 거예요 (gal geo-ye-yo) — I will go. 먹다 → 먹을 거예요 (meo-geul geo-ye-yo) — I will eat. 하다 → 할 거예요 (hal geo-ye-yo) — I will do. 보다 → 볼 거예요 (bol geo-ye-yo) — I will watch. Future time words: 내일 (tomorrow), 모레 (the day after tomorrow), 이번 주 (this week), 다음 주 (next week), 다음 달 (next month), 내년 (next year), 오늘 저녁 (this evening). Combine freely: 내일 서울에 갈 거예요 (nae-il Seo-u-re gal geo-ye-yo) — I will go to Seoul tomorrow.

To say you want to do something, use -고 싶어요: 먹고 싶어요 (meok-go si-peo-yo) — I want to eat. 가고 싶어요 (ga-go si-peo-yo) — I want to go. 한국어를 배우고 싶어요 (han-gu-geo-reul bae-u-go si-peo-yo) — I want to learn Korean. The negative is -고 싶지 않아요: 가고 싶지 않아요 — I don't want to go. For suggestions, use -(으)ㄹ까요?: 같이 갈까요? (ga-chi gal-kka-yo? — shall we go together?). For "let's," use -(으)ㅂ시다 in formal speech or -자 in casual: 갑시다 (gap-shi-da) — let's go. Accept with 좋아요! (jo-a-yo! — sounds good!).

Restaurant phrases. The staff greets you with 어서 오세요 (eo-seo o-se-yo) — welcome. Ask for the menu: 메뉴 주세요 (me-nyu ju-se-yo). Ask for a recommendation: 뭐가 맛있어요? (mwo-ga ma-shi-sseo-yo? — what is delicious?). Order with ...주세요 or the softer 주문할게요 (ju-mun-hal-ge-yo — I'll order): 불고기 주세요 (bul-go-gi ju-se-yo). React to food: 맛있어요! (ma-shi-sseo-yo! — delicious!). After eating, say 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meo-geo-sseum-ni-da) — thank you for the meal. Ask for the bill: 계산서 주세요 (gye-san-seo ju-se-yo). Common mistake: shouting or waving wildly for attention — a raised hand with 여기요 (yeo-gi-yo, over here) is polite and effective.

Travel phrases. 공항 (gong-hang, airport), 비행기 (bi-haeng-gi, airplane), 호텔 (ho-tel, hotel), 기차 (gi-cha, train), 표 (pyo, ticket), 예약 (ye-yak, reservation). At the hotel: 예약했어요 (ye-ya-kae-sseo-yo) — I have a reservation. 체크인 하고 싶어요 (che-keu-in ha-go si-peo-yo) — I'd like to check in. 조식은 몇 시부터예요? (jo-shi-geun myeot shi-bu-teo-ye-yo? — from what time is breakfast?). Problems: 여권을 잃어버렸어요 (yeo-gwo-neul i-reo-beo-ryeo-sseo-yo) — I lost my passport. 도와주세요 (do-wa-ju-se-yo) — please help me.

Dialogue 1 — at a restaurant:

Staff: 어서 오세요. 몇 분이세요? (Eo-seo o-se-yo. Myeot bu-ni-se-yo?) — Welcome. How many people?
Seo: 두 명이에요. 창가 자리 있어요? (Du myeong-i-e-yo. Chang-ga ja-ri i-sseo-yo?) — Two people. Do you have a window seat?
Staff: 네, 이쪽으로 오세요. 메뉴입니다. (Ne, i-jjo-geu-ro o-se-yo. Me-nyu-im-ni-da.) — Yes, this way please. Here is the menu.
Seo: 뭐가 맛있어요? (Mwo-ga ma-shi-sseo-yo?) — What is delicious?
Staff: 불고기가 인기 많아요. (Bul-go-gi-ga in-gi ma-na-yo.) — Bulgogi is very popular.
Seo: 그럼 불고기하고 밥 두 공기 주문할게요. (Geu-reom bul-go-gi-ha-go bap du gong-gi ju-mun-hal-ge-yo.) — Then I'll order bulgogi and two bowls of rice.
(later) Seo: 잘 먹었습니다! 계산서 주세요. (Jal meo-geo-sseum-ni-da! Gye-san-seo ju-se-yo.) — Thank you for the meal! The check, please.
Staff: 만 오천 원입니다. (Ma-no-cheon wo-nim-ni-da.) — That's 15,000 won.

Dialogue 2 — making weekend plans:

Yuna: 토요일에 뭐 할 거예요? (To-yo-i-re mwo hal geo-ye-yo?) — What will you do Saturday?
Jiho: 공원에 가고 싶어요. 유나 씨는요? (Gong-wo-ne ga-go si-peo-yo. Yu-na sshi-neun-yo?) — I want to go to the park. And you, Yuna?
Jiho: 저는 쇼핑하고 싶어요. 같이 갈까요? (Jeo-neun syo-ping-ha-go si-peo-yo. Ga-chi gal-kka-yo?) — I want to go shopping. Shall we go together?
Yuna: 좋아요! 몇 시에 만날까요? (Jo-a-yo! Myeot shi-e man-nal-kka-yo?) — Sounds good! What time shall we meet?
Jiho: 열 시에 역 앞에서 만나요. (Yeol shi-e yeok a-pe-seo man-na-yo.) — Let's meet in front of the station at ten.
Yuna: 알겠어요. 기대돼요! (Al-ge-sseo-yo. Gi-dae-dwae-yo!) — Got it. I'm looking forward to it!

Practice: Write three plans for next week using (으)ㄹ 거예요, and three wants using -고 싶어요. Write a full restaurant dialogue (8+ lines) where you enter, order two dishes and drinks, react to the food, and ask for the bill. Say it all aloud. Finally, invite a friend somewhere in Korean using -(으)ㄹ까요?, and answer your own invitation.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Conversation Practice Drills + Your 30-Day Practice Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson does two things: it gives you structured conversation drills that combine everything from Lessons 1–7, and it hands you a concrete 30-day plan so your Korean keeps growing after the course ends. A course can teach you the material, but only a routine turns material into skill — so treat this lesson as the most important one to actually do.

Drill 1 — The Two-Minute Monologue. Set a timer for two minutes and talk about your day — present for routines (매일 일곱 시에 일어나요 — mae-il il-gop shi-e i-reo-na-yo, I wake up at seven every day), past for what already happened (아침을 먹었어요 — a-chi-meul meo-geo-sseo-yo, I ate breakfast), future for what is next (지금 쇼핑할 거예요 — ji-geum syo-ping-hal geo-ye-yo, I'm going shopping now). Do not stop to look up words; describe around them. Keeping going matters more than being perfect. Do this drill daily — it is the single highest-value exercise in this course.

Drill 2 — Question Tennis. Write 20 question words and topics on slips of paper (뭐, 어디, 누구, 언제, 왜). Draw one and answer in two full sentences, then ask a follow-up question. Example: draw 어디 → 어디에 가요? 학교에 가요. Draw 뭐 → 뭐 먹었어요? 김밥 먹었어요. If you practice with a partner, rally: they answer your question, then ask you one back. Ten minutes of question tennis covers more ground than an hour of passive review.

Drill 3 — Situation Cards. Write real situations on cards: "Your hotel has no hot water — explain politely," "Ask a stranger for directions to the station," "Order dinner for two at a restaurant," "Small talk with a taxi driver for five minutes." Draw a card and perform it aloud, both roles. These force you to combine vocabulary, grammar, and particles under mild pressure — exactly what real conversations feel like. Rotate through all your cards weekly.

Two mistakes that stall learners at this stage. First, the perfection trap: refusing to speak until every particle is certain. Korean speakers are generous with beginners who try; they cannot help beginners who stay silent. Speak with 70% accuracy today rather than 100% accuracy never. Second, passive consumption: re-reading lessons and calling it study. Reading feels productive but builds recognition, not production. Every minute of speaking aloud counts triple compared to silent review — your mouth needs the reps, especially for the tense consonants and batchim.

Your 30-day practice plan. Week 1 — Foundations lock-in: 20 minutes daily. Days 1–2: re-read Lessons 1–2 dialogues aloud, reading hangul without romanization. Days 3–4: write all hangul consonants and vowels from memory, then check the chart. Days 5–7: number drills from Lesson 4 in both systems until 1–20 is automatic. Week 2 — Conversation ignition: 25 minutes daily. Daily two-minute monologue plus question tennis; re-do the Lesson 5 dialogues with changed details. Week 3 — Real situations: 30 minutes daily. One situation card per day performed aloud; write a daily journal of five Korean sentences about your day (present + past + future mix). Week 4 — Live fire: 30+ minutes daily. Have at least three real conversations — with a tutor, a language-exchange partner, a Korean-speaking neighbor, or ordering food in Korean at a restaurant. Note your three most frequent errors and drill them the following week.

Track it simply: a notebook page per day with the date, minutes practiced, and one line about what felt easier than last week. If you miss a day, never miss twice — the streak matters more than any single session. After 30 days, repeat the cycle with harder situation cards and longer monologues; you now own a system, not just a course.

Practice: Do Drill 1 right now — two full minutes about your day in Korean, out loud, no stopping. Then write out your personal Week 1 schedule with exact times (for example, "7:30 AM, 20 minutes, hangul writing"). Finally, write five situation cards of your own based on your life — travel you plan, restaurants you visit, people you meet — and perform the first one today. 화이팅 (hwa-i-ting) — you can do it! You are a Korean speaker now. Keep speaking.

courses.title: Leadership Mastery: Teams, Decisions & Communication
courses.tagline: Lead teams with clarity: communication, decision frameworks, feedback, and delegation.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Leadership Mastery is a written, self-paced course on the practical skills of leading people: communicating clearly, understanding team dynamics, making sound decisions, giving useful feedback, and delegating without micromanaging. It is written for new and aspiring managers, team leads, project owners, and anyone who influences a group without necessarily holding a title. The course treats leadership as a set of repeatable habits rather than a personality trait: you do not need charisma to run a clear meeting, and you do not need seniority to give feedback that actually helps. Each of the eight lessons teaches one skill with concrete scenarios, warns about common mistakes, and ends with a practice exercise so you apply the idea before moving on. By the final lesson you will have drafted a personal leadership plan with habits and ninety-day goals that fit your real role, team size, and calendar.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
