Beginners often say 'nao' flat like the English word 'now' — drill não daily until the nasal glide feels natural.

Key consonant rules. R at the start of a word or doubled RR is a throaty H sound in most of Brazil: rua (HOO-ah, street), carro (KAH-hoo, car). A single R between vowels is a light flap like the Spanish single R: caro (KAH-roo, expensive), para (PAH-rah, for). S between vowels sounds like Z: casa (KAH-zah), mesa (MEH-zah). At the end of a word, S often sounds like 'sh' in Rio or 's' in São Paulo — either is understood; this course uses the São Paulo 's'. CH sounds like 'sh': chave (SHAH-vee, key). LH sounds like 'ly': filho (FEE-lyoo, son). NH sounds like 'ny' in canyon: manhã, dinheiro (jee-NYAY-roo, money). QU before E or I is just K: que (kee, that/what), aqui (ah-KEE, here). The letter H is always silent: hotel (oh-TEHL).

Word stress usually falls on the second-to-last syllable: casa (KAH-zah), falar (fah-LAHR, to speak), mesa (MEH-zah). A written accent (á, é, í, ó, ú, â, ê, ô, ã, õ) marks the stressed syllable and often the vowel quality: é is open (café), ê is closed (você). Notice avó (ah-VOH, grandmother) versus avô (ah-VOH, grandfather) — same stress, different vowel openness, different person. A classic beginner mistake is stressing English-style — say fah-LAHR, never 'FAH-lahr'. Trust the rhythm: even syllables, gentle lift near the end.

Here is a short dialogue using only sounds from this lesson. Read it aloud slowly:

Mariana: Oi! Como você se chama? (oy KOH-moo voh-SEH see SHAH-mah) — Hi! What is your name?
Rafael: Me chamo Rafael. E você? (mee SHAH-moo hah-fah-EHL ee voh-SEH) — My name is Rafael. And you?
Mariana: Me chamo Mariana. Prazer. (mee SHAH-moo mah-ree-AH-nah prah-ZEHR) — My name is Mariana. Pleased to meet you.
Rafael: Prazer. Você fala português? (prah-ZEHR voh-SEH FAH-lah poor-too-GEHS) — Pleased to meet you. Do you speak Portuguese?
Mariana: Sim, um pouco. (seem oom POH-koo) — Yes, a little.

Say the whole dialogue five times today; it is your first Portuguese conversation.

Practice: Write out these ten words, mark the stressed syllable and any nasal vowel, and say each aloud three times: não, pão, manhã, coração, obrigado, chave, filho, dinheiro, rua, tempo. Next, drill the pairs caro/carro and para/barra until the single-R flap versus throaty-R difference is obvious. Finally, read the dialogue above aloud five times, then cover the pronunciation hints and read it again — you should be able to produce the sounds from the spelling alone.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully.

Start with greetings. Bom dia (boh-oom DEE-ah) means good morning. Boa tarde (BOH-ah TAHR-jee) is good afternoon, boa noite (BOH-ah NOY-chee) is good evening or good night. Oi (oy) is hi — warm, casual, and universal in Brazil. Olá (oh-LAH) is a slightly more neutral hello. Tchau (chow) is bye, até logo (ah-TEH LOH-goo) is see you later, and tudo bem? (TOO-doo beh-eem) means 'all good?' — the all-purpose greeting Brazilians actually use most. For introductions: Me chamo... (mee SHAH-moo) or Meu nome é... (meh-oo NOH-mee eh) means 'my name is'. Como você se chama? (KOH-moo voh-SEH see SHAH-mah) asks someone's name. Prazer (prah-ZEHR) means pleased to meet you; muito prazer is the warmer version.

Now the small-talk core. Como vai? (KOH-moo vigh) or Tudo bem? is 'how are you' — answer with Tudo bem (all good), Tudo ótimo (great), Mais ou menos (so-so), or Estou cansado (m) / cansada (f) (I am tired). E você? (ee voh-SEH) means 'and you?' — short and essential. Por favor (poor fah-VOHR) is please, obrigado/obrigada is thank you (men say obrigado, women say obrigada — match it to YOUR gender, not the listener's), de nada (jee NAH-dah) is you're welcome. A frequent beginner mistake is answering Tudo bem? with a long life story; a short answer plus E você? keeps the conversation balanced and gives you twice the practice.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. Não entendo (nah-oom ehn-TEHN-doo) — I don't understand. Pode repetir, por favor? (POH-jee heh-peh-CHEER) — Can you repeat, please? Fala mais devagar, por favor (FAH-lah migh jee-vah-GAHR) — Speak more slowly, please. Você fala inglês? (voh-SEH FAH-lah een-GLEHS) — Do you speak English? Com licença (koh-oom lee-SEHN-sah) — excuse me (to get attention); Desculpa (jees-KOOL-pah) — sorry (informal); Desculpe (jees-KOOL-pee) — sorry (formal). Sinto muito (SEEN-too MOOY-too) — I'm very sorry. O que significa...? (oo kee seen-yee-FEE-kah) — What does ... mean? These phrases will rescue you anywhere in Brazil, and people respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Watch for this social note: Brazilian Portuguese is warm and informal compared to European Portuguese — você is the standard 'you' everywhere in Brazil (tu is regional), and Brazilians happily use first names quickly. Physical warmth matters too: a hug or cheek kiss is normal among new acquaintances in social settings. A classic false friend: 'pasta' in Portuguese means folder or paste — the food is macarrão or massa. And 'parentes' means relatives, not parents (pais).

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with the translations:

Camila: Oi! Tudo bem? Como você se chama? — Hi! All good? What is your name?
Diego: Oi! Tudo bem. Me chamo Diego. E você? — Hi! All good. My name is Diego. And you?
Camila: Me chamo Camila. Prazer. — My name is Camila. Pleased to meet you.
Diego: Prazer, Camila. De onde você é? — Pleased to meet you, Camila. Where are you from?
Camila: Sou do Texas. E você? — I'm from Texas. And you?
Diego: Sou de São Paulo. Você fala português? — I'm from São Paulo. Do you speak Portuguese?
Camila: Um pouco. Fala mais devagar, por favor. — A little. Speak more slowly, please.
Diego: Claro. Como você está hoje? — Of course. How are you today?
Camila: Tudo ótimo, obrigada. E você? — Great, thanks. And you?
Diego: Tudo ótimo. Tchau! — Great. Bye!

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, one feeling word, goodbye) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then practice the survival phrases: cover the Portuguese column, read the English, and say the Portuguese from memory until you can do all seven without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with the nasal vowels from Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Ser, Estar, and the Present Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson tackles the two most important verbs in Portuguese — ser and estar, both meaning 'to be' — plus the present tense, which lets you describe what you do every day. Like Spanish, Portuguese splits 'to be' in two, and mixing them up is the single most common beginner error. Master this distinction now and every sentence you build later gets easier.

SER is for things that are permanent, essential, or defining: identity, origin, characteristics, time, and profession. Sou do Texas (I am from Texas — literally 'I am of Texas'). Ela é alta (She is tall). São três horas (It is three o'clock). Ele é médico (He is a doctor). ESTAR is for states, conditions, locations, and things in progress: Estou cansado (I am tired). A loja está fechada (The store is closed). Estamos em casa (We are at home). A simple memory rule: ser = what something IS, estar = how something is or WHERE it is. Location always uses estar: São Paulo fica no Brasil uses ficar, but Estou em São Paulo for 'I am in São Paulo'.

Conjugations (memorize these shapes — they never change):
SER: eu sou, você é, ele/ela é, nós somos, vocês são, eles/elas são.
ESTAR: eu estou, você está, ele/ela está, nós estamos, vocês estão, eles/elas estão.
TER (to have): eu tenho, você tem, ele/ela tem, nós temos, vocês têm, eles/elas têm.
Read them aloud now. Note the written accents distinguishing tem (he has) from têm (they have) — a small mark with a big job.

Now the present tense of regular verbs. Portuguese verbs end in -ar, -er, or -ir. For -AR verbs like falar (to speak): falo, fala, fala, falamos, falam. For -ER verbs like comer (to eat): como, come, come, comemos, comem. For -IR verbs like partir (to leave): parto, parte, parte, partimos, partem. In Brazilian speech, eu/tu/ele/nós/vocês/eles collapse in practice to eu, você, ele, a gente (= we, informal), vocês, eles — and a gente takes third-person singular verbs: a gente fala (we speak). Practice with trabalhar (to work): trabalho num escritório (I work in an office), and morar (to live): moro no Rio (I live in Rio). Notice that Brazilian Portuguese usually keeps the subject pronoun — 'falo' alone is correct but 'eu falo' is more natural in Brazil.

A few very common verbs are irregular — learn them as vocabulary: IR (to go): eu vou, você vai, ele vai, nós vamos, vocês vão, eles vão. Vou ao mercado (I go to the market). FAZER (to do/make): eu faço, você faz, ele faz, nós fazemos, vocês fazem, eles fazem. Faço exercício (I exercise). QUERER (to want): eu quero, você quer, ele quer, nós queremos, vocês querem, eles querem. Quero café (I want coffee). PODER (to be able to): eu posso, você pode, ele pode, nós podemos, vocês podem, eles podem. Posso ajudar (I can help). These four irregulars appear in nearly every conversation, so they repay memorization immediately.

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, the ser/estar swap: saying 'estou chato' when you mean 'sou chato' — the first means 'I am bored', the second means 'I am a boring person'. Adjectives change meaning with the verb, just like Spanish. Second, translating 'do' word-for-word: English 'Do you speak Portuguese?' is just Você fala português? — Portuguese does not use a helper verb for questions, so never say 'Você faz fala português?'.

Dialogue — two coworkers at lunch:

Bruno: Onde você trabalha? — Where do you work?
Fernanda: Trabalho num banco. Sou caixa. E você? — I work at a bank. I am a cashier. And you?
Bruno: Sou professor. Trabalho numa escola. — I am a teacher. I work at a school.
Fernanda: Você está cansado hoje? — Are you tired today?
Bruno: Não, estou bem. Quer almoçar comigo? — No, I'm fine. Do you want to have lunch with me?
Fernanda: Sim, quero. Vamos ao restaurante? — Yes, I want to. Shall we go to the restaurant?
Bruno: Vamos. Estou com fome. — Let's go. I'm hungry.

(Note: estou com fome — 'I am with hunger' — is how Portuguese says 'I'm hungry'.)

Practice: Conjugate these verbs fully in writing: falar, comer, partir, ser, estar, ter, ir. Then write six sentences about yourself: two with ser (identity/origin/profession), two with estar (feeling/location), two with present-tense action verbs. Say each sentence aloud. Finally, translate to Portuguese: 'She is a doctor. She works in a hospital. She is tired today. She wants coffee.' Check: Ela é médica. Trabalha num hospital. Está cansada hoje. Quer café.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Numbers are pure utility — prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules — and telling the time unlocks appointments, opening hours, and travel. Portuguese numbers are refreshingly regular, so this lesson is built for repetition and out-loud drilling.

Numbers 0–20 (memorize these exactly): 0 zero, 1 um/uma, 2 dois/duas, 3 três, 4 quatro, 5 cinco, 6 seis, 7 sete, 8 oito, 9 nove, 10 dez, 11 onze, 12 doze, 13 treze, 14 catorze (or quatorze), 15 quinze, 16 dezesseis, 17 dezessete, 18 dezoito, 19 dezenove, 20 vinte. Note dois/duas and um/uma change with gender: dois cafés, duas mesas, um ano, uma semana. Tens: 30 trinta, 40 quarenta, 50 cinquenta, 60 sessenta, 70 setenta, 80 oitenta, 90 noventa, 100 cem (cento before other numbers: cento e um). For 21–99, join with 'e': 21 = vinte e um, 47 = quarenta e sete, 83 = oitenta e três. So 33 = trinta e três, 99 = noventa e nove. Hundreds: 200 duzentos, 500 quinhentos, 1,000 mil.

Telling time: Que horas são? (What time is it?). For 1 o'clock: É uma hora. For all other hours: São duas horas, São três horas... São dez horas. In everyday Brazilian speech, people often drop 'horas': São duas, São três e meia. Minutes: São quatro e dez (4:10), São seis e meia (6:30), São quinze para as oito (7:45 — 'fifteen to eight', very common) or São oito menos um quarto. Meio-dia is noon, meia-noite is midnight. For appointments: a reunião é às três (the meeting is at three). A classic mistake is saying 'É duas horas' — remember, only 1:00 uses é, everything else uses são because the hours are plural.

Days of the week (feminine except sábado/domingo, never capitalized): segunda-feira, terça-feira, quarta-feira, quinta-feira, sexta-feira, sábado, domingo. Brazilians shorten them in speech: segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta. Use na/no for 'on': na segunda = on Monday. Months: janeiro, fevereiro, março, abril, maio, junho, julho, agosto, setembro, outubro, novembro, dezembro. Dates: cinco de maio, vinte de outubro. To say what day it is: Que dia é hoje? — Hoje é terça-feira. What is the date? Que dia é hoje? (date) — É dia dois de novembro, or simply dois de novembro. Note the order: day first, then month — 2 de novembro, never 'novembro 2'.

Practical money and shopping vocabulary, since numbers live there: Quanto custa? (How much does it cost?), Custa dez reais (It costs ten reais), É muito caro (It's very expensive), É barato (It's cheap), Tem troco? (Do you have change?), A conta, por favor (The check, please). Money amounts: 1,50 = um e cinquenta, 25 = vinte e cinco. In shops you will hear prices as bare numbers — 'quarenta e cinco' for 45 — so number fluency pays off immediately. The Brazilian currency is the real (plural reais), written R$.

Dialogue — at a market:

Vendedor: Bom dia! O que vai querer? — Good morning! What will you have?
Cliente: Quero dois quilos de maçã, por favor. — I want two kilos of apples, please.
Vendedora: São doze reais. Mais alguma coisa? — That's twelve reais. Anything else?
Cliente: Quanto custam as laranjas? — How much are the oranges?
Vendedora: Cinco reais o quilo. — Five reais a kilo.
Cliente: Me dá três quilos. A que horas fecha? — Give me three kilos. What time do you close?
Vendedora: Fechamos às oito. — We close at eight.
Cliente: Obrigado. Tem troco para vinte? — Thanks. Do you have change for twenty?
Vendedora: Sim, claro. — Yes, of course.

Practice: Count aloud from 0 to 100 without stopping, then backwards from 50 to 0. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in Portuguese. Then drill time: set a timer and say the current time in Portuguese every 15 minutes for two hours (Que horas são? — São...). Finally, memorize the market dialogue's price lines and role-play a shopping trip where you buy three different items, asking Quanto custa? each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to form every kind of question, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in a Portuguese-speaking place. The good news: Portuguese questions are simple — keep normal word order and raise your intonation, with no helper verbs.

To form a question, keep statement word order and raise your intonation at the end: Você fala português? (Do you speak Portuguese?), Onde fica o banco? (Where is the bank?). The core question words: o que (what), quem (who), qual/quais (which), onde (where), quando (when), por que (why — two words in questions), como (how), quanto (how much), quantos (how many). Porque (one word) means 'because' — a classic beginner mix-up is writing 'porque?' in a question. A very Brazilian pattern is adding 'é que' for emphasis: Onde é que fica...? (Where is it that... is?), O que é que você quer? (What do you want?).

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. Onde fica...? (Where is...?), Como chego a...? (How do I get to...?), É perto (It's near), É longe (It's far), à direita (to the right), à esquerda (to the left), siga em frente / reto (keep going straight), na esquina (on the corner), entre... e... (between... and...). When someone answers, listen for: vire (turn), atravesse (cross), siga (continue). Polite opener: Com licença, onde fica a estação? (Excuse me, where is the station?). And the lifesaver follow-up: Pode me mostrar no mapa? (Can you show me on the map?).

Shopping questions beyond prices: Você tem...? (Do you have...?), Tem...? (Is there...? / Are there...?), Posso provar? (Can I try it on?), Tem um número maior / menor? (Do you have a bigger/smaller size?), Aceita cartão? (Do you take card?), A que horas abre? (What time do you open?). Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: De onde você é? (Where are you from?), O que você faz? (What do you do?), Há quanto tempo você está aqui? (How long have you been here?), Você gosta da cidade? (Do you like the city?), O que você recomenda? (What do you recommend?). Two mistakes to avoid: saying 'Qual é seu nome?' instead of Como você se chama? (nobody says the first), and answering a question you only half understood — use Não entendi bem, pode repetir? instead of guessing.

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Turista: Com licença, onde fica o museu? — Excuse me, where is the museum?
Morador: É perto. Siga em frente e vire à esquerda. — It's near. Go straight ahead and turn left.
Turista: É longe a pé? — Is it far on foot?
Morador: Não, são cinco minutos. Fica entre o banco e a farmácia. — No, it's five minutes. It's between the bank and the pharmacy.
Turista: Muito obrigado. Como se chama esta rua? — Thank you very much. What is this street called?
Morador: É a Rua Augusta. — It's Rua Augusta.

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Beatriz: De onde você é? — Where are you from?
Gustavo: Sou da Argentina. E você? — I'm from Argentina. And you?
Beatriz: Sou daqui, de Belo Horizonte. Há quanto tempo você está aqui? — I'm from here, from Belo Horizonte. How long have you been here?
Gustavo: Há duas semanas. Gosto muito da cidade. — For two weeks. I like the city a lot.
Beatriz: O que você recomenda visitar? — What do you recommend visiting?
Gustavo: Quero ver o parque amanhã. Por que você não vem? — I want to see the park tomorrow. Why don't you come?
Beatriz: Boa ideia! A que horas? — Good idea! At what time?
Gustavo: Às dez. Nos vemos aqui. — At ten. See you here.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with rising intonation. Then memorize the direction-giving sequence (em frente, à direita, à esquerda, na esquina) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in Portuguese, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with a partner or alone, then change three details (city, time, place) and run it again — this is how small talk becomes automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The Pretérito Perfeito
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense — the pretérito perfeito — so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: O que você fez ontem? (What did you do yesterday?). The pretérito perfeito is for completed, finished actions with a clear end: yesterday, last week, this morning — and it is the everyday past tense of Brazilian speech.

Regular pretérito perfeito endings. For -AR verbs like falar: falei, falou, falou, falamos, falaram. For -ER verbs like comer: comi, comeu, comeu, comemos, comeram. For -IR verbs like partir: parti, partiu, partiu, partimos, partiram. Read those aloud and feel the rhythm — the endings carry the meaning: Falei com a Maria (I spoke with Maria). Comemos pizza (We ate pizza). Time words anchor the past: ontem (yesterday), ontem à noite (last night), semana passada (last week), ano passado (last year), hoje de manhã (this morning). In everyday Brazilian speech, você/ele/nós/vocês/eles forms are the ones you will hear most.

The verbs you use most in the past are irregular, so learn these as set phrases. IR (to go): fui, foi, foi, fomos, foram. Fui ao médico (I went to the doctor). SER shares fui/foi in the past — context decides: Foi um bom dia (It was a good day). TER: tive, teve, teve, tivemos, tiveram — Tive um problema (I had a problem). FAZER: fiz, fez, fez, fizemos, fizeram — Fiz a tarefa (I did the homework). ESTAR: estive, esteve, esteve, estivemos, estiveram — Estive doente (I was sick). DIZER (to say/tell): disse, disse, disse, dissemos, disseram — Ele me disse a verdade (He told me the truth). QUERER: quis, quis, quis, quisemos, quiseram — Quis te ligar (I tried to call you).

Two important beginner warnings. First, Portuguese has another past tense — the pretérito imperfeito, for ongoing and habitual past actions (falava = I used to speak / was speaking) — and this course teaches only the pretérito perfeito, which is enough for everyday conversation. Using the perfeito for everything at first is understandable and will not block communication. Second, watch the first-person ending: falei (I spoke) versus fala (he speaks) — one letter changes the person AND the tense. Write the endings carefully every time until your hand does it automatically.

Dialogue — talking about the weekend:

Larissa: O que você fez no fim de semana? — What did you do on the weekend?
Thiago: Fui à praia com minha família. — I went to the beach with my family.
Larissa: Como foi? Fez sol? — How was it? Was it sunny?
Thiago: Sim, fez muito sol. Nadamos e comemos peixe. — Yes, it was sunny all day. We swam and ate fish.
Larissa: Que bom! Eu fiquei em casa. Vi um filme e li um livro. — How nice! I stayed home. I watched a movie and read a book.
Thiago: Você gostou do filme? — Did you like the movie?
Larissa: Sim, adorei. O que você fez no domingo? — Yes, I loved it. What did you do Sunday?
Thiago: Dormi até tarde e visitei meus pais. — I slept in and visited my parents.

Practice: Write a paragraph of 8–10 sentences about what you did yesterday, using at least five different pretérito perfeito verbs (mix regular and irregular). Read it aloud twice. Then conjugate in writing: falar, comer, ir, ter, fazer — full pretérito perfeito, all persons. Finally, answer these aloud in complete Portuguese sentences: O que você comeu ontem? A que horas você acordou? O que você fez no fim de semana passado? Você viu um filme esta semana?

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Making Plans — Future Expressions + Restaurant and Travel Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to talk about the future — making plans, accepting invitations, and handling two of the most useful real-world conversations: ordering in a restaurant and navigating travel. Future talk is what turns you from a tourist into someone who can actually live in Portuguese: booking, inviting, promising, and planning.

Portuguese has two easy ways to express the future. The everyday Brazilian one is IR + INFINITIVE: Vou estudar (I'm going to study), Vamos viajar (We are going to travel), Você vai vir? (Are you coming?). Just conjugate ir (vou, vai, vai, vamos, vão, vão) and add any infinitive — this one structure covers nearly all future needs in Brazil. The second is the futuro simples, formed by adding endings to the infinitive: falarei, falará, falará, falaremos, falarão (I/you/he/we/they will speak); comerei, partirei follow the same pattern. Irregular stems: ser → serei, ter → terei, fazer → farei, poder → poderei, querer → quererei, vir → virei. Use it for promises, predictions, and formal plans: Vou te ligar amanhã is more Brazilian; Te ligarei amanhã is more formal. For this level, default to ir + infinitive in conversation and recognize the futuro simples when you hear it.

Restaurant vocabulary and phrases. O cardápio (the menu), o prato do dia (dish of the day), a entrada (starter), o prato principal (main course), a sobremesa (dessert), a bebida (drink). Ordering: Eu gostaria... (I would like... — polite), Para mim... (For me...), O que você recomenda? (What do you recommend?). During the meal: Está uma delícia (It's delicious), Pode me trazer...? (Can you bring me...?), A conta, por favor (The check, please). Common mistake: ordering with 'eu quero' barked at the waiter is grammatically fine but socially blunt — eu gostaria or por favor with a smile sounds much better. Tipping: the 10% service charge (taxa de serviço) is usually added to the bill — check before tipping extra.

Travel phrases. No aeroporto (at the airport): Onde fica o portão...? (Where is gate...?), Meu voo sai às... (My flight leaves at...), Tenho uma reserva (I have a reservation). No hotel: Gostaria de um quarto duplo (I'd like a double room), A que horas é o café da manhã? (What time is breakfast?), Tem wifi? (Do you have wifi?). Problems: Perdi meu passaporte (I lost my passport), Preciso de ajuda (I need help), Onde tem uma farmácia? (Where is there a pharmacy?). Note how much of this reuses Lessons 2–5 — the course is compounding.

Dialogue 1 — at a restaurant:

Garçom: Boa noite. Tem reserva? — Good evening. Do you have a reservation?
Renata: Sim, no nome de Renata. — Yes, under Renata.
Garçom: Por aqui, por favor. Querem ver o cardápio? — This way, please. Would you like to see the menu?
Renata: Sim, obrigada. Qual é o prato do dia? — Yes, thanks. What is the dish of the day?
Garçom: É frango com arroz. Está uma delícia. — It's chicken with rice. It's delicious.
Renata: Gostaria disso, e uma salada. E você, Bruno? — I'd like that, and a salad. And you, Bruno?
Bruno: Para mim, o peixe. Pode me trazer água, por favor? — For me, the fish. Can you bring me water, please?
Garçom: Já vou trazer. — I'll bring it right away.
(depois) Renata: A conta, por favor. — The check, please.
Garçom: São trinta e cinco reais. — It's thirty-five reais.

Dialogue 2 — making weekend plans:

Felipe: O que você vai fazer no sábado? — What are you going to do Saturday?
Aline: Vou visitar minha irmã. E você? — I'm going to visit my sister. And you?
Felipe: Vou à feira de manhã. Quer vir? — I'm going to the market in the morning. Do you want to come?
Aline: Sim, adoraria. A que horas nos vemos? — Yes, I'd love to. What time shall we meet?
Felipe: Às nove. Depois vamos almoçar juntos. — At nine. Afterwards we'll have lunch together.
Aline: Perfeito. Vou te ligar na sexta para confirmar. — Perfect. I'll call you Friday to confirm.

Practice: Write three plans for next week using ir + infinitive, and three promises using the futuro simples. Then write a full restaurant dialogue (8+ lines) where you order a starter, main, drink, and dessert, ask for the check, and react to the food. Say it all aloud. Finally, plan a real weekend in Portuguese: where you will go, who you will see, what you will eat — five sentences minimum, out loud.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Conversation Practice Drills + Your 30-Day Practice Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson does two things: it gives you structured conversation drills that combine everything from Lessons 1–7, and it hands you a concrete 30-day plan so your Portuguese keeps growing after the course ends. A course can teach you the material, but only a routine turns material into fluency — so treat this lesson as the most important one to actually do.

Drill 1 — The Two-Minute Monologue. Set a timer for two minutes and talk about your day — present for routines (Eu acordo às sete...), pretérito perfeito for what already happened (Tomei café...), future for what is next (Vou trabalhar...). Do not stop to look up words; describe around them (a coisa para escrever = the thing for writing, if you forget 'pen'). Fluency is built by keeping going, not by being perfect. Do this drill daily — it is the single highest-value exercise in this course.

Drill 2 — Question Tennis. Write 20 question words and topics on slips of paper (Onde...?, Quando...?, Por que...?). Draw one and answer in two full sentences, then ask a follow-up question. Example: draw 'Onde?' → Onde você nasceu? Nasci em Ohio. Draw 'Por que?' → Por que você estuda português? Estudo português porque quero viajar. If you practice with a partner, rally: they answer your question, then ask you one back. Ten minutes of question tennis covers more ground than an hour of passive review.

Drill 3 — Situation Cards. Write real situations on cards: 'Your hotel has no hot water — complain politely', 'Ask a stranger for directions to the pharmacy', 'Order dinner for two including a dietary restriction', 'Small talk with a taxi driver for five minutes'. Draw a card and perform it aloud, both roles. These force you to combine vocabulary, grammar, and politeness under mild pressure — exactly what real conversations feel like. Rotate through all your cards weekly.

Two mistakes that stall learners at this stage. First, the perfection trap: refusing to speak until every conjugation is certain. Brazilian speakers are generous with beginners who try; they cannot help beginners who stay silent. Speak with 70% accuracy today rather than 100% accuracy never. Second, passive consumption: re-reading lessons and calling it study. Reading feels productive but builds recognition, not production. Every minute of speaking aloud counts triple compared to silent review — your mouth needs the reps.

Your 30-day practice plan. Week 1 — Foundations lock-in: 20 minutes daily. Days 1–2: re-read Lessons 1–2 dialogues aloud. Days 3–4: conjugate ser/estar/present verbs from Lesson 3 out loud. Days 5–7: number and time drills from Lesson 4 until 0–100 is automatic. Week 2 — Conversation ignition: 25 minutes daily. Daily two-minute monologue plus question tennis; re-do the Lesson 5 and 6 dialogues with changed details. Week 3 — Real situations: 30 minutes daily. One situation card per day performed aloud; write a daily journal of five Portuguese sentences about your day (present + pretérito perfeito + future mix). Week 4 — Live fire: 30+ minutes daily. Have at least three real conversations — with a tutor, a language-exchange partner, a Portuguese-speaking neighbor, or even ordering food in Portuguese. Record one, listen back, and note your three most frequent errors to drill next month.

Track it simply: a notebook page per day with the date, minutes practiced, and one line about what felt easier than last week. If you miss a day, never miss twice — the streak matters more than any single session. After 30 days, repeat the cycle with harder situation cards and longer monologues; you now own a system, not just a course.

Practice: Do Drill 1 right now — two full minutes about your day in Portuguese, out loud, no stopping. Then write out your personal Week 1 schedule with exact times (e.g., '7:30 AM, 20 minutes, Lessons 1–2 dialogues'). Finally, write five situation cards of your own based on your life — travel you plan, restaurants you visit, people you meet — and perform the first one today. Boa sorte — you are a Portuguese speaker now. Keep speaking.

courses.title: Project Management
courses.tagline: Plan, lead, and deliver projects on time and on budget with practical frameworks anyone can use — no jargon, no experience needed.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Project Management is a written, self-paced course that teaches you to take a project from vague idea to finished result. It is written for complete beginners — no management background and no business experience are assumed. Every framework is explained in plain language and demonstrated with a realistic running example: planning a community fundraiser from scratch, so you see each technique applied to the same project as it grows. The course avoids jargon and certification-speak; instead of memorizing terminology, you learn the handful of practices that actually determine whether projects succeed: defining what is and is not included, breaking work into pieces, scheduling honestly, budgeting simply, communicating clearly, and handling risk and change without panic. The first lessons cover the project lifecycle, scope, scheduling, and budgeting. The middle lessons cover leading people, managing risk, and tracking progress. The final lesson is a capstone where you plan a complete sample project end to end. Each of the eight lessons states its goal up front, explains ideas with worked examples, warns you about common mistakes, and ends with a practice exercise.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Project Management is a written, self-paced course that teaches you to take a project from vague idea to finished result. It is written for complete beginners — no management background and no business experience are assumed. Every framework is explained in plain language and demonstrated with a realistic running example: planning a community fundraiser from scratch, so you see each technique applied to the same project as it grows. The course avoids jargon and certification-speak; instead of memorizing terminology, you learn the handful of practices that actually determine whether projects succeed: defining what is and is not included, breaking work into pieces, scheduling honestly, budgeting simply, communicating clearly, and handling risk and change without panic. The first lessons cover the project lifecycle, scope, scheduling, and budgeting. The middle lessons cover leading people, managing risk, and tracking progress. The final lesson is a capstone where you plan a complete sample project end to end. Each of the eight lessons states its goal up front, explains ideas with worked examples, warns you about common mistakes, and ends with a practice exercise.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: You will learn what project management is and the five phases every project moves through: starting, planning, doing, monitoring, and closing. You will learn to define scope — writing down exactly what the project includes and excludes — and to set goals that can actually be measured. You will learn to break work into small tasks, sequence them, estimate honestly, and build a schedule you can trust. You will learn budgeting basics: listing costs, adding contingency, and tracking spending against the plan. You will learn to lead a team without authority: clarifying roles, running useful meetings, and communicating so nobody is surprised. You will learn risk management: identifying what could go wrong, judging likelihood and impact, and preparing responses in advance. You will learn to track progress with simple status checks and to handle change requests without derailing the project. Finally, you will plan a complete sample project in the capstone and get a roadmap for continuing to learn.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: Work through the lessons in order, because each one builds on the previous. Pick a real project from your own life before Lesson 1 — a move, an event, a home repair, a product launch — and use it as your running example alongside the course's fundraiser example; project management learned on your own real stakes sticks far better than theory. After reading a lesson, do its Practice exercise before moving on; each takes thirty to sixty minutes and produces a real artifact (a scope statement, a task list, a budget, a risk register) that becomes part of your capstone plan in Lesson 8. Keep all your work in one document so the pieces accumulate into a complete plan. When a lesson describes a meeting or conversation, practice it out loud or in writing — people skills improve only with rehearsal. Plan roughly one to two hours per lesson including the exercises.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: You need no prior management experience, business training, or special software — a notebook or any document app is enough for every exercise in this course. Basic comfort with everyday arithmetic (adding costs, comparing dates) is all the math involved. A real project of your own to practice on is strongly recommended but not required; you may use the course's fundraiser example throughout if you prefer. Everything else — vocabulary, frameworks, and habits — is taught inside the lessons in plain language. If you can organize a to-do list and follow written instructions, you are ready.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This is a written course package: eight text lessons, this syllabus, and three practical reference materials (a project charter template, a risk register template, and a status report template) that you can print or keep open while you work. There is no video content, no audio, and no live sessions — everything is designed to be read, worked through, and kept as a reference you return to. The examples use realistic but illustrative numbers for practice, not claims about any real project. The course makes no promise of jobs, income, or certification; it teaches project management skills, and your results will depend on the practice you put in. Read at your own pace, repeat lessons as needed, and keep your exercises — together they form a complete sample project plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What Project Management Is and the Project Lifecycle
lessons.text:
This lesson defines project management in plain terms and walks you through the five phases every project moves through. By the end you will be able to tell a project apart from ongoing work, name the five phases and what happens in each, and explain what a project manager actually does all day. This is the map of the territory — every later lesson is a deep dive into one region of it.

A project is a temporary effort to create something specific: organizing a fundraiser, moving apartments, launching a website, renovating a kitchen. Three traits define it. It is temporary — it has a beginning and an end, unlike ongoing operations such as "running the shop day to day." It creates something unique — this fundraiser, not fundraisers in general. And it has constraints — limited time, money, and people. Project management is the discipline of delivering that unique result inside those constraints: deciding what will be done, by whom, by when, and for how much, then keeping reality matched to the plan. Notice the definition says nothing about authority or job titles — a volunteer organizing a charity run is doing project management, whether or not anyone calls them a project manager.

Every project, from a birthday party to a building, moves through five phases. Starting: someone decides the project is worth doing — you clarify why it matters, who wants it, and roughly what success looks like. Our running example: the neighborhood association wants to raise $5,000 for playground repairs with a Saturday fundraiser in eight weeks. Planning: you define exactly what is included, break the work into tasks, schedule them, budget the costs, and decide how the team communicates. This phase is where projects are won or lost — an hour of planning here saves many hours of chaos later. Doing: the team executes the tasks — booking the venue, printing flyers, recruiting volunteers. Monitoring: running alongside the doing, you track progress against the plan, spot problems early, and adjust. Closing: you finish the work, confirm everything is delivered, thank the team, and — the step everyone skips — write down what you learned for next time.

The project manager's real job, stripped of mystique, is five ongoing duties. Clarify: make sure everyone understands the goal and their part — most project failures are communication failures wearing other disguises. Plan: build and maintain the schedule, budget, and task list. Track: compare actual progress to the plan weekly and surface gaps early, when they are cheap to fix. Decide: when reality diverges from the plan, choose the response — adjust scope, add time, spend contingency — and communicate the change. Protect: shield the team from distractions and scope creep so they can do the work. None of this requires a title. If you are the person making sure the fundraiser actually happens, you are the project manager, and this course is your toolkit.

Two beginner mistakes start here. First, skipping the starting phase: jumping into tasks before agreeing on why the project exists and what success means. The fundraiser team that never agrees whether the goal is "raise $5,000" or "have a fun community day" will argue about every decision for eight weeks. Write the goal down in one sentence before anything else — Lesson 2 shows you how. Second, treating the phases as a strict one-way sequence: real projects loop back. Planning reveals the budget cannot work, so you return to starting and shrink the goal; doing reveals a task was underestimated, so you re-plan the schedule. The phases are a map, not a prison — expect to revisit them, and build that expectation into how you talk about the project.

Practice: (1) Name your running real-life project (or use the fundraiser) and write one sentence proving it is a project: temporary, unique, constrained. (2) Write one paragraph describing what each of the five phases would contain for your project — what happens in starting, planning, doing, monitoring, and closing. (3) List three duties from the project manager's five that you have already done informally in your life (organizing anything counts) and one sentence each on what happened. Keep this document — it becomes the cover page of your capstone plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Defining Scope and Goals
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches scope: writing down exactly what your project includes — and excludes — plus goals you can actually measure. By the end you will write a scope statement with inclusions, exclusions, and deliverables, and set goals that pass a simple five-part test. Scope is where projects are saved or doomed: most overruns, arguments, and disappointments trace back to people holding different unspoken assumptions about what "the project" covers.

Start with the goal, because scope serves the goal. A useful goal passes five tests: Specific (what exactly?), Measurable (how will we know?), Achievable (can this team do it?), Relevant (does it serve the real purpose?), Time-bound (by when?). "Raise money for the playground" fails four of the five. "Raise $5,000 in donations for playground repairs by the end of the fundraiser on June 14" passes all five — a stranger could verify whether it happened. Write one primary goal plus two or three supporting goals: "at least 150 attendees," "every volunteer shift filled," "event ends by 4 PM with the park clean." Supporting goals prevent the classic trap of hitting the money target by burning out every volunteer — they define what success looks like in full, not just in dollars.

The scope statement turns the goal into boundaries. It has three parts. Deliverables: the tangible things the project produces — "a Saturday fundraiser event, a donation collection process, a financial report." Inclusions: the work you will do — "venue booking, food vendors (three), children's activities, publicity, volunteer coordination, donation handling." Exclusions: what you will NOT do — stated explicitly, because unspoken exclusions are where arguments breed: "no evening entertainment program, no alcohol sales, no playground construction work (funds only)." Acceptance criteria: how you will know each deliverable is done — "venue booked means signed contract and deposit paid; publicity done means flyers in 20 shops plus three social posts." Write exclusions with the same care as inclusions — saying "we are not doing X" in week one prevents the week-six argument about why X is not happening.

Scope creep — the slow growth of "just one more thing" — is the force that destroys plans, and defending scope is a core project manager duty. It never arrives as a villain; it arrives as reasonable requests: "while we're at it, could we also..." Each addition seems small, but five small additions consume the contingency and then the schedule. Your defenses: the written scope statement (point to it — "that's outside what we agreed; here's what adding it costs"), a change process (Lesson 7 teaches it — every addition gets estimated before approval, never after), and the habit of asking "what should we remove to make room for this?" That last question is magic: it forces the requester to confront that additions are trades, not free. Protecting scope is not being difficult — it is keeping the promise the team made about what would be delivered.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, the invisible exclusion: assuming everyone knows something is out of scope without writing it down. You know the fundraiser is not building the playground; does the enthusiastic volunteer who offered to "coordinate construction" know? Write it. Second, goals without numbers: "make it a great event" cannot be planned for or verified. If a goal matters, find its number — attendees, dollars, deadline, satisfaction rating. Numbers turn wishes into targets the team can aim at and you can track.

Practice: For your project, write (1) one primary goal and two supporting goals, each passing all five tests — rewrite until they do; (2) a scope statement with at least five deliverables, eight inclusions, five explicit exclusions, and acceptance criteria for each deliverable; (3) three realistic scope-creep requests someone might make ("could we also...") and your written response to each using the scope statement and the "what should we remove?" question. Read the scope statement aloud to an imaginary team member — if any sentence could mean two things, rewrite it until it cannot.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Breaking Work Down and Scheduling
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to turn a scope statement into a trustworthy schedule. By the end you will break work into small tasks, sequence them by dependency, estimate durations honestly, and build a schedule that shows what happens when — including which tasks truly control the finish date. Big projects overwhelm because they are viewed whole; this lesson is the technique for viewing them as manageable pieces.

Break the work down until no task is bigger than a few days of effort and each has a clear done state. Take "publicity" from the fundraiser scope: it decomposes into "design flyer," "print 200 flyers," "distribute to 20 shops," "write three social posts," "publish posts on schedule." Each is assignable to one person, each has an obvious finish line. The test of a good breakdown: every task names a single owner and a verifiable result — "flyers in 20 shops, photo proof" beats "handle publicity." Keep decomposing any task you cannot picture doing: vagueness at this stage becomes delay later. A practical rule: if a task would take one person more than a week, split it; if describing it takes longer than doing it, you have split too far. For the fundraiser, expect thirty to fifty tasks — that is normal and healthy.

Sequence the tasks by dependency: what must finish before what can start? You cannot distribute flyers before they are printed; you cannot print before the design is approved; the venue must be booked before you advertise the location. Lay these out as a simple chain per workstream — publicity chain, venue chain, volunteer chain — then look across chains for the critical path: the longest dependency chain, which sets the project's minimum duration. If the venue chain takes five weeks and everything else takes three, the project takes at least five weeks, and any delay on the venue chain delays everything. Mark critical-path tasks clearly — these get your daily attention, your best people, and your contingency. Non-critical tasks have float: they can slip a little without moving the finish date, which tells you where flexibility lives when problems hit.

Estimate durations honestly, because every schedule is built on guesses and most guesses are optimistic. Three techniques beat gut feel. Ask the doer: the volunteer who has printed flyers before knows it takes three days including the print shop's turnaround — the person doing the work estimates better than the manager. Add explicitly for uncertainty: unfamiliar tasks get a wider estimate ("three to five days") and you schedule the upper end. And track reality: compare estimates to actuals as the project runs, and use what you learn to re-estimate the remaining work — estimation is a skill that improves with feedback. Then build the schedule backwards from the deadline: place the final tasks at the end date and work backwards through dependencies, which reveals immediately whether the plan fits the time available. If it does not fit, you have three honest levers — shrink scope, add people to parallel tasks, or move the date — and Lesson 7's change process governs which you pull. What you must never do is keep the date and the scope and just hope: hope is not a scheduling technique.

Two mistakes dominate scheduling. First, the student-syndrome schedule: tasks planned back-to-back with zero buffer, so the first delay cascades through everything. Protect the critical path with explicit buffer — a few unassigned days before the deadline that get consumed by reality. Second, scheduling people at 100%: nobody does project tasks eight hours a day alongside their life — volunteers have jobs, employees have meetings. Plan people at half to two-thirds availability for project work, and the schedule will survive contact with reality.

Practice: For your project, (1) break the scope into tasks until each is a few days at most with a single owner and a verifiable done state — aim for at least twenty-five tasks; (2) group them into three to five workstreams and map the dependencies within each; (3) identify your critical path and mark which tasks have float; (4) estimate each task using the "ask the doer" principle (write who you would ask and what you would ask them); (5) lay the schedule backwards from your deadline and note honestly whether it fits — if not, write which of the three levers you would pull and why. Save the task list; it becomes your tracking baseline in Lesson 7.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Budgeting Basics
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches project budgeting: listing every cost, adding sensible contingency, and tracking spending so there are no surprises. By the end you will build a line-item budget, choose a contingency reserve you can defend, and run a simple spend-tracking routine. Budgets fail for boring reasons — forgotten categories, optimistic guesses, and nobody watching — and this lesson's practices prevent all three.

Build the budget as a line-item list, one row per cost, grouped by workstream. For the fundraiser: venue deposit and rental, food vendor fees, flyer design and printing, children's activity supplies, sound equipment rental, donation-processing fees, volunteer refreshments, contingency. The technique that catches forgotten costs is walking the task list from Lesson 3 line by line and asking "does this cost money?" for each — tasks like "distribute flyers" hide printing costs; "children's activities" hides supply costs. Separate one-time costs from per-unit costs: the venue is one price, but food supplies scale with attendees — write per-unit costs as formulas ("$2 per attendee × 150") so the budget updates when the headcount changes. Get real numbers wherever money is significant: one phone call for a quote beats three guesses, and vendors expect it. For small items, honest estimates are fine — mark them as estimates so everyone knows which numbers are firm.

Contingency is not pessimism; it is arithmetic about uncertainty. Set aside a reserve — typically ten to twenty percent of the budget for familiar projects, more for unfamiliar ones — owned by the project manager, not distributed to task owners. The rule: contingency covers identified risks and estimating error, not scope additions (new scope needs new budget through the change process). When a risk from your Lesson 6 register materializes — the sound equipment costs more than quoted — you spend contingency and log it. Report contingency remaining at every status check, like a fuel gauge: "we've used $200 of $800 contingency with five weeks left" tells everyone the project's financial health in one line. A budget with no contingency is a promise that nothing will deviate from the estimate — a promise reality never keeps.

Track spending with a routine, not willpower. Keep one simple table: budgeted, spent, committed (ordered but not yet paid), and remaining per line item, updated weekly. Committed is the column beginners forget — the $400 sound system you ordered but have not paid for is already gone from your budget; tracking only paid invoices makes you feel richer than you are until the bills land together. The weekly review asks three questions: which lines are over pace, what commitments are coming due, and is contingency still adequate for the remaining risks? When a line threatens to overrun, you have the same three levers as scheduling: reduce scope in that area, find a cheaper approach, or move money from an under-spending line — decided openly, not by quietly hoping. For the fundraiser, the treasurer owns this table and reports the one-line health summary at each team check-in.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, the "we'll figure it out" budget: starting spending with costs still listed as "to be decided." Every undecided cost is a surprise waiting to happen — get the quote or set an explicit estimate with the uncertainty noted. Second, confusing the budget with the spending: a budget nobody reviews is decoration. The weekly fifteen-minute review is the entire difference between budgets that work and budgets that do not — put it on the calendar as a recurring appointment in week one.

Practice: For your project, (1) build the full line-item budget by walking your task list and asking "does this cost money?" for each task — include per-unit formulas where costs scale; (2) mark each line as quoted or estimated; (3) set your contingency percentage and write two sentences defending it based on how familiar this project is; (4) create the tracking table with budgeted/spent/committed/remaining columns and enter three sample weeks of plausible spending, including one line going over pace — then write the decision you would make about it using the three levers. Save the budget; the capstone assembles it with everything else.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Leading a Team — Roles and Communication
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the people side of project management: clarifying who does what and communicating so the team stays aligned without drowning in meetings. By the end you will assign clear roles, set up a communication rhythm, run meetings that respect everyone's time, and handle the two most common people problems. Projects are done by people, and people problems — confusion about ownership, surprises from silence, meetings that waste hours — sink more projects than technical difficulty ever does.

Clarify roles before work starts, because "I thought you were doing that" is the most expensive sentence in project management. For each major deliverable, name exactly one owner — the person accountable for it happening — even when several people contribute. The fundraiser's publicity has one owner; the flyer designer and the distributors contribute to that owner. Write the roster down where everyone can see it: name, role, what they own, how to reach them. Also name the decision-maker for the project (often you) and what decisions team members can make alone — volunteers should not need a meeting to choose flyer colors, but they should not sign contracts either. The test: pick any task and ask "who owns this?" — if the answer is a name within three seconds, your roles are clear; if it is a discussion, they are not.

Set up a communication rhythm with three parts. A weekly check-in (thirty minutes, same time): each workstream owner reports progress, next steps, and blockers — status, not discussion; discussions that need only two people happen after. A shared written status (one page or one message thread): what got done, what is next, what is blocked, updated before the meeting so the meeting itself stays short. And agreed response norms: how quickly messages get answered, which channel is for urgent versus routine, and that blockers get raised immediately rather than saved for the meeting — a blocker reported Tuesday gets fixed Tuesday; one saved for Friday's meeting costs three days. Match the weight to the project: a volunteer fundraiser needs this light structure, not corporate ceremony. The principle is constant though: regular, brief, written-first communication prevents the surprise, and surprises are what destroy trust.

Run meetings people do not hate with four rules. An agenda sent in advance with the decisions needed — no agenda, no meeting. Start and end on time, every time; ending late steals from the next commitment and teaches people your meetings are optional. Decisions get written down with an owner and a date before anyone leaves the room — "we decided X, Maya owns it, done by Friday" — because unwritten decisions evaporate by morning. And anyone who does not need to be there does not get invited; a five-person meeting that needs two people wastes three people's hour. For status meetings specifically, go around the owners with three prompts — done, next, blocked — and park any problem-solving longer than two minutes into a separate huddle with only the involved people.

Two people problems will find you; handle them early and directly. The disengaged contributor: someone who agreed to a role and went quiet. Talk to them privately within a week of noticing — not in the group meeting. Ask what changed; often the task was unclear or life intervened, and re-clarifying or reassigning solves it. What does not work is hoping they re-engage or complaining about them to others. The disagreeing stakeholder: someone with influence who wants a different direction. Hear them out fully first — sometimes they see a real problem — then decide openly against the written scope and goals: "I understand the concern; against our goal of $5,000 by June 14, I recommend we stay the course because..." People accept decisions they disagree with when the reasoning is transparent and the goals are shared; they revolt against unexplained ones.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, managing by broadcast: sending all information to everyone and assuming alignment. Targeted communication — the right update to the right people — beats volume; a volunteer does not need the budget spreadsheet, and the treasurer does not need the flyer drafts. Second, avoiding the hard conversation: the unclear role, the missed commitment, the brewing disagreement. Every hard conversation gets harder with waiting — address it in days, not weeks, privately and specifically, focused on the work rather than the person.

Practice: For your project, (1) write the role roster: every major deliverable with exactly one named owner, plus the decision-maker and what team members may decide alone; (2) design your communication rhythm — weekly check-in time and format, the written status template, and your response norms; (3) draft an agenda for your first team meeting with the decisions it must produce; (4) script two conversations: addressing a contributor who has gone quiet (private, specific, focused on the work) and responding to a stakeholder who wants to add out-of-scope work (heard fully, decided against the written goals). Rehearse both out loud — the words need to exist before the moment does.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Risk Management
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches risk management: finding what could go wrong before it does and preparing responses while they are cheap. By the end you will run a risk brainstorm, score risks by likelihood and impact, write response plans for the serious ones, and keep a risk register alive through the project. Beginners treat risk management as worrying; professionals treat it as buying insurance with planning instead of money — a few hours of thought that prevent the crises that destroy schedules and budgets.

Identify risks with a structured brainstorm, not anxious rumination. Gather the team (or think it through solo) and walk the project asking "what could go wrong here?" at each workstream, plus four universal prompts: people (what if a key person is unavailable?), suppliers (what if a vendor fails?), weather and environment (for anything outdoors or location-dependent), and dependencies (what are we waiting on that we do not control?). For the fundraiser: rain on the Saturday, the venue double-booking, half the volunteers not showing, the sound system failing, food vendors canceling, donation processing going down. Write each risk as a specific event with a cause — "rain forces cancellation of outdoor activities" beats "bad weather" — because specific risks get specific responses and vague ones get shrugged at. Aim for ten to twenty; fewer means you are not looking hard enough, and the exercise takes one focused hour.

Score each risk on two simple scales from 1 to 3: likelihood (1 = unlikely, 2 = possible, 3 = likely) and impact (1 = minor inconvenience, 2 = serious disruption, 3 = threatens the goal). Multiply them for a score from 1 to 9. This is not precise science — it is a sorting tool. Risks scoring 6 or 9 demand response plans; 3 or 4 get watched; 1 or 2 get noted and ignored. Rain on an outdoor June fundraiser might be likelihood 2, impact 3 (outdoor activities are core) for a 6 — plan needed. The treasurer catching a cold is likelihood 2, impact 1 — noted, not planned. Score quickly and move on; the value is in the ranking, not the arithmetic.

Write responses for the high scorers using four strategies. Avoid: eliminate the risk — book an indoor backup venue and the rain risk to the location disappears. Reduce: lower likelihood or impact — confirm volunteers twice and recruit 20% extras to reduce the no-show impact; rent the sound system from a vendor with on-call support. Transfer: shift the consequence — require food vendors to confirm in writing with a cancellation fee clause. Accept: for risks too small or too expensive to address — note them and move on, like brief passing clouds. Each response names an owner and a trigger: "if rain is forecast 48 hours out, Maya activates the indoor layout." Responses without owners are wishes; triggers without dates get debated while the rain falls.

Keep the risk register alive: a simple table of risk, score, response, owner, and status, reviewed for five minutes at each weekly check-in. Risks evolve — the venue contract signed means that risk retires; a vendor sounding flaky means a risk's likelihood rises from 1 to 3. Add new risks as they appear; the brainstorm was the start, not the whole. And connect the register to your contingency: the budget reserve from Lesson 4 exists precisely for the risks you accepted or could not fully reduce — "we hold $800 contingency against the vendor-cancellation and weather risks" is a sentence that shows the plan is coherent.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, the risk register as a write-once document: risks identified in week one and never reviewed are theater. The five-minute weekly review is the entire difference. Second, planning responses for everything: writing elaborate plans for 1-point risks burns the team's planning energy on trivia. Score honestly, plan the 6s and 9s well, watch the 3s and 4s, and let the 1s and 2s go — risk management is about focus, not completeness.

Practice: For your project, (1) brainstorm at least twelve specific risks using the workstream walk plus the four universal prompts — write each as a specific event with a cause; (2) score each 1–3 on likelihood and impact, compute the score, and sort; (3) write response plans for every risk scoring 6+ using the four strategies, each with a named owner and a trigger; (4) build the risk register table and write the five-minute review script you will use at check-ins ("any scores changed? any new risks? any responses to activate?"); (5) write one sentence linking your register to your contingency reserve. Save the register — the capstone and your status reports will reference it.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Tracking Progress and Handling Changes
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches the monitoring phase: tracking progress against your plan and handling change requests without derailing the project. By the end you will run a weekly status routine, read the warning signs of a slipping project, process changes through a simple approval flow, and re-plan honestly when reality diverges. Plans are predictions; this lesson is what you do when predictions meet reality — which is every week, on every project.

Run status as a weekly routine with three inputs. Task check: go down the task list and mark each task done, in progress (with percent honest — "80% done" for the third week running means it is stuck), or not started. Compare against the schedule: which tasks should be done by now and are not? Focus especially on the critical path from Lesson 3 — a two-day slip on a critical task moves the finish date; the same slip on a task with float does not. Spend check: update the budget table's spent and committed columns and compare to plan. Then produce the one-page status: what got done this week, what is next, what is blocked or at risk, and the project health in one line — "on track," "at risk," or "off track" — with the reason. Share it with the team and stakeholders the same day each week. This routine takes under an hour and is the single highest-value habit in project management: problems found in week three cost a fraction of problems found in week seven.

Learn the warning signs that a project is slipping before the schedule admits it. Tasks "90% done" for weeks — the last 10% is where the hard part hid. Growing silence — owners stop reporting, which usually means bad news they are hoping fixes itself. Shrinking contingency with most of the project remaining — the fuel gauge from Lesson 4 dropping fast early means the estimates were wrong. New tasks appearing that were never in the plan — scope leaking in without the change process. And the busiest warning sign: the team working nights and weekends to "catch up" — heroic effort masks a broken plan for about two weeks, then burns people out. When you spot one, name it in the status honestly: "publicity is two weeks behind because the design took three rounds; this threatens the June 1 flyer deadline." Early honesty gives you options; late honesty gives you a crisis.

Handle change with a process, not with reflexes. Every change request — and they will come — goes through four steps. One, write it down: what exactly is being requested, who asked, when. Two, estimate the impact: what does it cost in money, time, and displaced work? Never approve before estimating — "it's small" is how budgets die. Three, decide: approve (and adjust scope, budget, or schedule explicitly), reject (with the reason tied to goals), or defer (after this project). The decision belongs to the decision-maker named in Lesson 5, not to whoever was asked first. Four, communicate and update: the plan, schedule, and budget change on paper the same day, and everyone affected is told. For the fundraiser: "add a bake sale table" gets estimated (two volunteers, $50 supplies, one week of coordination), decided (approved — funded from contingency, Maya owns it), and the task list and budget update that day. Small process, enormous protection.

When reality diverges seriously — a key vendor cancels, half the timeline is lost — re-plan openly rather than improvising. Re-planning means rebuilding the schedule from today forward with honest estimates, re-scoring risks, and presenting the options: "we can still hit June 14 if we cut the evening program and move $300 from contingency, or we move to June 21 with everything intact — here is my recommendation and why." Bring options with trade-offs, not just problems; recommend one; decide together. Teams forgive bad news delivered with a plan — they do not forgive surprises at the deadline.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, status theater: reporting everything "on track" until it is undeniably off track. Status exists to surface problems early — a yellow "at risk" in week three is professionalism, not failure. Second, the invisible change: letting requests happen informally ("sure, we can add that") without the four steps. Every informal yes is a loan against the schedule that comes due later with interest. Kind, firm, procedural: "great idea — let me estimate it and we'll decide Thursday."

Practice: For your project, (1) create the one-page status template: done / next / blocked-or-at-risk / health line — and fill it with three sample weeks of plausible progress including one task slipping on the critical path; (2) write the status narrative for the slipping week, naming the problem and its impact honestly; (3) take two realistic change requests and run each through the four steps — written request, impact estimate, decision with reasoning, and the exact plan updates you would make; (4) draft a re-plan memo for a serious scenario (lose two weeks): the rebuilt outlook, two options with trade-offs, and your recommendation. Save all of it — the capstone needs your tracking and change approach.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Capstone — Plan a Sample Project End to End
lessons.text:
This final lesson is your capstone: assemble everything from the course into a complete project plan for a sample project, then review it like a professional. By the end you will have a single document containing the goal, scope, task breakdown, schedule, budget, roles, risks, and tracking approach — a genuine project plan — plus a roadmap for what to learn next. This is where eight lessons become one usable skill.

Use the community fundraiser as the sample project if you do not have your own ready: goal — raise $5,000 for playground repairs at a Saturday event on June 14, eight weeks out, with at least 150 attendees. Assemble the plan in order, pulling from your lesson exercises. One, the charter page: the goal statement with its five tests passed, the three supporting goals, and the one-paragraph project description from Lesson 1. Two, the scope statement: deliverables, inclusions, exclusions, and acceptance criteria from Lesson 2 — this is the contract the whole plan hangs on. Three, the work breakdown: your task list of thirty-plus tasks grouped by workstream, each with an owner and a done state, from Lesson 3. Four, the schedule: dependencies mapped, critical path marked, estimates honest, laid backwards from June 14 with buffer before the date. Five, the budget: line items walked from the task list, quotes versus estimates marked, contingency set with its defense, from Lesson 4. Six, the team page: role roster, decision rights, and the communication rhythm from Lesson 5. Seven, the risk register: scored risks with response plans, owners, and triggers from Lesson 6. Eight, the control approach: your status template, the change process steps, and the weekly routine from Lesson 7. Each section should reference the others — the budget's contingency names the risks it covers; the schedule's critical path names appear in the status template's watch list.

Now review the assembled plan like someone whose money is at stake, because that is the skill that separates planners from wishful thinkers. Read it end to end and attack it with five questions. Is the goal measurable and the scope free of weasel words — could two people read the exclusions and agree on what is out? Does every task have exactly one owner, or are there orphans everyone assumes someone else handles? Does the schedule fit the calendar — count the weeks yourself, check the critical path arithmetic, confirm the buffer exists? Does the budget's contingency match the risk register — are the 6-and-9 risks actually covered by the reserve? And what is the single weakest point — the one task, person, or assumption most likely to break — and what is your specific response when it does? Write the answers down; every weakness you find now is a crisis you prevented. A plan that survives this review is a plan you can trust.

Close the project properly in your plan too — Lesson 1's most-skipped phase. Write the closing checklist now, while you are clear-headed: confirm each deliverable against its acceptance criteria, settle every payment and collect receipts, thank the team specifically (name contributions, not generic praise), publish the financial report to stakeholders, and hold a thirty-minute lessons-learned session with three questions — what worked, what did not, what we will do differently. Write the answers into a one-page note filed where the next project can find it. This is how a one-time project becomes lasting capability: the next fundraiser starts from your note instead of from zero.

Where to go next depends on what engaged you. If the people side pulled you — roles, communication, hard conversations — study leadership and facilitation: running workshops, giving feedback, resolving conflict. If the analytical side pulled you — scheduling, budgeting, risk scoring — go deeper into estimation techniques, critical-path software tools, and quantitative risk analysis. If you want credentials, formal certifications exist in project management — research them only after you have run real projects, because the courses assume experience and the exams test judgment more than memory. Whatever direction you take, the foundation does not change: clarify the goal, bound the scope, break down the work, schedule honestly, budget simply, communicate constantly, plan for risk, track weekly, and close deliberately.

Practice: Assemble your capstone document — all eight sections above, in order, for your sample project, each section at least a solid paragraph or its full artifact. Then perform the five-question review in writing, fix what you find, and add the closing checklist with the lessons-learned questions. When the document reads as one coherent plan — goal through closing, every section consistent with the others — you have finished the course. Keep it: it is both your proof of skill and a template for every project you will ever run.

courses.title: Public Speaking Mastery
courses.tagline: Speak clearly and confidently in front of any room, with practical techniques you can practise and a routine that makes you better every time.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Public Speaking Mastery is a written, self-paced course for anyone who wants to speak clearly and confidently in front of a group — at work, in a class, at a community event, or at a family occasion. It assumes no speaking experience and no natural talent for performing. The course starts with nerves, because that is where most speakers get stuck, and then works through the craft step by step: structuring a talk, opening strong, using your voice and body language, making slides that help instead of hurt, handling questions, and telling stories that listeners remember. It finishes with a practice and feedback routine you can use for every talk you give from now on. Every lesson explains ideas in plain language with realistic examples, warns you about common mistakes, and ends with a practice exercise you can do alone or with a friendly audience. The advice is practical and honest: this course teaches speaking skills, and it makes no promise of fame, jobs, or income.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Public Speaking Mastery is a written, self-paced course for anyone who wants to speak clearly and confidently in front of a group — at work, in a class, at a community event, or at a family occasion. It assumes no speaking experience and no natural talent for performing. The course starts with nerves, because that is where most speakers get stuck, and then works through the craft step by step: structuring a talk, opening strong, using your voice and body language, making slides that help instead of hurt, handling questions, and telling stories that listeners remember. It finishes with a practice and feedback routine you can use for every talk you give from now on. Every lesson explains ideas in plain language with realistic examples, warns you about common mistakes, and ends with a practice exercise you can do alone or with a friendly audience. The advice is practical and honest: this course teaches speaking skills, and it makes no promise of fame, jobs, or income.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: You will learn what nerves actually are and how to work with them instead of fighting them. You will learn to structure a talk so listeners can follow it without effort: one clear message, a beginning, a middle, and an ending that lands. You will learn to open strong in the first minute, so the room pays attention. You will learn to use your voice — pace, pauses, volume, and tone — and your body — posture, gestures, and eye contact — to support your words instead of distracting from them. You will learn to design slides that help the audience and never replace you as the speaker. You will learn to handle questions, including hard ones and ones you cannot answer. You will learn to tell short, honest stories that make ideas stick. Finally, you will build a practice and feedback routine that improves every talk you give.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: Work through the lessons in order, because each one builds on the previous. Before Lesson 1, choose a real talk to work toward — a presentation at work, a class talk, a wedding toast, a community meeting, anything with a real audience and a real date if you can manage it. Use that same talk as your running example through every exercise, so your work accumulates into a talk you can actually give. After reading each lesson, do its Practice exercise before moving on; each takes thirty to sixty minutes and produces a piece of your final talk or your practice routine. Keep all your work in one document or folder. Plan roughly one to two hours per lesson including the exercises. Practise out loud, standing up, whenever an exercise says to practise — reading silently is not the same skill, and your mouth needs the rehearsal as much as your mind does.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no formal prerequisites. You need to be able to read and write in plain language, and to have — or to invent — a topic you can speak about for five to ten minutes. No speaking experience, performance background, or special equipment is required. A phone or computer that can record sound is useful for the practice exercises, so you can listen back to yourself, but it is not essential — a trusted friend listening live works just as well.
