— В десять. Увидимся здесь. (u-VI-dim-sya zdyes') — At ten. See you here.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with rising intonation. Then memorize the direction sequence (прямо, направо, налево, на углу) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in Russian, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with a partner or alone, then change three details (city, time, place) and run it again — this is how small talk becomes automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The Past Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: Что вы делали вчера? (shto vy DYE-la-li fchye-RA, what did you do yesterday?). Russian past tense is refreshingly simple: one form per gender, no person-by-person conjugation.

Forming the past: take the infinitive, drop -ть, and add -л for masculine, -ла for feminine, -ло for neuter, -ли for plural. Говорить → говорил/говорила/говорили (ga-va-RIL/ga-va-RI-la). So: Я говорил (ya ga-va-RIL, I spoke — said by a man), Я говорила (ya ga-va-RI-la, I spoke — said by a woman), Они говорили (a-NI ga-va-RI-li, they spoke). More: работать → работал/работала — Вчера я работал допоздна (fchye-RA ya ra-BO-tal da-paz-DA, yesterday I worked late). Делать → делал/делала — Что ты делал? (what were you doing?). Жить → жил/жила — Я жил в Москве (I lived in Moscow). The verb "to be" in the past is был/была/было/были: Вчера был хороший день (fchye-RA byl kha-RO-shy dyen', yesterday was a good day); Она была дома (she was at home). Notice the past tense agrees with the subject's gender, not the speaker's politeness level — был for a man, была for a woman, always.

A few verbs change their stem in the past — learn these as set phrases. Идти (to go, on foot) → шёл/шла/шли: Я шёл в магазин (ya shyol f ma-ga-ZIN, I was going/went to the shop). Ехать (to go by vehicle) → ехал/ехала: Мы ехали на автобусе (we went by bus). Мочь (to be able) → мог/могла: Я не мог прийти (ya nye mok priy-TI, I couldn't come). Есть (to eat) → ел/ела: Мы ели суп (we ate soup). Хотеть → хотел/хотела: Я хотел позвонить (I wanted to call). These cover most daily storytelling.

Time words are your best friends in the past tense: вчера (fchye-RA, yesterday), позавчера (pa-za-fchye-RA, the day before yesterday), сегодня утром (this morning), на прошлой неделе (na PROSH-lay nye-DYE-lye, last week), в прошлом году (f PROSH-lam ga-DU, last year), тогда (tag-DA, then). Two beginner warnings. First, Russian has two verb aspects — imperfective (ongoing/repeated) and perfective (completed) — and this lesson uses imperfective past forms, which is correct for describing what was happening or what you used to do. Do not worry about the perfective yet; using imperfective past for everything at first is understandable and will not block communication. Second, negation: Я не говорил (I didn't speak), Она не была (she wasn't) — не goes right before the verb, exactly like the present.

Dialogue — talking about the weekend:

— Что вы делали в выходные? (shto vy DYE-la-li v vy-khad-NY-ye) — What did you do on the weekend?
— Я ездил на дачу с семьёй. (YA YEZ-dil na DA-chu s syem-YOY) — I went to the country house with my family.
— Как было? Была хорошая погода? (kak BY-la? by-LA kha-RO-sha-ya pa-GO-da) — How was it? Was the weather good?
— Да, было очень тепло. Мы гуляли и ели шашлык. (TYOP-la, gu-LYA-li) — Yes, it was very warm. We walked and ate barbecue.
— Как хорошо! А я остался дома. Я смотрел фильм и читал книгу. (a-STAL-sya DO-ma, sma-TRYEL fil'm) — How nice! I stayed home. I watched a film and read a book.
— Тебе понравился фильм? (tye-BYE pa-NRA-vil-sya fil'm) — Did you like the film?
— Да, очень понравился. А что ты делал в воскресенье? — Yes, I liked it a lot. What did you do Sunday?
— Я спал допоздна и ходил к родителям. (spal da-paz-DA, kha-DIL k ra-di-TYE-lyam) — I slept in and went to my parents'.

Practice: Write a paragraph of 8–10 sentences about what you did yesterday, using at least five different past-tense verbs (mix masculine/feminine forms correctly for yourself). Read it aloud twice. Then write the past forms of: говорить, работать, жить, быть, идти — all four genders/numbers each. Finally, answer these aloud in complete Russian sentences: Что вы ели вчера? Во сколько вы встали? Что вы делали в прошлые выходные? Вы смотрели фильм на этой неделе?

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Making Plans — The Future Tense + Restaurant and Travel Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to talk about the future — making plans, accepting invitations, and handling two of the most useful real-world conversations: ordering in a restaurant and navigating travel. Future talk is what turns you from a tourist into someone who can actually live in Russian: booking, inviting, promising, and planning.

Russian has two ways to express the future, matching its two verb aspects. The everyday one uses буду (BU-du, I will) plus the imperfective infinitive: Я буду работать (ya BU-du ra-BO-tat', I will work / I will be working), Мы будем путешествовать (we will travel), Ты будешь звонить? (will you call?). Just conjugate быть in the future (буду, будешь, будет, будем, будете, будут) and add any imperfective infinitive — this one structure covers most future needs: plans, intentions, ongoing future actions. The second way is the perfective future: perfective verbs have no present tense, so their "present-looking" forms mean the future — Я скажу (ya ska-ZHU, I will say/tell), Я сделаю (ya SDYE-la-yu, I will do), Мы пойдём (my pay-DYOM, we will go). Use it for single completed future actions and promises: Я позвоню завтра (ya pa-zva-NYU ZAF-tra, I will call tomorrow), Я куплю билеты (I will buy the tickets). For this level, default to буду + infinitive in conversation and recognize the perfective future when you hear it.

Restaurant vocabulary and phrases. Меню (mye-NYU, menu), счёт (shchyot, check/bill), закуска (za-KUS-ka, starter), основное блюдо (as-nav-NO-ye BLYU-da, main course), десерт (dye-SYERT), напиток (na-PI-tak, drink). Ordering: Можно меню, пожалуйста? (may I have the menu, please?). Я буду... (I will have...) is the natural ordering phrase — Я буду борщ (I'll have the borscht). Это вкусно (E-ta FKUS-na, it's delicious), Очень вкусно! Что вы посоветуете? (what do you recommend?). During the meal: Можно счёт, пожалуйста? (the check, please). Common mistake: saying "Я хочу это" barked at the waiter is grammatically fine but socially blunt — Я буду... or Можно мне... (MOZH-na mnye, may I have...) sounds much better.

Travel phrases. В аэропорту (f a-e-ra-par-TU, at the airport): Где выход на посадку? (gdye VY-khat na pa-SAT-ku, where is the boarding gate?), Мой рейс в... (my ryeys, my flight is at...), У меня бронь (u mi-NYA bron', I have a reservation). В гостинице (f ga-STI-ni-tsy, at the hotel): Мне нужен двухместный номер (mnye NU-zhen dvukh-MYEST-ny no-MYER, I need a double room), Во сколько завтрак? (what time is breakfast?), У вас есть вай-фай? (do you have wi-fi?). Problems: Я потерял паспорт (ya pa-tye-RYAL pas-PART, I lost my passport), Мне нужна помощь (mnye nuzh-NA PO-mashch', I need help), Где аптека? (where is the pharmacy?). Note how much of this reuses Lessons 2–5 — the course is compounding.

Dialogue 1 — at a restaurant:

— Добрый вечер! У вас заказан столик? (u vas za-KA-zan STO-lik) — Good evening! Do you have a table booked?
— Да, на имя Анна. (na I-mya AN-na) — Yes, under Anna.
— Проходите, пожалуйста. Меню? (pra-kha-DI-tye) — This way, please. Menus?
— Да, спасибо. Что вы посоветуете? (shto vy pa-sa-VYE-tu-i-tye) — Yes, thanks. What do you recommend?
— Борщ очень вкусный сегодня. (borshch O-chen' FKUS-ny) — The borscht is very tasty today.
— Тогда я буду борщ и салат. А ты? (tag-DA ya BU-du) — Then I'll have the borscht and a salad. And you?
— Я буду рыбу. Можно мне воду, пожалуйста? (MOZH-na mnye VO-du) — I'll have the fish. May I have some water, please?
— Конечно. (ka-NYECH-na) — Of course.
(позже) — Можно счёт, пожалуйста? — The check, please.
— С вас тысяча двести рублей. (s vas TY-sya-cha dvye-STI ru-BLYEY) — That's 1200 rubles.

Dialogue 2 — making weekend plans:

— Что ты будешь делать в субботу? (shto ty BU-dyesh DYE-lat' f su-BO-tu) — What will you do Saturday?
— Я буду навещать сестру. А ты? (na-vye-SHCHAT' syest-RU) — I will visit my sister. And you?
— Я пойду на рынок утром. Пойдёшь со мной? (pay-DU na RY-nak, pay-DYOSH sa mnoy) — I will go to the market in the morning. Will you come with me?
— Да, с удовольствием. Во сколько встретимся? (s u-da-VOL-stvi-yem, fstrye-TIM-sya) — Yes, gladly. What time shall we meet?
— В девять. Потом пообедаем вместе. (pa-TOM pa-a-BYE-da-yem vmye-STYE) — At nine. Then we'll have lunch together.
— Отлично. Я позвоню в пятницу. (at-LICH-na, pa-zva-NYU f PYAT-ni-tsu) — Great. I'll call on Friday.

Practice: Write three plans for next week using буду + infinitive, and three promises using the perfective future. Then write a full restaurant dialogue (8+ lines) where you order a starter, main, drink, and dessert, ask for the check, and react to the food. Say it all aloud. Finally, plan a real weekend in Russian: where you will go, who you will see, what you will eat — five sentences minimum, out loud.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Conversation Practice Drills + Your 30-Day Plan
lessons.text:
This final lesson does two things: it gives you structured conversation drills that combine everything from Lessons 1–7, and it hands you a concrete 30-day plan so your Russian keeps growing after the course ends. A course can teach you the material, but only a routine turns material into fluency — so treat this lesson as the most important one to actually do.

Drill 1 — The Two-Minute Monologue. Set a timer for two minutes and talk about your day — present for routines (Я встаю в семь...), past for what already happened (Я завтракал...), future for what is next (Я буду работать...). Do not stop to look up words; describe around them. Fluency is built by keeping going, not by being perfect. Do this drill daily — it is the single highest-value exercise in this course.

Drill 2 — Question Tennis. Write 20 question words and topics on slips of paper (Где...? Когда...? Почему...?). Draw one and answer in two full sentences, then ask a follow-up question. Example: draw "Где?" → Где ты родился? Я родился в Огайо. Draw "Почему?" → Почему ты учишь русский? Я учу русский, потому что хочу путешествовать. If you practice with a partner, rally: they answer your question, then ask you one back. Ten minutes of question tennis covers more ground than an hour of passive review.

Drill 3 — Situation Cards. Write real situations on cards: "Your hotel has no hot water — complain politely", "Ask a stranger for directions to the pharmacy", "Order dinner for two", "Small talk with a taxi driver for five minutes". Draw a card and perform it aloud, both roles. These force you to combine vocabulary, grammar, and politeness under mild pressure — exactly what real conversations feel like. Rotate through all your cards weekly.

Drill 4 — Shadowing. Read any dialogue from this course aloud while tapping the stressed syllables, then read it again at natural speed trying to match the rhythm. Russian rhythm lives in its stress — one stressed syllable per word with everything else reduced — so shadowing dialogues trains your mouth faster than any grammar exercise.

Two mistakes that stall learners at this stage. First, the perfection trap: refusing to speak until every case ending is certain. Russian speakers are generous with beginners who try; they cannot help beginners who stay silent. Speak with 70% accuracy today rather than 100% accuracy never. Second, passive consumption: re-reading lessons and calling it study. Reading feels productive but builds recognition, not production. Every minute of speaking aloud counts triple compared to silent review — your mouth needs the reps.

Your 30-day plan. Week 1 — Foundations lock-in: 20 minutes daily. Days 1–2: re-read Lessons 1–2 dialogues aloud, exaggerating stress. Days 3–4: conjugate the Lesson 3 verbs out loud, all persons. Days 5–7: number and time drills from Lesson 4 until 0–100 is automatic. Week 2 — Conversation ignition: 25 minutes daily. Daily two-minute monologue plus question tennis; re-do the Lesson 5 and 6 dialogues with changed details. Week 3 — Real situations: 30 minutes daily. One situation card per day performed aloud; write a daily journal of five Russian sentences about your day (present + past + future mix). Week 4 — Live fire: 30+ minutes daily. Have at least three real conversations — with a tutor, a language-exchange partner, a Russian-speaking neighbor, or even ordering food in Russian. Record one, listen back, and note your three most frequent errors to drill next month.

Track it simply: a notebook page per day with the date, minutes practiced, and one line about what felt easier than last week. If you miss a day, never miss twice — the streak matters more than any single session. After 30 days, repeat the cycle with harder situation cards and longer monologues; you now own a system, not just a course.

Practice: Do Drill 1 right now — two full minutes about your day in Russian, out loud, no stopping. Then write out your personal Week 1 schedule with exact times. Finally, write five situation cards of your own based on your life — travel you plan, restaurants you visit, people you meet — and perform the first one today. Удачи — you are a Russian speaker now. Keep speaking.

courses.title: Singing Foundations
courses.tagline: Find your voice and sing with confidence, one steady breath at a time.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Welcome to Singing Foundations. This course takes you from your very first careful breath to singing a complete song with confidence. Across eight lessons you will learn how to breathe and stand for singing, find your vocal range, train your pitch and your ear, warm up safely, shape vowels and pronounce words clearly, sing a simple song from start to finish, sing harmony, and organize a daily practice routine. Each lesson ends with a structured practice assignment, and the included worksheets help you track your progress. Work through the lessons in order, and give each one the practice time it asks for before moving on.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Welcome to Singing Foundations. This course takes you from your very first careful breath to singing a complete song with confidence. Across eight lessons you will learn how to breathe and stand for singing, find your vocal range, train your pitch and your ear, warm up safely, shape vowels and pronounce words clearly, sing a simple song from start to finish, sing harmony, and organize a daily practice routine. Each lesson ends with a structured practice assignment, and the included worksheets help you track your progress. Work through the lessons in order, and give each one the practice time it asks for before moving on.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will: breathe with low, supported breaths and stand with balanced, relaxed posture; find your comfortable vocal range and know your lowest and highest easy notes; match pitch accurately and hear intervals by ear; warm up safely with gentle slides, hums, and lip trills; shape pure vowels and pronounce consonants clearly without tightening the jaw; sing a simple song with steady phrasing, clear words, and a planned breath map; sing a harmony part above and below a melody and hold your line against another voice; and follow a permanent twenty-minute daily practice routine with a clear map of what to learn next.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading and practice course. Read each lesson fully first, then work through its exercises in a comfortable room, then complete the Practice assignment at the end. Do not rush ahead: each lesson assumes the skills of the one before it. Aim for 20 to 30 minutes of practice per day, five or six days a week. Sing at a comfortable volume, rest your voice when it feels tired, and record yourself on your phone once a week to hear your progress honestly. Use the practice log worksheet to note what you worked on each day. If a lesson feels shaky, repeat it for another few days before continuing.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites beyond a willingness to sing. You need no prior musical experience, no ability to read music, and no theory background. A piano, keyboard, or tuning app is helpful for finding pitches, and any simple instrument or app that plays single notes will do. Everything is taught from zero, one step at a time, and every exercise is designed to be sung gently, within a comfortable range.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and printable worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes included. Everything you need is in the text: explanations, step-by-step exercises with repetition counts, common mistakes to avoid, and practice assignments. The materials section includes a breathing and warm-up reference card, a practice log worksheet, and a song practice worksheet. Learn at your own pace, and revisit any lesson whenever you need a refresher.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Breathing and Posture for Singing
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you how to breathe and stand for singing. Everything later in this course - holding long notes, singing in tune, shaping clear words - builds directly on the physical habits you set up today. Good breathing and posture prevent the two problems that stop most beginners: running out of air halfway through a phrase, and tension in the neck and shoulders that makes the voice sound tight and tired. Give this lesson a full practice session on its own. It may feel like you are not really singing yet, but this foundation work pays off every single time you open your mouth to sing.

Start with posture. Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart, your weight balanced evenly between both feet, and your knees soft - not locked straight and not bent deeply. Let your arms hang relaxed at your sides. Imagine a gentle thread pulling the top of your head upward, lengthening your spine, while your shoulders stay down and loose. Your chin should be level, neither tucked down toward your chest nor lifted high toward the ceiling. Your chest stays open and lifted, but not puffed out or stiff. Sit tall in the same way if you prefer to practice sitting: both feet flat on the floor, back straight but not rigid, arms relaxed. Good posture is not a military pose - it is a balanced, easy stance that lets your breath move freely.

Now the breath. Place one hand on your belly, just below your ribs, and one hand on your chest. Breathe in slowly through your nose and notice which hand moves: for singing, the lower hand should move outward while the upper hand stays almost still. This is low breathing, sometimes called belly breathing, and it gives you the steady air supply singing needs. Your belly expands as you breathe in, and it draws gently back in as you breathe out. Practice this for two minutes: breathe in for four slow counts, feeling the belly expand, then breathe out for four slow counts on a soft "sss" sound, feeling the belly draw in steadily. The hiss should be even and unbroken - if it sputters or fades, you are letting the air out in bursts instead of a steady stream.

The next skill is managing the air as you sing. Singing uses far less air than most beginners expect; the goal is a slow, controlled release, not a big blast. Try this: breathe in low for four counts, then sing a single comfortable note on "ah" for as long as you can, keeping the sound steady and even. Count how many seconds you last, and repeat the exercise five times, trying to keep the tone from wobbling or fading at the end. Most beginners find the note gets shaky near the end - that is the moment the breath support runs out, and it improves with practice. The trick is to start the note gently, with no push or burst, and to keep the belly engaged as the note goes on, as if you were slowly squeezing air out of a tube.

Time for drills. First, the belly-breath check: five slow breaths with hands on belly and chest, watching the lower hand move and the upper hand stay still. Second, the hiss exercise: breathe in for four counts, hiss out on "sss" for eight counts, keeping the sound perfectly even - repeat six times, then try hissing for twelve counts. Third, the long-tone exercise: breathe in low, sing one comfortable note on "ah" for as long as you can, five times, writing down how many seconds each attempt lasts so you can watch the number grow over the coming weeks.

Two common mistakes to watch for. The first is chest breathing: the shoulders rise and the chest heaves on every breath, which gives you a shallow, shaky air supply and a tight throat. If your shoulders move when you breathe in, stop and reset with your hands on your belly until the lower hand is doing the work. The second is pushing: forcing a big burst of air at the start of a note, which makes the sound blast and then fade. Singing is a steady stream, not a sneeze - start each note gently and let the breath flow out evenly.

Practice: Stand in your singing posture and do the belly-breath check five times. Then do the hiss exercise six times, aiming for eight even counts each time. Finish with five long tones on "ah," one comfortable note each, writing down the length of each one. Before every exercise, run the checklist: feet balanced, knees soft, shoulders down, chin level, belly breathing. End the session by singing a simple, familiar tune once through, standing tall and breathing low, just to feel the difference good posture makes.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding Your Range
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to find your vocal range: the span of notes you can sing comfortably, from your lowest easy note to your highest easy note. Knowing your range is practical, not a label - it tells you which songs will sit comfortably for your voice, which notes to avoid forcing, and where your voice naturally feels at home. By the end of this lesson you will know your comfortable range and you will have a simple map of it to use when choosing songs.

First, find your lowest comfortable note. Sit or stand in your singing posture, breathe in low, and hum gently on "mmm" starting on a note that feels easy and relaxed - for most people this is somewhere in the middle of their speaking voice. Now slide the hum slowly downward, one small step at a time, like walking down a staircase. Keep going until the sound starts to feel gravelly, weak, or strained, then step back up one note - that note is the bottom of your comfortable range. Write it down. Do not push below it: the lowest notes are not a contest, and forcing them only adds tension. Repeat the slide three times to check that you land on the same bottom note each time.

Now find your highest comfortable note. Start again on an easy middle note and slide the hum slowly upward, one small step at a time. The voice will feel lighter as you climb, and at some point the sound will start to feel thin, tight, or hard to control - step back down one note, and that is the top of your comfortable range for now. Write it down beside the low note. Your range today is simply the distance between those two notes, and it is a starting point, not a fixed limit: ranges grow slowly over months of gentle practice, and they grow by expanding a little at a time, never by forcing.

Between the bottom and the top, your voice has different feels, often called registers. The lower part of your range usually feels warm and speech-like - this is your chest voice, the sound you use when you talk. The upper part usually feels lighter and floatier - this is your head voice, the sound that feels as if it resonates higher up. In the middle there is a passage area, sometimes called the break, where the voice wants to shift from one feel to the other and the sound can wobble or crack. That wobble is normal and every singer has it. The goal of this lesson is not to erase the break but to know where it is: slide slowly through it on a hum, notice where the shift happens, and write that spot down too.

Time for drills. First, the downward slide: hum from an easy middle note down to your lowest comfortable note, three times, checking that you stop at the same note. Second, the upward slide: hum from the same middle note up to your highest comfortable note, three times, stopping at the same top note. Third, the siren: slide your voice slowly up and down across your whole range like a siren, on a gentle "oo" sound, three times, moving smoothly through the passage area without stopping or jumping. The siren teaches your voice to glide through the break instead of cracking at it.

Choosing songs by range is the practical payoff. Before you sing any song, check its lowest and highest notes against your range map. If the song's highest note sits above your comfortable top, the song will feel like a strain every time you reach it - choose a lower key, or choose a different song. If the song sits entirely in the middle of your range, it will feel easy and sound relaxed. As a rule for this course, pick songs whose notes stay inside your comfortable range with at least one note of room at the top and the bottom, so you never have to sing at the very edge of what you can do.

Two common mistakes. The first is confusing your range with your speaking voice: the notes you speak on are usually in the lower-middle of your range, and many beginners assume their singing range ends where their speaking voice ends. It does not - the hum slides in this lesson will show you notes above and below your speaking pitch. The second is forcing the top: pushing hard to reach a high note, which makes the throat tight and the note sharp and thin. High notes come from steady breath and a relaxed throat, not from effort - if a note feels like work, you are above your comfortable range for now.

Practice: Find your lowest and highest comfortable notes using the hum slides, and write both down on the range worksheet, with the passage area marked. Then sing the siren exercise three times on "oo," sliding smoothly across your whole range. Finish by singing a simple, familiar tune and checking whether its notes sit inside your range - write down the highest and lowest notes of the tune and compare them with your map.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Pitch and Ear Training
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to match pitch accurately and to hear musical distances - intervals - by ear. Pitch is the foundation of singing in tune: if you can hear a note clearly and reproduce it with your voice, you can sing any melody. Ear training is simply the habit of listening carefully before you sing, and it improves faster than most beginners expect. By the end of this lesson you will match single notes reliably and recognize the most common intervals by ear.

Start with single-note matching. Play a note on a piano, keyboard, or tuning app - choose a note in the comfortable middle of your range. Listen to it for a few seconds, then hum the same note on "mmm." Listen to yourself: does your hum sit exactly on the played note, or does it drift above or below it? If you are unsure, play the note again while you hum, and listen for the beating or wobbling sound that happens when two notes are close but not identical - when the wobble disappears, the notes match. Practice this with ten different notes, one at a time, taking your time on each. The goal is not speed but accuracy: one matched note is worth more than ten guessed ones.

Now learn to hear intervals, the distance between two notes. The smallest step is a half step, the move from any note to its nearest neighbor. Two half steps make a whole step. The most useful intervals to learn first are the ones that appear constantly in melodies: the major second (a whole step up), the minor third (three half steps), the major third (four half steps), the perfect fourth (five half steps), the perfect fifth (seven half steps), and the octave (twelve half steps, the same note higher). Play each interval on the keyboard - lower note first, then upper note - and sing both notes back. Give each interval a mental picture: the perfect fifth sounds open and strong, like the start of a fanfare; the major third sounds bright and cheerful; the minor third sounds softer and sadder.

The echo exercise is the fastest way to build your ear. Play a short pattern of three notes on the keyboard, listen carefully, then sing the pattern back without the keyboard. Start with simple patterns that move by step - up one, down one, up one - and gradually add small jumps. Do twenty echo patterns per session, and keep a tally of how many you get exactly right. When you miss one, play it again slowly, sing each note separately, and then sing the whole pattern again. The echo exercise works because it forces you to hold a sound in your mind and reproduce it - exactly what singing a melody requires.

Add the slide-and-match drill for notes that feel hard to reach. If a target note is above your comfortable starting point, do not jump straight to it: slide your voice slowly upward from a note you can match, and stop when you hear the slide meet the target note. The slide gives your ear time to compare the moving pitch with the target, and it teaches your voice to find notes by listening rather than by guessing. Practice five slide-and-match exercises per session, choosing target notes a little above and a little below your starting note each time.

Two common mistakes. The first is singing before listening: beginners hear a note and immediately blurt out a guess, and the guess is usually wrong. Build the habit of a silent beat - hear the note, hold it in your mind for a second, then sing. That one-second pause doubles your accuracy. The second is drifting flat on long notes: the pitch sags as the breath runs out. Keep the breath support engaged through the whole note, and imagine the note staying lifted, like a balloon you are holding up, rather than letting it sink.

Time for drills. First, single-note matching: ten notes, played then hummed, checking for the wobble that signals a mismatch. Second, interval singing: play and sing each of the six intervals above, five times each, naming the interval as you sing it. Third, the echo exercise: twenty three-note patterns, sung back from memory, with a tally of exact matches.

Practice: Do ten single-note matches, then the six intervals five times each, then twenty echo patterns, writing down your score. Finish by singing a simple, familiar tune slowly, stopping on each note to check whether it matches the melody you hear in your head - if a note feels wrong, play it on the keyboard and match it before moving on.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Warming Up Safely
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to warm up safely: gentle exercises that prepare your voice for singing without strain. A warm-up is not a performance - it is a slow, easy stretch for the voice, like walking before running. Singers who warm up regularly find their voices respond faster, stay in tune more easily, and feel less tired after practice. By the end of this lesson you will have a ten-minute warm-up routine you can use before every practice session and every song.

Start with the body, not the voice. Roll your shoulders slowly backward five times, then forward five times, letting them drop down and away from your ears. Turn your head gently from side to side, then tilt it slowly toward each shoulder, holding each stretch for a slow count of five - never force the stretch, and never roll your head in a full circle. Shake your hands out, then do five slow belly breaths from Lesson 1, feeling the lower hand move while the shoulders stay still. This two-minute body warm-up removes the tension that makes the voice sound tight, and it signals to your brain that singing time has started.

Now the voice, starting with the gentlest sound of all: the hum. Hum on "mmm" at a comfortable middle pitch for ten seconds, feeling a light buzzing in your lips and face. Slide the hum slowly up a few notes and back down, like a small wave, five times. Humming is gentle because the lips are closed and the sound is soft - it wakes the voice up without asking it to work hard. Next, lip trills: blow air through loosely closed lips so they flutter, like a horse, while sliding the pitch slowly up and down. Lip trills are one of the safest warm-ups because the fluttering lips keep the airflow steady and the throat relaxed. Do lip trills for two minutes, sliding through the middle of your range.

Add sirens on "oo" and "ee." A siren is a slow slide from the bottom of your comfortable range to the top and back down again, taking about ten seconds each way. Sing the siren on "oo" three times, then on "ee" three times, keeping the volume soft and the slide smooth - no jumps, no pushing, no holding your breath. The siren stretches the voice gently across its whole range and smooths the passage area where the voice shifts between its lower and upper feels. If the siren cracks or wobbles at the passage area, slow it down and make it softer - the goal is a smooth glide, not a perfect sound.

Finish the warm-up with gentle scales. Sing a five-note pattern - up five notes and back down - on "ah," starting on a comfortable middle note, then move the whole pattern up one step and repeat, climbing slowly through the middle of your range. Keep the volume moderate and the sound easy; if a note feels tight, stop climbing and come back down. Do five of these patterns, then sing the same five-note pattern on "ee" and on "oo," noticing how each vowel feels different in your mouth. End the warm-up with one minute of silence - no talking, no singing - letting the voice settle before you begin your practice.

Two common mistakes. The first is warming up too hard: beginners treat the warm-up like a performance, singing loudly and pushing for high notes, which tires the voice before the real practice begins. A warm-up should feel easy - if you are working hard, you are doing it wrong. The second is skipping the warm-up entirely on days when time is short. Even three minutes of humming and lip trills is better than none, and it protects your voice from the strain of starting cold. If your voice feels tired, hoarse, or sore, stop singing and rest it - rest is part of good practice, not a failure of it.

Time for drills. First, the body warm-up: shoulder rolls, gentle head turns, and five belly breaths, two minutes. Second, hums and lip trills: five hum slides and two minutes of lip trills, all soft. Third, sirens and scales: three sirens on "oo," three on "ee," and five five-note scale patterns on "ah," all at a comfortable volume.

Practice: Do the full ten-minute warm-up exactly as written - body, hums, lip trills, sirens, scales - before your next three practice sessions. Write down how your voice feels after the warm-up each time, using one honest sentence, and notice whether the feeling improves across the three days.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Vowels and Diction - Singing Words Clearly
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to shape vowels and pronounce words clearly while singing. In speech, vowels carry the sound and consonants carry the meaning; in singing, the same is true, but the balance shifts - vowels need to stay open and ringing so the note can sustain, while consonants need to be quick and crisp so the words stay understandable. By the end of this lesson you will sing the five main vowels with an open, relaxed mouth, and pronounce consonants without tightening your jaw.

Start with the five vowels: ah, eh, ee, oh, oo. Sing each one on a single comfortable note, holding it for four slow counts, and notice the shape of your mouth. For "ah," the mouth opens wide and tall, the tongue lies flat, and the jaw drops loosely. For "eh," the mouth opens halfway, the tongue lifts slightly. For "ee," the mouth is narrower, the lips spread gently, and the tongue rises toward the roof of the mouth. For "oh," the lips round into a soft circle and the mouth opens tall. For "oo," the lips round more tightly and the mouth opens smaller. Practice singing all five vowels in a row on the same note, slowly, feeling the mouth reshape for each one. The sound should stay steady and free - if a vowel sounds pinched or thin, the mouth is probably too closed or the jaw is tight.

Now the vowel ladder. Sing the five vowels in order - ah, eh, ee, oh, oo - on a single note, one vowel per beat, four times through. Then sing the ladder on a five-note scale, one vowel per note, climbing and descending. The ladder teaches your mouth to move cleanly between vowel shapes without disturbing the tone. A common trouble spot is the shift from "ee" to "oh": the mouth has to open and round quickly, and beginners often keep the "ee" shape too long, which makes the "oh" sound muddy. Slow the ladder down at that transition until the shift is clean, then speed it back up.

Consonants are the other half of diction. Unlike vowels, which you sustain, consonants are quick events: they start or end a sound and then get out of the way. Practice the consonant drill: sing "mah, nah, lah, dah, bah" on a single note, one syllable per beat, feeling each consonant land crisply at the front of the mouth and then release immediately into the vowel. The tongue and lips do the consonant work - the jaw stays relaxed and does not clamp down. Try the same drill with "tah, kah, sah, zah," noticing how each consonant uses a different part of the mouth. Then sing a line of a familiar song slowly, exaggerating the consonants slightly - not shouting them, just making them clear - and listen for whether every word is understandable.

The jaw deserves special attention because it is where most diction tension lives. Place your fingertips lightly on your jaw joints, just in front of your ears, and sing a line of a song: if you feel the jaw clenching or pushing forward, stop and let it hang loose. A useful check is the two-finger test: you should be able to fit two fingers stacked vertically between your upper and lower teeth while singing "ah" - if you cannot, your jaw is too closed. Practice singing "ah" with the jaw dropped and loose, and notice how much bigger and freer the sound becomes. Relaxed jaw, open mouth, clear consonants: those three habits are the whole of diction.

Two common mistakes. The first is mumbling: vowels that are too closed and consonants that are too soft, so the words blur together and the listener cannot follow the song. If you cannot understand your own words on a recording, the diction needs work - open the vowels and sharpen the consonants. The second is over-enunciating: biting off every consonant so hard that the singing sounds like spelling, with the flow broken by constant interruptions. Consonants should be clear but quick, like a tap on the shoulder, not a shove.

Time for drills. First, the vowel ladder: all five vowels on one note, then on a five-note scale, four times through. Second, the consonant drill: "mah, nah, lah, dah, bah" and "tah, kah, sah, zah" on a single note, four times each. Third, the jaw check: sing a line of a song with fingertips on your jaw joints, stopping and resetting whenever you feel tension.

Practice: Sing the vowel ladder four times, then the consonant drills four times each, then sing one verse of a familiar song slowly, focusing only on diction - open vowels, quick consonants, relaxed jaw. Record it and listen back, writing down one word that was unclear and one vowel that sounded pinched, and repeat that line five times with the fixes in place.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Singing a Simple Song from Start to Finish
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to sing a complete song from start to finish: learning it in sections, mapping your breaths, and putting the sections together into a performance you can be proud of. Singing a whole song is a milestone - it is the moment all the separate skills in this course become music. By the end of this lesson you will sing a simple song cleanly, in tune, with clear words and planned breathing.

Choose a simple song that fits your range. Pick one with a narrow span of notes - no big jumps, no notes at the very edge of your range - and with words you understand and like. A short folk song, a simple hymn, or a well-known children's melody all work well. Before you sing it, learn the melody by ear: play it on the keyboard or listen to it carefully, humming along until you can hum the whole tune without help. Then learn the words separately: speak them aloud slowly, as if you were reading a poem, noticing where the natural pauses fall. Melody and words learned separately are much easier to combine than melody and words learned together.

Now build the song in sections. Divide it into phrases - short musical sentences, usually two to four measures long - and learn one phrase at a time. Sing the first phrase slowly, checking each note against the melody you know, and repeat it until it is comfortable. Then learn the second phrase the same way. Then sing phrases one and two together. Add one phrase at a time until the whole song is joined. This section-by-section method works on every song you will ever learn, and it stops the most common practice trap: singing the whole song badly from the start and never fixing the weak spots.

Next, map your breaths. A breath map is simply a plan for where you breathe: mark a breath mark in the words at the end of each phrase, and practice breathing exactly there - nowhere else. Breathe in low and quickly at each mark, and sing through the whole phrase on one breath. If a phrase is too long for one breath, split it at a natural pause in the words and add a breath there. Practice the song with the breath map three times, breathing only at the marks. Planned breathing makes the singing sound calm and controlled; random gasps in the middle of a phrase make it sound panicked. Write the breath marks on your song worksheet so you can see them every time you practice.

Add phrasing and dynamics. A phrase is a musical sentence, and like a spoken sentence it has a shape: it begins gently, grows slightly toward the middle, and settles at the end. Sing each phrase with that shape - start at a comfortable medium volume, let the sound grow a little toward the most important word in the phrase, and ease back as the phrase ends. The most important word is usually the word that carries the meaning of the line - sing it with a touch more warmth and clarity, and let the other words support it. Practice the song once with exaggerated phrasing - big swells and clear phrase endings - then once with natural phrasing, and notice how the exaggerated version teaches your voice the shape that the natural version keeps.

Two common mistakes. The first is rushing the tempo: beginners speed up whenever the easy part arrives, and the song falls apart at the hard part. Choose a tempo slow enough for the hardest phrase, and keep it steady from the first note to the last - use a gentle tap of your foot to hold the beat. The second is stopping at every mistake and restarting from the beginning: this trains you to sing the opening brilliantly and the ending never. When you stumble, keep going, note the bad spot, and drill that spot alone afterward.

Time for drills. First, the phrase builder: learn the song one phrase at a time, singing each phrase three times cleanly before adding the next. Second, the breath-map run: sing the whole song breathing only at the marks, three times through. Third, the phrasing run: sing the song once with exaggerated phrasing and once naturally, recording both and listening for the shape of each phrase.

Practice: Choose a simple song inside your range and learn it phrase by phrase until you can sing it through without stopping. Write its breath map on the song worksheet, then sing the whole song four times: twice slowly with the breath map, once at a comfortable tempo with phrasing, and once recorded. Listen back to the recording and write down the one phrase that needs the most work, then drill that phrase ten times before you finish.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Harmony Basics - Singing with Others
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you harmony basics: singing a second part above or below a melody while someone else sings the main tune. Harmony is what makes group singing sound rich - two voices moving together, each on its own line, blending into a sound neither could make alone. By the end of this lesson you will sing a simple harmony part, hold it against the melody, and blend your voice with a partner.

Start by understanding what harmony is. A melody is a single line of notes. A harmony part is a second line that moves along with the melody, usually a third or a sixth above or below it - those are the intervals you learned in Lesson 3, and they sound warm and consonant together. When two voices sing a third apart, they move in parallel, like two friends walking side by side: when the melody goes up one step, the harmony goes up one step too. The simplest harmony to learn is the third above the melody: take any melody, and for each note, sing the note a third higher. Practice this on a simple tune you know well, singing the harmony line alone first, without the melody, until it feels like a tune in its own right.

The hard part of harmony is holding your line. When another voice sings the melody beside you, your ear wants to slide onto their notes - especially when the two lines come close together. The skill is to listen to the melody without joining it. Practice with a partner, or with a recording of the melody playing quietly: sing your harmony line while the melody plays, and if you slip onto the melody, stop, find your starting note again, and rejoin. A useful trick is to sing your harmony line while playing the melody on the keyboard at the same time - the keyboard holds the melody steady, and you learn to trust your own line against it. Do this for five minutes a day and the slipping stops surprisingly fast.

Blending is the second skill. Two voices blend when they match in volume, vowel shape, and timing: neither voice sticks out, and the two sounds melt into one. Practice blending by singing the same note as your partner on "ah," matching their volume exactly - not louder, not softer - and matching the shape of the vowel. Then sing a simple scale together in unison, listening for the moment the two voices fuse into a single sound. When you can blend in unison, try blending in harmony: sing the third above while your partner sings the melody, keeping your volume equal and your vowels matched. If one voice is much louder, the harmony disappears under it - the quieter voice is the one to bring up, gently, until the two are balanced.

Learn two harmony patterns you can use anywhere. The first is the third above: sing every melody note a third higher, which gives a bright, cheerful harmony. The second is the third below: sing every melody note a third lower, which gives a warmer, darker harmony. Practice both on the same simple tune, one after the other, and notice how different the song feels with each. Then try a call-and-response pattern: your partner sings a phrase, you echo it back, then you both sing the next phrase together in harmony. Call and response teaches you to listen and answer, which is the heart of singing with others.

Two common mistakes. The first is singing the harmony too loudly: beginners push their part to prove they are holding it, and the balance breaks. Harmony is a team sound - your part should be exactly as loud as the melody, no more. The second is watching the other singer's mouth instead of listening: your eyes cannot tell you the pitch. Close your eyes, listen to your own line inside your head, and trust your ear.

Time for drills. First, the harmony line alone: sing the third-above harmony to a simple tune by yourself, three times, until it feels like its own melody. Second, the hold-your-line drill: sing the harmony while the melody plays on the keyboard, five minutes, restarting whenever you slip onto the melody. Third, the blend exercise: sing a single note in unison with a partner or a recording, matching volume and vowel, then sing a scale together in unison, then in thirds.

Practice: Learn the third-above harmony to a simple song you know, singing the harmony line alone three times. Then sing it with the melody playing on the keyboard or sung by a partner, three times through, keeping your volume equal to the melody. Finish by singing the third-below harmony to the same song once, and write down which harmony felt easier to hold.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Your Daily Practice Routine + What to Learn Next
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your permanent daily practice routine and maps out where to go next. What separates singers who improve from singers who stall is not talent but the quality and consistency of their practice. This lesson gives you a repeatable session structure, a weekly plan, and a clear list of next steps, so you never again sit down wondering what to do.

The session structure has four blocks in about twenty minutes. Block one is warm-up, five minutes: the body warm-up, hums, lip trills, and sirens from Lesson 4, every single session without exception. Block two is technique, five minutes: rotate daily through pitch matching, interval singing, vowel ladders, and range slides, working on whatever is weakest. Block three is songs, ten minutes: your current song, worked phrase by phrase with the breath map, never just sung through on autopilot. Block four is fun, five minutes: sing anything you enjoy, even imperfectly, and end every session on a song you love. The order is fixed: warm-up, technique, songs, fun.

The weekly plan spreads the work. Practice five or six days a week rather than cramming: twenty focused minutes beats a two-hour weekend marathon because your brain consolidates the learning between sessions, while you sleep. Assign each day a small focus - Monday: pitch and ear training; Tuesday: vowels and diction; Wednesday: range slides and sirens; Thursday: harmony with a partner or recording; Friday: song work, recorded on your phone; weekend: one light session or rest. Keep the written practice log from your materials: date, minutes, what you worked on, and one honest note about what improved. Review the log every Sunday and set one specific goal for the coming week.

Where to go next: five directions. One, a second song in a different style - a slower ballad, where the challenge is sustaining long phrases and singing quietly with control. Two, a wider range: gentle slides that expand your comfortable range by one note at a time, over months, never by forcing. Three, a new time feel: learn to sing a song in 3/4 time, where the phrases breathe in threes instead of fours. Four, a harmony song with a partner: choose a song with a written harmony part and learn it together, trading melody and harmony between verses. Five, reading music: learn the treble clef and note values, so you can learn songs from written music instead of by ear alone. Learn these one at a time, one per few weeks, with the section method from Lesson 6.

Once a month, hold a review session instead of a normal practice. Sing through everything you have learned - your warm-up, your intervals, your vowels, and your songs - and record it all. Listen back with your practice log open and ask three questions: what is clearly better than last month, what has not moved at all, and what is the single weakest skill right now. Write the answers down, then set exactly one goal for the coming month, such as "match ten notes in a row without a miss" or "sing my song through with the breath map and no extra breaths." One goal keeps your practice focused; five goals means none of them happen. Date the goal in your log, and check it off the day you achieve it.

Two common mistakes. The first is practicing only what you already sing well: it feels good and improves nothing. Spend at least half of every session on the hardest thing, not the favorite thing. The second is the autopilot run-through: singing a song start to finish five times while thinking about dinner. If your mind wanders, stop, pick the weakest phrase, and drill it ten times - focused repetitions beat mindless ones by a wide margin. And remember the safety rule that runs through this whole course: if your voice feels tired, hoarse, or sore, stop and rest. A rested voice comes back stronger; a pushed voice does not.

Practice: Write out your weekly plan using the four-block session structure and the day-by-day focus above. Do one full session today, fill in the practice log honestly, and record your song from Lesson 6. Listen back, write down the single weakest spot, and make it tomorrow's technique block.

courses.title: Conversational Spanish: Levels 1-2
courses.tagline: Speak Spanish from day one: pronunciation, core grammar, and real everyday dialogues.
courses.syllabus_summary:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational Spanish: Levels 1-2 is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday Spanish from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. Level 1 builds your foundation — pronunciation, greetings, ser vs. estar, numbers, and asking questions. Level 2 takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day fluency plan so you keep moving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: Course Overview
syllabus.body:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Conversational Spanish: Levels 1-2 is a text-based course that teaches you to speak practical, everyday Spanish from your very first lesson. Instead of memorizing long word lists with no context, you learn the way real conversations work: how the sounds are made, the core grammar you need for daily life, and full dialogues with English translations so you always understand exactly what is being said. Level 1 builds your foundation — pronunciation, greetings, ser vs. estar, numbers, and asking questions. Level 2 takes you into the past tense, making plans, and longer conversations about food, travel, and daily life. The course closes with conversation drills and a 30-day fluency plan so you keep moving after the last lesson.

syllabus.heading: What You Will Learn
syllabus.body: By the end of this course you will be able to: pronounce Spanish words clearly using the five vowels and the main consonant rules; greet people, introduce yourself, and handle survival phrases when you do not understand; use ser and estar correctly and build sentences in the present tense with regular and common irregular verbs; count to one hundred and beyond, tell the time, and use days, months, and dates; ask and answer questions about directions, prices, and everyday topics; talk about things you did using the preterite tense; make plans for the future and hold a full restaurant or travel conversation; and run a simple daily practice routine that keeps your speaking improving.

syllabus.heading: How to Use This Course
syllabus.body: This is a self-paced reading course. Read one lesson at a time, out loud wherever you see Spanish — saying the words with your mouth, not just your eyes, is what builds speaking skill. Each lesson opens with what it teaches, explains the concept with concrete examples, includes full example dialogues with English translations, warns you about common beginner mistakes, and ends with a clearly labeled Practice exercise. Do the practice before moving on, even if it feels easy; the lessons build on each other, and Lesson 3's verbs depend on Lesson 1's sounds. Aim for one lesson per day, and re-read the previous lesson's dialogues the next morning as a warm-up. There are no grades and no timers — steady repetition beats cramming.

syllabus.heading: Prerequisites
syllabus.body: There are no prerequisites. This course starts from zero and assumes you have never studied Spanish before. Everything — even how to make each vowel sound — is explained from scratch. If you already know a little Spanish, Lesson 1's pronunciation rules are still worth reading, because correcting a bad accent habit early saves months later. You do not need any textbook, app, or prior grammar knowledge; a notebook for writing out the practice exercises is the only thing that will help.

syllabus.heading: About This Package
syllabus.body: This package contains written lessons and worksheets only. There are no videos, no audio tracks, and no live classes — it is a text/workbook course, and everything you need is on the page: explanations, example sentences, translated dialogues, and practice exercises. The materials section includes a vocabulary cheat sheet and a 30-day fluency plan template you can print and reuse. Work through the lessons in order, do the exercises in writing and out loud, and you will finish with usable, spoken Spanish for real everyday situations.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronunciation — The Five Vowels, Tricky Consonants, and Word Stress
lessons.text:
This lesson teaches you to pronounce Spanish clearly from the start. Spanish pronunciation is one of the most consistent in the world: letters almost always sound the same way, so once you learn the rules you can read almost any word correctly. That consistency is your biggest advantage as a beginner. Your goal in this lesson is not a perfect accent — it is clarity. If your vowels are right and your stress lands on the right syllable, Spanish speakers will understand you even while you are still learning words.

Spanish has exactly five vowel sounds, and they never change. Say them now: A (ah, as in father), E (eh, as in bed), I (ee, as in see), O (oh, as in go), U (oo, as in moon). That is it — no short-vs-long games, no silent-vowel surprises. Practice these three words slowly: casa (CAH-sah, house), mesa (MEH-sah, table), luna (LOO-nah, moon). Each vowel gets the same amount of time; do not stretch one vowel longer than the others the way English habits push you to. A very common beginner mistake is reading Spanish vowels with English values — for example, saying 'si' (yes) like the English word 'sigh' instead of 'see'. When in doubt, keep every vowel short and pure.

Next, the consonants that trip up English speakers. The rolled R (rr) is the famous one: pero (but) has a single soft R, perro (dog) has the rolled rr — mixing them up changes the word, so practice matters. To learn the roll, put your tongue behind your upper teeth and blow air firmly while relaxing the tongue tip; it takes days or weeks, and that is normal. The letter J sounds like a strong English H (as in 'hot'): jueves (Thursday) is HWAY-bes. LL and Y usually sound like the English Y: lluvia (rain) is YOO-vyah, and yo (I) is YOH. The letter Ñ is the 'ny' sound in 'canyon': mañana (tomorrow) is mah-NYAH-nah. B and V sound almost identical in Spanish — a soft sound between the two, like 'vino' (wine) with the lips barely touching. Finally, C before E or I sounds like S in Latin America (gracias = GRAH-syahs), and Z is also an S sound there — one less thing to worry about in this course, which uses Latin American pronunciation throughout.

Word stress follows simple rules, and they are worth memorizing today. Rule 1: words ending in a vowel, N, or S stress the second-to-last syllable — casa (CAH-sah), hablan (AH-blahn), mesas (MEH-sahs). Rule 2: words ending in any other consonant stress the last syllable — hablar (ah-BLAHR), ciudad (see-oo-DAHD). Rule 3: a written accent mark (tilde) overrides everything — the stressed syllable is the marked one: médico (MEH-dee-koh, doctor), café (kah-FEH, coffee). Notice how médico and medico would be different words if the accent moved. A classic beginner mistake is stressing English-style, like saying 'com-PU-ta-dora' for computadora (computer) when it is com-poo-tah-DOH-rah. Trust the rules, not your English ear.

Here is a short dialogue using only sounds from this lesson. Read it aloud slowly, stressing the right syllables:

María: ¡Hola! ¿Cómo te llamas? (OH-lah koh-moh teh YAH-mahs) — Hello! What is your name?
Carlos: Me llamo Carlos. ¿Y tú? (meh YAH-moh KAHR-lohs) — My name is Carlos. And you?
María: Me llamo María. Mucho gusto. (MOO-choh GOOS-toh) — Nice to meet you.
Carlos: Mucho gusto. ¿Hablas español? (AH-blahs ess-pahn-YOHL) — Do you speak Spanish?
María: Sí, un poco. (see oon POH-koh) — Yes, a little.

Notice every vowel is short and pure, and the stress falls exactly where the rules predict. Say the whole dialogue five times today; it is your first Spanish conversation.

Practice: Write out these ten words and mark the stressed syllable in each, then say them aloud three times: ventana, teléfono, español, gracias, mañana, biblioteca, hotel, familia, zapato, universidad. Next, write your own name and three English words you use often, then 'Spanish-ize' their pronunciation using today's vowel rules and read them aloud. Finally, record yourself (any phone recorder works) reading the dialogue above, listen back, and circle any vowel that sounded English — re-say those lines until the vowels sound short and pure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings, Introductions, and Survival Phrases
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you your first real social toolkit: greeting people politely, introducing yourself, and surviving conversations when you do not understand something. These phrases are the highest-value sentences in the language because they unlock every interaction — ordering food, asking for help, meeting people. Learn them cold before you worry about grammar, because even a flawless sentence is useless if you cannot open and close a conversation gracefully.

Start with greetings. Hola (OH-lah) means hello and works everywhere. Buenos días (BWAY-nohs DEE-ahs) is good morning, buenas tardes (BWAY-nahs TAHR-dehs) is good afternoon, and buenas noches (BWAY-nahs NOH-chehs) is good evening or good night. Notice that 'good' is plural here — that is just how Spanish says it, so do not 'fix' it to buen día, which sounds odd to native ears. For introductions: Me llamo... (meh YAH-moh) means 'my name is' — literally 'I call myself'. ¿Cómo te llamas? (KOH-moh teh YAH-mahs) asks someone's name informally; ¿Cómo se llama usted? is the formal version for strangers, elders, or officials. Encantado (if you are male) or encantada (if you are female) means delighted, and mucho gusto (MOO-choh GOOS-toh) — nice to meet you — works for everyone.

Now the small-talk core. ¿Cómo estás? (KOH-moh ehs-TAHS) is 'how are you' for friends; ¿Cómo está usted? is the formal version. Common answers: Muy bien, gracias (very well, thanks), Más o menos (so-so), and the wonderfully honest Estoy cansado/cansada (I am tired — masculine/feminine). ¿Y tú? (ee TOO) means 'and you?' — short and essential. De nada (deh NAH-dah) is 'you're welcome', por favor (pohr fah-VOHR) is 'please', and gracias (GRAH-syahs) is 'thank you'. A frequent beginner mistake is answering ¿Cómo estás? with a full life story; a short answer plus ¿Y tú? back keeps the conversation balanced and gives you twice the practice.

Survival phrases are your safety net — memorize these before anything else. No entiendo (noh ehn-TYEHN-doh) — I don't understand. ¿Puedes repetir, por favor? (PWEH-dehs reh-peh-TEER) — Can you repeat, please? Habla más despacio, por favor (AH-blah mahs dehs-PAH-syoh) — Speak more slowly, please. ¿Habla inglés? (AH-blah een-GLEHS) — Do you speak English? Perdón (pehr-DOHN) — excuse me / sorry. Disculpe (dees-KOOL-peh) — excuse me (to get attention, more polite). Lo siento (loh SYEHN-toh) — I'm sorry. ¿Qué significa...? (keh seeg-nee-FEE-kah) — What does ... mean? These eight phrases will rescue you in any Spanish-speaking country, and native speakers respect learners who ask for clarification instead of nodding blankly.

Watch for this common mistake: mixing up tú and usted forms at the wrong moment. Using tú with a stranger is not a grammar failure — it is a social one, and it can come across as rude with older people or in formal settings like banks and clinics. When in doubt, start with usted and switch to tú only when the other person does. A second mistake: saying 'estoy embarazado' thinking it means 'I'm embarrassed'. Embarazada means pregnant — a legendary false friend. Say tengo vergüenza (TEHN-goh behr-GWEHN-sah) for 'I'm embarrassed'.

Full dialogue — a first meeting. Read aloud with the translations:

Ana: ¡Buenos días! ¿Cómo se llama usted? — Good morning! What is your name?
Luis: Buenos días. Me llamo Luis. ¿Y usted? — Good morning. My name is Luis. And you?
Ana: Me llamo Ana. Mucho gusto. — My name is Ana. Nice to meet you.
Luis: Mucho gusto, Ana. ¿De dónde es usted? — Nice to meet you, Ana. Where are you from?
Ana: Soy de Texas. ¿Y usted? — I'm from Texas. And you?
Luis: Soy de México. ¿Habla español? — I'm from Mexico. Do you speak Spanish?
Ana: Un poco. Habla más despacio, por favor. — A little. Speak more slowly, please.
Luis: Claro. ¿Cómo está hoy? — Of course. How are you today?
Ana: Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? — Very well, thanks. And you?
Luis: Muy bien. ¡Hasta luego! — Very well. See you later!

Practice: Write a self-introduction of five lines (greeting, name, where you are from, one feeling word, goodbye) and memorize it — this is your personal script for the next month. Then practice the survival phrases: cover the Spanish column, read the English, and say the Spanish from memory until you can do all eight without peeking. Finally, role-play the dialogue above twice, switching roles, saying every line aloud with the correct vowel sounds from Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Ser vs. Estar and the Present Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson tackles the two most important verbs in Spanish — ser and estar, both meaning 'to be' — plus the present tense, which lets you describe what you do every day. English uses one 'to be' for everything; Spanish splits the job in two, and mixing them up is the single most common beginner error. Master this distinction now and every sentence you build later gets easier.

SER is for things that are permanent, essential, or defining: identity, origin, characteristics, time, and profession. Yo soy de Texas (I am from Texas). Ella es alta (She is tall). Son las tres (It is three o'clock). Él es médico (He is a doctor). ESTAR is for states, conditions, locations, and things in progress: Estoy cansado (I am tired). La tienda está cerrada (The store is closed). Estamos en casa (We are at home). A simple memory rule: ser = what something IS, estar = how something is or WHERE it is. Location always uses estar, even for permanent places: Madrid está en España (Madrid is in Spain).

Conjugations (memorize these shapes — they never change):
SER: yo soy, tú eres, él/ella/usted es, nosotros somos, ellos/ustedes son.
ESTAR: yo estoy, tú estás, él/ella/usted está, nosotros estamos, ellos/ustedes están.
Read them aloud now. Notice the accents on estás, está, están — the stress rule from Lesson 1 in action.

Now the present tense of regular verbs. Spanish verbs end in -ar, -er, or -ir, and each family has its own endings. For -AR verbs like hablar (to speak): hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan. For -ER verbs like comer (to eat): como, comes, come, comemos, comen. For -IR verbs like vivir (to live): vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, viven. The pattern: drop the -ar/-er/-ir and add the endings. Practice with trabajar (to work): trabajo en una oficina (I work in an office), ¿trabajas los sábados? (Do you work Saturdays?). Notice that Spanish usually drops the subject pronoun — 'hablo' already means 'I speak', so 'yo hablo' is only used for emphasis.

A few very common verbs are irregular — learn them as vocabulary: TENER (to have): tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen. Tengo dos hermanos (I have two brothers). IR (to go): voy, vas, va, vamos, van. Voy al mercado (I go to the market). HACER (to do/make): hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacen. Hago ejercicio (I exercise). QUERER (to want): quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren. Quiero café (I want coffee). These four irregulars appear in nearly every conversation, so they repay memorization immediately.

Two beginner mistakes to avoid. First, the ser/estar swap: saying 'estoy aburrido' when you mean 'soy aburrido' — the first means 'I am bored', the second means 'I am a boring person'. Adjectives change meaning with the verb: ser listo = to be clever, estar listo = to be ready. Second, translating 'do' word-for-word: English 'Do you speak Spanish?' is just ¿Hablas español? — Spanish does not use a helper verb for questions, so never say '¿Haces hablas español?'.

Dialogue — two coworkers at lunch:

Pedro: ¿Dónde trabajas? — Where do you work?
Sofía: Trabajo en un banco. Soy cajera. ¿Y tú? — I work at a bank. I am a cashier. And you?
Pedro: Soy profesor. Trabajo en una escuela. — I am a teacher. I work at a school.
Sofía: ¿Estás cansado hoy? — Are you tired today?
Sofía: No, estoy bien. ¿Quieres comer conmigo? — No, I'm fine. Do you want to eat with me?
Pedro: Sí, quiero. ¿Vamos al restaurante? — Yes, I want to. Shall we go to the restaurant?
Sofía: Vamos. Tengo hambre. — Let's go. I'm hungry.

(Note: tengo hambre — 'I have hunger' — is how Spanish says 'I'm hungry'. Another estar/ser trap avoided by using tener.)

Practice: Conjugate these verbs fully in writing: hablar, comer, vivir, tener, ir. Then write six sentences about yourself: two with ser (identity/origin/profession), two with estar (feeling/location), two with present-tense action verbs. Say each sentence aloud. Finally, translate to Spanish: 'She is a doctor. She works in a hospital. She is tired today. She wants coffee.' Check: Es médica. Trabaja en un hospital. Está cansada hoy. Quiere café.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers, Time, Days — The Everyday Vocabulary Core
lessons.text:
This lesson builds your everyday number vocabulary: counting, telling time, and using days, months, and dates. Numbers are pure utility — prices, phone numbers, addresses, schedules — and telling the time unlocks appointments, opening hours, and travel. There is no grammar trick here, just memorization plus a few patterns, so this lesson is built for repetition and out-loud drilling.

Numbers 0–20 (memorize these exactly): 0 cero, 1 uno, 2 dos, 3 tres, 4 cuatro, 5 cinco, 6 seis, 7 siete, 8 ocho, 9 nueve, 10 diez, 11 once, 12 doce, 13 trece, 14 catorce, 15 quince, 16 dieciséis, 17 diecisiete, 18 dieciocho, 19 diecinueve, 20 veinte. Notice 16–19 are compound words (diez + seis = dieciséis). Tens: 30 treinta, 40 cuarenta, 50 cincuenta, 60 sesenta, 70 setenta, 80 ochenta, 90 noventa, 100 cien. For 21–99, join the ten and the unit with 'y': 21 veintiuno (special single word), 22 veintidós, 23 veintitrés — but from 31 up it is treinta y uno, cuarenta y dos, cincuenta y tres, and so on. So 47 = cuarenta y siete, 83 = ochenta y tres. Hundreds: 200 doscientos, 500 quinientos, 1,000 mil. Uno becomes un before masculine nouns (un café) and una before feminine (una mesa).

Telling time: Spanish uses ser for time — ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?). For 1 o'clock: Es la una. For all other hours: Son las dos, Son las tres... Son las diez. Minutes: Son las cuatro y diez (4:10), Son las seis y media (6:30 — 'y media' = and half), Son las ocho menos cuarto (7:45 — literally 'eight minus a quarter', very common). Noon is el mediodía, midnight is la medianoche. For appointments: la cita es a las tres (the appointment is at three). A classic mistake is saying 'Es las dos' — remember, only 1:00 uses 'es', everything else uses 'son' because the hours are plural.

Days of the week (all masculine, never capitalized in Spanish): lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. Use 'el' for 'on': el lunes = on Monday, los lunes = on Mondays (habit). Months: enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre. Dates: el cinco de mayo, el veinte de octubre. To say what day it is: ¿Qué día es hoy? — Hoy es martes. What is the date? ¿Cuál es la fecha? — Es el dos de noviembre. Note the order: day first, then month, then year — el 2 de noviembre, never 'noviembre 2'.

Practical vocabulary for money and shopping, since numbers live there: ¿Cuánto cuesta? (How much does it cost?), Cuesta diez dólares (It costs ten dollars), Es muy caro (It's very expensive), Es barato (It's cheap), ¿Tiene cambio? (Do you have change?), la cuenta, por favor (the check, please). Money amounts: 1.50 = uno cincuenta, 25 = veinticinco. In shops you will hear prices as bare numbers — 'cuarenta y cinco' for 45 — so number fluency pays off immediately.

Dialogue — at a market:

Vendedor: ¡Buenos días! ¿Qué desea? — Good morning! What would you like?
Cliente: Quiero dos kilos de manzanas, por favor. — I want two kilos of apples, please.
Vendedor: Son doce dólares. ¿Algo más? — That's twelve dollars. Anything else?
Cliente: ¿Cuánto cuestan las naranjas? — How much are the oranges?
Vendedor: Cinco dólares el kilo. — Five dollars a kilo.
Cliente: Deme tres kilos. ¿A qué hora cierra? — Give me three kilos. What time do you close?
Vendedor: Cerramos a las ocho. — We close at eight.
Cliente: Gracias. ¿Tiene cambio de veinte? — Thanks. Do you have change for twenty?
Vendedor: Sí, claro. — Yes, of course.

Practice: Count aloud from 0 to 100 without stopping, then backwards from 50 to 0. Write today's date, your birthday, and three appointment times in Spanish. Then drill time: set a timer and say the current time in Spanish every 15 minutes for two hours (¿Qué hora es? — Son las...). Finally, memorize the market dialogue's price lines and role-play a shopping trip where you buy three different items, asking ¿Cuánto cuesta? each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Asking Questions — Directions, Shopping, and Small-Talk Dialogues
lessons.text:
This lesson turns you into someone who can get answers: how to form every kind of question, ask for directions, handle a full shopping conversation, and keep small talk going. Up to now you have mostly made statements; questions are what make you independent in a Spanish-speaking place. The good news: Spanish questions are simpler than English ones — no 'do/does/did' helpers, no word-order gymnastics.

The core question words (all carry a written accent — memorize them with it): ¿Qué? (what), ¿Quién? (who), ¿Cuál?/¿Cuáles? (which one(s)), ¿Dónde? (where), ¿Cuándo? (when), ¿Por qué? (why — two words), ¿Cómo? (how), ¿Cuánto/a? (how much), ¿Cuántos/as? (how many). Porque (one word, no accent) means 'because' — a classic beginner mix-up is writing '¿porque?' with no accent. To form a question, keep normal word order and just raise your intonation at the end, with inverted ¿ at the start: ¿Hablas español? ¿Dónde está el banco? You can also invert subject and verb for emphasis — ¿Dónde está ella? — but statement order works fine.

Directions vocabulary is survival-level. ¿Dónde está...? (Where is...?), ¿Cómo puedo llegar a...? (How can I get to...?), Está cerca (It's near), Está lejos (It's far), a la derecha (to the right), a la izquierda (to the left), siga derecho (keep going straight), en la esquina (on the corner), entre... y... (between... and...). When someone answers, listen for: gire (turn), cruce (cross), siga (continue). Polite opener: Disculpe, ¿dónde está la estación? (Excuse me, where is the station?). And the lifesaver follow-up: ¿Puede mostrarme en el mapa? (Can you show me on the map?).

Shopping questions beyond prices: ¿Tiene...? (Do you have...?), ¿Hay...? (Is there...? / Are there...?), ¿Puedo probármelo? (Can I try it on?), ¿Tiene una talla más grande/pequeña? (Do you have a bigger/smaller size?), ¿Aceptan tarjeta? (Do you take card?), ¿A qué hora abren? (What time do you open?). Small-talk questions that keep conversations alive: ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?), ¿A qué te dedicas? (What do you do for work?), ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas aquí? (How long have you been here?), ¿Te gusta la ciudad? (Do you like the city?), ¿Qué recomiendas? (What do you recommend?). Two mistakes to avoid: saying '¿Qué es tu nombre?' instead of ¿Cómo te llamas? (nobody says the first), and answering a question you only half understood — use No entiendo bien, ¿puede repetir? instead of guessing.

Dialogue 1 — asking directions:

Turista: Disculpe, ¿dónde está el museo? — Excuse me, where is the museum?
Vecino: Está cerca. Siga derecho y gire a la izquierda. — It's near. Go straight and turn left.
Turista: ¿Está lejos a pie? — Is it far on foot?
Vecino: No, son cinco minutos. Está entre el banco y la farmacia. — No, it's five minutes. It's between the bank and the pharmacy.
Turista: Muchas gracias. ¿Cómo se llama esta calle? — Thank you very much. What is this street called?
Vecino: Es la calle Juárez. — It's Juárez Street.

Dialogue 2 — small talk at a café:

Elena: ¿De dónde eres? — Where are you from?
Tomás: Soy de Colombia. ¿Y tú? — I'm from Colombia. And you?
Elena: Soy de aquí, de Madrid. ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas aquí? — I'm from here, from Madrid. How long have you been here?
Tomás: Llevo dos semanas. Me gusta mucho la ciudad. — I've been here two weeks. I like the city a lot.
Elena: ¿Qué recomiendas visitar? — What do you recommend visiting?
Tomás: Quiero ver el parque mañana. ¿Por qué no vienes? — I want to see the park tomorrow. Why don't you come?
Elena: ¡Buena idea! ¿A qué hora? — Good idea! At what time?
Tomás: A las diez. Nos vemos aquí. — At ten. See you here.

Practice: Write ten questions — two each for directions, shopping, time, personal info, and opinions — and say each aloud with rising intonation. Then memorize the direction-giving sequence (derecho, a la derecha, a la izquierda, en la esquina) and give directions from your front door to the nearest shop, in Spanish, out loud. Finally, role-play Dialogue 2 with a partner or alone, then change three details (city, time, place) and run it again — this is how small talk becomes automatic.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Talking About the Past — The Preterite Tense
lessons.text:
This lesson gives you the past tense — the preterite — so you can say what you did, where you went, and what happened. Without a past tense you are stuck in the eternal present; with it, you can tell stories, explain your day, and answer the most common small-talk question in any language: ¿Qué hiciste ayer? (What did you do yesterday?). The preterite is for completed, finished actions with a clear end: yesterday, last week, this morning.

Regular preterite endings. For -AR verbs like hablar: hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron. For -ER/-IR verbs like comer and vivir: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron.
